A Great mix of RPG and FPS. Very fun and exetremely fun with friends! Get to know the stories of Pandora more than once! Like an RPG, You can level up and earn new skills. For example, if you chose Maya, a mythical female, she can turn into a phoenix on kill. Or you could take Zer0, a man of mystery, capable of wiping out entire camps unseen. Maybe you'd love to play as Salvador, a short but strong man who can wield two guns. Maybe Axton, who can have a turret as a companion. I haven't even mentioned DLC. This is game is really fun, although it is a bit grinding at times.

A good game for sure. No doubt about that. Great gunplay, cool setting (if you're into post apocalyptic future stuff), fun characters and lots of content.
I'd recommend this to anyone who like RPG shooters (this is an RPG in the lightest of sense). Chances are, though, that you allready know what Borderlands is all about.
What made me stop playing it boils down to three points. First off, the unbalanced difficulty. I'm basically breezing through the game with little to no effort. Shields rarely gets depleted. Then suddenly a bossfight that totally steamrolls you. After a multitude of tries and lots of swearing (in my case) you finally manage to finish him/it/her off and you're back to EZ mode.
Secondly, timed delivery missions. Why put those in a shooter? Seriously.
And thirdly; it's too long. At least in my opinion. I typically prefer my games to last about 15-20 hours. Not 40. I have other games I want to play too. But hey, that's just me.

I'm hoping you'll click into this review as it's a positive one amongst a sea of negative ones, and I hope you'll take some time to read my views on why this game is getting an unfair drubbing from people who have no clue as to what goes into a game like this and an attitude that is all too common nowadays of 'I want it now!'. I've skimmed through the reviews here and most of them that have strong criticism of both the game and the devs are by people that have less than 200 hours in the game, far too little to provide an accurate or fair representation of the current state of DayZ. No, these people have spent a little time in the game and as soon as they come across what is, in their opinion, a 'game-breaking' bug they come here and rant about how their experience is completely ruined. Over the top and melodramatic, especially as the warnings on both the store page and in the game itself warn of exactly this issue. Are people really that stupid? Yes they are, and undoubtably they will continue with their ceaseless whining and counter-productive reviews until doomsday. What we need here is some facts, some sense amongst the senseless so I will try to provide that for those that are willing to jump off the 'this game is dead' bandwagon and enlighten themselves.
First of all, as I already mentioned above the warnings telling you the game may have bugs and issues and is unfinished are there for all to see, always have been since initial release, it was never released in a way that was deceptive or promising features that were not there. The dev team have been as open and honest about this game as they can be without falling into the trap of making false statements merely to please the masses. There is even a post on the forums entitled 'Should I buy this game?' and this post contains an honest and frank explanation of what you can expect from the game as it stands. It tells you that there will be features that don't fully work, bugs that may interrupt gameplay, that there will be database wipes, that it won't be to the tastes of everybody who expects a polished product. The dev's have in no way sought to deceive anyone at any time in regards to the state of the game in it's alpha stage. Now, I will admit that progress is slow or seems to be to the common game player but what you don't see is all the work that goes into the background stuff, net code, server stability etc. Have you ever opened a config file in a game's data folder and tried to make sense of the info contained within? Well there are literally thousands of files in one game that have to be edited to implement even the simplest of features, you don't see the poor guy that has the job of doing that, and because you don't see him he's automatically assumed to be, as one recent post put it 'spending all our money on booze and ♥♥♥♥♥s'. Get real, and take a moment to realize that just because you don't see any immediate progress in bugfixing, there may have been countless hours spent editing files to provide the groundwork for what will be a fix. Throwing wild accusations at the devs is couter-productive and lacks a certain maturity, so give them some encouragement instead if you want to be taken seriously.
Next, the big bad word ALPHA... Ooooh I see you all cringing and spitting like rabid dogs at the very thought of it. I know right? Cos Alpha is the stage where they add a load of stuff as well as bug fixing and making the framerate a gazzillion frames per milli-second right? It's where the dev's do everything the community asks of them and when doing that breaks everything else as an apology they send Patricia the stripper round to suck your♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and give you cookies.
Wrong!!!!!!!!!!
Alpha is purely for adding features until it is what they call 'Feature Complete'. Sorry, did that sound condascending? Well unfortunately most of the people writing negative reviews here need the information broken down for them to be able to take it in, spelling it out to them like magnetic letters on a refridgerator door in pretty colors so it can hold their tiny imaginations for more than six seconds. No, Alpha is not predominantly about fixing bugs, or increasing stability, or optimizing performance, it's for 'adding things'. A lot of people keep saying 'Stop adding things and fix the bugs!'. Ok, so let's for a second pretend they'd done that from the start, and every bug that they found was fixed as and when it appeared...
Everybody's sooo happy now huh?
Errr, no, cos now everyone is complaining that there seems to be very little being added to the game, that there's no animals, no working survival aspects, no vehicles at all. You see, all the time in this fictitious scenario that could have been spent making the game feature rich has been spent troubleshooting the few things that they had time to develop in between all the troubleshooting. And of course, there's the chance that anything new that's added after this point will break the fixes until eventually you'll have 80% troubleshooting for 20% features. Overall development would slow to a crawl and we'd be sitting now on a game that was only at a patch 0.45 level, if that. There's a good reason why Alpha and Beta are separate stages in the process and I personally am sick of reading posts from people naive enough to think the two stages can work together, they can't, they won't so shut up.
Onto the engine... Hmm, I've played Operation Flashpoint up to Arma 3 and they've always had clunky engines, I'm not going to defend this as it has caused me frustrations in the past, not just on DayZ. But you have to appreciate the origins of DayZ and the Arma series in that they originated from software developed to train real world military forces. The movement and clunkiness is there due to this to simulate realistic positioning of joints and limbs and therefore movement on the battlefield, it's there to force the player to think about reloading in safe areas, moving into cover to give or receive medical treatment and it's there to promote tactics and forward thinking in how you progress. It's not Call Of Duty where you run over medpacks and pull assault rifles out your♥♥♥♥♥♥and it's players that are used to this style of gameplay that are the biggest complainers about Bohemia's 'clunky' movement issues. Personally, after playing most of the Arma franchise I like the extra element it's movement adds and have no problem with all the CoD KiDs sodding off back to their 360 no-scope BS, might even cut the number of mindless complaints and KOS mentality.
There is one simple solution to everybody's complaints about the game as it stands, and that is to put it down and don't come back until well into Beta. I know you're gonna say it's ages away or may not even happen, but it will, and that's where you'll see the optimization, the bug fixing and the increased framerates, not a moment before. All the negative reviewers need to put the game down for a while and check back at a later date. You all keep saying the same thing over and over and over and over and over and over and (getting bored yet?) over and over and over, and it's pointless. You think the dev's are going to change the whole direction of development away from a system that works to one that just doesn't to please a few spoilt brats that feel they are entitled to have their way no matter what? Nope. I only have +/- 370 hours in the game but that's because I tend to come in and play a few hours to test new features, see how things are with each patch, I don't play this game and consider it one of my 'go to' games because as is so evident by the people that DO do that, it only leads to disappointment. When this game is well into Beta I will start spending more time with it as that's when it will become a more fulfilling experience for everyone, even the ones that claim it's dead, who will look really stupid, can't wait for that.
Buy this game, be patient, don't whine. Profit.

Dayz me rolling...
What is DayZ? At its finest moment, DayZ is an intense open world PVP survival simulator. The experience leaves you wanting more. You will curse for getting killed without ever seeing your killer. But, unlike life, you get to respawn and try again. DayZ isn't about hand holding, or guiding you to your objective because there are no objectives (yet). The only foreseeable objective is to survive the band of heavily geared players you hear talking down the street.
Run and zig till you can't zag no more to ensure a successful escape. Find a house, hope for a can of beans and a nice warm beer. Get your health status to a flourescent green "Energized" and "Hydrated". Scavenge houses for rememants of a lost society. Rip shirts for bandages. The more "pristine" clothes you have on, the more damage you can take. Once you are clothed and nicely fed, find a rope and burlap sack to make a courier bag. Then reinforce it with a stick to make an Improvised Bag.
Keep scavenging till you find some rounds and a decent rifle or pistol. There are many types of weapons and ammunition to find so make sure you have the correct caliber for the chamber. Now that you are equipped, go out and explore with the freedom of knowing you can defend yourself.
Now that you are equipped, DayZ's volume of problems start to unveil. For example, pressing V will allow your character to vault over a fence or if you are walking, to step over. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't. Sometimes you will lose a weapon in the process. It's not neccessarily lost, but lost in a sea of lag. Speaking of lag (desync) there is plenty of it. Most of DayZ's problems come from desync. You will find that not every item can be picked up because essentially your character isn't at that exact place to pick it up at that exact moment, they are basically lagged behind somewhere, maybe a few houses back even though physically you are above the item you want to pick up.
DayZ is also very problematic with close quarters combat as players appear to be animation-glitched or simply just all over the place which has a lot to do with lag. DayZ truly shines from a distance. If you can creep up on some unsuspecting players, you are more likely to take them out than just rushing up and spraying. Shooting ahead of where they are running helps combat the lag infestation of combat.
Zombies are basically broken, they just glitch out all over the place sometimes hitting you through walls. Again, thats lag at its finest. The Engine wasn't designed for DayZ's vision, so they are changing a lot of the components of the engine to handle the demand such a game requires. Zombies do provide a good indicator of potential enemies around you. If you are unsure if someone is around, just look for zombies and if they are just walking around, chances are no ones been through the area or at least fired a round. If a round is fired, you will wake up all zombies in the area and they will come beat you down.
When DayZ works and it works more often than not, its truly intense. Some of the best fire fights I've had have been in this game. Playing alone is tough, playing with friends is the best way to play. Remember, it is work in progress so problems will arise new and old.
Some tips: Don't fall in love with your gear. Spending four hours gearing up can be wasted in four seconds of combat or even if you are balls deep looking at loot on the ground someone can have you in their sights. Stay moving at all times.
DON'T TRUST ANYBODY! EVER! They may sound nice (in some cases might actually be) but 9 out of 10 times its a "baiter" or someone waiting for an opportunity to get you especially the "want some food?" trick. Sure, eat the food and get handcuffed as your animation plays out eating it.
Keep calm in gun battles. Losing your mind will get you dead real quick.
Have fun. Love you.

How do I explain Undertale? To a non-gamer its an 8-bit game like the type people used to play. Mario, Sonic and such. A non-gamer may enjoy Undertale, and would certainly play it once. Some people may hate it. Fair enough. But to those gamers, people dedicated to what they love, Undertale can be a masterpiece.
Think of the last time a game gripped you. Made you feel emotion for every single character. Can you remember? Maybe not. With Undertale, every character means something. You can choose to learn about them, or tear them apart. Its a game of choices. A game with a simple fight mechanic and an even simpler Mercy mechanic. Its a game that basically anyone could play.
But put it like this. In one of the endings (there are many) to Undertale, I actually hyperventilated. That has never in my life happened before, and I've played tons of games. I nearly cried (but I'm just a little too tough around the edges- NOT!) because it is just that good.
Simply put:
1) Great story
2) Amazing soundtrack
3) Toriel, Sans and Papyrus
4) Never put this game down
5) Unless you go pacifist. Then NEVER touch this game again!!!!!!!!!!!

If you're looking at the reviews for this game and you're unsure whether or not you would enjoy playing it, let me help you out.
This is by far one of my favourite games of all time, take that as bias or not however it really does earn the title.
The story is fantastic, no spoilers however it really does a lot to earn your respect and attempt to make the campaign enjoyable for the player with a variety of missions, ranging from shooting some dudes in a snowy landscape to shooting some dudes in a volcanic area!
Jokes aside the story tries it's hardest to stay as entertaining as it can, which, as far as FPS games go these days, is a blessing. The game features a variety of NPCs, featuring characters from the first game as primary NPCs! (That's right, you can talk to mother♥♥♥♥in' Brick!)
You may view them as a grab for money from the developers however the DLC is well worth the money paid, often adding what could be considered another game into a small price, especially Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon's Keep, I've yet to finish it myself however I've put a few hours into it and am looking to wrap it up sometime soon.
If I did have to complain about anything in the game, however, I would say that most content, be it DLC or not, tends to be for the endgame and is usually either a lot more enjoyable or only accessable once you're a high level, whilst I can understand this is mostly for the enjoyment of long-time players who have countless maxed out characters, playing the regular campaign without access to any of the fun bosses or DLC exploration can get a bit bland.
If you're looking to get Borderlands 2 or Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel then I would definitely go for Borderlands 2, not simply because I am a fanboy of this game nor am I an aussie hater, I prefer the game style and overrall feel of Borderlands 2.

Undertale is a game that may surprise you at any point in the game. Even after you finish it. Simply put, you're not going to expect some things to happen even if you think you've already seen the unexpected, if this makes any sense. Even after I beat the game for the first time, the game surprised me again and again. There are no clichés here (or very few).
When you first start the game, the first thing you notice is its distinctive graphics. Whether you like them or not, they are very unique and the designers should be proud of their work for breaking out of the typical sprites or cartoonish graphics that are so prevalent in RPGs. Not only the graphics are unique, but you will also see some very particular details in the areas because of them, because of the way the game is designed. A rock is just a rock, or maybe not, you'll see.
Speaking of rocks, you know how in other RPGs, there are items under certain rocks? I didn't find any here. I found something better, dialogue. It's easy to think that the only things that matter in games are better equipment and items, but when you think it through, isn't it more rewarding to have more content for exploring the game? You discover more about the game world and find things you wouldn't otherwise. What's the penalty for skipping side content in other games? You're less strong. Here, the penalty is you don't get to experience stories, you don't get to learn about the world and more importantly, find out if a rock is a rock or a dog. This reminds me of my favorite game (Final Fantasy 8), so I may be biased on this point.
The last point I'll bring up is a very crucial one and very important for me in any RPG: The soundtrack. I have nothing else to say, except it's amazing.
I won't say anymore, because the game is best experienced if you don't know or expect anything about it.
Enjoy it, it's an amazing game.

Dayz me rolling...
What is DayZ? At its finest moment, DayZ is an intense open world PVP survival simulator. The experience leaves you wanting more. You will curse for getting killed without ever seeing your killer. But, unlike life, you get to respawn and try again. DayZ isn't about hand holding, or guiding you to your objective because there are no objectives (yet). The only foreseeable objective is to survive the band of heavily geared players you hear talking down the street.
Run and zig till you can't zag no more to ensure a successful escape. Find a house, hope for a can of beans and a nice warm beer. Get your health status to a flourescent green "Energized" and "Hydrated". Scavenge houses for rememants of a lost society. Rip shirts for bandages. The more "pristine" clothes you have on, the more damage you can take. Once you are clothed and nicely fed, find a rope and burlap sack to make a courier bag. Then reinforce it with a stick to make an Improvised Bag.
Keep scavenging till you find some rounds and a decent rifle or pistol. There are many types of weapons and ammunition to find so make sure you have the correct caliber for the chamber. Now that you are equipped, go out and explore with the freedom of knowing you can defend yourself.
Now that you are equipped, DayZ's volume of problems start to unveil. For example, pressing V will allow your character to vault over a fence or if you are walking, to step over. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't. Sometimes you will lose a weapon in the process. It's not neccessarily lost, but lost in a sea of lag. Speaking of lag (desync) there is plenty of it. Most of DayZ's problems come from desync. You will find that not every item can be picked up because essentially your character isn't at that exact place to pick it up at that exact moment, they are basically lagged behind somewhere, maybe a few houses back even though physically you are above the item you want to pick up.
DayZ is also very problematic with close quarters combat as players appear to be animation-glitched or simply just all over the place which has a lot to do with lag. DayZ truly shines from a distance. If you can creep up on some unsuspecting players, you are more likely to take them out than just rushing up and spraying. Shooting ahead of where they are running helps combat the lag infestation of combat.
Zombies are basically broken, they just glitch out all over the place sometimes hitting you through walls. Again, thats lag at its finest. The Engine wasn't designed for DayZ's vision, so they are changing a lot of the components of the engine to handle the demand such a game requires. Zombies do provide a good indicator of potential enemies around you. If you are unsure if someone is around, just look for zombies and if they are just walking around, chances are no ones been through the area or at least fired a round. If a round is fired, you will wake up all zombies in the area and they will come beat you down.
When DayZ works and it works more often than not, its truly intense. Some of the best fire fights I've had have been in this game. Playing alone is tough, playing with friends is the best way to play. Remember, it is work in progress so problems will arise new and old.
Some tips: Don't fall in love with your gear. Spending four hours gearing up can be wasted in four seconds of combat or even if you are balls deep looking at loot on the ground someone can have you in their sights. Stay moving at all times.
DON'T TRUST ANYBODY! EVER! They may sound nice (in some cases might actually be) but 9 out of 10 times its a "baiter" or someone waiting for an opportunity to get you especially the "want some food?" trick. Sure, eat the food and get handcuffed as your animation plays out eating it.
Keep calm in gun battles. Losing your mind will get you dead real quick.
Have fun. Love you.

One of the most anticipated and popular games, certainly the best known within its own genre.
At start i was certainly optimistic, but it's been about 2 years now and it's still in alpha.
The graphics and the gameplay is true to it's original mod-version for Arma II, even properly improved in terms of visuals.
Except that though, it's a disgrace to the gaming industry, and a shame on Dean Hall.
In later times, the DayZ mod for arma II was more popular and had more people playing it than battlefield 3.
Turning that mod into a standalone game was an obvious next step, and we as players were hyped from when we first heard it as a rumor. The first playthrough was fair enough - It was alpha, i didnt expect too much. Loot was scarce, it was poor, the entire map had about 3 zombies on it in total, but then again they were superzombies that could run straight through walls and buildings and hit you while being invisible. Most the loot you can find now, 2 years later, is still the same from back then. You've got some additions here and there, more books, different clothing, a new backpack, and even a little crafting - but all in all, the BIG things like vehicles, weaponry, group systems, bases - are either on a complete status quo or only seeing minor updates at a far too slow rate.
There's no excuse for launching an early access game to a fanbase that big, with a hype so high, and not drive development forward more than they have.
For those familiar with Bohemia's games and the Arma series in particular, it's evident that this is taking far longer than necessary. DayZ mod was handcrafted in a boy's bedroom - now he's a grown man, filthy rich on early access money, and the game we all paid for is turning into that old classic car rusting in the backyard that you and your dad never got around to.
Dont get me wrong, i am a big fan of DayZ and the mod, the communities within it, the standalone aswell and the direction it is taking. Therefore, i plead to Dean Hall:
Please, Dean Hall. Well played, gg. You can keep the money. Hell, i'll even pay for it a second time over if you just shut down the project, stop giving us ridiculous and absolutely minor updates, so few and far between - and instead let it be as it is and
There are already WAY better working versions as mods to Arma 3, and even far more fun modes than DayZ A3 have been made since then. You have Breaking Point and Epoch already as mods, kicking your Standalone Game's♥♥♥♥♥
Please for the love of god -STOP- and let the community go nuts to create what you SHOULD have had ready this year!

Undertale isn't exactly Final Fantasy. It certainly doesn't have the length, even if you account for multiple playthroughs. And the graphics? They do a good job - with some good design work too - but they're not exactly triple-A. (
, at least, is truly top-notch. It helps that the developer is a music composer by trade.)
Normally, I wouldn't even pay any mind to its Overwhelmingly Positive rating, with around 45,718 reviews as of my own review. Here's the thing, though: if a game isn't wowing so many people with its graphics, or its scope - and good music alone does not a good game make - there must be
to it. And that 'it' in Undertale's case is a whole lot of genuine heart, complimented by some actually good writing.
This is basically a JRPG for people who don't really like JRPGs, and I know this because I am one of those people. No matter where you stand on the JRPG-liking scale, I would advise you to at least try
. It is, at the very least, something genuinely different, and it really does have heart.
As for the rest of the game? I dislike bullet hell even more, and the combat system comprising of mini bullet-hell games was nothing short of brilliant - at the very least better than the bog-standard 'select an attack, hold down the speed key in your emulator and watch stuff happen' system of other JRPGs.
Perhaps most importantly, Undertale gives you the choice of not killing any enemy you come across.

, perhaps, but more elegantly implemented than any other game I've seen yet. Even an attempt at a pacifist run here counts for more than in some other games.
Tying into this, Undertale is the rare example of video game writing that isn't some value of bad or otherwise effortless/nondescript, a distinction that puts this game in the leagues of Alpha Centauri and Deus Ex for me. I will say that it gets somewhat cloying and heavy handed at times, but the fact remains Undertale's writing isn't good because it manages to pull off speculative, philosophical hard sci-fi or just because it tells a rollicking tale of conspiracy and action with corny yet genuine voice acting. Undertale's writing...
...made me laugh, and laugh
it, and I'm
a person who laughs with a game very often. It made me think, not only of the enemies I killed, but of the ones I killed in other games. It started sincere and only became more sincere the further I progressed, although it might have helped that I was invested early on. On my second playthrough, it started to actually kind of get to me. The most important aspect here, however, is the gameplay and story segregation.
There is almost none. In a genre where developers generally don't even care about that sort of thing.
You truly live with your choices here. This game's encyclopedic recall of the decisions you make and the enemies you kill, and the tight interlacing of the aesthetic with the gameplay in general, really do make this game stand out for me...and I've played a lot of games. Even if it isn't the Best Game Ever, it's absolutely one of the best games to come out of 2015, or at least the best one with an androgynous player character which I think is pretty neat either way.

After playing this game for about a year. Ive decided to give my honest review. This game is very buggy. Yet everyday i see people ♥♥♥♥♥ing about the lag, bugs, and problems with the game. Please, understand that you are dealing with a game thats in progress and work your way through or around the bugs.
Now that ive gotten that out of the way. Lets be straight. This game is full, i mean FULL, of people who go into highly populated servers and kill eachother in towns. 75% of the community that is.(Not acctually sure but thats an estimate.) You barely see people playing the game for the survival aspect. Its a constant shoot on sight and betrayal. I barely find people who i would consider forming a friendship with. Although, the first day i got this game i met the group of friends i play with everyday. And i thank this game for that. With that said it is possible. Now lets review some pros.
PROS:
+Dev team is very involved with community. There is a bug tracker in the forums that you can report bugs too and the devs will fix them. Literally. In the next update. If there is a wall glitch, a texture glitch, a world based object glitch. It doesnt matter they will fix them.
+Large map 10km wide, that is.
+Very decent loot economy. The loot is randomized since .57 patch. Everything spawns random. Some buildings spawn only shirts. But none only spawn guns. Meaning it takes more time to loot and find exactly what you need.
+Many guns and melee weapons. They add guns almost every patch lately.
+Many, many, many clothing items. You can customize your survivor to whatever you want. You can be a complete asshat and dress in pink, yellow, bright green, red. Or you can dress in camo. What ever you want!
+Very easy inventory system. The inventory system is very user friendly. Simply drag and drop. Or you can double click. Simple.
CONS:
-DESYNC DESYNC DESYNC. This video will explain it all.
-No persistance. Currently in .57 they have disabled persistance. When persistance is enabled the world items are reset every wednesday. Which means you can have bases for a week. ♥♥♥♥ing blows.
-Not being able to pick up items. There is a fix. Just enter a building and re-enter. Although if you are in a situation when you are trapped and you need something off the ground your ♥♥♥♥ed.
-Random leg breaks. This doesnt happen often but when it does, and it ruins YOUR PRISTINE BLACK CARGO PANTS THAT YOU HAD TO SWIM THE OCEAN FOR, It sucks more than Mia Khalifa.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Thats all i can think of off the top of my head. This game is no where near finished. And dont expect it to be any time soon. If you dont have a well trained temper, dont buy this game.

It's freakin' Borderlands! C'mon now, the outstanding ''Looter-Shooter'' RPG/FPS hybrid game. With hilariously freakish enemies, bright, iconic characters, and A LOT of emphasis on a ''Bazillion'' of guns, and for good reason. Because it's considered a looter-shooter, there are millions of items to find and loot, aswell as unlimited weapon combinations, because a lot of the stuff is randomly generated so you will very rarely discover 2 items that are exactly the same. With guns with technology integrated into them that are capable of shooting explosive, fire and shock (because ♥♥♥♥ it, why not?) rounds to name just a few, along with a wide variety of shields, grenade mods, passive relics, and weapons from simple handguns/revolvers, to freakin' rocket launchers that basically fires a nuke, the game will always make you crave for new and more weapons and items with crazy different combinations and attachments/parts. Now, to organize all these amazing items, it includes a color-coded quality system. From White (being the most common/basic tier) to Green (Uncommon) Blue (Rare) Purple (Very Rare) and Orange (being Legendary grade/quality items that includes a special effect) which certainly keeps your eyes open for the next and best items/loot. There are unique and different characters with a level-up system, each with their own personal special or, ''skill'' along with 3 different unique skill trees for each character. Hence the RPG part. It still continues to be my favorite game series to this day. There's also so much other stuff and content I'm not mentioning, because it would make this review an entire damn page essay.
This also still remains as my favorite game.
Game also really encourages you to play Co-Op with friends. Later on, especially with a harder playthrough option, it becomes quite difficult.
BUT LOOK, GAME'S GOO- ABSOLUTELY AMAZING. Otherwise I wouldn't have this many hours into it. Oops.

Undertale is quite a remarkable little game.
It's kind of like... like when you go to an old relative's house for Thanksgiving and you're surrounded by so many people that you havn't seen since you were a little kid. And then everything goes wrong. The turkey falls on the floor and the dog eats it. Your sister catches her hair on fire on a nearby candle, and everyone is forced to get by on all the other food, save the turkey. Everything seems to go wrong, but in the end everyone is all smiles and much laughter is shared. You'll wish you could stay in that warm house by the fire with your friends and family forever, but alas the time comes to return home. Part of you worries that you may never get to see them again, but deep down you know that even if that's true, that your experiences and memories made that risk worth it.
It's not about the journey that you took to get to where you are now, it's about the people who were with you along the way.
That's Undertale.

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Rust is a brutal game, you are going to die in this. A lot. If you're in one of the official servers, you're going to be killed for comically small stakes- your starter torch, your starter rock, the animal fat another player can rip out of your carcass. For a long while, when you die- you will lose everything you've been building, and gathering up. It will be painful, It will show you the darker sides of the human condition with no effort at all, no real enticement on it's part. For a while, you will bolt- like some Sisyphusian  deer in a hunting season of eternal torment.
Some time later, you'll have some semblance of a strategy- you'll squirrel away enough wood, stone, and metal to create the most basic bunker box to build from. You'll sneak through bushes- hoping you see the people with guns before they see you. You'll balk at the ruins of settlements, hoping no one is currently plundering them.
You might even run around in the nude, simply because it might dissuade your hunters from shooting you.
Then, somewhere along the line you'll spot some relic of the world that was- a power plant, a rail yard, a warehouse, and you'll find fragments of the world that was- and after some time, you'll study them. You'll start to learn how to make better buildings- better tools. Maybe you'll sell yourself as a labor slave to some other player, who already has some semblance of a base built. You'll forage, you'll learn, you'll construct the weapons of the missing culture.
Then, there you will sit- master (because at this point, every player is a dude) of a tiny keep. You'll venture brazen into the fields, knowing it would take far more than your number to fell you. Perhaps you have a group of friends with you- there is power in numbers after all. You'll build a grand wall around your home- you'll have a compound- and you'll stop feeling unsafe.
That's the point when Rust reminds you that no one is untouchable. Some naked guy in a bush, or a prefab bear will launch itself through your doorframe as you're tapping out the key code, to go get more rocks. They'll steal your right to build, they'll rip your bed in half, they'll render the fat from your carcass into low grade fuel. If they like what you built, they'll keep it for themselves- if they don't, they'll leave signs all around, informing anyone who wanders through that this land is tainted by the horror you once were. Perhaps they'll make jokes about your mother.
And you, will either appear nearby- in some sleeping bag you hid in a bush near your camp (that no one has destroyed yet) or else you'll wake up somewhere down the river, with a rock, a torch- and the savagery of humanity looming over you- grinding their spears, ready to break you apart, for nothing more than the fat of your carcass, your rock, and your torch.
It's like a gritty reboot of Philip Jose' Farmer's Riverworld, if you were in a section where no one was important.

I played this game for the first time this afternoon, but it was nothing like the experience that I had on the previous mod for Arma 2. This game felt...different. Everything felt different...
It all started when I spawned on the southern side of Chernarus (the game's map) in a rather large town called Elektrozavodsk. This place had been popular in the previous mod, being a central area for out of control firefights, from who knows where, and frolicking throughout the city in search of loot that didn't seem to help you in the end. Surprisingly, I was given a Lee Enfield when I spawned, but with only two magazines. I told myself as I began my journey, "It's better than nothing."
As I was running down the main road heading west, I heard several gunshots in the distance. Curious as to what was going on, I continued toward the sounds of lead, that were, in my mind at the time, spewing out of someone's barrel at another helpless survivor. But, when I approached the area, all I saw was a lot of zombies pacing; some even dead. They seemed distressed, like they just...chased someone. I proceeded onward until I reached a lone shack. It had a dark, blood-like red look to it on it's roof, and its walls had hundreds of bullet holes placed throughout it. Then, something clicked in my head. I realized that this was a high loot spawning area for things such as food and clothing. Becoming overwhelmingly excited, I moved toward the shack.
Upon entry, I became utterly terrified, I jolted to an immediate stop. I could feel a twitching in my jaw, coming and going. My stomach began twisting uncontrollably. My mouth was dry, my legs quaking, and my eyes became out of focus. Then my vision cleared. I switched to my Lee Enfield, turned the corner, and ran inside. I knew that something didn't feel right. My horror returned. I was in an empty room. There was a flight of stairs right above my head, and I could hear a faint voice coming from the top, saying, "...are you friendly?" Confused, I frantically switched to direct communication and replied, "Come again?" There was no reply. I refused to go upstairs, terrified of what would happen to me. But I told myself, "I bought this game to get into circumstances like this just for the thrill of it." Escape was impossible now. So, I ran up the stairs, which seemed like forever and saw a player, that was a blur to my right. I wheeled that way, crouched, gripped the Enfield in both hands, and fired. Not only was he the first player I had ever shot at in this game; he was the only one I had seen at close quarters. He was a small, stern looking man with thick, stubby legs dressed in faded khaki pants and the rest of him squeezed into a uniform that was too tight for a man of his size. Unlike me, he was wearing a gas mask, dressed to kill. His rifle was strapped on in a sniper’s harness, and though he had heard me, and was trying to run toward me, the harness sling had him trapped. He couldn’t disentangle himself from it. His eyes were rolling in panic. Realizing that he couldn’t retrieve his arms and defend himself, he was backing toward a corner with a crazy, crab like motion. My first shot had missed him, embedding itself in the wall, but the second caught him dead-on just under his liver. I saw an explosion of blood shoot out from his back. His left thigh blossomed, swiftly turning to mush. A wave of blood gushed from the wound. Silently, he looked down at it. He dipped his hand in it and smeared his dirty cheek red. Then he slumped down slowly, and died. I kept firing until about half of my clip was gone. The smoke from my barrel blocked my view of what I had just done.
A sour, pervasive feeling hit me when I saw his body, which is different from anything else you have ever known. Yet witnessing someone die at that range, the smell of it, requires no previous experience. You instantly recognize the convulsion of what you have just done. I don’t know how long I stood there just staring at his mangled body. A feeling of disgust and self-hatred clotted darkly in my throat, gagging me.
Shaking my head, I slipped a new, fully loaded magazine into the slot of my Enfield. Then I began to tremble and shake all over. I sobbed uncontrollably and told the man: "I’m sorry." I threw up all over myself and recognized the half-digested Baked Beans dribbling down my chest, smelling the vomit. At the same time I noticed another odor; the horrendous stench of the man's body that I had just taken the life of. It seemed as if he was not going to harm me, but just simply ask for my assistance. I pondered fleetingly with thousands of feelings that became so loathsome the instant they left my body.

Very good game overall, aside from the occasional bugs and glitches than may or may not crash your game. For an Alpha game, the Standalone is very robust, but it also has that flare most games find hard to grasp... an intense atmosphere that makes the player feel as if he/she is there.
Now, I know that there are a lot of glitches, and it's one thing to completely immerse yourself and dedicate much time and effort to equipping your character with the most effective and deadly amount of gear, and another to one day log on, only to lose it all due to a stupid mistake. I get that this game has bugs, but hell, it's one-of-a-kind. In fact, most game development processes take well over a few  years to successfully release a product and this title is no different.
This is a game with an extreme learning curve, but if you manage to look at some guides or some YouTube videos on how to play the game effectively, you too can become a master at this game. You can't win in DayZ. You just do a little better every time.
Pros:
- This game has one of the highest replay values. It consistently immerses the player almost as if they themselves are the character they have control over.
- Player interaction is very high, unless you only play on lower population servers to purposefully avoid people. Interacting with players is key in the standalone version of DayZ as it allows safety and the ability to always have someone watching your back to the occasional rogue zombie.
- The setting of DayZ is absolutely beautiful and it is perfect for projecting an atmosphere of a zombie apocalypse.
Cons:
- Buggy Zombies (Now somewhat fixed, they *usually* don't faze through walls of buildings anymore.)
- Lots of connection issues such as the infamous desync
- Way too much banditry (for those of you that don't know what this is, it's the people that will shoot you on sight regardless)
- Slow development process (I'll return to this in just a moment)
- Large learning curve that requires skill to master
Development: While to the untrained eye it may appear that DayZ is going nowhere and hasn't since release (as almost all the negative comments for DayZ will say), the developers have implemented many different things over the year since this game has been released. Many people pushed for vehicles early due to the fact that it takes so long to travel across the <225km of Chernarus. Since they have implemented it, most likely due to the consumer push for them, it so far has been extremely buggy mostly because they did not take the time to refine it due to the persistent insistence of the people who want to play this game quickly. What many people don't realize (surprisingly), is that although it would be great to add vehicles and more weapons sooner, they need to let the developers do their job of refining the game. Those pushy people who want more content should realize this, THIS GAME IS STILL IN ALPHA. It even states every time that you load the game that this game is in Alpha. It does not reflect the final representation of the game and you must work through the bugs and possible game-ending crashes that result from it. The developers have so far done a wonderful job advancing the game through it's rocky beginnings and in fact, by comparing the release build to the current one, it would be hard not to see the monumental progress this game has made.
So the ultimate question:
Would I recommend this game or buy it again?
That answer is a definite yes. I love to support the development of games myself and watch the amazing community that takes origin from it. Aside from it's glitches and its constant banditry, I find this game one of the best I have ever played.
Overall Rating:
5.5/10

Alright casuals, time for some history.
Some philosophers of the 18th century like Hobbes and Rousseau developped the concept of the Natural State of humankind. The Natural State is humanity without society ; where survival of the fittest rules and backstabbing others in hope to live one more day is the norm.
Rust is that shît.
Don't come here expecting to make alliance with everyone you cross on a road ; killing on sight is the safest way to play and making sure you survive one more day. Alliance with random people are either frail or successful, and I can tell you I've been stabbed in the back more than once trying to befriend someone.
Also, dying is part of the game ; you will die and have your base raided by other players. You will loose everything. You will rage. There are no rules.
Now of course, this whole mess won't appeal to everyone. Those seeking a cooperative game will often cry playing this, expecting everyone they cross to be friendly. Well if you're looking for someone to play with, bring some friends along, or look in the forum chats to find like-minded players, or team up with other fresh-spawns of a server ; those are usualy more willing to team up because they stand nothing to loose if you betray them. Just don't run to a guy in full armour holding a gun and say "I'm friendly, wanna team?" then cry like all those negative reviews pointing out this "major flaw" of Rust.
Alright, now if you still have the nuts to play this game, let me tell you that it can be the most rewarding experience you've ever lived. Fending off a raid or pulling one, rockets wizzling by your head, is the most intense experience i've ever had in a video game. Forming a clan and managing your little town and it's citizens is insane fun. Going solo is a harsh experience, and one will quickly find out he needs to team up with other if he wants more chances at survival.
If someone tells me this is a bad game, he is wrong. This brutal stone age-wannabe game won't click for everyone. But if the idea of the Natural State appeals to you and you've got some decent-sized pair of balls, you'll enjoy this gem.

After putting just under one hundred hours into this game, by that I mean 99 as of the time writing this, I feel like I could give my input on the game.
*Before I can truly recommend this game to anyone, I highly encourage watching many different YouTubers' videos on this game to get an idea of what it's like. Also, don't just read one review and make up your mind, read many and decide from there.
I would highly recommend this game to those who like this type of game or like the idea of the game. With said recommendation, there are a few warnings with it; this game has problems. It's buggy at times, has it's fair share of issues, and can be frustrating at times, but I would still recommend this to anyone who can deal with the occational frustrating glitch, i.e, guns disappearing, items falling through the floor when taken off, and also some optimization issues.
This game may take time to get used to as well. Don't expect to buy the game, join a server, and be amazing at everything. You won't know where to find good gear when you first start, unless you use YouTube videos, which I would also highly recommend. You won't know the map unless you have the map pulled up on another screen, or phone, which I would also highly recommend. You also won't be that great at using weapons, or knowing what items do what, and how to do some things. The game takes some getting used to, and also some experience to really get the hang of it and really enjoy it.
If anyone is on the fence about getting this game, I would say buy it. The game is still updated fairly often, and those updates often come with new and interesting content. Yes it has it's issues, but if you look past the glitches and bugs in the game, it can be a very fun and interesting game.
Overall, I would say if you can deal with some problems in the game, and understand the fact that this game is in very early alpha stages, and was originally a mod for Arma II, then I would say buy it.

A survival game where you can build a base and craft everything from a spear to a sniper rifle sounds fantastic, but the reality is so much less. It ends up being just that: players with wooden spears and another group with sniper rifles, where potshots at the defenseless from tall towers is the expected norm. A sadist's dream, kindness has no place in rust, and the amount of work and time this game requires to get anywhere past wooden spears is always more than you'll be able to put in. It's disappointing that such a promising game ends up being a power session for preteen boys who can't make friends at school, and losers in their early thirties who have to take a smoke break every twenty minutes. I wish I could get my money, and time, back.

Rust is a brutal game, you are going to die in this. A lot. If you're in one of the official servers, you're going to be killed for comically small stakes- your starter torch, your starter rock, the animal fat another player can rip out of your carcass. For a long while, when you die- you will lose everything you've been building, and gathering up. It will be painful, It will show you the darker sides of the human condition with no effort at all, no real enticement on it's part. For a while, you will bolt- like some Sisyphusian  deer in a hunting season of eternal torment.
Some time later, you'll have some semblance of a strategy- you'll squirrel away enough wood, stone, and metal to create the most basic bunker box to build from. You'll sneak through bushes- hoping you see the people with guns before they see you. You'll balk at the ruins of settlements, hoping no one is currently plundering them.
You might even run around in the nude, simply because it might dissuade your hunters from shooting you.
Then, somewhere along the line you'll spot some relic of the world that was- a power plant, a rail yard, a warehouse, and you'll find fragments of the world that was- and after some time, you'll study them. You'll start to learn how to make better buildings- better tools. Maybe you'll sell yourself as a labor slave to some other player, who already has some semblance of a base built. You'll forage, you'll learn, you'll construct the weapons of the missing culture.
Then, there you will sit- master (because at this point, every player is a dude) of a tiny keep. You'll venture brazen into the fields, knowing it would take far more than your number to fell you. Perhaps you have a group of friends with you- there is power in numbers after all. You'll build a grand wall around your home- you'll have a compound- and you'll stop feeling unsafe.
That's the point when Rust reminds you that no one is untouchable. Some naked guy in a bush, or a prefab bear will launch itself through your doorframe as you're tapping out the key code, to go get more rocks. They'll steal your right to build, they'll rip your bed in half, they'll render the fat from your carcass into low grade fuel. If they like what you built, they'll keep it for themselves- if they don't, they'll leave signs all around, informing anyone who wanders through that this land is tainted by the horror you once were. Perhaps they'll make jokes about your mother.
And you, will either appear nearby- in some sleeping bag you hid in a bush near your camp (that no one has destroyed yet) or else you'll wake up somewhere down the river, with a rock, a torch- and the savagery of humanity looming over you- grinding their spears, ready to break you apart, for nothing more than the fat of your carcass, your rock, and your torch.
It's like a gritty reboot of Philip Jose' Farmer's Riverworld, if you were in a section where no one was important.

The experience is awful. Full of broken game mechanics, terrible performance on even the highest end of machines, and the worst player base I've ever seen. I wish I could get my money, and time, back.

Call for help, screaming on mic to the defenders to get me out.
I bang on the walls with my bone clubs.
They send naked men with machetes to take me down.
I kill one of them with my trusty waterpipe shotgun.
Out of ammo, take machete.
Continue to kill 3 more nakeds with the machete.
One of the defenders become disarmed and wounded.
I help him up.
We're both stuck in slave pit.
I compliment his body features (especially the lower body)
We become buddies.
Ends up glitching up the wall and boosting him up to allow him to leave.
I hear a fall, followed by screams, he dies from wooden spike traps.
Rust in Peace Vengeance.
"BIG DADDY DAN" comes along and gives me food, clothes, and resources through a tiny crack in the pit.
We become best buddies.
He dies to an AK from the defenders.
Rust in Peace Daniel.
Spend an hour sitting there playing the guitar.
Friend comes along to boost me out.
True "Saving Private Ryan" moment.
Run free to the north like a black slave in the 1800's.
10/10 game would tell my tale of escaping slavery to grandchildren.

I woke up naked and afraid. Other naked guys with long wooden pigstickers jabbed at me while dancing around howling like monkeys. I ran, still naked and afraid. The distant fields and wooded areas offered little solace and I was soon slumped over in a pool of my own frothy blood simply because I had no time to react from the thunderous crack that ripped through the air from behind me. I couldn't even clothe myself and these guys had guns. FML.
Respawning, over and over, I came to learn the ways of this strange and wonderful land. I brought down my first kill and, for a single night, feasted like a King! With hunger at bay I could explore my surroundings some more and, ultimately, carved out my own remote corner where I could buld a small, but sturdy, structure to make it through the night in. I fashioned simple garb to keep warm with. I crafted primitive weapons. I learned to harvest the land's bouty and turn what I unearthed into better and better items. Soon, I too had guns.
The prey was now the predator and I learned to strike at those who would take what I had. I could defend myself. I could force my will upon others. I could take what they had. Now I was a King!

This game is the type of game that you can really lose yourself in, you can play dozens of hours a day, and still have fun!
This was in the good old days of Rust. I recieved this game as a gift from a friend for christmas (2015). Back then you connected to people and you "Roleplayed" and truly interacted with all of the players on a server. On these servers you got to know most people and you knew them as a community, and interacted with them more than just in any other game. Before I played as much Rust as i did back then, I played a fair bit of CS:GO and Unturned, one of which is a round based First Person Shooter, and the other one, a Zombie survival game with graphics all based on square models.
Even though I came from these games that are considered very different from Rust, I still fell in love with the game and lost yself in it. Now i nearly have 2500 hours in the game and i have completely lost the spark to play it.
Updates and development was shifted from what the games core was (Blueprint system) and was tergetting  bigger audience by putting out quick, not-well-thought-out updates, many of which (In my opinion) ruined the game and the way it was played.
Nowadays, the game doesn'thave a goal for the week, the 'wipe' used to consist of you and your friends farming and getting those recourses needed to get that one base, or that one outpost, after that, you spent the wipe interacting, PVP:ing and gathering for Blueprints, this knowledge that followed you till the next wipe, where you could build better things from the start and it gave you an insentive to stay on the server for more than the timeit took you to die the first time.
Nowadays, Rust is completely changed, everything that the developers do in terms of progress is being hidden away, the old branches barely have anyt population because not a lot of people know about them, the new resource system only involves farming and if you die or get raided, you lose all the progress that you had made to that point, nothing was gained from the hundreds of hours you put in that wipe, just to have to reset and do the exact same thing again next wipe, and so on.
The playerbase got more and more agressive due to the increased rarity of items, people now have to work extra hard, jut to get a stone wall up. Now KOS is one of the most reoccuring themes in the Rust chatroom.
For me, the devs have to drastically change the way the game is played so that it better matches the playerbase, no need to farm for the entire wipe and invest that much time, just so that you can lose it immediatey to a clan of 20 or more players. (Obviously one can try to avoid this, but what is the point in selective playing due to that) What the developers desperately has to do is to give the players something to hold onto on a server for the next wipe, knowledge on item crafts, specific components, something, just so that when a player joins a server, he has something to hold on to, something to bring with him to prove that his efforts was worth the while.
I loved this game, now I am sad to see what it has become, I still have hopes for it but I think it has a long way to go still.
I would give this game a 2/10, due to the reason that I have so much nostalgia from it, however changes need to be made, drastically.

DayZ is fun in a way that compares to jamming forks up ones behind. It hurts like hell the first couple of times but after a few hundred hours of doing it with your friends it becomes somewhat likeable. (At this point you might notice I have about 30 hours in the standalone but trust me, I've played the mod plenty.)
Better loot is rare unless you actively hunt the airfields and firestations for scraps that clans left behind. I've yet to encounter anything besides an empty can or a roll of toilet-paper in a deerstand so I assume the spawns are a bit screwed.
Even if you do encounter a pistol, crossbow or god forbid, an actual rifle with bullets, you're still left with the moral choice of killing the newspawn for his beans or not. (Assuming you'll ever spot anyone new. All I found were either straight up military-tier gearmonsters or half-dead looters who took a couple of shots from the beforementioned militants.)
All in all I'd love to recommend DayZ for a weekend experience for anyone who wants to hike for a good 30 minutes only to end up finding nothing or an axe-murderer jolting about in the woods near Electro.

Might as well talk about it, as its been two years.
Undertale was one of those games that was illusive when it first came out those 2 short years ago. the only way i would've known about it was jesse cox' fan friday, where he play the begining of the game. I remember witnessing the first boss' death, and just felt awe struck, based on that performance. the fact that the game memorized your choices was what made it a unique experience. The fanbase at its begining was good, to say the least. there was a bunch of art and music being made from the game that it was such a massive gathering of people. The game had an amazing affect on people.
Two years have passed ever since then. The fanbase went to hell and back, and it kind of hampered the fun of the game because people who enjoyed the game so much spoiled anything for new players. I would know, i was kind of the problem, ruined it for one of my friend because i thought they werent ever going to play it. but it was that sense of the compasion of sharing this game that had a wonderful effect on people that probably drove them to doing such actions. Were here talk about the game, however, so lets get this underway.
Undertale is a role playing game that follows a nameless human that you control.  you awaken in this place called "The Underground", more specifically, "The Ruins". you awaken on a bed of flowers, and you walk into the next room to meet the first thing you come across, a talking flower by the name of flowey. he tries to kill ya, but a friendly figure known as toriel comes in to rescue you. you follow her around the ruins, until she leaves all by herself to do some tasks, which leaves you all by yourself. The game teaches you that you can simply talk your way out of fights, which is encouraged in this game, whereas killing enemies is refrained from doing. you adventure around, collect some healing items, then you go confront toriel at her house, and she invites you inside for a slice of pie. you then have to tell her that you have to leave, in which she retreats to the basement in an attempt to close off the door to the rest of the underground. you simply must stop her, either with negotiation or confrontation, and then you are free to leave. the game opens up in the next area, simply called snowdin. anything beyond this point is a potential spoiler, as you could only go as far as fighting toriel in the demo of the game.
so what about the rest of the game?
The rest of the game is a standard affair of solving puzzles, fighting, and making different choices throughout the game all the way up until the end. certain things get revealed to you, which are spoilers to talk about, so we wont speak of them here. The games ending is dictated on 2 sets of things: Which bosses you spared or killed, and if you spared or killed all enemies. if you spared everyone no matter what, you're on the pacifist route, but if you killed everyone, you're on the genocide route, each having different events and stories following them. if you wish to leave the route you are on, you can simply spare or kill 1 enemy, and the game throws you onto a regular normal route, which i recommend for a first time playthrough.
The music, whether you love or hate this game, is pretty good. its one of the high points of the game, with each boss having a unique boss theme that sets the tone for the whole fight. the boss fight with toriel at the begining of the game set a tone that would make actions seem regretable, but also give the idea of an adversary that urges you to challenge them, despite what you know.
The art is also good. most of the concept art was made by Toby Fox, but Temmie Chang gave her contribution as the co-artist for the game, and the game looks really nice because of it. the game gives off a retro pc game feel from the combat, and a wacky theme for the overworld that works really well together.
The uniqueness of the game comes from the main gimmic the game throws at you: the morality system. The game judges you based on what you do in fights, ie. sparing or killing enemies. the problem with this is that people claim that this game has a good morality system, even though its just like every other morality system in other games, just disguesed well enough to look different from others. The only good thing i like about it, however, is that the game records what happens with the each encounter with the bosses, which results in the game going through a checklist to see if you spared or killed any of the bosses. Killing and sparing bosses has a varying affect on the games normal ending, which doesn't matter if you're going for the games good ending, or the games bad ending.
My issues start to arrise when it comes down to the different story pathways. I do not like how the game deliberately punishes you for choosing to do the genocide runs, and it praises you for doing a pacifist run. if you have played dishonered, you know that the game will give you skills most of which will kill people, which killing people gets you the bad ending in dishonered. the problems start to arise when the game deliberately makes it more fun to do one route more than the other, because the route the game wants you to play is the more fun route of the two. undertale punishes you a bit too much for doing the route it doesnt want you to do, and if you have to take away fun from people who just want to explore everything, then how does that make a better game? theres a point where you should just tell the player that what they are doing is wrong, but it shouldn't retain permanent damages to future playthroughs of the game. The game also pins the blame on the player alot for doing the genocide runs, but then it makes you think: Who's more twisted? The player for playing through the elaborate, negative story, or the developer for making such a route in the first place?
If you have been ruined by the fanbase to sway your reasoning to avoid playing this game, you have every right to do that. I won't say you're missing much, but if you want to give it a shot, you can go right on ahead. Its extremely fun for your first playthrough, but after a few repeated playthroughs, you'll just wish there was something more than just slight nuanced endings to the same story over and over.

Easily one of the most unique franchises in the past decade, Borderlands targets a somewhat niche but unsurprisingly populated demograph of gamers who enjoy FPS games and RPG elements. The overall charm, humor, and complicated--though not convoluted-- combat is hard not to appreciate.
Borderlands 2 builds upon the  sucesses of its predecessor and patches up its numerous flaws. It contradicts the common trend of mediocre titles producing sequels that are of even lesser quality. This is truly a sequel in all respects. Not only does it build upon the story, but it learns from its mistakes and also expands upon all the positive qualities of its predecessor. Hardcore gamers might find it difficult to enjoy the game for all its worth due to  reoccuring "end game" problems with "lootfest" genre style games that lack a real PVP mode. However, the mindset in which you approach this game is important. Play this like it's Diablo or Torchlight, and not like it's Call of Duty. If you are the type of person who tires of things quickly and you don't want to burn out too fast, then I highly reccomended that you play this game as more of a stress reliever on the side that you sink no more than ~10-15 hours a week playing if possible, and not as your main go-to game.
-Oscar

Undertale was one of those games that was illusive when it first came out those 2 short years ago. the only way i would've known about it was jesse cox' fan friday, where he play the begining of the game. I remember witnessing the first boss' death, and just felt awe struck, based on that performance. the fact that the game memorized your choices was what made it a unique experience. The fanbase at its begining was good, to say the least. there was a bunch of art and music being made from the game that it was such a massive gathering of people. The game had an amazing affect on people.
Two years have passed ever since then. The fanbase went to hell and back, and it kind of hampered the fun of the game because people who enjoyed the game so much spoiled anything for new players. I would know, i was kind of the problem, ruined it for one of my friend because i thought they werent ever going to play it. but it was that sense of the compasion of sharing this game that had a wonderful effect on people that probably drove them to doing such actions. Were here talk about the game, however, so lets get this underway.
Undertale is a role playing game that follows a nameless human that you control.  you awaken in this place called "The Underground", more specifically, "The Ruins". you awaken on a bed of flowers, and you walk into the next room to meet the first thing you come across, a talking flower by the name of flowey. he tries to kill ya, but a friendly figure known as toriel comes in to rescue you. you follow her around the ruins, until she leaves all by herself to do some tasks, which leaves you all by yourself. The game teaches you that you can simply talk your way out of fights, which is encouraged in this game, whereas killing enemies is refrained from doing. you adventure around, collect some healing items, then you go confront toriel at her house, and she invites you inside for a slice of pie. you then have to tell her that you have to leave, in which she retreats to the basement in an attempt to close off the door to the rest of the underground. you simply must stop her, either with negotiation or confrontation, and then you are free to leave. the game opens up in the next area, simply called snowdin. anything beyond this point is a potential spoiler, as you could only go as far as fighting toriel in the demo of the game.
so what about the rest of the game?
The rest of the game is a standard affair of solving puzzles, fighting, and making different choices throughout the game all the way up until the end. certain things get revealed to you, which are spoilers to talk about, so we wont speak of them here. The games ending is dictated on 2 sets of things: Which bosses you spared or killed, and if you spared or killed all enemies. if you spared everyone no matter what, you're on the pacifist route, but if you killed everyone, you're on the genocide route, each having different events and stories following them. if you wish to leave the route you are on, you can simply spare or kill 1 enemy, and the game throws you onto a regular normal route, which i recommend for a first time playthrough.
The music, whether you love or hate this game, is pretty good. its one of the high points of the game, with each boss having a unique boss theme that sets the tone for the whole fight. the boss fight with toriel at the begining of the game set a tone that would make actions seem regretable, but also give the idea of an adversary that urges you to challenge them, despite what you know.
The art is also good. most of the concept art was made by Toby Fox, but Temmie Chang gave her contribution as the co-artist for the game, and the game looks really nice because of it. the game gives off a retro pc game feel from the combat, and a wacky theme for the overworld that works really well together.
The uniqueness of the game comes from the main gimmic the game throws at you: the morality system. The game judges you based on what you do in fights, ie. sparing or killing enemies. the problem with this is that people claim that this game has a good morality system, even though its just like every other morality system in other games, just disguesed well enough to look different from others. The only good thing i like about it, however, is that the game records what happens with the each encounter with the bosses, which results in the game going through a checklist to see if you spared or killed any of the bosses. Killing and sparing bosses has a varying affect on the games normal ending, which doesn't matter if you're going for the games good ending, or the games bad ending.
My issues start to arrise when it comes down to the different story pathways. I do not like how the game deliberately punishes you for choosing to do the genocide runs, and it praises you for doing a pacifist run. if you have played dishonered, you know that the game will give you skills most of which will kill people, which killing people gets you the bad ending in dishonered. the problems start to arise when the game deliberately makes it more fun to do one route more than the other, because the route the game wants you to play is the more fun route of the two. undertale punishes you a bit too much for doing the route it doesnt want you to do, and if you have to take away fun from people who just want to explore everything, then how does that make a better game? theres a point where you should just tell the player that what they are doing is wrong, but it shouldn't retain permanent damages to future playthroughs of the game. The game also pins the blame on the player alot for doing the genocide runs, but then it makes you think: Who's more twisted? The player for playing through the elaborate, negative story, or the developer for making such a route in the first place?
If you have been ruined by the fanbase to sway your reasoning to avoid playing this game, you have every right to do that. I won't say you're missing much, but if you want to give it a shot, you can go right on ahead. Its extremely fun for your first playthrough, but after a few repeated playthroughs, you'll just wish there was something more than just slight nuanced endings to the same story over and over.

This was in the good old days of Rust. I recieved this game as a gift from a friend for christmas (2015). Back then you connected to people and you "Roleplayed" and truly interacted with all of the players on a server. On these servers you got to know most people and you knew them as a community, and interacted with them more than just in any other game. Before I played as much Rust as i did back then, I played a fair bit of CS:GO and Unturned, one of which is a round based First Person Shooter, and the other one, a Zombie survival game with graphics all based on square models.
Even though I came from these games that are considered very different from Rust, I still fell in love with the game and lost yself in it. Now i nearly have 2500 hours in the game and i have completely lost the spark to play it.
Updates and development was shifted from what the games core was (Blueprint system) and was tergetting  bigger audience by putting out quick, not-well-thought-out updates, many of which (In my opinion) ruined the game and the way it was played.
Nowadays, the game doesn'thave a goal for the week, the 'wipe' used to consist of you and your friends farming and getting those recourses needed to get that one base, or that one outpost, after that, you spent the wipe interacting, PVP:ing and gathering for Blueprints, this knowledge that followed you till the next wipe, where you could build better things from the start and it gave you an insentive to stay on the server for more than the timeit took you to die the first time.
Nowadays, Rust is completely changed, everything that the developers do in terms of progress is being hidden away, the old branches barely have anyt population because not a lot of people know about them, the new resource system only involves farming and if you die or get raided, you lose all the progress that you had made to that point, nothing was gained from the hundreds of hours you put in that wipe, just to have to reset and do the exact same thing again next wipe, and so on.
The playerbase got more and more agressive due to the increased rarity of items, people now have to work extra hard, jut to get a stone wall up. Now KOS is one of the most reoccuring themes in the Rust chatroom.
For me, the devs have to drastically change the way the game is played so that it better matches the playerbase, no need to farm for the entire wipe and invest that much time, just so that you can lose it immediatey to a clan of 20 or more players. (Obviously one can try to avoid this, but what is the point in selective playing due to that) What the developers desperately has to do is to give the players something to hold onto on a server for the next wipe, knowledge on item crafts, specific components, something, just so that when a player joins a server, he has something to hold on to, something to bring with him to prove that his efforts was worth the while.
I loved this game, now I am sad to see what it has become, I still have hopes for it but I think it has a long way to go still.
I would give this game a 2/10, due to the reason that I have so much nostalgia from it, however changes need to be made, drastically.
