This game is practically dead. I would advise you NOT to buy the game as the page description says.
You probably wonder why I have played this game so much. The answer is: I don't even know the answer myself.
"Why is DayZ Standalone dead?", you might ask. Well, it's very simple.
It was promising in the beginning. A year of delay and suddenly a Standalone pops up. Hype to the maximum, this game was balls when it was released. Fun, fast-paced, reminded me of the Mod. I bought it.
Then something changed. For the worse.
The development shifted from VERY FAST to very very VERY slow. I understand that it's a relatively small dev team working on this game + Dean Hall, the creator of DayZ bailed out from the project, and I see no point in playing this game anymore.
The essential features and aspects of the game were not completed in time or have not been completed at all. And yes, I'm talking about the dreaded optimization that everyone has been complaining about. I have an overlocked 4.6GHz quad-core i5 4670K along with 16GB of 2166MHz RAM and a GTX 970. They manage to BARELY squeeze 20 FPS on LOW settings.
The "Real Virtuality" engine is a pile of steaming♥♥♥♥♥♥and is a complete abomination that should not be called software. Literally. It uses only 15% of my GPU no matter where I am in the game world. While I belive it would be easily fixable, the dev team has done nothing to improve the performance of the engine. Instead, they add seven ♥♥♥♥ing varieties of wool coats and more and more content (thus meaning more objects in the game world) that the engine obviously can NOT ♥♥♥♥ing handle because DayZ dev team's official motto is "quantity over quality".
Servers that have 40+ people on them are the worst. Because the servers simply can not handle such amount of "requests" happening in-game. Some of you would call that "bad netcode". I simply call it unoptimized piece of software. It's just not working right now. Actually, it hasn't worked properly from the beginning, but now it's even worse.
If you want the purest DayZ survival experience, play the mod. Vanilla. 'Cause that's how DayZ should be.
For Standalone, you should wait a couple of decades before the dev team pulls their heads out of their asses and actually start developing real software, a real game, real DayZ that everybody has been waiting for since the two-thousand ♥♥♥♥ing twelve.
Over and out.

На планету Пандору прибыли 4 наёмника, чтобы отыскать некое "Хранилище» - кладенец инопланетного оружия и эридианских технологий. Им противостоит корпорация "Hyperion" в лице Красавчика Джека, ставшего президентом этой корпорации и имеющий свои виды на Пандору. Вследствие чего, Джек присылает станцию доставки грузов корпорации в виде буквы "Н", на орбиту Пандоры, и начинает захват планеты. Данная игра представляет собой "Diablo от 1 лица, исполненная в лице шутера": прокачка персонажа, бесконечный опыт за убийство огромных толп врагов, большое количество квестов, к такому количеству приблизился разве что Skyrim. Процесс игры представляет собой формулу: убить и обобрать, а также споры по поводу снаряжения в кооперативе, ибо в игре случайно генерируется ВСЁ, включая награды за квесты. Графика в игре не однозначная, но красивая, присутствует технология nVidia PhysX, что делает бои, более красочными. Из минусов можно отметить унылый однообразный геймплей, присущий играм данного жанра.

I really tried to like this game. But I can't. It's been over a year since its release, and it still seems as though very little development progress has been made. I put tons of hours into the original Arma II mod, and I bought this with the intention of helping development and eventually getting a good standalone game. Unfortunately, that hasn't been the case.
First, the game's updates have been nothing special since launch. Beyond a few new weapons and the addition of a vehicle (I think? I've never actually seen it before) there have been almost no remarkable updates to the game, with the exception of the occasional bug fixes. However it seems that with every bug fixed, more and more annoying ones arise, taking development priority over everything else.
The game runs terribly, since day one, seemingly regardless of how impressive your specs are. My computer isn't the absolute best, but it is certainly powerful enough to max out games like Crysis or Battlefield. It's very hard for my system to maintain 30 fps while in cities, and usually I am stuck around the lower 20s. When running in the wilderness, with nothing but trees and the ground to render, I manage to get a whopping 40-50 at best. Woo hoo! Perhaps if the devs put half as much effort into optimizing the game as they did into adding gardening to the game, it would actually be playable.
Lastly, I feel like DayZ's community has gotten significantly worse since the release of the standalone on Steam. Back in the days of the mod, I remember encountering people that weren't solely out to kill every other player on sight. Don't get me wrong, I know that hostile players do add to the difficulty and realism of the game. But it just seems like now that's the only thing the game has going for it. The zombies are hardly a threat, there's very few at any given time, and they're very easy to escape from.
The game used to (sort of) reward you when you helped other players (giving blood, sharing food, etc.) by giving them the "Hero" skin. On the other hand, violent players would be given the "bandit" skin. This was a feature that was actually interesting and worth while. It served as a kind of goal for people to reach for with every new character. And now it's been taken away, and hasn't returned since. Just like vehicles, helicopters, and gear that is actually good and worth playing/fighting for.
Like I said before, I really wanted to like this game. I knew that it was early access, and I knew what I'd be getting into wouldn't be perfect, but after over a year, I can't say it's been worth my time or my money.

but that's not the problem with rust. i think it actually adds a lot of thrill and a little bit of difficulty to the game.
the actual problem with rust is it's emptiness.
after more than 2 years of development it still feels like an empty shell. once you got all the craftable stuff and a nice home base there's nothing more to do. the game ends. of course you could team-up with other players and raid some bases. of course you could expand your home base - make it huge. but for what? after less than 100 hours of gameplay you already saw everything. researched everything. explored everything. did almost everything you could do. the experience comes to an abrupt halt as you reach the limits of this game.
the real problem is rust's lack of content.
another thing that bothers me is more technical in nature.

altogether i enjoyed the game so far and i'm looking forward to more content. and yes i'm going to play it in the future. but i really can't recommend it as it is right now. buy a game with more content till they fixed some bugs and added content that increases rust's replay value - that's my advice.

So I'm nearing on 300 hours clocked for DayZ and have been playing since the Alpha was first launched in December 2013. I've always enjoyed playing and being a part of the development process and seeing the game evolve over time. I've also always hated seeing all of the negative comments over how long this game is taking to progress and up until now have always defended the Devs.
But now, I've absolutely had enough... Since Rocket left, the updates have been poor, sporadic and show almost NO PROGRESS... With the amount of money the game has made for the developers so far, you cannot argue that progress is much, MUCH slower than it should be. A Friend of mine has just arrived back from a year of travelling, and returned to DayZ to notice almost no difference in the year he's been away, except less Z's and more bugs.... Oh and a truck.
There is just no explanation for what is taking so long and why. Look at Ark: Survival Evolved, for example... Development STARTED in Oct 2014.... Less than a year later they already have a great Alpha, with features DayZ has only ever talked about (Advance base building, persistence, decent crafting system) and updates for Ark are being churned out almost weekly.
It just seems now that every single DayZ Status Report states the SAME things every time.... "We're still working on this bug" "Persistence will be fixed soon" "While development continues, the team would like to talk about an idea we had that won't actually happen for another three years"... "Here, look at these fan videos to keep you entertained"

Now that I am better able to connect to servers, I can post a new review.
Is it a good game? Yes. Is it the ultimate survival game? No. Or atleast not what I'm looking for personally.
In order to like this game, you have to ask yourself, are you more interested in PvP or PvE? I tend to go for the latter. The environmental threat in this game at this stage in development I'm writing this (11 Mar -16) consists of two entities: the bear and the wolf. For the most part even these are pretty easy to dodge if you see them from a distance. And... that's about it for the environmental threat. Hunger, thirst and cold are very easily satiated.
The game is geared for PvP. Defending one's base, and raiding other bases. For what it does I find it does pretty well. Base building mechanics are easy to learn, but designing a safe base is not easy.
My personal issue with the game, from the personal experience of playing the game in solo or in a pair is that it's just a matter of time when your base will be raided. It could be as short as two days in real time from the time you've set up. It could be even less. I also find it's a bit of a chore to keep collecting resources, upgrading your base, creating maybe other bases for security etc. It's not what I'm looking for in a survival game - I don't want to chop trees and mine ores, I want to lead a more of a "nomadic" existence. But, it's not the game's fault, it's just not what I'm looking for. It can also feel very frustrating at times to get raided, so also be aware of this. It's not an easy game in more ways than one.
But, if you're interested in the PvP aspect the game offers, then it's a very recommended buy. If you're more like me who likes PvE better, then maybe look elsewhere. I still do feel I got my money's worth out of the game.

Undertale is a MUST OWN for any fan of the RPG genre and for players with a sense of humor.
Quirky, fun and amazingly deep, Undertale tells the story of a child who falls into a hidden world filled with monsters.  What is unique about the gameplay is the system for which you avoid attacks.  Instead of standard turn-based RPGs where your avoidance of hits are based on your "agility" stat or something of the like, you play a mini-game that involves dodging obstacles for a period of time.
Another unique aspect of this RPG is that you can complete the game without killing a single enemy.  (In fact, without spoiling anything, I HIGHLY recommend doing this on your first playthrough!)  Achieving this involves solving a puzzle as opposed to knocking hit points off of the monster.  I found these puzzles to be way more interesting than just bashing on enemy monsters all day to begin with, thus making the "pacifist" route more enjoyable.
The graphics for this game are stylistically low-key, providing a nostalgic feel that brings you back to the old SNES days.  The music is delightful, written by the creator of the game, Toby Fox who is also a talented video game composer.
So I definitely recommend this for all RPG and indie game fans, and gamers in general will find it a treat as well!  Play it now!

The one and only significant problem with this game is that the community cannot contsin themselves with their excitement, and while that does put people off talking about it sometimes, that doesn't mean the game isn't worthy of all that praise.
Gameplay
Oh yes. Nobody can really appreciate this battling system until they've experienced it. If you're already into it, that's a different story though. If you're reading this, you already know how the battle system works, and the only question is whether it's satisfying.
Once again, oh yes.
Exploration is about as RPG as you could expect. Toss in environmental ambience and atmosphere, a few puzzles here and there, and many secrets that STILL haven't been found, you got a good gameplay. Game. Play. Words.
Music
Yes.
Characters
Definitely comes with a large package of humour. That's a perk though, considering the two or three characters that are entirely focused on seriousness. And some others who have brilliant serious sides and perhaps even backstory. These characters drew me in even after spoiling the game like a doofus.
Boss Fights
What's there is brilliant. Great adaptational gimmicks on some of these bosses make fighting much better. Every boss has their own theme, which is something more games really need. Really really need. Some get a bit too easy or too hard. Actually, no bosses are too hard. Some are almost impossible, though.
I'm impressed by these boss fights, and I'm sure many people have figured out already that one more is likely to come...

This is a NEGATIVE positive review, but I'm still giving it a thumbs up, because it wasn't "bad," and I deeply appreciated the "good/evil" mechanic. However, I purchased this game after it was already cool, and so my expectations were pretty high. I thought it would be a clever or emotional game on par with Gone Home or The Binding of Isaac, but by the end, I was mostly unmoved.
In large part, that's because the middle was unable to carry the excellent beginning and end sequences, which had real choices and a sense of gravity to them. A full 80% of the game is a tedius grind with only token RPG elements and shallow exploration to drive you on. The characters are purposefully shallow, which was fine at times, but got old really fast. Even the main game mechanic, which had so much promise, never really felt like it developed to its full incarnation by the end. Which is all a shame, because the beginning especially had a real sense of innovation and personality.
Frustratingly, a good chunk of the game's cleverness (and, honestly, most of its plot) relies on time-consuming multiple runs to unlock different story patterns. Which would be fine and clever if I finished the game with a burning desire to retry it, but I didn't.
The main redeeming innovation in this game is its take on killing monsters, which is pretty unique and hard to forget. But don't buy this game thinking it's some shoe-in for Treasured Game I Keep Close to My Heart. Because it may not be, like it wasn't for me.

My original opinion on
mostly still applies, althought I would like to note that the game does have a couple flaws that are entirely subjective, personally speaking.
The combat system; while unique, does take some practice to ultimately get the hang of. This is especially the case toward some of the more difficult encounters from the midpoint on. If you've never played a "bullet hell" style game as they are sometimes referred to, then you will definitely get a taste here.
Morality systems in games can be a tricky thing to do right, and some might find
's to be a bit ambitious for what the game is trying to do. I believe this was intended, as to my knowledge there hasn't really been a game that has attempted to persuade its players to think about their actions as a participant as well as a bystander. The best advice I can give is just make your choices as you yourself would personally make them were you in the protagonists position in actuality, at least for your first playthrough.
Other than noted above, there is very little I can say I found negative about
. It's charming, creative, and does its darndest to break some kind of mold that I can't even properly describe what through words. I still recommend
wholeheartedly, truthfully.
As with anything popular however, be cautious of
's rabid fanbase though. Yeesh.

allows this, and I daresay it encourages you to think differently about even the simplist decisions made throughout the course of its plot.

The one and only significant problem with this game is that the community cannot contsin themselves with their excitement, and while that does put people off talking about it sometimes, that doesn't mean the game isn't worthy of all that praise.
Gameplay
Oh yes. Nobody can really appreciate this battling system until they've experienced it. If you're already into it, that's a different story though. If you're reading this, you already know how the battle system works, and the only question is whether it's satisfying.
Once again, oh yes.
Exploration is about as RPG as you could expect. Toss in environmental ambience and atmosphere, a few puzzles here and there, and many secrets that STILL haven't been found, you got a good gameplay. Game. Play. Words.
Music
Yes.
Characters
Definitely comes with a large package of humour. That's a perk though, considering the two or three characters that are entirely focused on seriousness. And some others who have brilliant serious sides and perhaps even backstory. These characters drew me in even after spoiling the game like a doofus.
Boss Fights
What's there is brilliant. Great adaptational gimmicks on some of these bosses make fighting much better. Every boss has their own theme, which is something more games really need. Really really need. Some get a bit too easy or too hard. Actually, no bosses are too hard. Some are almost impossible, though.
I'm impressed by these boss fights, and I'm sure many people have figured out already that one more is likely to come...

This review was taken from my early game experience
I awoke on some Strange Island, I had a Rock and a Torch ( Flaming one )
I hit some trees with my Rock and beat up some Bigger rocks to get Stone and metal, I found Cloth plants and made a bow, Then started Hunting.
Killed 2 or 3 Stags and got Raw Chicken Breasts from them as well as: Leather,more cloth, bone Fragments and Animal fat.
I decided to find a town/looting place. Heading alongside a Mountain and I look into the Forest and Whats this ?
A strange army green box was there. It was a Airdrop.
I looted a Bolt action rifle ( with 2 Bullets) and a SMG ( with 6 Bullets) I thought that these would come in handy.
I found some big broken Satellites and decided to loot. Found no loot and it was getting dark. I heard a noise and hid in some Small metal room and waited... I ran out and fled for the hills but came back at Dawn. I hit a barrel and ran away, It did not explode so I beat it up and it game me loot ! I went around hitting all the barrels I could find and soon I had: a Crossbow, Salvaged Ice Pick and some blueprint fragmets, Lots of those ! I then thought that I will build a base, I built a 2x2 block wooden base with a wall 1 wall high and I furnished my base with a Forge and set some metal to forge. While the Forge was doing its magic I went around and found more barrels to smash. I went back to base and found that my forge was empty. I went back to busting up barrels but then... I found ... candy bars... on the floor in bags... I took those like a little child, Eating food on the floor ! I then was heading back to base and I stoped to cheak my inventory but was interrupted by a Golden light and a Loud noise. They had come. Bandits. I ran to a Bush while I was being shot and the Shooting stopped... I pulled out my SMG and waited , I man came and looked at me , I knew what Rust players were like and I thought that I would rather Defend my homeland or die trying so I pulled the trigger and let off my 6 bullets like a mad man, all missing his head, I waited for a few secounds and I was on the floor crying for help and I died. I respawned by my sleeping bag that I had hidden in the bush and I saw them, I ran to the base and closed my door... My door would protect me but no... they just opened it like a civilized person would, I screamed into my mic Please don't kill me ! They then said ok Daniel is friendly, game me back my Bolt action rifle and a random Pipe shotgun and left... I went back to my base and logged out. Rust is Unpredictable.

Being a gamer since the NES era, one will most likely develop a standard that would help one define if a game is a work of art or a brainless time-waster. Seeing this game being in a lot of discussions, with youtube, imageboards, and forums being flooded by tons of content regarding this game. It took me quite a while to convince myself to get Undertale. And when I did. Oh boy! It sure was one hell of a ride. And let me share too all of you folks why.
I'm not finicky when it comes into graphics. What I care for is the experience. I don't care about the length of the gameplay. As long as it serves its purpose to immerse you, entertain you, and give you the quality time you deserve. I am not picky if the music is 8 bit. As long as it carries the mood. Undertale puts you in the shoes of a protagonist wearing a striped shirt. And it is all up to you. Be a typical RPG character or be a pacifist. BUT the way it connects you to the characters, the way the story flows, the way the BGM fits with every situation and the way it brings excitement due to the variety of mechanics it introduces for every creature you stumbled upon will surely leave a mark.
I'd say it is more of an experience than a game. And if I could, I want to erase my memory and go back to the time when I still don't have an idea what this game is all about. Just so I could experience it all over again.

UNDERTALE is truly a magnificently crafted piece.
It brings homage to older RPG games that have influenced the modern gaming age so greatly, and yet puts its own amassment of twists and feelings on the classic RPG genre.
One might even say that Undertale isn't a normal RPG at all.
The combat system is extremely unique, and the karmic system's massive impact on the game's storyline feel like inFamous, but multiplied by ten.
Be warned, this game has its own unhealthy counts of fourth-wall breaks, so watch out!
If one puts the rather unlikable and generally alienating fanbase of Undertale aside, they will most likely realize that this game is a very good one, and can easily be recommended to others!
If you are one of the few users who has not heard of this game yet, or have managed to not spoil yourself of the entire game, then dive head-first into this game!  Plot progression feels slow at times and navigation through various areas sometimes feels like a waste of time, but that's just my own opinion.
I would easily tell anybody to go play this game for themselves, as Mr. Toby Fox has truly crafted a successful masterpiece that (might) will be remembered in everyone's hearts someday as a great milestone in indie gaming.
Happy gaming!

Quite possibly the best game I have ever played.  It tells a story that is much deeper than it first appears to be.  The graphics are very low-res, but full of emotion and detail (besides which, they're an homage to the Mother/Earthbound series.)  The game mechanics are a genuine improvement on the general set of RPG turn-based battles; most RPGs feel very hands-off, since your accuracy and attack strength are based entirely on invisible dice rolls, while Undertale gives you the visceral feeling of evading enemy attacks and lining up your own, as well as the myriad other options that can be performed in combat.  This action-based set of mechanics also makes repeat fights more interesting; if a boss fight kicks your♥♥♥♥♥ rather than level grinding for two hours and coming back to see if your numbers are high enough this time, you can try to improve by getting better at evading the boss's attack patterns and timing your attacks better.  The game's word and characters are also much more responsive than most games, and I'm not just talking about the multiple endings.  There are a ton of little interactions all over the game world that change based on different actions you've taken; the developer thought of EVERYTHING.  To top it all off, the soundtrack is incredible and very catchy, bringing to mind the best chiptunes on the NES, SNES and Sega Genesis.
Anything else I could say would be a spoiler, and it's best to play this game with no spoilers at all.  This game is incredible.  Every serious reviewer loves it.  Yahtzee loves it.  Yahtzee hates everything, but he loves this.  Also, it's ten bucks, and not a two-hundred-hour time sink.  How much are you really risking by just giving it a shot?

There's a lot about this game I have really enjoyed so far but I really cannot reccomend it.
It's three years into it's alpha and it's still ridden with bugs and performance issues. I have a more than capable computer but the rendering is terrible and frame rate drops are awful even though I'm playing with a spotless internet connection.
It's a beautiful game with lots of atmosphere and a very strange dystopian feel. I really expect the final product to be something quite amazing but most of the satisfaction I get is balanced by boredom and frustration. Animals can run up sheer cliffs to escape or attack you,  the hit detection for weapons can be awful, hacking is abundant, and eveyone wants to kill you.
Now, that last point is fine. It gives the game an edge, with every human encounter being excpetionally complex and dangerous. However I have never made an ally, and whenrver I don't kill somenone they stalk me and blow my brains out. I know it's a complex social experiment but when someone is never on your screen for more than a second because of lag or hacking, and you've spent 4 and a half hours getting all your equiptment together it gets frustrating. Most of my close range engagements with human beings end in failure because the game doesn't know where either of us should be. Long rang encounters end with me dead, as I've just spwaned in with a rock in my hands and someone has build a mile-high tower and just sits at the top sniping people with the bolt action and scope he just made.
I want this game to work, and I could put up with the terrible animal behaviour, floating rocks, almost impossible to aquire upgrades, and all that other atmosphere destroying nonesense if it wasn't for the god-awful performance as a whole.
Buy it when it's finished (in 10 years time) because right now it's not worth the money.

Now that I am better able to connect to servers, I can post a new review.
Is it a good game? Yes. Is it the ultimate survival game? No. Or atleast not what I'm looking for personally.
In order to like this game, you have to ask yourself, are you more interested in PvP or PvE? I tend to go for the latter. The environmental threat in this game at this stage in development I'm writing this (11 Mar -16) consists of two entities: the bear and the wolf. For the most part even these are pretty easy to dodge if you see them from a distance. And... that's about it for the environmental threat. Hunger, thirst and cold are very easily satiated.
The game is geared for PvP. Defending one's base, and raiding other bases. For what it does I find it does pretty well. Base building mechanics are easy to learn, but designing a safe base is not easy.
My personal issue with the game, from the personal experience of playing the game in solo or in a pair is that it's just a matter of time when your base will be raided. It could be as short as two days in real time from the time you've set up. It could be even less. I also find it's a bit of a chore to keep collecting resources, upgrading your base, creating maybe other bases for security etc. It's not what I'm looking for in a survival game - I don't want to chop trees and mine ores, I want to lead a more of a "nomadic" existence. But, it's not the game's fault, it's just not what I'm looking for. It can also feel very frustrating at times to get raided, so also be aware of this. It's not an easy game in more ways than one.
But, if you're interested in the PvP aspect the game offers, then it's a very recommended buy. If you're more like me who likes PvE better, then maybe look elsewhere. I still do feel I got my money's worth out of the game.

Undertale is a Single-player Role-Playing Game(RPG) written, developed, and published all by one person, Toby Fox. He also composed all of the music for the game himself, and drew most of the art as well; only receiving help from Temmie Chang with the art. It was released on September 15, 2015, and has won (as of 1-20-2016) five different game of the year awards!

Most RPG’s have some kind of combat system, and while Undertale does, it is extremely unique for this kind of game. In this turn based system you have two options for dealing with your enemies; Fight, or Act. Fighting is a lot simpler, and ends with you just killing your opponent, and you gain EXP and gold. If you Act instead, you can appeal to the “Monsters”, and convince them to like you and lose the will to fight, then spare them. This way you gain some gold, but no EXP, and it is possible to beat the game this way; without killing anyone. When they attack you however, it puts you into a box area, where the enemies throw attacks at you, which the player must control the character's soul (represented by a heart) to dodge. While this is original enough as is, some of the boss fights even mess with the way the player controls the heart, adding even more character to this already novel system.

Speaking of character, Monsters aren’t different only by their appearance like in most RPGs, but each type has their own personality and dialogue, and their own way of being pacified through Acting. The characters are what truly made this game amazing; all of the bosses have profoundly Unique, dynamic, and round personalities. Throughout the game you fight several bosses, and have the chance to make them realize that there is no reason to fight, and you can be friends instead. All of the decisions you make this way contribute to what happens in the game and the ending you get, and the changes are not slight either. If you choose to spare everyone, the game is much more light hearted and friendly to the player.  if you kill everyone however, the game takes a much more eerie and dark turn, where you are the evil one. There are also many different endings for what happens when you only kill some of them, varying on who you spare and kill.

... I gotta get this off my chest.
When I first heard about Undertale, I absolutely hated the idea of it. A perfect game? That everyone felt the need to talk about? How absurd.
Now I'm the guy who thinks it's a perfect game that I feel the need to talk about.
Though I will admit that I didn't play much of the game myself. A friend gave it to me but I got really annoyed with it in the first part so I just watched Game Grumps play it and by the time I realized it was worth the trouble I was already too far in and some of my friends on Facebook had spoiled some parts for me...
And that concludes the part of the review where I establish that I am a hypocrite.
The game's creator, Toby Fox, has somehow managed to create a game that is worth more than the sum of its parts. Normally sprites like these would bring down a game released in this day and age, but the game's excellent meta-humor justifies it enough to where I don't even care. The RPG elements are extremely light, though I feel that this was to do away with aspects that would have made the game grindy and overall boring. The bullet hell-like combat is fun and not overly challenging (unless you deserve it; see below), but can be a bit repetitive if a fight takes longer than it probably should.
To me, the best part of the game is the story.
Before I continue, I must note that you must do absolutely everything in your power to go into this game as blind as possibly can be. The less you know about the game, its shenanigans, and its plot, the better your experience will be.
On paper, the plot is only a bit more interesting than what we're used to nowadays, but the way that it's revealed over the course of the game is stunning. It's extremely difficult not to get engaged, wondering what comes next after each scene, each part of the game.
Thing is, how the plot unravels is heavily player-influenced.
Almost every single action you take has an effect on the plot, be it small or large. This especially plays into the whole "you don't have to destroy anyone" thing. Trust me when I say that you really shouldn't.
In an RPG, enemies are just... enemies. Monsters that want nothing but destruction of some sort and can't be reasoned with. Undertale is different. French television producer Arnaud Desjardins once said "There are no bad people, only badly loved people." Every single being that tries to attack you in this game is their own person, with their own personalities, faults, and viewpoints. All of them can be pacified if you just take the time to see from their viewpoint and deal with them without resorting to violence (well, there are only two times in a Pacifist run (don't kill anyone and be everyone's friend) where you will actually need to attack, but I won't say exactly where those are (only that they're at pretty much the end of the game)).
Or, alternatively, you can kill everyone. This is what you usually do in video games and, thus, what you first think you have to do here. Thing is, though, you WILL feel bad for doing it. Remember how I said that everyone has their own personalities, faults, and viewpoints? They will respond to your actions how they feel is necessary. On a Genocide run, where you have to kill each and every enemy you come across, you will go from the hero of the story to being the villain. The two hardest fights in the entire game are heroes trying to stop you in this storyline.
The fact that the world is so responsive to your actions makes it feel living and breathing. There is some fourth-wall breaking, but miraculously it serves to further establish the world of Undertale as living and breathing. I'm pretty sure this is why the true final boss, only encountered at the end of the Pacifist route, is actually one of the easiest... the game doesn't want you to lose. It wants you to get your happy ending, and it's not afraid to break its own rules in order to do that.
The soundtrack is fantastic, and can be bought here on Steam along with the game. Every track was composed by Toby Fox and is great in its own way. More details on that in a review of the soundtrack itself, if I get around to it.
If you're still skeptical, I understand, but please take my word for it. I am a perfect example of a non-believer turned believer, and I really hope that that is enough to convince anyone that this is probably their cup of tea. Want to know how it plays first? There's a free demo built off of an earlier version of the game available on the official website. Cannot stand the gameplay? At least watch a playthrough of the game on YouTube, like I did. Though, again, you really should try to play it for yourself. Blind.
... wow, and I said I wasn't gonna ramble.
That concludes my thoughts on Undertale, I guess. If you can't take my word for it, then see just how many other people have praised this game and consider THEN if you don't think this game deserves the praise it gets. This is no Five Nights at Freddy's.
This is so much more interesting.
Note that I'm pretty sure I'm a really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ reviewer so I won't probably make any more of these.

A solid game with solid humor throughout, Undertale constantly defies expectations. Frequently the game will "teach" you how to play the game, only to change things up and leave the game feeling completely new again. There's a ton of great humor tied to these mechanics, as well as the occasional clever story moment.
The story itself is fine, if not somewhat predictable. It follows a lot of the same tropes as anime, where logic isn't always needed when connecting the dots, which is the main reason the predictable plot is a bit of a letdown. I loved the feel of the game, and as stated previously it constantly defies your expectations when it comes to gameplay...and maybe that's why the rather straight-forward story is left feeling that much more bland by comparison. Yes there are some great meta moments, yes there are great jokes and visual gags, but if there was one thing Undertale could be criticized for it's the story. And yes, that's taking into consideration the fact that the story branches in different ways depending on who, if anyone, you kill in your playthrough; it still plays out pretty much exactly how you would expect. That's not to say I want crazy twists in my story driven games, but even the characters are mostly one dimensional, for better or worse. Certainly, being simple makes it much easier to focus on the humor element, and other games that Undertale was clearly influenced by (like the Mother series) are fairly similar in that regard.
The music is great throughout, and the graphics are charming. There's a few moments where a little more polish would have been appreciated, mostly in areas that have only 2 or three colors; striking at first due to the contrast, these areas tend to have really hard edges that clash with earlier high quality pixel art.
If you enjoy JRPGs, games driven by humor, or games with upbeat music, then you'll likely love Undertale. It's an indie darling for good reason, and you could do much worse even when choosing from powerhouses like Square-Enix or Atlus.
I'd give it a solid A, and would certainly place it in my top games of 2015. Would it take the top spot? No, not for me personally, but don't let that keep you from checking it out; there's room in your schedule/collection for Undertale.

Undertale is not a good game. This is a traditional RPG, right? So logically I thought the first step would be to grind out for levels, money, and items. But after awhile, enemies stopped showing up and the game began to slowly punish me for just playing it. How many games can you say punish you for simply going along with the genre norms? How was I supposed to know that the apparent 'good' path was to just let monsters beat the crud out of me and do nothing. How is that logically what I should do?
The game starts with some dog lady coddling you, it's kind of creepy for someone she just met honestly. She scares the monsters away, solves puzzles for you... It's rather insulting. How am I supposed to grow as a player if she just does everything for me at the start? Clearly the creator of this hasn't had kids themselves, or else they'd allow us to take a more hands on approach to learn for ourselves too. Not only that though, she then tries to bar you from leaving her house, as if she abducted us. Creeeepy.
After I completed the game, I looked around all over the internet, read many people's reviews and comments... And so many had shown pity or sentiment towards the boss characters, saying it'd be impossible to ever harm them. But seriously? Each boss in this game just wanted to kill you for their own selfish reasons. Because of that, I felt no pity or remorse, but rather, I felt invigorated by killing the fiends one by one. I killed the spider that wanted to eat me, I crushed the gay bone dude, beat up the metrosexual robot's precious face, and I smashed that butch fish's face in. So to cut a long review short - I think I see why this game is so popular. It 's just difficult to explain how and why without spoilers. Undertale  takes the concept of Breaking the Fourth Wall, turns it into an Existential Crisis, loads it up with guilt trips, gives it a slice of butterscotch-cinnamon pie, and sends it on its way. It does all of this while being a homage to classic rpgs, making the experience both nostalgic and refreshing. (You will also never look at those smiley flower decorations that were popular in the 90's in the same way again.)
I recommend playing blind -if that's possible at this point. The storytelling is most effective when the player lacks foreknowledge. What begins as a seemingly average RPG setup at best very quickly expands into something unique. There are moments which made me burst out laughing, then metaphorically stabbed me in the heart.  The music is good, and the atmosphere is consistent. I spent the final battle on the edge of tears.  The characters are all endearing and well rounded, each with their own lives and concerns that have little to do with you. Throughout the game I genuinely felt like an (albeit not unwelcome) trespasser into somebody else's world.
The battle mechanics are also great fun. Puzzles are challenging without being hair-tearingly frustrating, and the blend of Bullet Hell with RPG is cleverly implemented with each battle having its own unique appearance, execution, and solution.
The game is, surprising as this may seem to some, not without flaws. Here are some of my personal nitpicks:
I understand that Undertale isn't to everyone's taste (and there's a lot of hype aversion going on) but I appeal to everyone to give it a try. It's as much an experience as a game, and while I can see the problems some have with it, for me it was a very worthwhile experience -one I am grateful to have had, and which I will remember for a long, long time.

is different from most survival games you see on Steam today. Most of them consist of nothing but shooting zombies (or, you know, surviving) or basically idiots trying to run up to people and ask them for free stuff.
is nothing like that. The server I played on for this review was a server named Rusty Trombone and a Facepunch Manhattan server. Your gameplay may differ from how I experienced it due to the hardened nature of the regulars that go on these servers, but, that's how the game is supposed to be, I'd assume.
When you start, you start with a rock and a torch. That's it. It's nothing like
where you have a guide right next to you telling you how you can craft things, instead, you have to find blueprints that you can collect by using blueprint fragments that you can find in boxes or barrels that are next to roads or huge landmarks which have a very inflated number of players (presumably armed with M249s and shotguns) fighting to the death for rare blueprints. Seems scary, but this doesn't always happen at all of the landmarks because on most maps that the majority of people play on, there is more than just a power plant for a landmark. Instead, you have a satellite, roads (which are less-traveled and yield less loot for lower risk) and other places that are worth your time checking out if you are a naked.
Refering back to what I said before, most servers have very hardened regulars that don't have time for reasoning and pretty much go by two rules: Shoot now, questions later, and nakeds (players who have just or recently spawned) are always killed on sight. Although some people are moving away from some of these rules and fabricating ones of their own, these are the two I usually see (espesically when joining a group of people that are more than just two people).
Among some of these regulars, you have 10, 20, possibly even 30-player groups that do nothing but raid your hard-earned base. Although I myself are in one of those groups (it consists of 15+ players and the last raid we did, we turned up with incendiary rockets and we blew up a tower!), if you are defenseless, then you might aswell just call it quits. I can recall this one time I was playing on Rusty Trombone, I ran into a group of 10+ players in a circle, all armed with assault rifles. I ask them what they are doing, and I was abruptly shot.
Moving away from the discussion of all the looters of Rust, you can also encounter some good people that are willing to help you at any costs. I can recall one time where I have met one of these people. I was looting a satellite beacon, where I found somebody trying to shoot me with a bow. Since I had the upper advantage because I possessed a pistol, I shot him and moved on. Eventually, there were two people armed with bolt-action rifles running towards satellite. This same person that I have shot ran up to me and told me to get out while I still can, and I ran far. I still know that person to this day, and he is such a nice guy. But, that's not important.
You can also encounter some people who just don't want to fight at all and want to make peace. One time this happened was when I was on a road leading up to a power plant, and I saw somebody travelling on the road. I told them that it is my duty to fight him, and he dropped high quality metal (the highest form of metal used for weapon mods and firearms) and ran away. I still don't know who this person is (I wish I said their name in the TeamSpeak server I was in, but it wasn't the time since they were taking down a helicopter) and I wish I knew to this day. I guess playing
really did pay off, huh?
Not only that, but instead of the usual gamemode that you're thinking of, survival mode, there are also other gamemodes as well. These include, but are not limited to, a battlefield server where you start with weapons, ammo, and modifications to your weapons and the goal is to kill as many people as you can, and servers where there is no PVP at all, the only goal is to just survive. In addition to these community servers, there are also modded servers where... Well, I haven't been on one yet and I could write a whole new review on modded servers in general.
A lot of games have pros and cons, and I think now is the time I should dive right into the cons. One con is that if you are a new player, you don't really gain much help from anybody at all. At least 90% of players who play Rust will always try to shoot a naked they find out of nowhere, for absolutely no reason whatsoever, just to gain the loot (and to harvest the flesh and cloth) they had and to move on. Another disadvantage is that some weapons have rediculous recoil, like the assault rifle, a very good example. If you played
then the recoil shouldn't really be much of a disadvantage, but it's certaintly challenging to use one without any experience prior.
In conclusion,
is a survival game consisting of grinding designed for new players to build their way to the top, and veterans to sharpen their skills in raiding clans and raids in general. It may be an expensive game for some people ($20 is a lot for me, I get at least $100 a year for gaming!) and the learning curve is very steep, but once you get in and you get to know the surroundings and you understand your enviroment, it'll be pretty fun mowing down nakeds with your newly-created assault rifle.
TL;DR: A survival game that relies on your server's (or community's) taboos and what-not for a new experience every time you wake up. Although it's expensive and some weapons have highly uncontrollable recoil, it is still a very great game that I would recommend to anybody looking for a survival game on Steam.

Undertale is one of the beat games i have played my entire life, lately (and by that i mean in the past few years) there haven't been many good story based/RPG games coming out, but undertale combines both of the genres and makes up to a wonderful game.
Not only that it has both an amazing story behind it, but also unique gameplay, unlike any other RPG game, in this game you dont have to kill, or even attack anyone (except 1 enemy wich i will not say the name of cuz' spoilers...), you can attack and spare the enemies, or just do certain things and spare them without even having to fight.
Long story short, this game is more then worth the amount you have to pay for it, and honestly, it should cost more, so if you have the money for it, definetly buy this game.

Note: as of this writing I am actually rage-quitting Undertale for a while because of a particular boss that is giving me a headache.  I tried to go for a pacifist run and some of the late game battles will make you pull your hair out considering I still only have 20hp.  That said,  I have played a significant amount into the game so I would at least like to put my thoughts down on paper though.
First off:  Undertale is not going to change your life, get off the hype mindset.  It has an extremely creative battle system which I would say is the main draw here.  When I say no two battles are the same I mean in extremely literally; EVERYTHING about the battle system warps and changes and alters itself to make the situation more interesting.  I think a genuine argument can be made that Undertale, with its live-action bullet hell inspired battles, has the most progressive and inspired battle system any Jrpg has had in memory.  The game also has a really good, occasionally great soundtrack.
That said I don't love it.  The art is wildly inconsistent in quality (this is coming from a man who LOVES pixel art), the humor is very funny at best and grating/annoying at worst, and the world Tobyfox has dreamed up for this game just doesnt inspire wonder in me.  There is also a variety of minutiae from its insistence on handling item stores differently to the frequently frustrating/long boss battles that just wears on me after a while.  I have been told by every person on the internet that the ending will blow my mind, but for the time being I just am not motiviated to go further.
There is very likely something you will love in Undertale.  I suggest you play it.  Just try to be level headed about it.

For a game that is currently at its Alpha Stage - I find it sensational (9/10).
Initially I found it quite difficult to get started with but after approximately 100 hours of game play - I felt I had a genuine grasp of the game.
The real hook for me was the 'time investment' factor into to tasks and how ruthless/fragile the game can be. A perfect example was when I first started, I spent a solid 2.5 hours gathering timber and stone to prep a base / I then spent 30 minutes crafting boxes / shelves and upgrading my base to stone until I realised I required a Furnace to generate Metal Fragments to create a Sheetmetal Door + Code Lock. Hence I had to venture out and hunt local animals to acquire the animal fat (for low-grade fuel) to produce the furnace and after about 45 minutes of hunting I had attained enough cloth and animal fat for 3 furnaces (of course now I am far more efficient). On my venture back I was attacked from an absolute savage camping in a bush with a pipe shotgun - and then polished off with an arrow to the spine only moments from my front door. To my grief the key to my wooden door was taken by the savage - he then accessed my front door killed me as I awoke from my sleeping bag, then hacked at my sleeping bag before I respawned and cleared my building rights.
I swelled with Rage - but then moments laughed it off "reminding me that it’s just a game."
My cheeky brain then took over from the disgust of what just happened and realised that
the 2.5hours of gathering + 30minutes of setting up + 45minutes hunting and then being assassinated took up 3hrs & 45 minutes of my time just like that.. Giving that ‘filthy wanka’ 3.75hrs of my hard earned effort... i.e. -3.75hours "time investment" for me became +3.75 for the savage stranger - in literally 2 minutes.
**I then punched my dog, my wall and my family portrait in fury**
This forced me to ironically 'adapt' 'evolve' my early-game play style to:
a. Box-out my tool box so no others can access it - even when my base is breached (unless extreme measures are used)
b. Create an airlock to my base (second layer of passage for those who don't know the expression)
c. Bury a small stash in a secret location before doing my errands so that if I am killed before returning - there is no risk of my base being breached (this of course a temporary measure until I acquire my code lock and metal door)
d. Do not annotate on my map the exact location of my base so that I am not traced
etc etc etc.
Long story short this is the best survival game I’ve played - It truly is cruel and rewarding and can be addictive so
don't get too involved.
I do recommend this game for 16years + as it requires a higher degree of logic and "mental prowess" to be successful
as a solo player.
For those who are wondering – l too have become a ‘filthy wanka’.

People who give Rust a bad rating really have no idea what they are talking about nor do they know how to play the game.  I guarantee that if you were to look at thier profil they will have less that 500hrs in the game and most of those hours were spend sitting in their 3x3 house thinking that gathering and crafting were the goals of the game till a team that knows how to play comes and raids them and all they have to fight with are a bow and a rock.  Then they come and cry about it on here giving fauls information about the game because they have 0 clue themselves what the game is really about.  Most alwawys go back to the Legacy days and when we had that one map every server and it was easy to hide in rocks and stuff.  But, those days are over and the new version of rust is not any different then Legacy.  Legacy was a KOS based system and this new version is noooooo different.  Kevlar's owned Legacy, and most of them would take over main recource valleys so no one could gather.  At least now the maps are bigger and you can always find a spot to build and places to gather in peace.  So if you like a game that will have your heart racing and your adrenaline flowing everytime you step outside or start gathering something, this is the game for you my friend.   The advice I give to you is this...Never....and I mean NEVER...Trust anyone 100%.  Rust is a Kill or be Killed game and even the person, who you might of been playing with for days now, and sleep right next too on the cold stone floor of the house you two build together, can be your worse enemy in seconds.  So be ready for that and always watch your own back.

EDIT: Im rewriting this review because orginally, my review was negative because i experienced a horrible glitch, so I wrote the review with an angry mindset and my opinion of the game has also changed in the last few months.
This game is not the best right now (DO YOUR RESEARCH!!!)
1) Bugs are still a prevelent factor when thinking of purchasing this game, (For a full scope and understanding of the bugs and glitches, do a little research before spending your money, there are quite a bit which is why im not going to list any of them in this review)
2) The community for the most part is not friendly in terms of the in-game aspect, most people will kill you on sight if you're on a public server, but there are role playing servers that have strict KOS = ban from server rules in place, which can improve player interaction heavily.
3) The dev team does not do the greatest job of letting players know when updates are going hit. It has mechanics in it that could only exist in an Indie game, which isn't a bad thing - in fact, some of it is very inventive. It went on for a bit too long for me, though, given that part of the idea, as far as I can tell, is that you play through it multiple times for different interations and endings. I'll get around to that someday, perhaps, but I wasn't eager to jump back into it immediately.
I liked the game, but I didn't love the game. I appreciate what it's doing - something a bit different, arguably even subversive.

It's fine. It's just fine. It's worth playing so you can talk about it with other people. I don't get why everybody's fawning over this particular game, though.

I gave it a shot.  But the game just doesn't do anything other games don't do better.
Mainly the game is about bullying.  People and groups of people try to build a base, and other groups come by and raid them.  If you don't have people online at the time of the raid, you base is gone.  And even if you do, if the raiders have more people you base is probably gone.
So building isn't going to be a satisfing aspect for anyone.  That leaves raiding other people's bases.  Which pretty much comes down to how many people you have with you.  The bigger group generally wins.  And as far as the fighting aspect of the game goes, there are much better games out there for team/group fighting.  Basically this game adds nothing other games don't do better, except that simply bigger groups will win.
You can see all this just by logging onto a server for a bit.  You have people taunting that they will destroy so-and-so base... and other people begging not to have their base destroyed.  The people I have talked to that enjoy the game simply like going around raiding, and generally messing up what other people have built.  Some play the modded servers, which are really just like every other first person shooter out there, only with more bugs, less balance, and often completly luck based (battle Royal - whoever finds a weapon in the first crate they search has a massiv advantage over others).
And of course it will be in alpha forever... animals clip rocks, sometimes right into you base and kill you.  But they can't go up steps... it rains inside...

Highly recomend if you're ready to say goodbye to your life :)

I can't sum up everything I think about Undertale in a review. So I'll just put in what really matters...
In a way, Undertale reminds me of Half-Life 2.
No, wait, where are you going? Hear me out, okay?
When I played each, I had not seen much gameplay and did not know too much about the story.
I tried to avoid walkthroughs for both.
And I found that I enjoyed both an incredible amount without knowing why.
Maybe it's the feel of freedom. Or maybe it's the interesting story and characters. (Okay, HL2 had less of those last two.)
Whatever it is, I loved them both.
Anyway. Undertale as an RPG is pretty underwhelming. There are less than ten pieces of armor and weapons respectively (I think), only a total of 95 enemies, excluding special and boss monsters, (I also think) and minimalistic pixel graphics (Which I know for sure) (and which actually help to add character to the game).
But that's the thing... Undertale is more than an RPG.
A couple of things make it prety unique as a game. Firstly, it's the only RPG I know of where you dodge enemy attacks in a bullet-hell environment. Secondly, it gives you the option to spare every enemy you fight.
I'm not going to spoil the story, only say that it and the characters are really great and could probably rival Telltale Games. A bold statement, but then again that's how I like my fonts. (Reference, I guess...?)
Case in point: Buy Undertale instead of watching someone play it if you can, because having the choice to spare something and making that choice is something else. If you can't then watch someone play it. It's not the same, but you still see what the game has to offer.
If you ignore this game without even looking at it...
. . . Y o u ' r e  g o n n a  h a v e  a  b a d  t i m e .
A game where you don't have to kill anyone, and feel guilty when you do.
And still has good jokes.
And, if you play the game and see, still has a better love story than Twilight. (Reference.)

For a game that is currently at its Alpha Stage - I find it sensational (9/10).
Initially I found it quite difficult to get started with but after approximately 100 hours of game play - I felt I had a genuine grasp of the game.
The real hook for me was the 'time investment' factor into to tasks and how ruthless/fragile the game can be. A perfect example was when I first started, I spent a solid 2.5 hours gathering timber and stone to prep a base / I then spent 30 minutes crafting boxes / shelves and upgrading my base to stone until I realised I required a Furnace to generate Metal Fragments to create a Sheetmetal Door + Code Lock. Hence I had to venture out and hunt local animals to acquire the animal fat (for low-grade fuel) to produce the furnace and after about 45 minutes of hunting I had attained enough cloth and animal fat for 3 furnaces (of course now I am far more efficient). On my venture back I was attacked from an absolute savage camping in a bush with a pipe shotgun - and then polished off with an arrow to the spine only moments from my front door. To my grief the key to my wooden door was taken by the savage - he then accessed my front door killed me as I awoke from my sleeping bag, then hacked at my sleeping bag before I respawned and cleared my building rights.
I swelled with Rage - but then moments laughed it off "reminding me that it’s just a game."
My cheeky brain then took over from the disgust of what just happened and realised that
the 2.5hours of gathering + 30minutes of setting up + 45minutes hunting and then being assassinated took up 3hrs & 45 minutes of my time just like that.. Giving that ‘filthy wanka’ 3.75hrs of my hard earned effort... i.e. -3.75hours "time investment" for me became +3.75 for the savage stranger - in literally 2 minutes.
**I then punched my dog, my wall and my family portrait in fury**
This forced me to ironically 'adapt' 'evolve' my early-game play style to:
a. Box-out my tool box so no others can access it - even when my base is breached (unless extreme measures are used)
b. Create an airlock to my base (second layer of passage for those who don't know the expression)
c. Bury a small stash in a secret location before doing my errands so that if I am killed before returning - there is no risk of my base being breached (this of course a temporary measure until I acquire my code lock and metal door)
d. Do not annotate on my map the exact location of my base so that I am not traced
etc etc etc.
Long story short this is the best survival game I’ve played - It truly is cruel and rewarding and can be addictive so
don't get too involved.
I do recommend this game for 16years + as it requires a higher degree of logic and "mental prowess" to be successful
as a solo player.
For those who are wondering – l too have become a ‘filthy wanka’.

If you hadn't guessed it by now Undertale is a game that brilliantly presents you with choices, but unlike most games that try to include choice, it will remember every choice you made, and jusge you for it- changing character dialogue and endings to fit your in game choices. Sure, the graphics aren't great, I will admit, but I feel the game doesn't need flashy graphics and that the classic 8-bit style adds to it's quirkyness.
All the characters are lovable, deeply though and fleshed out characters (If you choose to get to know them, even the antagonist can't be despised for long.), hell even the tiny characters all have their own unique personalites! Somehow, the game manages to be fun and uplifiting but also heavily stresses the idea of consequences and delivers either a heartwarming or somber message, depending which path you choose.
If you choose to fight however, the game quickly turns from adorable and heartwarming to completely isolated, no characters, more ominous music. Blasting through areas make you feel empty and cold-blooded- it feels no need to cushion our the story for the player's enjoyment, as you caused the game to change so drastically. It really feels like a completely different game.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone. With such loveable characters, unique battle system, lovely settings, brilliant soundtrack (Which I too bought after playing the game), for such a small price this game sure delivers.

If you hadn't guessed it by now Undertale is a game that brilliantly presents you with choices, but unlike most games that try to include choice, it will remember every choice you made, and jusge you for it- changing character dialogue and endings to fit your in game choices. Sure, the graphics aren't great, I will admit, but I feel the game doesn't need flashy graphics and that the classic 8-bit style adds to it's quirkyness.
All the characters are lovable, deeply though and fleshed out characters (If you choose to get to know them, even the antagonist can't be despised for long.), hell even the tiny characters all have their own unique personalites! Somehow, the game manages to be fun and uplifiting but also heavily stresses the idea of consequences and delivers either a heartwarming or somber message, depending which path you choose.
If you choose to fight however, the game quickly turns from adorable and heartwarming to completely isolated, no characters, more ominous music. Blasting through areas make you feel empty and cold-blooded- it feels no need to cushion our the story for the player's enjoyment, as you caused the game to change so drastically. It really feels like a completely different game.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone. With such loveable characters, unique battle system, lovely settings, brilliant soundtrack (Which I too bought after playing the game), for such a small price this game sure delivers.

I can't sum up everything I think about Undertale in a review. So I'll just put in what really matters...
In a way, Undertale reminds me of Half-Life 2.
No, wait, where are you going? Hear me out, okay?
When I played each, I had not seen much gameplay and did not know too much about the story.
I tried to avoid walkthroughs for both.
And I found that I enjoyed both an incredible amount without knowing why.
Maybe it's the feel of freedom. Or maybe it's the interesting story and characters. (Okay, HL2 had less of those last two.)
Whatever it is, I loved them both.
Anyway. Undertale as an RPG is pretty underwhelming. There are less than ten pieces of armor and weapons respectively (I think), only a total of 95 enemies, excluding special and boss monsters, (I also think) and minimalistic pixel graphics (Which I know for sure) (and which actually help to add character to the game).
But that's the thing... Undertale is more than an RPG.
A couple of things make it prety unique as a game. Firstly, it's the only RPG I know of where you dodge enemy attacks in a bullet-hell environment. Secondly, it gives you the option to spare every enemy you fight.
I'm not going to spoil the story, only say that it and the characters are really great and could probably rival Telltale Games. A bold statement, but then again that's how I like my fonts. (Reference, I guess...?)
Case in point: Buy Undertale instead of watching someone play it if you can, because having the choice to spare something and making that choice is something else. If you can't then watch someone play it. It's not the same, but you still see what the game has to offer.
If you ignore this game without even looking at it...

A game where you don't have to kill anyone, and feel guilty when you do.
And still has good jokes.

This is a beautiful well thought out game!  It has it's bugs/irritants (what game doesn't), but then again it's a pre-release test version that is constantly being updated & improved.  The stable version I'm currently playing is well worth the price of admission.
The environment is very realistic and the world area is huge and exquisitely detailed; puts to shame even the biggest maps in other games I've played.  The equipment is very detailed and you can craft and repair things as well.  There are some restrictions/limitations on what you can do with things (i.e. give yourself an IV?) but they are minor when compaired to what you CAN do. And while your are exploring and collecting loot, you'll need to keep yourself healthy, well fed/hydrated, and warm.
One thing to consider is that this game is not a quickie "Oh I'll just play for 5 mins" and then move on.  This is unscripted survival and you're in it for the long haul.  Also, because it's online, you'll be up against other players ... some good, some bad ... all trying to do the same thing.  Even better, you can choose to play in a server thats almost empty or be one of 50 duking it out in a small town.

It's a pretty good game.
There's lots of loot, as every gun is randomly generated using a system of different parts and puts them together upon spawning. Although to be honest, they all pretty much do the same thing. The only guns with truly unique properties are legendary guns (orange colored text) and unique guns (i think blue text?) That's besides the point though.
The gameplay is really solid, and your playstyle is determined by the character you use and which part of the skill tree you invest in. Each character has three different branches in their skill tree, each of which caters to a different kind of playstyle. For example, Zer0 has a melee focused branch. Each character also has a unique action skill, which is activated with F and can be used for a certain time and then you have to wait for the skill to recharge before you can use it again. The charge time can be reduced with certain skills or items that affect your character.
The story is very good as well, you're basically chasing around this guy in a mask for revenge. All the characters from the first Borderlands appear in the storyline as important characters that help you along the way. The story gets pretty good, especially near the end too. There's also a lot if hilarious moments in the story as well. The sidequests are pretty good as well, and usually have their own story unrelated to the main questline.
The graphics have a very unique style, it's really nice. Everything looks really good, and to be honest I don't think this isn't even a very graphicallly intensive game as I can run it on high settings even though I only have an average video card. The music is pretty neat as well.
Overall, I'd score this game around the neighborhood of 8-9/10.
Also, if you bought the first borderlands, and didn't like it, I'd give this one a try. It's basically the first borderlands, just done the right way.

I gave it a shot.  But the game just doesn't do anything other games don't do better.
Mainly the game is about bullying.  People and groups of people try to build a base, and other groups come by and raid them.  If you don't have people online at the time of the raid, you base is gone.  And even if you do, if the raiders have more people you base is probably gone.
So building isn't going to be a satisfing aspect for anyone.  That leaves raiding other people's bases.  Which pretty much comes down to how many people you have with you.  The bigger group generally wins.  And as far as the fighting aspect of the game goes, there are much better games out there for team/group fighting.  Basically this game adds nothing other games don't do better, except that simply bigger groups will win.
You can see all this just by logging onto a server for a bit.  You have people taunting that they will destroy so-and-so base... and other people begging not to have their base destroyed.  The people I have talked to that enjoy the game simply like going around raiding, and generally messing up what other people have built.  Some play the modded servers, which are really just like every other first person shooter out there, only with more bugs, less balance, and often completly luck based (battle Royal - whoever finds a weapon in the first crate they search has a massiv advantage over others).
And of course it will be in alpha forever... animals clip rocks, sometimes right into you base and kill you.  But they can't go up steps... it rains inside...

Undertale became an instant cult-classic, almost as soon as it was released, and for a good reason. Before Undertale, I had never enjoyed any story based game, or turn based game I had ever played. I've allways cared much more about the gameplay, and aesthetics of a game than the storyline, or characters, but Undertale really can't be compared to any other game. Not only does Undertale have one of the most compelling and deep storylines of any RPG, but it takes classic RPG turn based gameplay in a very unique direction, with engaging bullet hell mechanics, and story driven encounters. The game challenges the very most fundamental elements of RPG games, with a complete lack of boring or repetitive stuff like grinding. As Dunkey says, "Undertale says more in 5 hours of gameplay than most do in 70". Undertale brings together the perfect combination of a fantastic soundtrack, and a genuine and engaging storyline. Undertale is the only game I honestly believe anyone can enjoy, regardless of preferences in game genre.
I'm a hard to please gamer and this game is phenomenal. I would recommend it to anyone and have. Seriously, you wont be disappointed.

I've never felt so conflicted about a game. I love what it tries to do, but hate how it does it. Addicting and compelling loot-motivated gameplay, RPG leveling-up, creative weaponry, and wonderful worlds of creative and extremely effective dialogue with references of memes to retro gaming, the first game to do such of what I can recall. But then, once the game loses that honeymoon luster, the game derails and becomes a heartless loot quest with bullet-sponges in the way, but your friends to liven the experience. A game that can't stand alone without the help of being enjoyed with friends comes as a weakness in design. I could have fun with my friends doing things none of us enjoy solely based on the fact we're suffering together. I love this game, one I might have played too much, but it could do so much more to take away its artificial difficulty and push beyond the comfort zone it created for itself.

Difficulty scaling in co-op can make this game incredibly bullet-spongey, so if the humour gels with you, don't be afraid to play solo. You might actually complete it instead waiting for the stars to align and the four of you, none of whom want to be left behind, have time to play together. You'll actually be able to play the DLC as well.

As of this writing, I don't recommend this game. Not because of the community, not because of the graphics or sound, not because of the features.
The only reason I don't recommend this game is because the developers took the game from a
(i.e. Rust Classic) to a

I have  a number of interesting stories and enjoyable experiences stemming from Rust Classic. It had a certain magic to it. At the time, no one really understood the game too much and the game wasn't so focused on FPS. With threats ranging from zombies, wildlife, radiation, and hunger, you could work with people and create a group of players all struggling to survive. When I played, I tended to be more diplomatic - and you could do that in Rust Classic. See what each player's about, build "alliances" with certain people, while defending said alliances when necessary. At one point, my house was a meeting spot for a good part of the community I played on. People could go to my place to make trades and meet up, knowing they wouldn't be shot at unless they came across the wrong way. At one point the community we created was so tight, that when a band of raiders started attacking people's homes, a domino effect occurred. An all-out war across the server sprung up. Some people died and lost everything, however the bandits were hit hard and lost their explosives. It easily ranked as one of my tensest and most enjoyable times while playing a video game.
The gameplay now doesn't seem to get like that anymore. It could just be how I'm playing nowadays, but my experience with the game has become solitary due to the nature of the current state of the game.
Rust isn't really a bad game, but I can't recommend it. Over three years of the development and it seems to be running in place. They add graphical improvements and update regularly. I've played this game when it first came out and play still today... My experience has largely stayed the same. There's no venturing into new territory for this game. Because they don't want to try something new within Rust and stick with improving features already present, it inadvertently shaped the game from a survival sandbox to a survival FPS.
My review may have come across a little harsh, especially since it's still in Early Access - don't get me wrong, it's a good game in its own right. My fear is that it's becoming stale over the course of its development, and may end up becoming a game stuck in Early Access because of a lack of direction. I'll make changes to my review later in the future.

No description does this game justice. I've already spent 30 minutes on this review only to erase everything and start over several times now.
But hey, think of it like this:
Take a dash of the Yume Nikki/Earthbound gameplay, with a bit of Cave Story artstyle, add a bit of classic JRPG battles (but ones where you can be friends with everyone instead of killing them, if you so choose). Then imagine the story unfolding in different ways depending on if you're good or bad, with critical plot points to be found in the details of the game that make you realize how wonderfully crafted it all is. The game is littered with all these small hints that are left to the fans to speculate about their meaning, kind of how some parts of the Dark Souls series is intentionally left open to interpretation. These details will change as you do new playthroughs of the game, giving you extra information regarding all the background story to the game.
Undertale has made me feel kind of how it would be if you were in a Hayao Miyazaki movie like Spirited Away, but where the story can take a very, very dark turn if you are so inclined. Like other reviewers have already said, this is more of "an experience" than a game. It certainly has an active gameplay component, but it's basically a Yume Nikki style visual novel with moral choices for each battle. The battles themselves are usually kind of lackluster if you're used to more intense gameplay, but you don't really have to any grinding if you're going through a pacifist run. In genocide however it's a different story so if you chose to kill everyone: it will take a bit of extra time and it can get tedious.
Overall I would recommend everyone to at least give the demo for this a try. This is a game that has storytelling at it's core. Just make sure to ignore the community. I haven't really had a problem with the community myself, but I guess when people are deeply affectionate towards something that really stirred their emotions, they can have a harder time recognizing other people might not feel the same way.
Summary: I really liked this title and will remember it forever. If you do decide to get this, play it however you want but I recommend it this way: spare everyone in the game, explore the world and talk to the characters, become friends with the main characters and let the story unfold to the natural end. Then if you want more, there is more. This is the point where you might want to look up a wiki or talk to a friend who has played the game.
