I really loved this game when I first purchased it, but until the game leaves early access, it is dead to me. When I first bought this game back in 2015, updates were dropping roughly every 1 or 2 months. However, at one point, the updates just stopped coming. Not a single update came for HALF A YEAR. Fast forward to 2017 and the updates that have been released have not really moved this game forward by much. Plenty of bugs still exist since when I first played this game in 2015. Regarding the actual gameplay, if you are doing nothing but looking for loot, 95% of the game is searching for valuable gear, and the other 5% is player interaction once every two hours. Most often it is someone with a weapon, and if they kill you then you get sent back to looking for more gear to go kill some people.
Here are some pros and cons for nitty bitty details.
Pros:
-Friendly player interactions are pretty funny to experience.
-Combat can induce an adrenaline rush.
-Lots of areas to go to and loot (excluding high level gear).
-Items slowly wear over time, forcing you to search for more loot every now and then.
Cons:
-Player encounters rarely occur when you venture away from the coast, especially FRIENDLY encounters.
-Despite the new game engine, game still lags with computers over the recommended specs.
-Infected are more of an annoyance than an actual threat.
-Oftentimes all you need to do to get rid of an infected is to simply run away from it until it runs out of energy.
-Your character gets dehydrated/hungry way too quickly.
-The best loot is all placed in the corner of the map so that the game forces players in land, instead of being more random. If you spawn on the coast, it can take an hour just to get there, and unless you join an empty server you will only find items other players left behind.
-The updates never fix problems in DayZ that need to be addressed, such as an item not being moveable into your inventory, black faceless heads, and being able to randomly die in a police station when walking down the stairs.
In my opinion, don't buy this game until 1) the game's problems are resolved and the game makes a full release, or 2) if the game becomes a F2P (lets be fair these outcomes won't ever happen with the rate updates are being released).

Look, I'm not a great gamer or a great writer, and I've never written a review before, but I feel like I need to say something, anything about this wonderful game.
Buy it. Even if you're on the fence, just get it. The humor is worth it alone, not to mention the absolutely stellar soundtrack and amazing, well fleshed-out characters. I know that the fandom sometimes pushes people away from this game because of their craziness, but this game is worth way more than $10. Honestly, I would pay good money to have my memory wiped so I could play it again.
Although it makes me sad that I can never bring myself to load up this game again after finishing it, I'm so happy that I got to meet such wonderful characters. Each one of them reminded me of a part of myself, and I had so much personal resonance with each character that I wish I could meet them in real life. Like most of the fandom, I guess, heh.
Even though this game is not impressive looking at first glance, you can tell that a lot of love went into every detail of its crafting, from the level design to the minor enemies, and so on. I'd like to say that I have just as much love for this game as its creator. Mr. Fox really poured his soul into this game, and I appreciate that so much.
So, yeah. And please, don't kill, and don't be killed. Okay?

I've never felt so conflicted about a game. I love what it tries to do, but hate how it does it. Addicting and compelling loot-motivated gameplay, RPG leveling-up, creative weaponry, and wonderful worlds of creative and extremely effective dialogue with references of memes to retro gaming, the first game to do such of what I can recall. But then, once the game loses that honeymoon luster, the game derails and becomes a heartless loot quest with bullet-sponges in the way, but your friends to liven the experience. A game that can't stand alone without the help of being enjoyed with friends comes as a weakness in design. I could have fun with my friends doing things none of us enjoy solely based on the fact we're suffering together. I love this game, one I might have played too much, but it could do so much more to take away its artificial difficulty and push beyond the comfort zone it created for itself.

Difficulty scaling in co-op can make this game incredibly bullet-spongey, so if the humour gels with you, don't be afraid to play solo. You might actually complete it instead waiting for the stars to align and the four of you, none of whom want to be left behind, have time to play together. You'll actually be able to play the DLC as well.

Before I start my more in depth review, let me say to anyone reading this I know if you loved Borderlands you need to play this game, if you liked Borderlands, you need to buy this game.  Now if you really did not like or enjoy Borderlands you prob will not like this game, I would say go look at some game play videos and judge it yourself.  Now on to my review :)
This game is bigger, badder, better, and in a shock to me fleshes out each hero from the original game into someone with a backstory, and depth to each one.  I felt closer not only to the 4 new vault hunters (5 if you count the mechromancer class released at launch as a .99 DLC), as well.  Borderlands 2 made me laugh out loud at least 2 to 3 times an hour.  The writing in this game is damn funny, totally outrageous, and totally Pandora's own Borderlands esque.  The introduction of some new faces and people, as well as the Doc, Moxi, Scooter, and Marcus all will make a Borderlands fan smile.  An then there is Jack.... one of the best villians in a game I have seen in a long long time. With some clever put down's, and a character by the end you seriously start to dislike and dare I say hate...
However most people do not play these types of game's (myself aside) for the story.  They play it for the loot fest, loot porn, frenzy, fast, fun, addictive, 4 player ,drop in, drop out, loot ♥♥♥♥♥ in all of us.  An let me say again, as with every aspect of Borderlands 2 this game again goes FAR BEYOND the original.  From types of guns, to unique looks, to even a few made as quest rewards that you simply want to hang on too.  Add in to that numerous easter eggs and homage to nerd and geek favorites like Minecraft, Batman, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, and thats just a few of the over the top omfg did you see that easter Eggs.
Overall I play games for Story, Immersion, Gameplay, and Fun.  An this game hit on many of the right notes for me. I will say the menu for both skills and gun compare is a pain, and something I am sure Gearbox will hear from fans needs to improve for Borderlands 3.  I also would like to see more dun with car combat, perhaps new modes, perks, or a co op campaign centered around it.  Having said all that I smiled every moment I played this game.  It made me know the original 4 members in a real in depth way, gives you a great great villian to loathe, and adds to what is becoming quickly my favorite co op shooter to date.  If you have some friends to play with this will be a fun ride.  They have already released 4 new DLC packs for this game. Putting the time invested easily at 40 to 50 hours and that is just counting one play through, as in the orginal the game truly starts after the first play through.  As in the second play through different loot is accessable and new mobs are in the lands as well.
Lastly, I will say Jack aside, and the true warmpth and feelings I have now for the original vault hunters, and the new four this game gives us my two stand out additons were both Sir Hammerlock.  A new British man of mystery type who is interested in all mobs of pandora andhas his own DLC.  An Tina.... Tiny Tina was spell binding, laugh out loud, she just said WHAT.....  I was thrilled to hear she is a key part of either the 2nd or 3rd DLC pack, and the 4th centers around her almost entirely.
In closing this is one of the best co op drop in drop out, loot fest games of all time, and in time will rank right up there with Diablo 2 and others of it's kind.  While people that never played the first can still enjoy Borderlands 2, they will not get the numerous in game refrences to past quests an places, nor understand the "hero's" of this game as we who played the original.  An while the single player game is fun, this is made and built to play with friends, as that is 50% of the fun.  As for me I will be starting the DLC for this game in a month or two and plan on putting a few hundred hours into this game as I still have friends I want to layand share these memories, and characters with.

I have  a number of interesting stories and enjoyable experiences stemming from Rust Classic. It had a certain magic to it. At the time, no one really understood the game too much and the game wasn't so focused on FPS. With threats ranging from zombies, wildlife, radiation, and hunger, you could work with people and create a group of players all struggling to survive. When I played, I tended to be more diplomatic - and you could do that in Rust Classic. See what each player's about, build "alliances" with certain people, while defending said alliances when necessary. At one point, my house was a meeting spot for a good part of the community I played on. People could go to my place to make trades and meet up, knowing they wouldn't be shot at unless they came across the wrong way. At one point the community we created was so tight, that when a band of raiders started attacking people's homes, a domino effect occurred. An all-out war across the server sprung up. Some people died and lost everything, however the bandits were hit hard and lost their explosives. It easily ranked as one of my tensest and most enjoyable times while playing a video game.
The gameplay now doesn't seem to get like that anymore. It could just be how I'm playing nowadays, but my experience with the game has become solitary due to the nature of the current state of the game.
Rust isn't really a bad game, but I can't recommend it. Over three years of the development and it seems to be running in place. They add graphical improvements and update regularly. I've played this game when it first came out and play still today... My experience has largely stayed the same. There's no venturing into new territory for this game. Because they don't want to try something new within Rust and stick with improving features already present, it inadvertently shaped the game from a survival sandbox to a survival FPS.
My review may have come across a little harsh, especially since it's still in Early Access - don't get me wrong, it's a good game in its own right. My fear is that it's becoming stale over the course of its development, and may end up becoming a game stuck in Early Access because of a lack of direction. I'll make changes to my review later in the future.

The games PVP is one of the best designs in the market currently, base raiding and defending is extremely fun and entertaining. The biggest problem in Rust currently is the amount of time it takes. Sometimes it feels like you have to be online 24/7 and can't even go to sleep in fear of getting offline raided. There is no such thing a unraidable base, you just have to have enought brains and C4 (or after the updates rockets, their splash damage is something that one might call ridiculous).

I've never felt so conflicted about a game. I love what it tries to do, but hate how it does it. Addicting and compelling loot-motivated gameplay, RPG leveling-up, creative weaponry, and wonderful worlds of creative and extremely effective dialogue with references of memes to retro gaming, the first game to do such of what I can recall. But then, once the game loses that honeymoon luster, the game derails and becomes a heartless loot quest with bullet-sponges in the way, but your friends to liven the experience. A game that can't stand alone without the help of being enjoyed with friends comes as a weakness in design. I could have fun with my friends doing things none of us enjoy solely based on the fact we're suffering together. I love this game, one I might have played too much, but it could do so much more to take away its artificial difficulty and push beyond the comfort zone it created for itself.

Difficulty scaling in co-op can make this game incredibly bullet-spongey, so if the humour gels with you, don't be afraid to play solo. You might actually complete it instead waiting for the stars to align and the four of you, none of whom want to be left behind, have time to play together. You'll actually be able to play the DLC as well.

This isn't an easy game to review. Whether Undertale impacts you deeply in a good or bad way (or anywhere in-between) is entirely dependent on your own experience.
Think for a moment about hypothetically attending a theatre to watch a play. You become a member of the audience. How the audience experiences and percieves a play is dependent on how they suspend their disbelief. For instance, one member of the audience may have a really good time while others feel like it was a waste of money on account that they simply felt "it wasn't realistic". That's just a single example.
Much of your experience with Undertale will be shaped in the same manner. This is partially due to the retro-esque style of graphics it utilizes. It's easy to dislike the game based off its appearance--which would be a valid opinion on it's own. Yet, I feel like this would be a subjective approach. I rarely see people consider the options that the creator(s) of any game had based off the systems they used to create it (this isn't even counting finance) into their opinion. Undertale was made in "Game Maker Studio". For those who don't know, Game Maker Studio is one of the most easily-accessible and "low-end" systems you could use to create a game. With that perspective in mind, much of what Undertale provides can easily become impressive.
However, perhaps an even larger portion of the experience provided by Undertale is that it incorporates the use of frequent "4th-wall breaking" and that it "(does something else I can't quite mention)". There's not much more I can say on that matter without spoiling the experience of the game...
And that's exactly why Undertale is so difficult to review. There's simply not much I can say about the game that won't spoil some sort of aspect it contains. And, strangely or brilliantly enough, this is also the exact reason why I find it so interesting.
I will say this, however: If you're looking for a game with gameplay that will leave your jaw on the floor, Undertale isn't the game for you. If you play Undertale with this intention, you'll most likely grow bored--which hinders your ability to become immersed by affecting your ability to suspend disbelief. I sometimes feel like many fans of Undertale overhype its gameplay--which would be misleading, to say the least.
If you, on the otherhand, end up enjoying its gameplay--that's great! It's gameplay is constructed this way on purpose to enhance the other aspects of the game. The gameplay is not supposed to obstruct the rest of the game--it's simple so that it can compliment the rest of the game. Why? Well, again, there's not much else I could say on the matter. It's important for the story that Undertale tells.
Yet, Undertale is a "fragile" game. This is to say that your very experience of it can EASILY become corrupted or altered based on your expectations. Unfortunately, the fervor of many fans seems to have no end. I have seen quite a few people enjoy the game less than they could have due to how much some fans have egged them on about it.
I speak with experience. I immensly enjoyed this game, even though my initial experience was vicarious by watching other people play it. That being said, I do think it would have had an even larger impact on me if I had played it myself first. This is why I highly recommend playing this game completely blind (or at least as blind as possible) to get as much of the experience it provides as possible.
What else could I say...
Oh yes! The soundtrack is quite nice.
The writing and characters are quite nice, too. I relate the writing of Undertale to the quality of writing from Earthbound and its characters to the quality of characters in Paper Mario: The Thousand Year Door. If you're a fan of either of those games, that's most likely good news for you.
What else...
Oh! Before I forget, I have one piece of advice for anyone who plans on playing Undertale:
You might want to pay close attention to the possibilites alluded by the context of its various dialogue. This game is much more than what it initially leads itself into being...

I have  a number of interesting stories and enjoyable experiences stemming from Rust Classic. It had a certain magic to it. At the time, no one really understood the game too much and the game wasn't so focused on FPS. With threats ranging from zombies, wildlife, radiation, and hunger, you could work with people and create a group of players all struggling to survive. When I played, I tended to be more diplomatic - and you could do that in Rust Classic. See what each player's about, build "alliances" with certain people, while defending said alliances when necessary. At one point, my house was a meeting spot for a good part of the community I played on. People could go to my place to make trades and meet up, knowing they wouldn't be shot at unless they came across the wrong way. At one point the community we created was so tight, that when a band of raiders started attacking people's homes, a domino effect occurred. An all-out war across the server sprung up. Some people died and lost everything, however the bandits were hit hard and lost their explosives. It easily ranked as one of my tensest and most enjoyable times while playing a video game.
The gameplay now doesn't seem to get like that anymore. It could just be how I'm playing nowadays, but my experience with the game has become solitary due to the nature of the current state of the game.
Rust isn't really a bad game, but I can't recommend it. Over three years of the development and it seems to be running in place. They add graphical improvements and update regularly. I've played this game when it first came out and play still today... My experience has largely stayed the same. There's no venturing into new territory for this game. Because they don't want to try something new within Rust and stick with improving features already present, it inadvertently shaped the game from a survival sandbox to a survival FPS.
My review may have come across a little harsh, especially since it's still in Early Access - don't get me wrong, it's a good game in its own right. My fear is that it's becoming stale over the course of its development, and may end up becoming a game stuck in Early Access because of a lack of direction. I'll make changes to my review later in the future.

This game... This game is just so fantastic. Let's start at the beginning- I got Undertale because I was curious about all of the hype surrounding it. The first hour or so I played it, I was disappointed. The puzzles weren't difficult and the fight system confused me. After playing for another couple of hours I started to get attached to the characters and soon could not stop playing and jamming out the the wonderful music that Undertale had to offer. I now see what all the hype was about and it is completely justified. When you play Undertale, it's less like playing a game and more like experiencing a work of art. You will truly remember every action that you do. If you are even thinking about getting this game, get it. You will not regret it one bit. But that is just my 2G...

Undertale is by no means a perfect game...but it has provided me far more entertainment and downright FUN than most other games I've played recently. It beats out numerous AAA titles in terms of story and originality. You really come to care about the NPCs in this game (my personal favorite is the GREAT PAPYRUS!) which cannot be said as often as one would wish. In fact, it is a game that, though I love it so much, I cannot bring myself to play again lest I destroy the happy ending everyone has achieved.
Positives:
-Story, while not complicated, is engaging
-The NPCs are alive with personality
-The game 'breaks the rules' of typical rpgs in ways that I will not spoil but find absolutely delightful.
Negatves:
-The puzzles really aren't all that impressive (A small complaint)
-Defeating some bosses takes some lateral thinking that requires one to bend one's mind into unusual shapes.
-Sometimes, the jokes can get a bit stretched. (But not often)
All in all, I'd still rate this game 10/10. It is everything I could have expected and more from a title of this price.

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

This review concentrates on the original Rust, which was a great game.
(I am not so impressed with the new Rust.)
The original Rust had a good minimalist feel about it.
Farm materials, build a base, and fight your enemies.
When you had a lot to lose (carrying a huge load of materials), it added an element of fear of loss to any engagement you participated in.
If you were gathering materials, you really didn't want to get into a fight and lose the lot.
It would be late at night in a forest, you couldn't see if an enemy was behind a tree nearby, you were trying to get a massive load of material back to base, had your gun out ready for a fight, and your heart would be pumping.
Good times.
Had great fun building massive bases.
Most servers I played on had set their decay rates at about a week, which was ok. So long as you opened a door in your base once a week, the base didn't decay.
Some servers had set very high decay rates, which meant you had to log in every day just to maintain your base - which was ridiculous (most people have to go to work or school, so having to log on to Rust every day was a bit much).
Unfortunately, when your Rust server updated its version of the game, it would mean a complete server wipe, whereby every base would be wiped off the map, and you had to start all over again. That was always pretty hard to take, especially when you had built a huge base, defended it against various enemy attacks, kept all your resources safe, only to lose it all due to a server wipe.
There were quite a few hackers around on the old Rust. Apparently, this was due to the game being based client-side, rather than server-side, so hackers could just change the code on their computer.
But despite that, it was a great game.
The new Rust looks more cartoonish, has less scope to build big bases, and is more fiddly with opening doors, etc.
For me, the new Rust is a bit ho-hum.
Give it a go if you want to - plenty of people seem to like it.
But if they ever brought back the old Rust, with the game being based server-side, count me in!

.................................................................................................................................................
CONS:
Community can be toxic and having nothing other than PvP and raiding to do has made it even worse.
PvE, AI, virtually non-existent and causes frustration with community who hold it in higher priority than developers.
Update results vary, sometimes content is lost and changed without explanation.
Performance is an issue for many users even with decent PC's (personally Rust performs well for me)
Game is well into development, PvE and vision of game is still not fully understood or explained; the game still appears to be very open ended fairly late into development.
"Clones" and other games are catch up and passing Rust content wise are hitting the market.
Legacy players disappointment and expectations vs. new or current players wants cause a rift in community.
No vehicles (3 years of discussion of them coming someday Legacy-Current)
Developers tend to try to ignore what the community wants (Garry saying they need to ignore what people ask for and do whats 'right', Devblog comments turned off, lack of direct communication on regular basis with developers on reddit and other means)
Game profits from presales have not all been used to expand Rust development or expedite it.
Game is still very hard for casual enjoyment - servers wipe very frequently losing progress and large clans still dominate raiding and servers.
No character progression other than blueprints which also get wiped, procedural maps even wipe away any advantage veterans players may have knowledge wise over map and landmarks.
Game focuses too much on PvP and gun play yet the gunplay is not as good as most shooters out there available - the game needs PvE and other things to focus on challenge wise to make the gunplay not the 'be all' of the game.

Play it by yourself, with very little info about it and this game will quickly become one of the most interesting experiencies you will ever have. This game makes important questions about its genre and about the medium.
Be mindful about what you're doing once you actually get the game, though. You're playing the game. You're not joining a phenomenon nor checking what everyone's talking about to give the "final and most important opinion about this game ever". No, dude, you're playing a piece of art. Enjoy it.

[no spoilers, don't worry]
Pros:
- The characters are absolutely fantastic. They all have their own backstories, unique personalities, and I'd be suprised if anybody didn't get attached to at least one of them.

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

With over 200 hundred hours played, I can say I definitely have mixed feelings about this game. I'll go through some pros and cons for DayZ Standalone in the summer of 2015.
Pros:
- The developers are really starting to work on connectivity. (no or less rubberbanding, little to no desync, etc.)
- The heart racing battles against other players whether you are alone or with your friends. There's really nothing else like it.
- There are constant updates being put out for the game, increasing the overall quality of the game.
- A vehicle has actually been introduced (even though it sucks.)
- More customization options than ever before. There are really so many combinations of camos, gear, weapons, etc. Because so many new items are being implemented in each update.
- Overall the game has come a long way, even though it's still "early access alpha".
Cons:
- There's little to no reason to actually interact with other people other than to take their things. (Unless you're both nice people which is very rare)
- "Early Access Alpha"
- Persistence is still a problem.
- Some items do not spawn even though it says they do :/.
- There haven't been any signs of base-building or saving something to a server.
- Overall the game could be much further through development than it currently is.
Final Verdict:
I think DayZ has a long way to go before really becoming a great game. Right now it is a pretty good and fun game in which you could use to throw away some hours while sitting at your pc. Do I think the game should go to console? Absolutely not. But, I still love DayZ and I have to say that you should really give this game a shot if youre thinking about it. I've met a bunch of my friends through the game and had so many good times and all of it was worth losing my hard earned loot over and over and over again.
Sidenote - Sorry, I'm really bad at writing official review, but I wanted to share my opinion on DayZ. I hope you found this helpful.

Rust isn't very good in making you feel like you're trying to survive. Everytime you spawn into a world, everyone has already made a huge city around the spawn, making the world feel less like a huge expanse of land that needs to be explored and more like a city with an outer wall that you go an look at for some reason. You can find basic materials like wood and stone laid out on the ground, presumably the excess from the owner of the towering castle in front of you. And to top it all off, the game feels more like an fps with the end game being able to craft or find a gun and mess with other people. This is also apparent in the newly adapted Battle Royal mode, which it totes it borrowed from Arma 3 on every official server screen. The problem with it being an fps, is it's not even a good fps. Controls feel clunky in a fire fight and even worse when trying to fight someone in melee range. One time, I had a guy actually kill me at melee range and he didn't even make a swinging animation.
The game looks nice, but is poorly optimized. My rig is able to handle most games on high pretty fine, but chugs like a used car powered by soda when I try to get anywhere close to it. And I don't know if it's me, but it feels like there's this smeared-on white type filter over the screen. It makes everything seem brighter than it is and it's kind of annoying.
I think the icing on this dirt cake is this game has been in alpha for about 2 years. They had revamped the game once, at one point calling it Rust Experimental. The move was nice, making the game look more refined and even changing the island. The game got a little better, but personally not enough. Now the devs are selling people's creations as store items. I'm not big fan of this from games who aren't even out yet. Especially when some of them get as pricey as $20. Fine as long as you want to support the devs, but it seems this game doens't have a release date in sight.
There are better survival games on Steam. There are better fps games on Steam as well. This game isn't quite steer clear. Many people like it, so there's a possiblility you might too. However, if you were to ask me, I cannot reccomend this game.

Worst game ever. The story is - back in 2012 when Dayz mod launched it literally exploded, everyone was so hyped and even if it was bugged, every patch seemed to fix some issues. The dev team was much bigger, everything was going smoothly until Hall annoucned he's going to create standalone. Early access Dayz Standalone. Even though the mod was doing great, they abandoned it (gave back to community) and focused on their released pile of crap. Hyped people purchased SA and kept playing it, because it was newer. The mod kept going on with updates, but player's pool drastically decreased. Meanwhile we're currently in 2015 and SA barely moved and I mean it. The game even lacks key aspects like zombies, but devs keep focusing on adding new jackets. In the same time Mod got improved tremendously. There is everything more, better, smoother, but on the older engine, that's it. If you're looking for real survival challenge with zombies, cars, guns and more for no price and wish to experience Dayz in much better shape I highly recommend Dayz Mod (Vanilla). There are still some good servers.

This game started off as a magnificient survival game set up in a sombre atmosphere, with a unique art style, a huge map with tons of details, a building system like no other we've ever dreamt of, an unbelievably caring and cooperative community and lots of adrenaline rushes caused by strangers, zombies, and rad animals. In short, it was about primitive men—some better geared than others—versus nature, making friends and enemies along the way.
At some point Rust was rebooted from scratch. That made a lot of sense back then because the amazing concept behind the game was being hidden by its modest technical level, and the messy code in Good Ol' Rust supposedly hampered developers’ progress to an ill extent. Getting more features and a better game seemed optimal. This new thing was labeled Rust Experimental.
Now, two years later, Rust Experimental is simply known as Rust. A lot has changed since the beginning of said massive revamp. I'll give you one thing: it looks fantastic. It totally does.
The negative side? The game has totally turned from a survival to an FPS. The community is now crowded with players who are intellectually uncurious at large: they are not interested in interacting, they will never ask for food nor will they try to convince you about letting them in to spend the night, and they will not cooperate in any way. If any of the previous ever happens to you, it will be to kill you and to raid your house. Most of the times they will refrain from using these old tricks and just shoot on sight with an AK-47, rocket launcher, flamethrower, or sniper rifle with a 4x-zoom scope if they are able to. Everyday they stay late at night with one goal in mind: use C4 to raid as many houses as possible right when everyone's logged off.
People are simply not open to expanding their friend circle, and so the hilarious and creepy dialogues and situations that made Rust the best game I've ever played they're all gone. The developers' ill emphasis on military weapons has taken this too far away, to the point that I've found myself playing DayZ trying to recover some of this experience while still visiting Rust from time to time to check on the progress of users' devastating mindset and the building system, which I still enjoy quite a bit.
Some other bad bits that are in no way nearly as defining as the ones above: developers are poorly organised and seem to tackle issues randomly instead of as a team, developers' progress is tedious to follow mostly because of their lack of focus, realism and priorities (although they manage to pull some decent weekly devlogs), performance is poor and seems to be slowly getting worse, the building system hasn't received barely any update in a year (bugs are virtually the same ones as back then), developers' only goal in life is adding modern weapons to the point that even this new FPS-addicted hostile community is feeling wrong about it, procedurally generated maps are losing features for no apparent reason (amazing desert and snow biomes, forests and canyons suddenly just flew away), caves have never worked properly and old Rust's rock formations which allowed players to hide, build shelters where they'd never in a hundred years be found simply don't exist anymore. Animals have not worked at all for two whole years and they want to have it fixed by June (!).
Now let me tell you a story. Facepunch didn't like the zombie fashion, they took them out of the game, put rad animals instead and took them out again when moving to the new Rust. After that, they spent years deliberating about adding NPC hostiles (there are none), doing intellectual work on the topic, coming up with amazing new beings that would terrify survivors, thinking of refined concepts that would shatter the world as we know it. After all that effort on a paramount subject, the only NPC threat now in the game is... guess what. A cannibal tribe? An ancestral monster? A wizard in a tower? I cannot say enough good things about this game. There are many many more eloquent reviews out there than this one, so if you're undecided about this game, please read them. However I will try to sum up my feelings about Undertale:
This game is charming; visually, in the play style, the feel of the world, the characters.... Every single character feels alive, like they have so much more backstory than you could ever find out. The general play style is cute and funny, the combat is engaging and with it's own mini puzzles unique to each enemy. You can be friends with all the bosses (under the right conditions) who are complex, likeable (nay, adorable) and each with their own distinct "voice" in terms of writing style. You can hug them, date them, try to give them good advice... Or not, if you don't feel like it.
Your choices actually make a difference. Not just the obvious ones. Everything you do, every kill, every death, every choice, is remembered. The story changes dramatically based on what you do or don't do, and resetting may not have the effect you hope for. It makes everything feel so much more real. Especially when the combat screen says something like "You consider telling this character you saw them die. But that's creepy." That stuck with me.
The feels. Near everything I did in this game felt like a gut-wrenching choice that would haunt me. And it has, this game is literally all I can think or talk about and I haven't played anything else since the first time I launched it.
This game is so detailed and well thought out, full of secrets, references and squee. The puzzles, while not unduly challenging, are clever. But don't think this game isn't hard; at times it got so hard (at least on first playthrough) I thought I'd be stuck there forever. There's one part where the game TELLS you you'll be stuck there forever. This game breaks the fourth wall in a way that is self conscious without unnecessary navel-gazing and everything seems, in a tangential way at least, to lead to the main point of the story. The moral, if you will. It's a bit of a spoiler so I won't lay it out.
The sound design is fantastic. The only music in the game that I ever grew tired of hearing (and I heard some of it A LOT) was the "Game Over" music, but even that is bright and sweet, perfect to recharge your DETERMINATION. The bosses' theme tunes are memorable and feel fitting to the characters.
EDIT: Some of the music can feel a little grating after playing more than 50 hours, my remedy to this is to put on a Slipknot playlist on youtube. I was surprised how well it worked.
The story. Oh my gOODNESS THE PLOT TWISTS. Plucked all my heartstrings.
Honestly, the only other coherent thing I can say about Undertale is: BUY THIS GAME.

I highly enjoy this game because of it's great dev team and astounding progression and different ways to go about said progression.
You start out completely naked with nothing else but a rock and a torch. Its from this point right here, how you decide to progress.
You can progress by gathering materials, making yourself a nice home with a metal door and codelock, or you can make yourself a bow and some bandages, and kill other starting players for their materials. You can also sit by monuments and farm blueprints, which allow you to make a specific item, and that knowledge to make said item stays with you, no matter what, until there is a server wipe, or you exit to a different server. No matter what method you use of getting higher in the game, People will attempt to kill you or break into your home, and take everything you own.
What makes this game so enjoyable is the fact that it just gives you the tools, and the community itself makes about 90% of the game. This game is made for the community to build on it. There are raiders, people who build impregnable bases and camp their tower all day firing at people, and people who partner with others, to stab them in the back within 1 hour - 1 week. You shouldn't feel bad for killing anyone, and I mean anyone. Whether it comes to killing new spawned people, or fully geared assailants, you shouldn't feel bad for killing anyone.
Now you may say, "Why should I kill a newly spawned player? They can't hurt me, and they aren't a threat". Although this is true at the time, it's what they're gonna do TOMORROW is what matters. You battle for resources, and eventually if he outfarms you, you are on the losing hand, and you have to waste more materials protecting yourself against them.
So you've farmed up and geared yourself with metal and everything needed. What next?
Raiding. Raiding is the main endgame of rust and it still manages to keep things interesting, no matter what. You may find a base with so many walls and defenses, it may just be full of so much loot and goodies that you can't wait to start to invade their home. Or, you may hate someone so much because they stole your stuff, drew hilarious signs in front of your house, or are just straight up disgusting bandits that probably need a lesson. All fixed with a little clever invasion strategy. To invade someone, you need to know a few basics.
1. The base layout. How large is their base? How many walls are there? What kind of walls are they? Do I have the materials to get inside? Are they online? Can they retaliate?
2. Invasion tools. There are MANY tools you can use to invade someone's home. If they don't have a tool cupboard, you can build straight over their main walls. What if they have a roof? Find the weakest spot of the base, and use any explosive you have to attempt to get inside. The tools you will most likely use to break in are C4, Rockets paired with a Rocket Launcher, Grenades, or pickaxes/axes/bone-clubs.
3. A raid base. One of the most important things when raiding, is a small base you create to make yourself a spawning point, extra materials, and a safe place to keep all the enemy's stolen belongings.
There is so much more to this game. Finding weapons, exploring monuments, and clever decision making in dangerous situations is what builds a smart player in Rust. Always think a situation through, and never trust anyone holding a gun, shouting "Stop for a second".

lets look at some facts.
Fallout 3, a great AAA game for its time, came out in 2008.
It took Bethesda 7 years of development, and re-development to finally give people Fallout 4 this coming november.
Now, the team working on DayZ have only been working on it for 2 years. They have also had members leave, and new people come on to the team. They are, as compared to Bethesda, a very small team. The smaller your team is, the longer development takes. With that said, it still took Bethesda 7 ♥♥♥♥ing years with a huge team to create Fallout 4.
The reality of it is this; it could be another 2-5 years before DayZ is finished, or at the least is out of Alpha. So, if you want to help that team along, and get to play a game that IS STILL BEING DEVELOPED, then by all means buy the game.
But if all you want to do is buy the game and then give it♥♥♥♥♥♥reviews then ♥♥♥♥ off. they have a very clear disclaimer telling you that the game is in its infancy.

Bit of a side note here. It seems like people expected this game to be finished or be in Beta by now. What people seem to forget, is that this game was created from scratch. My thoughts on Borderlands 2 are long overdue, but better late than never. I enjoyed the first game since I loved the different characters skill builds that worked exteremely well with the weapon variety. I see Borderlands as an FPS-RPG  blend because it has the obvious shooty parts, but also unique character skill builds to accomodate my playstyle or yours.
To be exact, every character has the potential to be aggressive, tank or support.Salvador is better at tanking while Zer0 is best at hit-and-run tactics. Maya and Axton both fill the role of crowd control/debuffer, but Maya is specialized in single targets and Axton does better at crowd controls thanks to his turret. Regardless of that, I would welcome anyone to buy this game on sale and invite me to play with you. The loot hunt does not get old if you like shiny dropping out of fleshy pinatas. The killing of enemies is as inventive as the gun manufacturers themselves. Eridian guns that shoot triple barrelled plasma balls, Hyperion 100% accurate weaponry from miles away, Maliwan elementally charged bullets ** Think the power of shooting lightning/fire/acid/slag **
The game is a mature for a reason and the jokes made here will poke funny at you especially thanks to our one and only charismatic jackass: Handsome Jack. I've rarely had an anti-hero as likeable as Jack. To some extent he is a tragic figure, but once you get over the fact that he murders those closest to you ... there ain't to rest for the wicked.
Co-op is a great deal with this game, but I higly discourage you play with anyone except friends. You can find decent folks online, but remember that anyone can pick up loot so would you rather have a trusty sidekick to share or an Anon hoping that he won't ninja loot you? Either way, there are ways to combat ninja looting, but it is best overall to have a friend to play with as the experience is enhanced. Trust will be created, fun will be had, and loot to be dropped.
Final verdict: Fantastic game when played with friends. Average with strangers, yet still enjoyable.

Rust isn't very good in making you feel like you're trying to survive. Everytime you spawn into a world, everyone has already made a huge city around the spawn, making the world feel less like a huge expanse of land that needs to be explored and more like a city with an outer wall that you go an look at for some reason. You can find basic materials like wood and stone laid out on the ground, presumably the excess from the owner of the towering castle in front of you. And to top it all off, the game feels more like an fps with the end game being able to craft or find a gun and mess with other people. This is also apparent in the newly adapted Battle Royal mode, which it totes it borrowed from Arma 3 on every official server screen. The problem with it being an fps, is it's not even a good fps. Controls feel clunky in a fire fight and even worse when trying to fight someone in melee range. One time, I had a guy actually kill me at melee range and he didn't even make a swinging animation.
The game looks nice, but is poorly optimized. My rig is able to handle most games on high pretty fine, but chugs like a used car powered by soda when I try to get anywhere close to it. And I don't know if it's me, but it feels like there's this smeared-on white type filter over the screen. It makes everything seem brighter than it is and it's kind of annoying.
I think the icing on this dirt cake is this game has been in alpha for about 2 years. They had revamped the game once, at one point calling it Rust Experimental. The move was nice, making the game look more refined and even changing the island. The game got a little better, but personally not enough. Now the devs are selling people's creations as store items. I'm not big fan of this from games who aren't even out yet. Especially when some of them get as pricey as $20. Fine as long as you want to support the devs, but it seems this game doens't have a release date in sight.
There are better survival games on Steam. There are better fps games on Steam as well. This game isn't quite steer clear. Many people like it, so there's a possiblility you might too. However, if you were to ask me, I cannot reccomend this game.

Day 16.... I'm still alive, but barely.  I am on the outskirts of some town... the roadside says Gorka... there is a police station that I want to explore. I have found that police stations usually contain some good gear, and I badly need good gear.  I quietly sneak up to a bunch of bushes, and zoom my scope in on the police station. Nothing. No movement. No one is there. I run up the hill, heart racing. I don't like towns... not since Berizino when they got Ronnie.  I hold up behind a wall, catching my breath, breathing heavy, my senses alert. That's when I hear it... "I'm Stuffed! Ha! I ate too much!"  Followed by laughing. What are they eating? Are they cannibals? My heart starts racing again... what do I do?  Call out to them? Find a tall building and shoot them?  Run away?
This game is awesome. Every time I play it is a new experience... from finding gear. fighting off zombies, hiding from bandits - to exploring new places, to crafting new things.  Even in early Alpha, the game is immersive.  Realistic.  One life to lose. No Respawn.  Just like "The Walking Dead" a lone zombie is no problem, but a group can be deadly.  Being killed when newly spawned is not that big a deal - after all when you have nothing, you have nothing to lose. But later on, loaded with gear and invested in the character... you really start trying to survive.
And trusting other players doesn't happen easily.
I have found that the private servers, where the character you create  is locked to only that server, is my preference.  A level playing field, if you will.   No server hopping is possible to collect the best loot.  You have to earn it.
Looking forward to see where the game goes as it reaches Beta and eventual Production Release.

This is, I believe, the best game of 2015 when it comes to story and nature. Obviously the graphics are not anything like The Last of Us or Until Dawn, but I believe that is what allowed for the game to be so excellent. Not bashing those two games in any way, I should mention, as I'm also a fan of AAA games. Many games become caught up in the sea of how realistic it can appear to the eye, but they tend to lose their meaning within that sea. Undertale has the ability to make you happy, sad, angry, meloncholy, and everything inbetween. You become attached to every single character in the game, no matter how small. So many games can hardly even make the main characters interesting with so much backstory and exposition, while, in Undertale, EVERY SINGLE CHARACTER is different. Even Frisk, who never even says a word, is given a personality based on your own desicions. At surface level, I did not think I would be remotely interested in this game, but I fell head over heels into it. With tonnes of laugh-out-loud moments and scenes filled with emotion, this game is so worth the money paid. Toby Fox did an amazing job with the story, mechanics, music, art, etc. Speaking of the music, BUY THE SOUNDTRACK AS WELL! It's so well made and helps move the plot and causes emotion so much more so than many other games. And as for the mechanics, the game is difficult at times, but does not drag on. For some fights, this is very obvious to whom have played the game in the genocide route, they are formulated so perfectly in order to make you feel so much more empathy-less when they are over. I honestly cannot praise this game anymore so than I have... amazing. Great job, Toby Fox.

I'm a huge rust fan. I started in the wee early stages of Alpha when the game had quite a heavy load of bugs.  If you're someone who is giving the store page a quick look and you have no clue whether or not to buy this game, I'll give you a few reason why NOT to buy this game.  And i'm not picking at the game here, legacy was quite enjoyable, but if you're coming here thinking that you're going to buy a game to enjoy, then turn away quickly. If you're someone who is willing to wait for the Alpha stages to work these bugs out just so you can play the game, then by all means get the game and sit behind a loading screen and wait because you'll be doing a lot of it. In a list below, i'll be trying to make a quick and easy way to explain to you why this game simply just doesn't work.
1. This game is not compatible with Windows 10. If you are of the lucky few that get this game and are able to play it on Windows 10 without any issues, bless the gods around you 'cause everyone else is failing at the moment.
2. Memory leaks.  Even if you somehow figure out a way by going on the forums and getting through the long loading screens, you'll most likely crash and figure out that you cannot play the game without turning your setting to the lowest settings possible. Get used to slick textures and pixelated materials.
3. Rust doesn't like win32 users.  For all of those who use 32bit Windows, I feel for you. Even though you should probably upgrade your rig, you shouldn't have to for a game like this. I've played much more developed games than Rust and still had some FPS to spare even in the most crowded of areas.
4. The game is still in Alpha. You just have to remind yourself that even though there are a bagillion bugs, this game is still in Alpha. How? I don't know this game has been out on the market for like forever. But they still are developing the game so even if you do complain about how horrible it is to load or play the game, give it some credit, the devs are doing the best of their abilities.
I gave this review a 'thumbs down' only because I don't want people to get their hopes up and not being able to play the game. Go read the forums, there are countless amounts of people refunding their copies because they simply cannot play it.  Yes, they could of done some better research, but if you're someone excited about playing games, you just gotta have it.

This is, I believe, the best game of 2015 when it comes to story and nature. Obviously the graphics are not anything like The Last of Us or Until Dawn, but I believe that is what allowed for the game to be so excellent. Not bashing those two games in any way, I should mention, as I'm also a fan of AAA games. Many games become caught up in the sea of how realistic it can appear to the eye, but they tend to lose their meaning within that sea. Undertale has the ability to make you happy, sad, angry, meloncholy, and everything inbetween. You become attached to every single character in the game, no matter how small. So many games can hardly even make the main characters interesting with so much backstory and exposition, while, in Undertale, EVERY SINGLE CHARACTER is different. Even Frisk, who never even says a word, is given a personality based on your own desicions. At surface level, I did not think I would be remotely interested in this game, but I fell head over heels into it. With tonnes of laugh-out-loud moments and scenes filled with emotion, this game is so worth the money paid. Toby Fox did an amazing job with the story, mechanics, music, art, etc. Speaking of the music, BUY THE SOUNDTRACK AS WELL! It's so well made and helps move the plot and causes emotion so much more so than many other games. And as for the mechanics, the game is difficult at times, but does not drag on. For some fights, this is very obvious to whom have played the game in the genocide route, they are formulated so perfectly in order to make you feel so much more empathy-less when they are over. I honestly cannot praise this game anymore so than I have... amazing. Great job, Toby Fox.

I highly enjoy this game because of it's great dev team and astounding progression and different ways to go about said progression.
You start out completely naked with nothing else but a rock and a torch. Its from this point right here, how you decide to progress.
You can progress by gathering materials, making yourself a nice home with a metal door and codelock, or you can make yourself a bow and some bandages, and kill other starting players for their materials. You can also sit by monuments and farm blueprints, which allow you to make a specific item, and that knowledge to make said item stays with you, no matter what, until there is a server wipe, or you exit to a different server. No matter what method you use of getting higher in the game, People will attempt to kill you or break into your home, and take everything you own.
What makes this game so enjoyable is the fact that it just gives you the tools, and the community itself makes about 90% of the game. This game is made for the community to build on it. There are raiders, people who build impregnable bases and camp their tower all day firing at people, and people who partner with others, to stab them in the back within 1 hour - 1 week. You shouldn't feel bad for killing anyone, and I mean anyone. Whether it comes to killing new spawned people, or fully geared assailants, you shouldn't feel bad for killing anyone.
Now you may say, "Why should I kill a newly spawned player? They can't hurt me, and they aren't a threat". Although this is true at the time, it's what they're gonna do TOMORROW is what matters. You battle for resources, and eventually if he outfarms you, you are on the losing hand, and you have to waste more materials protecting yourself against them.
So you've farmed up and geared yourself with metal and everything needed. What next?
Raiding. Raiding is the main endgame of rust and it still manages to keep things interesting, no matter what. You may find a base with so many walls and defenses, it may just be full of so much loot and goodies that you can't wait to start to invade their home. Or, you may hate someone so much because they stole your stuff, drew hilarious signs in front of your house, or are just straight up disgusting bandits that probably need a lesson. All fixed with a little clever invasion strategy. To invade someone, you need to know a few basics.
1. The base layout. How large is their base? How many walls are there? What kind of walls are they? Do I have the materials to get inside? Are they online? Can they retaliate?
2. Invasion tools. There are MANY tools you can use to invade someone's home. If they don't have a tool cupboard, you can build straight over their main walls. What if they have a roof? Find the weakest spot of the base, and use any explosive you have to attempt to get inside. The tools you will most likely use to break in are C4, Rockets paired with a Rocket Launcher, Grenades, or pickaxes/axes/bone-clubs.
3. A raid base. One of the most important things when raiding, is a small base you create to make yourself a spawning point, extra materials, and a safe place to keep all the enemy's stolen belongings.
There is so much more to this game. Finding weapons, exploring monuments, and clever decision making in dangerous situations is what builds a smart player in Rust. Always think a situation through, and never trust anyone holding a gun, shouting "Stop for a second".

В игре открытый мир, состоящий из трех десятков отделенных друг от друга локаций. Каждый кусочек Пандоры обставлен по-своему: помимо ландшафтного эксклюзива на диких территориях встречаются градообразующие предприятия, пещеры монстров, лагеря бандитов, небольшие деревушки, пустыни, трубопроводы, индустриальный завод, лаборатория с удивительными растениями и животными, высоченные ледники. Дизайн каждого объекта, каждого населенного пункта – изумителен; уникальный, рисованный графический стиль; тщательная проработка каждой детали. В игре многообразие оружия. Игра автоматически генерирует характеристики находимых или «выпадающих» из монстров экземпляров, создавая огромнейший арсенал: начиная от обычных пистолетов и заканчивая снайперками с разрывными патронами и кислотными гранатометами. В игре много юмора и побочных и сюжетных миссий. Музыкальное сопровождение восхитительно: мелодия чутко реагирует на появление больших скоплений агрессивных врагов и очень хорошо сочетается с общим стилем локаций. Есть сетевая игра на четверых игроков. Моя оценка 10/10.

This is, I believe, the best game of 2015 when it comes to story and nature. Obviously the graphics are not anything like The Last of Us or Until Dawn, but I believe that is what allowed for the game to be so excellent. Not bashing those two games in any way, I should mention, as I'm also a fan of AAA games. Many games become caught up in the sea of how realistic it can appear to the eye, but they tend to lose their meaning within that sea. Undertale has the ability to make you happy, sad, angry, meloncholy, and everything inbetween. You become attached to every single character in the game, no matter how small. So many games can hardly even make the main characters interesting with so much backstory and exposition, while, in Undertale, EVERY SINGLE CHARACTER is different. Even Frisk, who never even says a word, is given a personality based on your own desicions. At surface level, I did not think I would be remotely interested in this game, but I fell head over heels into it. With tonnes of laugh-out-loud moments and scenes filled with emotion, this game is so worth the money paid. Toby Fox did an amazing job with the story, mechanics, music, art, etc. Speaking of the music, BUY THE SOUNDTRACK AS WELL! It's so well made and helps move the plot and causes emotion so much more so than many other games. And as for the mechanics, the game is difficult at times, but does not drag on. For some fights, this is very obvious to whom have played the game in the genocide route, they are formulated so perfectly in order to make you feel so much more empathy-less when they are over. I honestly cannot praise this game anymore so than I have... amazing. Great job, Toby Fox.

Rust isn't very good in making you feel like you're trying to survive. Everytime you spawn into a world, everyone has already made a huge city around the spawn, making the world feel less like a huge expanse of land that needs to be explored and more like a city with an outer wall that you go an look at for some reason. You can find basic materials like wood and stone laid out on the ground, presumably the excess from the owner of the towering castle in front of you. And to top it all off, the game feels more like an fps with the end game being able to craft or find a gun and mess with other people. This is also apparent in the newly adapted Battle Royal mode, which it totes it borrowed from Arma 3 on every official server screen. The problem with it being an fps, is it's not even a good fps. Controls feel clunky in a fire fight and even worse when trying to fight someone in melee range. One time, I had a guy actually kill me at melee range and he didn't even make a swinging animation.
The game looks nice, but is poorly optimized. My rig is able to handle most games on high pretty fine, but chugs like a used car powered by soda when I try to get anywhere close to it. And I don't know if it's me, but it feels like there's this smeared-on white type filter over the screen. It makes everything seem brighter than it is and it's kind of annoying.
I think the icing on this dirt cake is this game has been in alpha for about 2 years. They had revamped the game once, at one point calling it Rust Experimental. The move was nice, making the game look more refined and even changing the island. The game got a little better, but personally not enough. Now the devs are selling people's creations as store items. I'm not big fan of this from games who aren't even out yet. Especially when some of them get as pricey as $20. Fine as long as you want to support the devs, but it seems this game doens't have a release date in sight.
There are better survival games on Steam. There are better fps games on Steam as well. This game isn't quite steer clear. Many people like it, so there's a possiblility you might too. However, if you were to ask me, I cannot reccomend this game.

Undertale is incredibly unique amongst the slews of shooters and RPGs that have become so prevalent these days. It doesn't have breathtaking graphics or incredible gameplay, but it doesn't need it. It doesn't even necessarily have the strongest story. But it has an incredible cast of characters, an intricate way of handling the player's morality and choices, and above all else, it makes you think about what you're doing and feel for the characters around you. Wacky hijinks and clever wit aside, Undertale has a way of making the player feel like both a wonderful and horrible person, sometimes simultaneously. (Sure, everyone knows that killing things isn't the right way to go in Undertale, and you can remove wonderful from the previous descriptor if you run around mass-murdering, but this isn't the place to discuss the specifics of that particular path, chilling as it is.) It really brings you to task for the things that you normally do in games - not the character you play, but you, the player controlling the character. Suffice to say that not everything in Undertale is wiped away and forgotten by reloading a past save. I can't say very much without spoilers, but there's a reason its fans are so passionate about and defensive of its characters - just how attached they can become after a few hours of sprites and text, bringing them to life without fancy graphics or long infodumps detailing their backstories. Undertale pulls through on wit, introspection, and ability to move the player, and its experience is in no way lessened by its lack of more prevalent modern gaming elements.
(Okay, and the soundtrack. It has an awesome soundtrack.)
The amount of detail put into the writing is amazing - for example, the game has accounted for pretty much every weird, contrived thing the character can do with the world, and characters will react accordingly. There are also plenty of hidden secrets, right down to datamining, for those who are into those sorts of mysteries.
My only complaint with Undertale is that it has no replay value. Or negative replay value. Because it actively makes me feel like a♥♥♥♥♥♥if I try to replay the game. Like I said, it's effective.

If you consider yourself even somewhat of a fan of this game, just don't bother reading this review, you've already downvoted it. Just move on. For those of you who are actually interested in what I have to say, then feel free to read.
Alright, so there are several reasons I don't like and don't recommend Undertale.
1) Style. This one is all but entirely subhective, but the barebones 8-bit style graphics and chiptunes do absolutely nothing for me. I have no nostalgia for the days of the NES or SNES, thus have no love for the style. The environments feel repetitive after a very short amount of time, and don't look very interesting to begin with.
2) Repitition. This game just repeats itself over and over and over and over. The random encounters become boring and overly samey after you face the same enemies more than once or twice, as they do not change even slightly. You'll want an option to disable these encounters as they only serve to slow the pace of the game to a crawl. Also, if a puzzle has a mechanic, expect that mechanic to be the sole gimmick of the next few puzzles.
Writing and characters also get extremely repetitive. Characters come off as one-note and boring, and take far too long to actually feel like they are changing. Characters instead rely on some quirk to entice the player, but seem to offer little beyond that. It's quirky character after quirky character, and they eventually start to belnd together. Jokes get beaten to death far after they stopped being funny, and then they keep going. The referential humor can easily be lost one you, especially if you don't get it or just don't like that style,
3) Gameplay. The gameplay is a very mixed bag. The "bullet hell" segments of turns start to get boring as you see the same attacks from the same enemies over and over. They provide a good deal of challenge, and can be fun the first time you try them, but otherwise they feel stale quickly.
One of my biggest issues with the gameplay is the difference between fighting and sparing, in that there almost isn't any. Killing something requires you to stay alive and attack your enemy until it dies. When you spare it, you stay alive, acquire some basic information, and perform actions until you spare the enemy. These sound different at first, but it just boils down to "press button, dodge bullets, press another button". Outside the bullet hell segments, the battles are simply menu options, feeling extremely similar. If this thought is kept in mind while playing, you realize sparing an enemy feels about the same as killing an enemy, with all but one extra step involved.
There are a couple things I liked about this game:
1) The music, on occasion, kicks♥♥♥♥♥ Boss themes can be very strong, and some background music is used to good effect.
2) First impressions of characters are strong, and can be very enjoyable before the repitition sets in.
Overall, I didn't care for Undertale. It wasn't my type of game. Maybe you love it, maybe you hate it, but for me, it did nothing.

This game started off as a magnificient survival game set up in a sombre atmosphere, with a unique art style, a huge map with tons of details, a building system like no other we've ever dreamt of, an unbelievably caring and cooperative community and lots of adrenaline rushes caused by strangers, zombies, and rad animals. In short, it was about primitive men—some better geared than others—versus nature, making friends and enemies along the way.
At some point Rust was rebooted from scratch. That made a lot of sense back then because the amazing concept behind the game was being hidden by its modest technical level, and the messy code in Good Ol' Rust supposedly hampered developers’ progress to an ill extent. Getting more features and a better game seemed optimal. This new thing was labeled Rust Experimental.
Now, two years later, Rust Experimental is simply known as Rust. A lot has changed since the beginning of said massive revamp. I'll give you one thing: it looks fantastic. It totally does.
The negative side? The game has totally turned from a survival to an FPS. The community is now crowded with players who are intellectually uncurious at large: they are not interested in interacting, they will never ask for food nor will they try to convince you about letting them in to spend the night, and they will not cooperate in any way. If any of the previous ever happens to you, it will be to kill you and to raid your house. Most of the times they will refrain from using these old tricks and just shoot on sight with an AK-47, rocket launcher, flamethrower, or sniper rifle with a 4x-zoom scope if they are able to. Everyday they stay late at night with one goal in mind: use C4 to raid as many houses as possible right when everyone's logged off.
People are simply not open to expanding their friend circle, and so the hilarious and creepy dialogues and situations that made Rust the best game I've ever played they're all gone. The developers' ill emphasis on military weapons has taken this too far away, to the point that I've found myself playing DayZ trying to recover some of this experience while still visiting Rust from time to time to check on the progress of users' devastating mindset and the building system, which I still enjoy quite a bit.
Some other bad bits that are in no way nearly as defining as the ones above: developers are poorly organised and seem to tackle issues randomly instead of as a team, developers' progress is tedious to follow mostly because of their lack of focus, realism and priorities (although they manage to pull some decent weekly devlogs), performance is poor and seems to be slowly getting worse, the building system hasn't received barely any update in a year (bugs are virtually the same ones as back then), developers' only goal in life is adding modern weapons to the point that even this new FPS-addicted hostile community is feeling wrong about it, procedurally generated maps are losing features for no apparent reason (amazing desert and snow biomes, forests and canyons suddenly just flew away), caves have never worked properly and old Rust's rock formations which allowed players to hide, build shelters where they'd never in a hundred years be found simply don't exist anymore. Animals have not worked at all for two whole years and they want to have it fixed by June (!).
Now let me tell you a story. Facepunch didn't like the zombie fashion, they took them out of the game, put rad animals instead and took them out again when moving to the new Rust. After that, they spent years deliberating about adding NPC hostiles (there are none), doing intellectual work on the topic, coming up with amazing new beings that would terrify survivors, thinking of refined concepts that would shatter the world as we know it. After all that effort on a paramount subject, the only NPC threat now in the game is... guess what. A cannibal tribe? An ancestral monster? A wizard in a tower? Nope: a chopper, a ♥♥♥♥ing chopper with a machine gun. You still think it's not that bad, huh? Okay, picture Facepunch staff would be replaced by one CoD-mad 14 year-old, tell him to develop a concept for The Boss of a game like this and give him two hours instead of two years. You and I know even he would've thought of something better.
And have I said this game requires too much time? Several hours daily. And also that it includes a few pre-gun powder weapons who no one can use thanks to the mindblowing number of guns?
There are a lot of minor points I could make too, but I'm lacking the energy and time for it.
In case you are considering this as an FPS purchase, I firmly believe it makes no sense for you to go through the annoyance of building a house, gathering blueprints and resources, crafting weapons, trying not to die at night, and moving from wipe to wipe if all you want is to simply shoot down some people. Of course, this game allows you to shoot down some people who really care about what they're doing and who're expending a sick lot of time putting effort into building their place, which I have come to understand motivates a bunch of people. (Sigh)
If you are still going to play it, bring some friends from real world and enjoy the bloodbath or simply get abused non-stop playing solo.

Borderlands 2 took everything they did right from Borderlands and made it even better. From game options to gameplay, everything has been tweaked to satisfy a greater audience and they did it without dumbing down much of what made Borderlands so great.
With the three DLC's that have been released so far, you will have a lot more variation in scenery and gameplay if you get bored of the main story line. Pirate Butts is a medium length story but the end missions will usually pay off with some amazing loot. Some people complain about reskinned enemies but there's plenty of new things that keep it visually interesting. The new weapons are definitely unique, some of them are considered "cursed" which can give them amazing bonuses but they will have a drawback that can be just as devestating to you as the bonuses are to the enemies.
The Torgue DLC is filled with the great comedy that made Borderlands so memorable and the final raid boss is amazingly fun to fight unlike Gee in Pirate Butts. Seraph items have actually become useful in this one: For grenades, the O-Negative, Crossfire and the Meteor Shower are simply amazing and replace some of the legendary gear for sheer mass destruction. The Hoplite is the seraph equivalent of the Fabled Tortoise with less of a speed impact, so technically it's even better and should be used over the FT. Oh yeah, EXPLOSIONS!
Sir Hammerlock's Big Game Hunt is a rather short DLC but it takes you to a very different part of Pandora. Instead of wastelanads you visit an underground oasis for rare and unusual (for Pandora) animals. While the main plot isn't too long, there's plenty of side missions to keep yourself busy with. The seraph dealer has found some amazing weaponry this time like the new Interfacer which is now the absolute strongest shotgun in the game and The Hawkeye sniper rifle. The Hawkeye may be weak for body shots, it has one of the highest crit bonuses for any sniper and has great accuracy. The vast manjority of enemies are new and there's a returning enemy from Borderlands which may or may not make some people rage. Along with the missions you will get a new vehicle, new heads and new skins to customize your character and a terribly designed raid boss with unavaoidable shock novas.
Borderlands 2 is worth picking up if you're a fan of the original game and it's often silly humor. Just be warmed, you may lose track of time very easily so don't play this before work. :P
