EDIT: I will start off by saying that I did not buy this game, it was gifted to me.
Undertale is not a game, and it's not art, either.
The game is entirely story-driven, which wouldn't be a bad thing if it meant that the game has zero replayability once you know everything. And knowing the fandom, you already know absolutely everything.
The thing with replayability is that it gives a game reasons to be played even after you've beaten it, but with little to no worthwhile gameplay (or even a new game+), there's no replayability to offer.
The music is good, but only five remotely memorable tracks feels a little lacking at times.
The characters are witty, but the game is so short to the point where it's trying to cram in as much character development as possible over the course of three hours, which ends with the game lacking any real gameplay or difficulty.
Ironically, the game's main problem is the difficulty, and it's one of the dumbest design decisions I've ever seen. I'll get to that later, but I'll explain one thing firsthand. There are three paths, in order of easiest to hardest; Pacifist, Neutral and Genocide.
The choice that people pick the most often is Pacifist, and although it gives a rather touching story, it's severely lacking in difficulty, especially near the end.
The next one that's usually the middle ground is Neutral, which also gets very easy near the end.
The previous two paths both had final bosses where dying serves almost no penalty to the player since they start back in the middle of the battle anyway, but the third path is a much different story. Genocide is the only path I had any fun with, not because I'm a masochist, but because it was actually challenging.
This leads into my main complaint with the game; It punishes you for making it difficult. Throughout the entirety of Genocide, you're constantly berated by the characters and environment in a way that's supposed to make you feel bad for even choosing the path in the first place (this isn't mentioning the overdramatic fits the fandom would have if you told them you played through Genocide). Does it work? For some people, yes, but only because they grow attached to the characters, which I honestly feel fall kind of flat since once you've played through it once, there's no variety.
Don't get me wrong, I found this game humorous, and it shares alot of my kinds of humor, but when it's punishing me for choosing to make the game difficult? Why? That's just stupid.
Also, I understand that Genocide is supposed to make you feel like a "monster" or whatever, but regardless, it's still the hardest path. It's still the most fun out of all of the paths. Why should I be punished so severely for playing a game how I want to play it?
All in all, Undertale is comparable to The Walking Dead if you're only given one choice in the dialogue options; It's a graphic novel. You play it for the story, maybe for the characters, and that's it. It's not hard, and it's not worth playing again unless you're doing it to give the game actual difficulty, but even then, the game tries to make you feel bad for doing so.
I wouldn't say it's worth $10 when you can buy something more enjoyable and replayable for that much during a sale.

As of today 1-20-16, with over 150+ hours I cannot endorse this game. I endorse the potential, but the game itself is shallow and lacks any form of immersion or character.
Rust is currently a player-survival-simulator. In the beginning of the game you will spend a great deal of time gathering materials by (1) using tools to gather them directly from nodes or (2) killing other players you find walking around and taking their stuff. After you finish gathering materials you will ultimately craft weapons to kill other players. That is the end-game of Rust in its current state and honestly that has been the end-game of Rust since its creation.
GAMEPLAY: CRAFTING
The crafting system in Rust is shallow but effecient. It lacks any form of character to separate itself from other games such as Minecraft, Reign of Kings, 7 Days to Die, or any other "survival sim" on the market currently. Objects require a minimum number of materials and you select what you want to craft from a list on the side of the screen. If you have it, you can craft it. Materials are readily available throughout the randomly generated maps. Need fuel? Need wood? Need metal? Have no fear because material nodes have no fixed spawn points. You can literally live in a hole and never have to travel anywhere in particular to obtain special resources other than blueprints.
The blueprint system Rust employs makes it a bit more involved which is a good thing. You go to monument/dungeon sites on the map, such as an abandoned trainyard, and collect actual blueprints or blueprint fragments which you then study to add craftable items to your crafting list. Blueprint fragments can be used to learn low-level items or upgraded multiple times, each time giving you a rarer blueprint opportunity. At first this is exciting as you lurk through abandoned buildings trying to learn new things to craft while you hear gunshots and people killing eachother around you (if you play on a populated server). After a few hours of gameplay constantly obtaining new blueprints, you are done with this portion of the game. You will be able to craft gear that can effectively kill other players, and that's what the game boils down to.
GAMEPLAY: PVP
There is no PVE in this game. Starving to death is not possible unless you intentionally avoid every opportunity thrown at you to not starve. You could die to a bear in the game, but once you get even the basic revolver bears are a joke.
Your life will be taken by other players and you will take their lives as well. Repeatedly. In its current state you do not need top-tier firearms to kill other players who are wearing full armor. You could potentially end someones life with a bow even from the beginning of the game if your aim is alright. Put any firearm in the hands of a decent FPS player and the game quickly revolves around just landing your hits, no matter what weapon you use. I have killed people with the waterpipe shotgun (basic weapone veryone can craft) while they used fully automatic rifles. And to be fair, it is VERY EASY to obtain fully automatic rifles even on vanilla non-modded servers. Just travel to a monument/dungeon while completely naked and open boxes. Eventually you will find the blueprint for the firearm itself. Bam. Done. Now you just get some metal from any rock on the map and craft a gun. Proceed to murder. Done with the game. GG.
GAMEPLAY: CONSTRUCTION
Rust has moved away from cube-building to fixed object construction. Minecraft for example uses cube construction. So does Reign of Kings. In Rust you lay down a foundation object, which can only be placed at certain elevations and build adjacent to that elevation. It essentially tells the game what level is the ground floor or "level 0" on a plane. Keep in mind that foundations have to be a certain distance from the ground. It becomes extremely difficult to construct *meaningful* structures with this system. Because of that, bases repeatedly look the same over-and-over-and-over. All of them are the same ugly flat pieces of planks/stone/sheet metal. You lay foundation, select the wall option, put walls up, put whatever up, and all of them are the same.
At first you may be tempted to construct a building with separate rooms for all of your operations. This is stupid unless you don't care about losing your stuff. The only way to destroy a player made building that is protected by a toolbox (Rust's version of a protection block in Minecraft) is to use C4. This explosive might seem rare in the beginning, but can be easily obtained by running naked to dungeons and hitting random boxes until you find the blueprints.
Any building made out of wood can be destroyed by hand-made tools. This automatically removes wood as a viable structure because anyone can break into your home. Stone requires C4 to be destroyed. But only 2 of them. If you only have 1 layer of walls, anyone with the blueprint for C4 can just blow open a wall and take your stuff. This means everyone builds two types of structures - TOWERS and HONEYCOMB bases. A tower is just...a bunch of levels going up with doors at every level. A honeycomb base just has door after door after door. Both of these attempt to force raiders to use all of their C4 before reaching any of the real loot.
Think about that. The number one way to defend your base is to force the enemy to use waste all of their ammo. And it doesn't work. C4 is easy to craft for anyone who has an hour to gather materials. Let alone a group of people working together.
IMMERSION:
Everything in Rust lacks character. The first time you walk through a trainyard or water treatment plant might seem amazing. But after an hour or two you quickly feel as though everything lacks a soul. It is hard to describe. Nothing feels valuable in the game itself. You cannot craft any objects which might feel like you belong to the world. Chairs, tables, bathrooms, aesthetic objects etc. are almost non-existant. You can craft a very limited number of clothing pieces (some of which you can now buy on the market for real life money by the way$$$!!!). You can craft placeable signs but why? All the ones I have seen are filled with bad♥♥♥♥♥♥♥drawings or just telling you to die in a fire. As of right now there is essentially no RP server and I do not see how you could even have one.
PC REQUIREMENTS:
For some reason, even fully tricket out computers can have problems running this game. If you have 4GB of RAM do not even bother trying to run it. I have played this with 4GB of RAM and with higher-end PCs. Something is wrong when a game like Minecraft can give Rust a run for its money in the graphics department after downloading a texture pack. All while running far better. If you have a minimum requirement crap-computer you should totally expect 5 - 10 minute loading screens with studder lag all over the place.
OVERALL:
Rust sucks. I'd rather eat burnt toast. If you just want to run around the map looking to shoot another player who doesn't know you are there, then sure buy the game. The combat is not particularly difficult to master for anyone who plays FPS games. If you are looking for something that has a soul and depth, pass this up for another 2 years until they actually create a game with it.

EDIT: I will start off by saying that I did not buy this game, it was gifted to me.
Undertale is not a game, and it's not art, either.
The game is entirely story-driven, which wouldn't be a bad thing if it meant that the game has zero replayability once you know everything. And knowing the fandom, you already know absolutely everything.
The thing with replayability is that it gives a game reasons to be played even after you've beaten it, but with little to no worthwhile gameplay (or even a new game+), there's no replayability to offer.
The music is good, but only five remotely memorable tracks feels a little lacking at times.
The characters are witty, but the game is so short to the point where it's trying to cram in as much character development as possible over the course of three hours, which ends with the game lacking any real gameplay or difficulty.
Ironically, the game's main problem is the difficulty, and it's one of the dumbest design decisions I've ever seen. I'll get to that later, but I'll explain one thing firsthand. There are three paths, in order of easiest to hardest; Pacifist, Neutral and Genocide.
The choice that people pick the most often is Pacifist, and although it gives a rather touching story, it's severely lacking in difficulty, especially near the end.
The next one that's usually the middle ground is Neutral, which also gets very easy near the end.
The previous two paths both had final bosses where dying serves almost no penalty to the player since they start back in the middle of the battle anyway, but the third path is a much different story. Genocide is the only path I had any fun with, not because I'm a masochist, but because it was actually challenging.
This leads into my main complaint with the game; It punishes you for making it difficult. Throughout the entirety of Genocide, you're constantly berated by the characters and environment in a way that's supposed to make you feel bad for even choosing the path in the first place (this isn't mentioning the overdramatic fits the fandom would have if you told them you played through Genocide). Does it work? For some people, yes, but only because they grow attached to the characters, which I honestly feel fall kind of flat since once you've played through it once, there's no variety.
Don't get me wrong, I found this game humorous, and it shares alot of my kinds of humor, but when it's punishing me for choosing to make the game difficult? Why? That's just stupid.
Also, I understand that Genocide is supposed to make you feel like a "monster" or whatever, but regardless, it's still the hardest path. It's still the most fun out of all of the paths. Why should I be punished so severely for playing a game how I want to play it?
All in all, Undertale is comparable to The Walking Dead if you're only given one choice in the dialogue options; It's a graphic novel. You play it for the story, maybe for the characters, and that's it. It's not hard, and it's not worth playing again unless you're doing it to give the game actual difficulty, but even then, the game tries to make you feel bad for doing so.
I wouldn't say it's worth $10 when you can buy something more enjoyable and replayable for that much during a sale.

It's not without its flaws, but you should at least play it once.
This game is actually very scripted. It tries to make it seem like you have a lot of choices, but the game is actually very scripted. There are three endings: one for killing everyone, one for sparing everyone, and one for doing literally anything else. The game tries to pressure you into being a pacifist, and gives you a very rewarding ending for doing so, while the neutral ending and genocide endings are a bit of a letdown. There are around ten weapons and armors in the game, and almost all of them are impossible to miss.
The game is small, and it is short. There are few areas, and you'll have beaten the game within 10 hours (more likely half that). The maps are very dull, and very linear. If a map splits, it's either taking you somewhere that lets you warp back to a previous stage, further on into the game, or to some sort of shop. Many times, the map splits just to take you to other maps that split, ultimately making a grid that eventually has only one exit.
The game's graphics are not great. It was made by a small team, and it's excusable. Sure, the graphics don't make the game. And the story even has an explanation for why things look so unpleasant. But the point is, the game is not pretty. No matter what spin or excuse someone slaps on it, the graphics of the game are not good.
Many fights get very tedious or frustrating. Relatively few of them are outright difficult, it's mostly about doing the right thing enough times. In pacifist mode, you gain no health or damage, so you stay relatively weak. This means you get killed in less than five hits by any given enemy. It's also worth pointing out that quite a few attacks can in fact hit you five times (but you pretty much have to try to let that happen). The greatest challenge in this mode comes from the fights dragging out for so long, and all you do is stall for time turn after turn after turn. There is a boss fight where you win by just staying alive for seventeen turns (you can also hold onto an item from early in the game and break it out here to shorten that time, but there is no indication that you can do so or expect to do so). I get it, 17 turns isn't excessive by RPG standards. But you're basically playing a dumbed down Touhou in that time, over and over. It gets repetitive. Sparing enemies usually involves finding the actions you need to take to make them willing to leave you be, and then sparing them. It's almost like you're punished for not reading a guide or getting lucky, because many of these enemies will wear you down to nothing in the three turns you lose by choosing the wrong action, then choosing the right one, and then the next correct answer. In genocide mode, you will have almost no challenge in one-shotting most of the enemies you fight. Fights can get pretty boring.
There's another big problem with the combat system: hitboxes can be a little off sometimes. Sometimes you may blame the game, "That didn't hit me! I dodged that!" That only happened once or twice to me. In actuality, it's more common that an attack will scrape the edge of your icon and not actually damage you. That practically happened every other fight.
Now, flaws are out of the way. Let's talk about what this game does right to still make it recommendable after so many negatives.
You will never find a game with characters more charming than Toriel, Sans, and Papyrus. Pretty much every character you meet, you will fall in love with. This game's sense of humor makes it very likely the funniest game I have ever played. There is a scene where a character is attempting to get you to make friends with another character, and then flips through and smashes a window to leave you alone. In another scene, a character tells you to hide behind a "conveniently shaped lamp" with pixel dimensions identical to your character. Toriel, the designated mom character, is absolutely touching to interact with. She guides you through the early game, being supportive all along the way. I was so attached to her that I reset the game when I accidentally killed her just so I could make sure she stayed alive.
The story takes a backseat to the character development. The same ten or so characters will constantly pop up throughout the game, and you get to see how these characters interact with each other.
The music in the game, while oftentimes not even present, is simple but perfectly fitting, and usually fun.
The last hour or so of pacifist mode has incredible pay-off. Everything you've worked towards, and everything you've liked about the game, comes together perfectly. The characters you love and friendships you make matter. Everything the game has tried to teach you matters. The game ultimately motivates you to be good, and then it rewards you for goodness.
This game is meeting all of my standards. (One a side note, this is one of those games you absolutely must play. Buy it already! )

The game's graphics are not great. It was made by a small team, and it's excusable. Sure, the graphics don't make the game. And the story even has an explanation for why things look so unpleasant. Many fights get very tedious or frustrating. Relatively few of them are outright difficult, it's mostly about doing the right thing enough times. In pacifist mode, you gain no health or damage, so you stay relatively weak. This means you get killed in less than five hits by any given enemy. It's also worth pointing out that quite a few attacks can in fact hit you five times (but you pretty much have to try to let that happen). The greatest challenge in this mode comes from the fights dragging out for so long, and all you do is stall for time turn after turn after turn. There is a boss fight where you win by just staying alive for seventeen turns (you can also hold onto an item from early in the game and break it out here to shorten that time, but there is no indication that you can do so or expect to do so). I get it, 17 turns isn't excessive by RPG standards. But you're basically playing a dumbed down Touhou in that time, over and over. It gets repetitive. Sparing enemies usually involves finding the actions you need to take to make them willing to leave you be, and then sparing them. It's almost like you're punished for not reading a guide or getting lucky, because many of these enemies will wear you down to nothing in the three turns you lose by choosing the wrong action, then choosing the right one, and then the next correct answer. In genocide mode, you will have almost no challenge in one-shotting most of the enemies you fight. Fights can get pretty boring.
There's another big problem with the combat system: hitboxes can be a little off sometimes. Sometimes you may blame the game, "That didn't hit me! I dodged that!" That only happened once or twice to me. In actuality, it's more common that an attack will scrape the edge of your icon and not actually damage you. That practically happened every other fight.
Now, flaws are out of the way. Let's talk about what this game does right to still make it recommendable after so many negatives.
You will never find a game with characters more charming than Toriel, Sans, and Papyrus. Pretty much every character you meet, you will fall in love with. This game's sense of humor makes it very likely the funniest game I have ever played. There is a scene where a character is attempting to get you to make friends with another character, and then flips through and smashes a window to leave you alone. In another scene, a character tells you to hide behind a "conveniently shaped lamp" with pixel dimensions identical to your character. Toriel, the designated mom character, is absolutely touching to interact with. She guides you through the early game, being supportive all along the way. I was so attached to her that I reset the game when I accidentally killed her just so I could make sure she stayed alive.
The story takes a backseat to the character development. The same ten or so characters will constantly pop up throughout the game, and you get to see how these characters interact with each other.
The music in the game, while oftentimes not even present, is simple but perfectly fitting, and usually fun.
The last hour or so of pacifist mode has incredible pay-off. Everything you've worked towards, and everything you've liked about the game, comes together perfectly. The characters you love and friendships you make matter. Everything the game has tried to teach you matters. The game ultimately motivates you to be good, and then it rewards you for goodness.
This game is meeting all of my standards. (One a side note, this is one of those games you absolutely must play. Buy it already! )

Ok, third time writing this review. In the Arma 2 mod, you could find a fairly decent gun with at least 1 magazine of ammo for it within the first 15-30 minutes. Also, in Arma 2, if you aren't very familiar with the map, you can just find a map, open it, and find your position on the map and what city you are in. However, in the Stanalone, gun spawns are less frequent and more useless clothes spawn instead. And when guns do spawn, they spawn with no ammo. Normally, this would be fine, if you can't find ammo next to it, search around for a bit and maybe you'll find some stray ammo for it. This is sadly not the case, as ammo almost never spawns unless you know everything about the map and know exactly how to get to military bases no matter where you are. Don't know exactly where you are? Don't worry, I'm sure you can find your location with ease when you find a map! Whats that? Maps are completely useless and you could get the same if not better results just google imaging "Dayz Map"? Huh? They don't tell you your location on the map? Not even the names of the cities? Yeah, this game makes it even harder for new players to get into the game than Arma 2 does. You'll just get crushed by people who have a few hundred more hours in the game than you do and know everything about the map, or you'll get bored and just leave the server you are in and sigh since most of the game is just walking very slowly and annoyingly up a tiny incline. Just save your money and buy Arma 2 or 3 if you can afford it and have a nice PC.

I have played rust for some decent time by now. I judge i can point out the details i most consider relevant about the game. IF you are p[ondering wether to buy this game, and made your research in gameplay streams and stuff, you might have some doubts yet. I had these, so i am also evaluating the game over these aspects.
AMMOUNT OF PLAYERS --
I played in 3 ways - either alone, or in a clan, or with a friend in a double team.
I can say that each of them has their own fun into it.
Most of the solo plays were somewhat successful. Even though not resource rich and a raider, you can live decently at solo building, as long as you are skilled with hiding and find a very good spot. This demands patience and building far from hotzones, but hey, that's how you do it.
Solo playing is mostly farming and carefully examining it. If you play aggressivelly, you want to be the trapper, and kill people outside rather than raid someone.
As a Clan, i can tell you that farming is quick and fast, and you will almost always hold giant buildings. Lots of loot, weaponing and stuff. And raiding too. Not only doing it, but suffering it a lot, from other clans. With 6~8 you can have a big enough base so that whoever wants to raid you lose more than they earn, making a stronghold worth building - Safety is uncommon, but a bit of it is assured with big clans and a well designed base. You want the flattest area too, for radial expansion.
And as a team, you will have the middle tier between those. You will mostly be more exposed, but more defendable, with resources enough to build tall and weaponing enough to eventually even raid something.
MORALITY --
I have been strictly moral so far. I have carefully picked people i would "befriend" (Being the weakest) and never been batrayed so far. I have never betrayed either. Don't stick around in just random people running, and often you can have a depth of honor into it. Joining forces with random people, specially other solo, can be done.
I have also never betrayed anyone weaker, though i have been attempted to. I have aided many, even donated blueprints to some people, and i do not regret it at all. Being honorable in this game (And raiding only "Guilty" people) is possible, and tho harder, i enjoy it most.
PVP --
Rust is a PvP based game. You will always want to have at least 2 weapons, a main one and a secondary (Usually a bow). Mastering them might be somewhat hard. I am particularlly bad at most weapons, tho i have learned how to decently whoot with bows and thompsons along this time. This is probably me being unskilled tho. No crosshairs, and physics can trick a guy who mostly play CS:GO as shooters.
UPDATES --
The team weekly updates the game with new content, in some ocasions biweekly. New content not only include new items, but graphical upgrade, tweaks in engine, building changes, balancing, etc. They are active and this forces some servers to wipe down everything.
I personally hope it always remain like that, for 3 reasons: Because it forbids huge clans to literally take over a whole world, because it allows you to start over new worlds (Which is one of the most fun parts) AND because this makes you know that anything is temporary, so you dont rage over being fully raided, since everything is temporary.
IN OVERRAL, a summing up review here - you can enjoy this game. In whichever way. Even if you want to be the nice solo guy, it's hard, but you can.
It's an excelent game.
No naked guy jokes.
This game is excelency in sandbox and shooting and social interaction.
9.9/10
(minus 0.1 points for slightly worse interface on macs) (It's the least developed part tho, will be solved afterwards)

I've never played Legacy Rust, so I wouldn't know if the game actually improved with the revamped version, but perhaps that gives a more honest review of the game as it is right now.
I've recently picked up Rust in the steam sales for a few bucks and been logging into the game from time to time. The game is still in the alpha / early access stage so it can still go both ways.
As it stands right now, it's definitely an enjoyable game, if you like the survival genre at least. It might take a few goes to get into it and perhaps joining a proper server will play a part in the enjoyment aswell. Joining the 'wrong' server may result in getting fed up with the game really fast. Community and modded servers may use increased gathering rates, better loot, more loot, redeemable kits (e.g. you get some starting equipment) which can result in alot of people being fairly heavy geared and having major bases built, which as a newbie can be quite intimidating,
You'd hope to run into friendly people, but in reality people playing these sorts of games, survival games, tend be not as friendly as you'd want them to be. Getting shot on sight and stripped from whatever loot you've struggled to collect or getting killed while trying to construct a fairly simple house for yourself, with a bunch of materials you just spent an hour to collect. I suggest you find some friends to play with so you can gather, build and gear faster aswell as having more of a chance to defend yourself against other players. It's every man for himself.
Having found some friends to play with and a nice server to play on, i've spent countless hours collecting loot to get by. I've built bases, some of them lasted, some of them got raided overnight. That's all part of the game, don't get too attached to your stuff.  I found myself playing deep into the night several times, while I should be sleeping. The thought of my base getting raided haunted me. Just a little more wood to expand a part of my base. Just some more stone to fortify my base. Let me just smelt these ores real quick so I can make these sheet metal doors to keep intruders out. Before I knew it, it was 6am already again. That's the first sign of addiction.
Once you're 'done' building your base - you are never really done to br honest - the time to walk around and explore the map starts. Going on loot runs to collect weapons and other useful items and gear to defend against other players or be one of those unfriendly bandits running around the map with a hunting party, making life difficult for people, just as they did yours. Revenge is sweet! Until you die and lose all your gear. Rinse and repeat.
Current state if the game is not too bad, depending on how busy the server you play on is, the longevity might vary. The game definitely needs some more fun stuff to do besides looting, building and shooting people, but that doesn't make it less thrilling or less exciting. I'm sure I'll log a few more hours in this game, casually.

In my opinion, this game is one of the best early access games on the market. They have come such a long way from zombies. Now there is everything from helicopters, to rotten apples. The developers really thought of everything when they were developing the game. The step they took from legacy to the new rust version was the descision to make the game the best it could be, and that they could not reach the games full potential on the unity enigine. It was a very contriversial descision, but in my opinion it was a good one. This game also reaches a part of your brain that no other game ive played has reached. The very specific part of the lizard brain that this game tickles is a very special experience. Something about losing everything that you have every worked for just pisses you off in a way that normal video games can't do. This game also is updated bi-weekly with new features to keep the entire experience new and interesting. Across my 3 accounds, i have nearly 1200 hours and and still haven't gotten the least bit burnt out on the exciting experience that is rust. I can't really do a pros and cons list, because everything about the game i enjoy. The only thing i miss about legacy is the skill gap. It didnt matter what kind of gun or gear you had in legacy. Someone could still kill you with a rock if they had the necassary skill. In the new version, its really hard to get on your feet with all these players with guns running around. You cant take them on either, since the game is highly gear based and not entirely skill based. That doesnt take away from the fact that you could technically take down as many people as you want if your opponent is bad at the game, but it doesnt matter how good your skill level is. If someone has a better weapon then you, chances are you will get killed. Aside from that, i think the game is entirely accessable to everyone and is something anyone can just pick up and enjoy. It will take practice, but once you get the hang of it its one of the most amazing, beautiful and immersive gaming experiences in existence.

However, if you're the type who wants the "best" ending without having to replay many hours because you made one mistake, it's worth peeking at how to accomplish that without spoiling story. I know if I had gotten to the end and found out I had to play all over again I would have never done it.
I also really enjoyed playing the game "with" people. It's great to play for streams or videos or to watch people expirience it on their own.
It's story and character heavy so it's worth checking out all the lore you can find. And if you're up to it, it's worth doing things the "bad" way at least once. Otherwise you're only getting half the story.

Welcome to Rust.  That is a phrase any new player must severly become accustomed to hearing when you first try this game.  The game itself is a great idea, but since this application has been in "Alpha" for who knows how long it takes some time to come to terms with game aspects.  The game is perfect if you love open world survival, intense fire fights, massive areas, and fighting over resources.  Caution: DO NOT GAME ALONE.  The community is usually a solid 50/50 between extreme toxicity and friendly players. With massive amount of community, modded, and specialized servers therer is a place for everyone in Rust.  I would recommend this game to any person and/or group that has alot of time to spend playing and becoming "king of their server", but playing this game casually comes at a steep price.  Usually you can run to find a small area to begin establishing your base by collecting allllllooootttt of materials and the game is very appealing at its ability to always keep you busy....however other players are constantly on the look out for the new players and will use very underhanded tactics to utilize game mechanic flaws and leave you back at square one.  To the people that play this game be aware that you will be stalked, murdered, and cannabalized for resources whenever you are offline.  If you enjoy a game that tests your strategic ability to overcome enemy players and survive then this game is for you.  Thankfully with the amount of servers and admins that are usually on they are able to help guide and find the perfect place for you in the magical land of Rust.  Live free or Die a rock carrying Nooblet.........choose wisely

Back in the day I actually ran/co-owned a Rust server. Back then, because there were no admin tools to detect cheaters, I thought the easiest way to combat cheaters was to simply "be" a hidden cheater, and walk around with a full inventory of loot with esp and god mode on, and hide in a crevass somewhere, where no one would even bother to visit.
Sure enough, as soon as I spawned and started walking to my position, two individuals had started to follow me from a distance away. Changing direction did not help, although I admit i was quite sneakily pretending to hit trees while watching their distances. Soon I went to my very very secluded location, still keeping an eye on those individuals. They found me, killed me, took my loot. I respawned. They triangulated my position almost immediately, and then killed me again, this time laughing.
Shortly after that, I received a vac ban due to cheats detected on my system.
I did of course, contact support about this, and tell them that I co-owned a server AND had the receipt to prove it, which was the reason behind the cheats.
I was told that it is illegal to cheat and no exceptions would be made.
I pretty much told myself that THAT was the last time I'd ever play an alpha, or even buy an alpha through steam again, (mainly PVP oriented dedicated server based games). The game was glitchy, full of cheaters, felt like a massive cash grab, given that the reason for downloading cheats was actually for a noble cause. But not to matter, how Steam wants to do business is their choice, but that is BAD business.
One Vac-ban in over 6-8 years, and with reason, for an alpha game, and you refuse to lift the ban or refund me money back then? Shame on you.
/Endrant.

This game is pretty good, and outright amazing if you've never played anything like it before. I have however, so I don't rate it as highly as some other people would.
Undertale is not really a game you play for the gameplay aspects. It has an eccentric combat system which combines a couple minigames to reach it's goal of allowing you not to kill anyone in the game, as advertised. It also cleverly combines it's mechanics with narrative to humorous effect (humor is a large part of the game, so if you're not okay with that, don't buy). However, the combat itself I found borderline annoying as it kept coming back on random intervals while I was trying to progress. It was not engaging enough for me to try and seek it, much less have it shoved in my face every now and then. That said, the boss fights felt fresh and fun, especially due to changing patterns of the bullet hell minigame, which the random engagements didn't have and thus became a monotonous chore really fast.
The narrative is where the game really shines, and Undertale is one of those games with a strong ending that just blows you away. My main criticism here would be that the game feels bland at first. I understand what the author was going for there as the game keeps one-upping itself as it goes, but the very first area maybe ended up being a bit too bland, and, to be brutally honest, if I didn't know it would get better from all the goddamn overhyped fans, I swear I'd uninstall the thing 2 hours in.
The strong narrative is largely helped by the amazing music. Together with the very simplistic graphical representation, it helps draw the mental image and makes you feel like you're actually there. This is one part that most "retro" indie games tend to fall flat on, and AAA games don't bother with anymore - the same kind of imagination-driven atmosphere that you get when reading a book, except taken to a new level. This is one more thing that a lot of gamers never got to experience, or maybe just forgot about, before playing Undertale, which brought it back.
Undertale might not be as amazing as it's hyped to be, but I can wholeheartedly recommend it without hesition. It's not perfect. It has it's issues and shortcomings. But for the most part, it finds clever ways to work with them rather then pretending they don't exist. It's not something that I can recommend to absolutely anyone - if you don't like humor in heaps, or aren't big for largely narrative-driven experiences, steer clear. But when playing it, my expectations couldn't be any higher, and while it definitely did not exceed them, it still delivered at the very least, which is already quite impressive.

Welcome to Rust.  That is a phrase any new player must severly become accustomed to hearing when you first try this game.  The game itself is a great idea, but since this application has been in "Alpha" for who knows how long it takes some time to come to terms with game aspects.  The game is perfect if you love open world survival, intense fire fights, massive areas, and fighting over resources.  Caution: DO NOT GAME ALONE.  The community is usually a solid 50/50 between extreme toxicity and friendly players. With massive amount of community, modded, and specialized servers therer is a place for everyone in Rust.  I would recommend this game to any person and/or group that has alot of time to spend playing and becoming "king of their server", but playing this game casually comes at a steep price.  Usually you can run to find a small area to begin establishing your base by collecting allllllooootttt of materials and the game is very appealing at its ability to always keep you busy....however other players are constantly on the look out for the new players and will use very underhanded tactics to utilize game mechanic flaws and leave you back at square one.  To the people that play this game be aware that you will be stalked, murdered, and cannabalized for resources whenever you are offline.  If you enjoy a game that tests your strategic ability to overcome enemy players and survive then this game is for you.  Thankfully with the amount of servers and admins that are usually on they are able to help guide and find the perfect place for you in the magical land of Rust.  Live free or Die a rock carrying Nooblet.........choose wisely

Back in the day I actually ran/co-owned a Rust server. Back then, because there were no admin tools to detect cheaters, I thought the easiest way to combat cheaters was to simply "be" a hidden cheater, and walk around with a full inventory of loot with esp and god mode on, and hide in a crevass somewhere, where no one would even bother to visit.
Sure enough, as soon as I spawned and started walking to my position, two individuals had started to follow me from a distance away. Changing direction did not help, although I admit i was quite sneakily pretending to hit trees while watching their distances. Soon I went to my very very secluded location, still keeping an eye on those individuals. They found me, killed me, took my loot. I respawned. They triangulated my position almost immediately, and then killed me again, this time laughing.
Shortly after that, I received a vac ban due to cheats detected on my system.
I did of course, contact support about this, and tell them that I co-owned a server AND had the receipt to prove it, which was the reason behind the cheats.
I was told that it is illegal to cheat and no exceptions would be made.
I pretty much told myself that THAT was the last time I'd ever play an alpha, or even buy an alpha through steam again, (mainly PVP oriented dedicated server based games). The game was glitchy, full of cheaters, felt like a massive cash grab, given that the reason for downloading cheats was actually for a noble cause. But not to matter, how Steam wants to do business is their choice, but that is BAD business.
One Vac-ban in over 6-8 years, and with reason, for an alpha game, and you refuse to lift the ban or refund me money back then? Shame on you.
/Endrant.

Ok...I honestly don't know where to start with this game. I never cried, laughed, or actually felt bad in a video game before, then Undertale happened. For a game with roughly only 8-10 hours of gameplay, 8-bit graphics, and your average RPG backstory (At least it seems that way when you start)...it has a lot to offer. A lot. Friendly flowers, goat moms, reptile weeaboos, pun-cracking skeletons, even a fish warrior. And that's just for starts. There's a lot to this game, and you will find yourself laughing, crying, and jumping in fear all along the way.
Undertale is a truly inspirational game, a game that showed me there's still hope in the world, that people
be good, and that violence isn't always the answer. It showed me that the no matter what path you take, you should stay to it, and stay determined along the way, because no one should ever stop you, no matter what.
Ok, that was really deep. Apoligies.
It was made by only a handful of people, but mainly by a guy named Toby Fox. You may have heard of his Earthbound Halloween ROM Hack before (under the name FwugRadiation). He actually appears in-game as a little white dog. There's a lot of dogs in this game. Too many to count. I counted 10, but it turned out the 7th dog was the 3rd dog, and the 3rd dog was the 10th dog, and the 6th dog somehow disappeared, so I gave up trying.
This game is best played without any knowledge, so I'm not going to say anything else. So just buy the game, if you haven't gotten it already.

Hype culture ruined this game for me, honestly.
I was reccomended this game by a friend who showed me a Youtube video of the Sans genocide fight.
I quickly was turned onto the game by a unique combat system with a myriad of ways to progress. Sadly, this is one of the only things that I feel was fleshed out in this game enough for me to
like it.
The emotional aspect of the game feels akin to something of a high schooler going through an internal crisis. Emotion is flung all around in this game, mostly to no avail. There were a few scenes where I laughed or said, "Oh, that's sad.", but no points where I felt genuinely emotionally invested in this game.
As stated above, if Toby Fox were to have fleshed this game out to possibly even 3 or 4 hours longer, I would be giving this game a positive review.
The game's progression is also seemingly all over the place, especially twoards the end. The final scenes seem to show up out of nowhere, and the ending is mediocre at best.
Maybe I just don't see something in this game that others do.
It's a great game, don't get me wrong, but there's just so many things about it that culminate into me having to give this negative review.

A solid game, well desigend and keeps the feel of the original. For the replayability alone this game is worth the price, but get the Game of the Year edition, as it contains all the DLCs you really need, with the rest being the Headhunter packs and a bunch of heads/skins for the 6 different characters which you really don't need (but get a few if you're so inclined). The only downside is that to truly max out your character, Overpower levels aside, you're going to have to play the main campaign 3 times per character as each of the 3 play modes have a level cap, which can start to feel boring.
The DLCs offer a lot of additional content, however they're not as massive as the ones from Borderlands, and some of them (Like Hammerlock's Hunt) are ones you just want to get through as quickly as possible, so don't expect them to take a long time to complete.
The game has its share of bugs and glitches, but most of them are minor and don't effect your gameplay.
Also, taking this game to open-to-all online co-op is risky, as people hacking the game (or even your character) is a major issue. So it's safer to co-op with people you know, but the game is still a lot more fun with a full squad of players, even if you can do everything solo.

It's was a cool co-op adventure game, that I expect to be now too. I like co-op adventures :)

Imagine if you were playing Pokemon for the first time, and when you fought your rival (You probably named him "Sir Garbage") at the beginning of the game he died and was completely out of the story. No more taunting you throughout your adventure like an the annyoing brat Sir Garbage was. Just dead, and you are the murder. Right in front of his own grandpa, Dr Oak, who cries out, and then he dies too. Soon you meet other well known characters in the franchise. They too die after you fought them. The world becomes a dark and lonley place. It's a shock for the whole population. Until now murder was an unknown concept. The other Pokemon trainers now starts to fear you, others seeks to punish you for your crimes. They too starts to fall one by one, and soon whole villages flees you. Some seeks the protection of Team Rocket in hope of having enough people to counter attack you. A last desperate defence from all Pokemon trainers are made. But they all die. You leave trail of dead pokemons and humans everywhere you go. At last your own pokemons , the once who has always served you, has had enough. In one last epic final, they go against their whole life of training, to finally follow their own hearth, the whole world prays they succeed. But they too fall, and in the end, you are the very best, like no one ever was. Because everyone else is dead.
Or, instead, of killing Sir Garbage, you refuse to fight him entirely, and you become friends, and share this lovely little adventure together to two of you, and your Pokemons, who are released from captivity.
Thats Undertale.

Ah, Undertale. What can I say about Undertale that hasn't already been said so many times? Probably nothing new. But this game deserves recognition regardless. It's a shining example of what someone can accomplish with simple tools. It does not bathe in the graphical serenity that most modern games do. It does not have an insane physics engine that allows for interactivity down to the smallest object. It does, however, show you how much can be done with what you already have.
This game may not be the first thing you think about when you think "innovative". But is that right? Not entirely. It may not have the latest tech behind it, but it really pushes the boundaries. Toby Fox, the creator, really thought "outside of the box". And that's not something you see too often these days. It best shows with the combat - regardless of which route you take, the combat is really unique and interesting, to say the least. Especially the "boss battles". It's not at all what you'd expect from an RPG. No, each battle is instead its own minigame, and it does it really well. You're never truly bored when you're "fighting" your opponents, and the game is always throwing something new at you. Something you weren't expecting. Something that often makes you rethink your strategy.
The characters are all so well written. Again, regardless of which route you take, these characters will be true to themselves. This isn't the only game with well written characters, but it's one of the few games that really makes you care about each one respectively. Each character brings something of their own to the table, and when you've met them all, you really do feel enriched by them. Character development like this is so rare. And it inspires me to do even better when I myself attempt to write. This entire game inspires me. And that's not something I feel often.
Undertale is well worth the little money it costs. It's got replayability pouring out of itself like you wouldn't believe. There are so many different ways to approach this game, so many different endings. And each one of them will contribute to the whole experience - the whole story of the world, and the characters within.
Definitively one of the best things to come out of 2015. And continues to remain a masterpiece in the years to come.

Imagine if you were playing Pokemon for the first time, and when you fought your rival (You probably named him "Sir Garbage") at the beginning of the game he died and was completely out of the story. No more taunting you throughout your adventure like an the annyoing brat Sir Garbage was. Just dead, and you are the murder. Right in front of his own grandpa, Dr Oak, who cries out, and then he dies too. Soon you meet other well known characters in the franchise. They too die after you fought them. The world becomes a dark and lonley place. It's a shock for the whole population. Until now murder was an unknown concept. The other Pokemon trainers now starts to fear you, others seeks to punish you for your crimes. They too starts to fall one by one, and soon whole villages flees you. Some seeks the protection of Team Rocket in hope of having enough people to counter attack you. A last desperate defence from all Pokemon trainers are made. But they all die. You leave trail of dead pokemons and humans everywhere you go. At last your own pokemons , the once who has always served you, has had enough. In one last epic final, they go against their whole life of training, to finally follow their own hearth, the whole world prays they succeed. But they too fall, and in the end, you are the very best, like no one ever was. Because everyone else is dead.
Or, instead, of killing Sir Garbage, you refuse to fight him entirely, and you become friends, and share this lovely little adventure together to two of you, and your Pokemons, who are released from captivity.
Thats Undertale.

The combat system is turn based, but you have 4 options. You can fight and deal a good amount of damage to your opponent depending on where you stop the dot on the meter, perform an action (such as talking, approaching, etc), use an item which will most likely be food to restore health, and then the mercy option. You can spare an opponent- tell them you dont want to fight, or flee the battle if possible. You gain experience if you kill the monsters which levels you up, as you level up, the enemies do too. This ups the challenge but not by much, your HP also increases. If you spare the opponent somehow though, you wont gain any XP, but only your casual gold amount or maybe something else. To survive,
I give the combat system a 9/10 just for how unique and unpredictible it can be. Sure, every enemy has a specific pattern, but you'll have to spare a few food items or die a few times before you adapt to it. Also, every monster has different actions, to perform on them. some benefit you, some dont. All about adaptations.

As I said before, Undertale made me become the player. And the puzzles certainly add to it as well. Undertale is a constant game of puzzle solving, assuming, adapting, and guessing. The ruins is all about puzzles, so much that the entire game is one. You'll have to set things together piece by piece like "Oh, this enemy wants me to make fun of him, guess I should do that, haha!!" The game also has a good way of giving the player momentum. Musicless sections set up the drama nicely, and hard hitting drums and other instruments help as well to give intensity. Bosses will either make you want to quit, or vow revenge with all your might.
You can also talk to every monster you meet who either gives you a full damn conversation, or just simple flavor text with no real meaning but better than nothing I guess.

I finally caved into the hype and decided to buy Undertale, and, for what it's worth, I was satisfied.
The characters are well written and likable, and I haven't laughed so many times at any piece of fiction in a long time. The visuals are simplistic, but appealing, and Toby Fox pulls off a fantastic soundtrack.
If I had to complain about Undertale, my only complaints would really be small nitpicks.
The few that pop into my head immediately are
- You can normally speed up text scrolling, but can't on the game over screen, which is minor, but kind of irritating.
- The game will occasionally crash intentionally, which, while technically kind of ominous, also slows things down when you need to reopen it.
- At some story-related points you are not permitted to restart the game, you have to progress further in the game to re-unlock resets.
That's really about it.
If you're a fan of rpgs, or just strong stories in general, Undertale will probably entertain you.

Most of my hours have been as a "lone wolf". It is possible to play as a lone wolf, but this is certainly a social game so at some point you're going to run into someone else.  Scroll to the bottom for helpful hints / tl:dr if you are going to buy this game. Review may be slightly out of date as was written when the XP system was in, it should still be fairly relevent though.
Will that person be friendly?
OFFICIAL SERVERS:
If you are on an official server (as I started out) the friendlies make up about 1 in 30 people, so the likelyhood is that you will get KOSed (killed on sight). You'll loose everything and it will wholey♥♥♥♥♥♥on your parade. The important thing is to (depending what point you are at in the game) remember names, take your revenge when you can.
The fact that you can get jumped at any moment is one of the major adrenaline sources in the game. Out mining stone and having to watch your back, sneaking past a huge base full of geared guys.
Your game experience will change drastically depending on what server you play on.
If you choose a community server, that ratio gets smaller, and you'll find more friendlies.
Personally, for the first few months I started out on an official server. I wanted "pure rust". I wanted to play the game as close to "vanilla" as was humanly possible. I recommend doing this, although many would most likely disagree. Official servers are usually looked upon as the place where the real toxicity in rust is, where the cheeters are, where the huge clans are.  As a solo player, you can make it slightly easier on yourself by choosing a server in a different timezone. This will give you "downtime" hours where the population drops from 200 down to 80 or 90, you'll still get action, but the chances of you getting wiped out by a group of 8 people go from 100% down to a more managable 50%.
I met small groups, fell out with others, raided, built, hid, attacked; official servers are great for action.
The bottom line in rust, currently, is build - raid -build -raid (server wipe) build - raid -build -raid
A server wipe happens every month, to every server it is forced and puts everyone back on a level playing field. It also stops servers from filling up with bases (many of which are dead and raided) which could eventually kill the server due to lag etc.
Once you've been through a few wipe cycles it can get very old. It did for me. At 140hours I almost gave up, bored. Then I thought I would play a little longer but set my own goals.
On the offical server I created a "survival outpost" where noobs could run past, use a furnace, repair bench, research table etc...
After that I started setting goals "get a rocket launcher this wipe" (this was back in the days of BPs where getting a rocket launcher was actually a big deal and unlikely to happen to a solo).
I decided to try a modded server.
MODDED/COMMUNITY SERVERS
(Modded) "Pure PVE"
In this server there is no raiding, no killing other players. It is "Pure Person Vs Enviroment" it had a huge gather, so within a few taps of a rock you have 3k wood. etc. You also get Airdrops delivered right to your door. You call them in with your daily smoke grenade. It was basically rust handed to you on a platter. It was cool to be able to run around without the anxiety of having to look over shoulder, build a castle in just an hour. But then what? After a few hours getting myself to the same state that would have taken a week in any othe server, I left. Bored.
Currently there aren't enough enviromental threats for this to really work; and if you're just using rust as a glorified chat room (which is fair enough) you need to be able to gel with the players already in there. I'd like it to work...perhaps oneday it will.
Server 2 (Vanilla), Noob friendly.
I'd racked up probably 700 hours on official servers, exhausted from constant adrenaline I wanted to kick back and retire for a while. Noob friendly servers are the hardest ones to run. KOS is looked down on, and the servers are generally full of 3 types of people. Genuine noobs. Players who want easy PVP because offiical servers are too much for them and finally retired helpful old folk. It's a very tough combination to balance and control. They are great servers for chatting, kicking back. In my opinon they are actually a little counterproductive to the actual noob. It is Rust easy mode. Noob friendly servers are often low population, everybody generally knows everyone else which makes the sting of being raided even more personal, on top of it being a "noob friendly" server. The salt is even more real, and far more painful for the noob than it would have been on a lawless official server with 200 people, where a noob wouldn't have known their raider.
Server 3, Modded Community
Faster Gather, Better Loot? The problem I find with these is that it devalues everything.
In a vanilla server, say, you may get attacked by a group with 2 C4. Your base will need to be able to withstand 2 C4. As soon as the gather rate goes up, you now have to compensate for the fact that 2 C4 will now be 6C4. The base size grows. If you find 5HQM in one barrel that means nothing, as the next time you hit a rock you'll get 50HQM...Everything gets bigger, everything looses value.
Finding the balance, playing on other servers will help you find your home. I am still a fan of starting on Official servers, to get a taste of lawless rust and then use that as the bar to measure other servers against. There are loads of better servers out there than offiical, but you won't know that until you experience a good amount of time on one.

I played this game with the help of a walkthrough, and I spoiled the story for myself. Even then, I only partially understood what to expect; I heard loud praise about this being one of the greatest games ever made, but I also read comments about it being some kind of smarmy "Tumblrina" politically correct meme game. Well, reviewers were wrong on both counts: It's not the greatest game ever made, nor is it the political soapbox that its detractors desperately wished it to be. It is, however, the only game I have ever played to profoundly affect me emotionally. I was emotionally attached to this game within the first 15 minutes, and it only got worse. It impacted me so strongly that I actually lost sleep, and if that sounds overly dramatic, I can assure you, I definitely was NOT expecting such a response.
Undertale's magic, I believe, is from the ever-present feeling that the game isn't just happening to the characters, with you (the player) as a detached observer, as in most other RPGs. It's as if the game is happening TO YOU. The choices you make in the game don't just matter (after all, RPGs like King's Quest and Ultima have had meaningful choices for nearly 30 years,) but they impact the game in an organic way that makes you feel like you're living through an experience, rather than simply plugging options into a choose-your-own-adventure.  Undertale is a real-life Neverending Story... and you're Bastian, reading the book out of curiosity at first, but then slowly realizing that you're an inextricable part of how the story unfolds.
The gameplay itself, comprised mostly of battles which combine typical RPG sensibilities with a kind of hybrid "bullet hell" dodging mini-game, is fun and highly varied. However, this is not an RPG with gameplay as its core value. There is no item hunting. No grinding. No crafting. No overworld, and no map, for that matter (not that you'll need one.) Its closest RPG cousin is probably the 16-bit classic Earthbound, with its incorrigible charm and quirky atmosphere, but even with that comparison in mind, don't go into Undertale expecting a vast, sprawling adventure. Some reviewers have expressed the idea that Undertale might not even be an RPG at all, but rather a linear, interactive story, along the same line as the Stanley Parable, or Journey on the PS4. This comparison is a little off the mark, I think. Although Undertale is extremely story-driven, it also maintains familiar RPG trappings like interactive objects and NPCs, an explorable game world with optional areas and secrets, and "combat"-driven narrative.
Perhaps now that Toby Fox has made quite a bit of money, he can hire the personnel to make a more expansive sequel or spin-off. It's almost sad to think that fans will be disappointed if he's content to rest on his laurels. Undertale has a strange cult-like ability to convert its players into fanatics clamouring for more content... not necessarily more content as we understand it, but for more of the unique experience that Undertale offers. The game's hysteria is so pronounced that fans tend to tremendously overhype the experience, sometimes ruining the whole thing for new players. Upon learning that you're about to play Undertale, don't be surprised if people DEMAND that you play the game a certain way, often in a desperate, almost accusational tone, as if to prevent you from doing anything to harm the characters whom they've grown to love. This is a very strange and unfortunate phenomenon, since it can lead to people being turned off from having anything to do with Undertale.
I will say that players with absolutely no nostalgia for retro greats like Chrono Trigger, Earthbound, and Super Mario RPG will probably miss out on part of this game's appeal. Undertale masterfully recalls those innocent childhood memories of playing RPGs without a care in the world. Its aesthetic and especially its soundtrack tread familiar ground, but they're so convincingly and expertly composed that the entire game will seem fresh. I'd be shocked if the music wasn't stuck in your head for days after playing it.

If you are anything like me, you probably looked at the trailer and screenshots but still had a hard time figuring out why this game had so much hype surrounding it. On the face of it seems to be just another Retro-style RPG with a generic story about monsters and humans.
Neither of these really do the game justice... I mean come on, the screenshots don't even have any cool skeletons in them!
But let me tell you, I haven't cared this much about video game characters since I played Telltale's The Walking Dead, and unlike that game, your actions HEAVILY influence the outcome of the story.
Undertale is all about the storytelling and the characters. The monsters all have their own personalities, the 'boss' monsters are all main characters to the story, they are hilarious, likeable, sometimes formidible and sometimes tragic, and you will want to get to know them all.
Combat is fun, all the enemies have unique 'mini-games' where you have to dodge their attacks, (and which combine with other attacks if multiple monsters are present!) and finding out how to defeat them are puzzles in themselves.
The game is not too long, but its an experience that will stay with you for a long time afterwards. Or at the very least you'll end up watching undertale videos and listening to the amazing soundtrack endlessly for weeks afterward...

Undertale is an interesting game. Not because it offers particularly good gameplay, graphics, or because it’s challenging – but the simple exterior hides a surprisingly engaging and complex story, told in a way that defies convention and makes Undertale stand out from the endless brown goo of mediocrity that the Steam store occasionally resembles. It styles itself like a JRPG but it really isn’t one, taking every opportunity to subvert existing tropes and play with the format.
Unfortunately, the brilliant writing makes the lacklustre gameplay stand out all the more, because it quickly becomes a chore that you must plow through in order to get to the next parcel of story. And then again, because the game withholds some (story-critical) content unless you go through it at least twice, or manage to hit all the critical flags on the first run – probably impossible without a walkthrough.
Undertale prides itself on being a game where nobody has to die – which is represented in each battle by the option to “spare” the monster. This option only becomes available after certain actions are taken, and so is a mini-puzzle in itself, but the solutions are often obvious and so most battles can be resolved in seconds, especially if the same monster has been encountered before. When attacked, you are faced with a short “bullet hell” minigame, where you must dodge incoming projectiles of various sizes and shapes. There are enough variations on the formula that this doesn’t immediately become tedious, and some of the later battles can be quite challenging.
The graphics, as I’ve mentioned, vary from simply bad to acceptable; the game is presented in faux 8-bit – that is, blocky graphics in variously low resolutions, but with high resolution effects. There are a number of art shifts throughout, which are used sparingly but effectively, typically in expectation of a major event. The excellent soundtrack also contributes greatly to the ambience and helps set the tone of each encounter.
Apart from the story, what I think makes Undertale stand out is how it plays with itself as a medium. Actions such as saving, loading and even exiting to the desktop are woven into the story in a way that few games have ever even tried. Restoring a save file to try something different, you may find that NPCs still remember your actions from before, although this mostly affects dialogue.
While I still don’t feel that Undertale quite lives up to the hype, I’ve come to overlook its faults and appreciate it much more after seeing the whole story through to the end. It delivers a unique experience and a story that manages to be emotionally engaging while still delivering a lot of laughs. And you’ll be filled with determination.

There are few games that I find myself personally invested in any of the decisions one would make while progressing from beginning to end. From the start Undertale empowered the value of ones choices, and then, maintained it through the game all the way to the last moment.
The writing was both clever and informative. The game is not shy when showing the results, and later, the consequences to your actions. Any piece of text, in dialog or observation, would provide more depth to the world and the characters that exist within it.
Undertale game play made two changes to the mechanics common in role playing game.
First) You have the option to spare your opponents in combat. Second) You can maneuver your character during your opponent action to dodge incoming attacks. These changes make both random encounters and boss battles more unique.
Undertale is a well crafted gem that has been a rich experience to play.

Undertale is an interesting game. While it doesn't seem impressive at first glance, the story, characters and game world's reactions to your actions make it a great excellent experience.
It's a metagame and toys with your expectations. I recommend not reading a guide for your first playthrough. Being able to make your decisions based on what you know at the time is a big part of its charm and this is one of those games where going in blind is important.
The combat is alright. After your turn you'll go into bullet-hell mode to dodge enemy attack. All enemies have different ways to act with and have a variety of attack patterns, making sure you won't tire of repetition too soon. The difficulty level seemed alright, not too easy, not too hard.
The characters are unique and there are several particularly notable ones. How much of the humor or references you enjoy depends on you. But all of the monsters are nicely written.
In the story itself there are a lot of good moments. As a whole it was very enjoyable and stands multiple playthroughs. There's plenty of optional text to read as well to tell you more of the world, but not too much.
b]Playtime[/b] of one of the endings took me about 12 hours and the game's good for at least 2 playthroughs. There's more than that if you're willing to dig deeper into the various endings and tidbits of lore.
Undertale was a great experience and made it to my list of things to replay every year or two or whenever I've managed to forget enough of it. I'd highly recommend it.

Undertale shouldn’t be spoiled in advance. You’ve seen the score, you’ve seen from the screenshots that it’s a JRPG-style game, and I’ll tell you up front, it’s one of the funniest and best designed RPGs you’re likely to play this year. Beyond that, I’ll try to stay light on details—as much as I can while still telling you why it’s great—but avoid Google, avoid forums, avoid picking away at the scab of not knowing much. The less you know about Undertale before diving in, the better it can work its magic.
The basic secret is that it’s not entirely what it looks like: a goofy 8-bit RPG parody that owes a debt and at least two limbs to EarthBound/Mother. It’s partly that, sure, and it’s brilliant at it. After a slow and not particularly fun intro area, it opens up into a world more densely packed with jokes and puns and adorable characters than pretty much anything out there. Papyrus, the skeleton guard desperate for recognition and friends. His brother Sans, mocking RPG puzzles by just dumping a Junior Jumble to block your way. Crazy monsters like Woshua, who just wants you to be clean, and a ghost who only lowers his HP when you attack to be polite.
I haven’t laughed this hard at a game in years, and if Undertale was purely a joke RPG like Cthulhu Saves The World or Barkley Shut Up And Jam: Gaiden, it’d honestly be enough. Even its weaker moments where it veers too close to reference and inside joke oversaturation—the stuff of many a comedy RPG Maker game—just about work, if only because they’re always over quickly.
But that’s just what’s happening on the surface, and it’s disarming in just the right way. The cleverness builds as you play, and systems that originally seemed throw-away usually end up being more than they seem. The big gimmick is that nobody has to die: there are ways to spare everything and everybody, from the random monster encounters to the bosses. Combat plays out via a series of minigames, mostly unique to each monster, in which you move your pixel heart around in a small box—dodging bullets, blocking shots with shields, simple platforming, getting past shields, often layered to make things more complicated when you face off against multiple enemies at once.
As a really basic example of the mechanics being more than they seem, Undertale often uses them to convey the character’s mental state: faster attacks when they’re annoyed, bolder attacks when they’re feeling confident, or even aiming to miss when they don’t really want to fight. There’s the vegetable who just wants you to eat your greens and will leave you alone if you do. A late game encounter with a character who gets a mid-battle telegram from a previous zone to tell them that it’s cool, you’re a friend. Papyrus, who's so desperate to have cool attacks that he’s forgotten to actually make them deadly, and who's interrupted by a dog stealing the bones he intended to throw at you in his next turn.
How you choose to handle things affects how the story plays out. It also affects your replays, with Undertale interested in experimenting with what happens if certain characters remembered what you did the last time, and what the implication of that power might be. Finishing the story only takes about 5-7 hours, but to dig into its secrets takes another couple of loops, and a strong stomach. We’re also not just talking a few line changes. Going for a genocide run, where you murder literally everybody, essentially turns the whole thing into a pitch-black horror game. A peaceful run meanwhile leads to one of the most charming and heartfelt RPGs ever made. Murder followed by a reload to see what might have been… well, you get what you deserve.
You can spare the monsters. Not always their feelings. You can spare the monsters. Not always their feelings.
Undertale obviously has its faults, including a couple of puzzles that wear out their welcome, a first play that’s a little too easy to be satisfying, and occasionally relying a bit too much on players getting jokes like a jealous aircraft called the ‘Tsunderplane’. If you can’t stand those, or the JRPG style in general, it won’t likely win you over. Every player also seems to have one area that they dislike, though rarely the same one—for me it was the Hotlands, not because the action was bad, but because the puzzles were time consuming without being satisfying. Luckily, the same location also had one of my favourite characters, as well as one of Undertale’s best direct parodies.
To miss it though is to miss out. Undertale isn’t simply like Earthbound, like Chrono Trigger, like Final Fantasy VI in its graphical and mechanical style, but a worthy successor to the way they took the JRPG genre and experimented with it, evolved it, took it in new and interesting directions. It’s an old-school game, but one designed with modern sensibilities and an eye for deconstruction matched only by Knights Of The Old Republic 2’s brutal assault on the Star Wars universe.
The fact that this is basically a one-person project only makes it more impressive, from the excellent use of simple graphics to convey emotion, to the fantastic lo-fi soundtrack. It may or may not be the best RPG you play this year, but it’s certainly going to be one of the most worthwhile—as memorable as anything in, say, The Witcher 3, and every bit as worthy.
THE VERDICT

Disclaimer: As you guys might know this game is early acess. Considering that I bought it with a clear warning that the game was unfinished I'll write my review ignoring all the bugs and problems I faced.
In this game you start as a fresh, newbie, zombie apocalypse survivor with a bunch of possibilities in front. You want to be a good person? You can! You want to be an outlaw? You also can! Want to be a mix of both? Why not!? Just remember the golden rule of DayZ, you die, you loose everything to the ground free for everyone to pick up (even you, if you are fast enough). It might be extremely frustating but it's all designed to be that way, you feel the need to survive in a way that no other game could do before it. The moral choices in this game are one of it's core components but beware since every other player will be able to choose them. It's as hard to find someone to survive as it is to survive alone. But it ain't only about other survivors, you will have to face other dificulties like hunger, thirst and (obviously) zombies. The zombies might be hard to kill since at this point in the game they aren't really perfect and some frustrating encounters might happen.
Don't forget 2 things tough; the game is a standalone version of the original sensation mod for Arma 2 so be ready to see a better version of it and the fact that the game is sold cheaper while it's Early Acess.
