Undertale shouldn’t be spoiled in advance. You’ve seen the score, you’ve seen from the screenshots that it’s a JRPG-style game, and I’ll tell you up front, it’s one of the funniest and best designed RPGs you’re likely to play this year. Beyond that, I’ll try to stay light on details—as much as I can while still telling you why it’s great—but avoid Google, avoid forums, avoid picking away at the scab of not knowing much. The less you know about Undertale before diving in, the better it can work its magic.
The basic secret is that it’s not entirely what it looks like: a goofy 8-bit RPG parody that owes a debt and at least two limbs to EarthBound/Mother. It’s partly that, sure, and it’s brilliant at it. After a slow and not particularly fun intro area, it opens up into a world more densely packed with jokes and puns and adorable characters than pretty much anything out there. Papyrus, the skeleton guard desperate for recognition and friends. His brother Sans, mocking RPG puzzles by just dumping a Junior Jumble to block your way. Crazy monsters like Woshua, who just wants you to be clean, and a ghost who only lowers his HP when you attack to be polite.
I haven’t laughed this hard at a game in years, and if Undertale was purely a joke RPG like Cthulhu Saves The World or Barkley Shut Up And Jam: Gaiden, it’d honestly be enough. Even its weaker moments where it veers too close to reference and inside joke oversaturation—the stuff of many a comedy RPG Maker game—just about work, if only because they’re always over quickly.
But that’s just what’s happening on the surface, and it’s disarming in just the right way. The cleverness builds as you play, and systems that originally seemed throw-away usually end up being more than they seem. The big gimmick is that nobody has to die: there are ways to spare everything and everybody, from the random monster encounters to the bosses. Combat plays out via a series of minigames, mostly unique to each monster, in which you move your pixel heart around in a small box—dodging bullets, blocking shots with shields, simple platforming, getting past shields, often layered to make things more complicated when you face off against multiple enemies at once.
As a really basic example of the mechanics being more than they seem, Undertale often uses them to convey the character’s mental state: faster attacks when they’re annoyed, bolder attacks when they’re feeling confident, or even aiming to miss when they don’t really want to fight. There’s the vegetable who just wants you to eat your greens and will leave you alone if you do. A late game encounter with a character who gets a mid-battle telegram from a previous zone to tell them that it’s cool, you’re a friend. Papyrus, who's so desperate to have cool attacks that he’s forgotten to actually make them deadly, and who's interrupted by a dog stealing the bones he intended to throw at you in his next turn.
How you choose to handle things affects how the story plays out. It also affects your replays, with Undertale interested in experimenting with what happens if certain characters remembered what you did the last time, and what the implication of that power might be. Finishing the story only takes about 5-7 hours, but to dig into its secrets takes another couple of loops, and a strong stomach. We’re also not just talking a few line changes. Going for a genocide run, where you murder literally everybody, essentially turns the whole thing into a pitch-black horror game. A peaceful run meanwhile leads to one of the most charming and heartfelt RPGs ever made. Murder followed by a reload to see what might have been… well, you get what you deserve.
You can spare the monsters. Not always their feelings. You can spare the monsters. Not always their feelings.
Undertale obviously has its faults, including a couple of puzzles that wear out their welcome, a first play that’s a little too easy to be satisfying, and occasionally relying a bit too much on players getting jokes like a jealous aircraft called the ‘Tsunderplane’. If you can’t stand those, or the JRPG style in general, it won’t likely win you over. Every player also seems to have one area that they dislike, though rarely the same one—for me it was the Hotlands, not because the action was bad, but because the puzzles were time consuming without being satisfying. Luckily, the same location also had one of my favourite characters, as well as one of Undertale’s best direct parodies.
To miss it though is to miss out. Undertale isn’t simply like Earthbound, like Chrono Trigger, like Final Fantasy VI in its graphical and mechanical style, but a worthy successor to the way they took the JRPG genre and experimented with it, evolved it, took it in new and interesting directions. It’s an old-school game, but one designed with modern sensibilities and an eye for deconstruction matched only by Knights Of The Old Republic 2’s brutal assault on the Star Wars universe.
The fact that this is basically a one-person project only makes it more impressive, from the excellent use of simple graphics to convey emotion, to the fantastic lo-fi soundtrack. It may or may not be the best RPG you play this year, but it’s certainly going to be one of the most worthwhile—as memorable as anything in, say, The Witcher 3, and every bit as worthy.
THE VERDICT

The single greatest storytelling experience made possible by gaming.  Undertaled has been reviewed by and approved by tens of thousands of players the world over, so saying something profound and new is unlikely at best.
Still, Toby Fox's creation is full to the brim with experiences that will surprise and change even the most veteran of RPGers.  No matter your background, Undertale is ready for you.  The experiences you have with the game will shift and change based on how you play.  You may laugh, you may cry, you may even experience emotions you never considered possible from this gaming genre.  The game is a mere 5-6 hours long at the most, made even shorter by being spoiled about how to best play the game by other people.
For anyone who reads this review, I strongly urge you to stop reading now and simply play the game.
Still, I imagine it's hard to just get up and walk away when gaming reviews are so prevalent these days.  But hunting for secrets and spoilers or discussions on the game's narrative and style will severely diminish your experience of the game.  No one playthrough of Undertale is the same because it draws so heavily on the player's Gaming Style, and that is what gives this charming game its magic.
It's akin to the commentary of the Toy Story films. Have you considered the "realness" of the video game worlds you visit?  In a game filled to the brim with the power of a true and impactful moral choice system, how will you respond when, as you stare into the great expanse of possibilities that gaming provide, the game stares back into you.
I close with this, ALL of the Endings of Undertale are TRUE Endings.  There is no CORRECT way to play this game, but if you are willing to explore the underground, you will find YOUR way to experience it.

Disclaimer: As you guys might know this game is early acess. Considering that I bought it with a clear warning that the game was unfinished I'll write my review ignoring all the bugs and problems I faced.
In this game you start as a fresh, newbie, zombie apocalypse survivor with a bunch of possibilities in front. You want to be a good person? You can! You want to be an outlaw? You also can! Want to be a mix of both? Why not!? Just remember the golden rule of DayZ, you die, you loose everything to the ground free for everyone to pick up (even you, if you are fast enough). It might be extremely frustating but it's all designed to be that way, you feel the need to survive in a way that no other game could do before it. The moral choices in this game are one of it's core components but beware since every other player will be able to choose them. It's as hard to find someone to survive as it is to survive alone. But it ain't only about other survivors, you will have to face other dificulties like hunger, thirst and (obviously) zombies. The zombies might be hard to kill since at this point in the game they aren't really perfect and some frustrating encounters might happen.
Don't forget 2 things tough; the game is a standalone version of the original sensation mod for Arma 2 so be ready to see a better version of it and the fact that the game is sold cheaper while it's Early Acess. The playability during the early acess is messy and you have trouble picking stuff from the ground, zombies are buggy and there are some hackers. If it's worth buying? I personaly don't regret it since I've been an DayZ enthusiast since the early Arma 2 Mod and I think the team behind it deserves it.
Overall: 7.5/10

DayZ consistently reminds you that simplicity creates the most potential. You will rediscover what the game is again and again, as your play style shifts from terrified scavenger to tactical adventurer. There is always something to do and there is always somewhere to go. As open and undefined as DayZ is, there is always a narrative with every new spawn. Sometimes you may begin on the East coast and work your way up North with little interaction, slowly becoming more equipped. Other times you will find yourself smack in Elektro or Cherno with gun shots firing and you hiding in the bushes waiting to scavenge the remains.
You will realize that in a post-apocalyptic world, the biggest threat is not the zombies, but the people. 9/10 times I have died by the hands of another, and each time I learn from my mistakes.
But your deaths are what drive you the next time around.
This game is hard. And down right terrifying a lot of times. But it is also incredibly rewarding. There is nothing more satisfying than finally getting that long scope for the Mosin, cooking with a fire in the wilderness, or working with a friend to fight a bandit (even if you end up dying). Whether you prefer to stick to the outskirts and live off the land, or test your luck looking for friends on the coast, there is always room for the unexpected. Things can and will change in an instant. And it is always a blast.

DayZ looks like fun, but it just boils down to a looting simulator where hours of boredom are punctuated by a brief moment of excitement before some guy guns you down for fun. I would really rather have my money back.
Apart from my problem with the premise of the game I also find that the development and maintenance is poorly done.
. Servers are laggy duplication glitches and hacks are pretty common
. The game runs poorly
. The game is not balanced correctly. By this I mean that depending on the patch, it may be too difficult to survive (like when they introduced freezing to death or made food spawns drop) or it may be too easy to get top gear.
. Sometimes on the second floor of buildings you fall through the floor and die
A seperate issue i'd like to talk about is the login/logout system. players can out whenever they like, but their character only disappears 20-30 seconds after they log out. this is to prevent someone from escaping combat by logging out.
. This system works, but only at close range. otherwise they duck behind cover and have enough time to log out
. Sometimes I log out and come back dead. It's possible I didn't know about a nearby player, but given the population of the servers at the time this is unlikely.
. I believe that being able to attack someone and log out when things get rough makes it a tempting option and icreases KOS and by extension the general suckage of the game.
edit:
A lot of people will hide behind the excuse that this game is in Early Access. Yes, but its been there too long. Keep in mind that they have your money, finishing the game isn't high on their priorities.
DayZ will probably go down in infamy for being the game with so much promise that was just never done.

I'm torn on whether to recommend Undertale. Undertale has clever, cute, funny and subversive moments that really stand out. When I was enjoying Undertale, I really enjoyed it. At the same time, the gameplay is weak and at times frustrating.
The game leans very hard on the characters, story, and the choices the player makes. The problem is what the player wants to do is often at odds with the gameplay. It's hard to say whether this was the intent of the developer or a flaw in the game design. There were multiple times that I nearly quit the game, but the story and character hooks were strong enough to keep me playing.
Since those hooks kept me playing until I beat the game twice, I give Undertale one, shakey thumbs-up.
An early problem with Undertale, is that the beginning area is slow, it's boring, and it takes longer than necessary to get through. After playing for about 45 minutes, I had nearly given up on the game. For a game that's probably 6-8 hours to complete, having to spend 45 minutes on poor puzzles and repetative combat is a bad sign.
At one point, I made a choice in the game that I regretted immediately. I hated the results of my choice. So, I save scummed. I save scummed and found an alternate solution, and the game called me out on the save scumming. It was clever and witty and I thought to myself, "These interactions are why people are raving about the game!" Unfortunately, these moments are very rare, and the lack of their use feels like wasted potential on the developer's part.
The characters and the story you create with them is where the game shines. There's a tongue-in-cheek silliness to most of the characters you meet. There are also characters that are irritating, and be prepared to be hit over the head with puns and running jokes. If you're enjoy silliness, then you'll likely enjoy Undertale.
Unfortunately, there's a barrier between making the most of interacting with the characters - tedious backtracking. Even with the limited fast-travel in the game, I spent a fair amount of time backtracking. The backtracking is a real shame, because some of the better interactions with the characters are hidden behind the need to do this. If you weren't aware, or simply aren't enough of a completionist to go back and talk to characters, you will miss out on story and funny interactions.
Combat is a weird mix of ideas that don't come together well. As the player you have four different options for how you interact with monsters in combat. Attacking opens a simple, time-based attack meter where your ability to time a button press impacts the damage dealt. Taking an action allows you to choose an action you wish to perform on the monster. Each monster has a different set of action options with certain actions working better than others. Using an item is almost exclusively healing your character (it's incredibly rare you'll have the opportunity to do anything else with an item). Showing mercy allows you to either show the monster mercy or flee. Upon choosing one of the options, the monster will generally react with an attack.
Monster attacks introduce you to a mini-bullet hell where you dodge their attacks by moving around the screen. This dodging mechanic is OK in small doses, but it quickly wears out it's welcome, especially on boss fights where you may end up replaying the battle many times. Even when the game changes up the rules for the bullet hell, it's rarely an enjoyable experience. I realize the game needed to include some mechanic to dodge attacks, but this is a situation where I wish the game subverted player expectations and eased up on the bullet hell. When a line of dialog is, "You've killed me X times already," then maybe the game needs to use that data in a clever way to make the dodge sequences more managable.
The puzzles are basic and generally uninteresting and uninspired. There is some humor around the puzzles that makes a few of them enjoyable, but this wears off pretty quickly. Other than as a running gag (I guess?), there's really no reason for them to be in the game.

Now, we've all heard that this game is apparently the "Best game ever made" according to online polls that put many classics head to head, and seeing that an indie game that was released only a few months ago had actually topped the charts, I couldn't help but buy this game, wondering what the fuss was about. Well, straight off the bat, is this the best game ever? The relevance of a game can make it the most popular, so is that why the game has received its title as the greatest game of all time? I don't think anyone can really say.
Everyone has different tastes, and this game is an RPG. RPG's are really well known to be story rich games with fantastic personalised gameplay, but like I said, it's not for everyone. I for one can play an RPG for about an hour before I realise that I don't like having too many choices to make at once, and go for a more linear experience.
This game however, surpassed all my expectations. It's the result of several faithful years of work from one man, and yes I know that he got some help with the art, but it's pretty much 99% his work. From the characters, to the writing, to even the freaking music! The music is amazing, and I will even go as far as to buy it on Steam. I thought that buying soundtracks on Steam was pointless, but now I can see why it's there.
The game takes inspiration from many JRPG's, and it's clear to see, even from someone who never plays them. While some RPG's (not all) have stories that are very serious and hard to stay focused on, this game has a comedic spin to it, which kept me coming back. All the characters are whacky and unique, and their text boxes/attacks reflect it. For instance, a character named 'Sans' speaks in Comic Sans.
I have to mention the fighting system in this game. Your life is represented as a red heart in a box. You must move the heart away from obstacles to avoid taking damage. Different enemies will have different attacks, and some of their attacks will deliberately miss you or troll you depending on their feelings towards you. You can ATTACK them, or ACT. Through acting, you can talk to the enemies, and convince them to stop fighting, and you can do that for the whole game. That's right, you can go through the whole game, and not kill anyone or gain any EXP. You can also kill everyone, which adds another layer to this game.
Now, the genocide route of the game deserves a separate review, because the tone is completely inverted. People are terrified of you, cheery locations are eerie and deserted, and anyone who dares to fight you is either trying to turn you back onto the right path, or wants to grind you to dust for what you have done. That bright and cheerful atmosphere of comedy and lightheartedness is completely removed and replaced with something that's rather unsettling. There is also many endings if you play the game neutrally, by killing some monsters while sparing others. And the game also uses your save files to recognise your choices in later playthroughs, which breaks the fourth wall. To go into that would ruin the game. It's a relatively short game, but there's a good reason for that. There are several endings, and 3 different ways to play the game (Pacifist, Neutral, and Genocide), so this game is designed to be played more than once. With every playthrough, dialogue changes, and the dark backstory that is covered up by a true pacifist run comes together. Make no mistake, this game is made to be played through more than one and even twice, but it still manages to be a great game with only one playthough.
The idea of making a game friendly and nice in one playthrough, and creepy and mysterious in another, is just fantastic. Not entirely original, but fantastic.
The game also has many little touches that some will appreciate, and others may even miss. For instance,
, and the name selection screen refuses to let you name your character after any of the game's bosses.
This game has some of the best boss fights I have ever seen, like seriously, there's at least 4 boss fights that are all shocking the first time you see them.
So, is this game the best game ever? I could say that this game is the best indie game ever made, but then I would be giving an opinion and claiming it to be a fact. Just play the game at least twice through (to experience the other endings), and keep an open mind. It didn't disappoint me, and I think that it truly deserves its fame.

Now, we've all heard that this game is apparently the "Best game ever made" according to online polls that put many classics head to head, and seeing that an indie game that was released only a few months ago had actually topped the charts, I couldn't help but buy this game, wondering what the fuss was about. Well, straight off the bat, is this the best game ever? The relevance of a game can make it the most popular, so is that why the game has received its title as the greatest game of all time? I don't think anyone can really say.
Everyone has different tastes, and this game is an RPG. RPG's are really well known to be story rich games with fantastic personalised gameplay, but like I said, it's not for everyone. I for one can play an RPG for about an hour before I realise that I don't like having too many choices to make at once, and go for a more linear experience.
This game however, surpassed all my expectations. It's the result of several faithful years of work from one man, and yes I know that he got some help with the art, but it's pretty much 99% his work. From the characters, to the writing, to even the freaking music! The music is amazing, and I will even go as far as to buy it on Steam. I thought that buying soundtracks on Steam was pointless, but now I can see why it's there.
The game takes inspiration from many JRPG's, and it's clear to see, even from someone who never plays them. While some RPG's (not all) have stories that are very serious and hard to stay focused on, this game has a comedic spin to it, which kept me coming back. All the characters are whacky and unique, and their text boxes/attacks reflect it. For instance, a character named 'Sans' speaks in Comic Sans.
I have to mention the fighting system in this game. Your life is represented as a red heart in a box. You must move the heart away from obstacles to avoid taking damage. Different enemies will have different attacks, and some of their attacks will deliberately miss you or troll you depending on their feelings towards you. You can ATTACK them, or ACT. Through acting, you can talk to the enemies, and convince them to stop fighting, and you can do that for the whole game. That's right, you can go through the whole game, and not kill anyone or gain any EXP. You can also kill everyone, which adds another layer to this game.
Now, the genocide route of the game deserves a separate review, because the tone is completely inverted. People are terrified of you, cheery locations are eerie and deserted, and anyone who dares to fight you is either trying to turn you back onto the right path, or wants to grind you to dust for what you have done. That bright and cheerful atmosphere of comedy and lightheartedness is completely removed and replaced with something that's rather unsettling. There is also many endings if you play the game neutrally, by killing some monsters while sparing others. And the game also uses your save files to recognise your choices in later playthroughs, which breaks the fourth wall. To go into that would ruin the game. It's a relatively short game, but there's a good reason for that. There are several endings, and 3 different ways to play the game (Pacifist, Neutral, and Genocide), so this game is designed to be played more than once. With every playthrough, dialogue changes, and the dark backstory that is covered up by a true pacifist run comes together. Make no mistake, this game is made to be played through more than one and even twice, but it still manages to be a great game with only one playthough.
The idea of making a game friendly and nice in one playthrough, and creepy and mysterious in another, is just fantastic. Not entirely original, but fantastic.
The game also has many little touches that some will appreciate, and others may even miss. For instance,
, and the name selection screen refuses to let you name your character after any of the game's bosses.
This game has some of the best boss fights I have ever seen, like seriously, there's at least 4 boss fights that are all shocking the first time you see them.
So, is this game the best game ever? I could say that this game is the best indie game ever made, but then I would be giving an opinion and claiming it to be a fact. Just play the game at least twice through (to experience the other endings), and keep an open mind. It didn't disappoint me, and I think that it truly deserves its fame.
Edit: Just adding this here so that I can get the steam achievement for updating a review that I nominated for an award.

OKAY, WOW I CAN'T BELIEVE I CAN FINALLY RECOMMEND THIS GAME.
It was a 1star out of 5 back in 2015-2016 now it's about a 3 star game. It lacks a lot of content but at least performance has improved and if you get lucky enough to find enough resources to survive, then great. I die a lot out of hunger/hypothermia before I even get to do anything like grow crops and really explore.
BUT BUT BUT
It was soooooo bad before. Performed like a dookie stain a year ago. So today, I can do a lot more and actually think of strategy because it actually performs adequately on even low-ish end GPU that I have now.
Today I get 72 avg FPS outside of town with 32 avg FPS inside medium villages or around large factory complexes on AMD R9 380 STRIX 4GB ( a gpu that performs right in the middle of GTX960-GTX970)
2560x1080 resolution 32bit color, VERY HIGH TEXTURES, HIGH FXAA antialiasing. Can be optimized to run better but I like it pretty and the standard settings work great.
Today I have a 3.3Ghz turbo 24 core xeon. Works great when assigned 3 or 4 cores. It nearly maxes out 3 real cores and more cores really won't make a difference, but 1 or 2 cores will be a bottleneck as I tested.
In theory it should still run ok on a dual core with HT but 4 real cores are more preferable over 2 real and 2 logical. When I tried simulating a dual core with HT on my xeon by using onlt those respective threads for the game, it actually worked just as well as 4 real core scenarios worked and it took full advantage of GPU.
Hope this gave you guys an insight on performance. Definetly pick this game up when it's under $20 as that's about all it's worth at this point in development, and don't go in having too many expectation.
Your experience won't be quite as those explosive youtube videos you see. Those people are basically entertainment professionals and could make you think even a pile of pooh looks amazing. But if you have smaller expectations, like you just want to stay alive, run from a zombie or two, grind to get good, then you can have fun.
And for the love of GOD if you are new, here is a tip, don't get stuck behind obstacles that you cant climb out of...I got stuck between two buildings and my only choice was to jump off to die. Yay.

It's so hard to do a review of this game because you can't say anything else other than what it made you feel; you can't and shouldn't play this, knowing even a little about the game. You have to go in blind, absolutely no spoilers, you have to play it as if it was your first game ever: Without knowing what a game is or what it wants you to do. It's impossible to write anything about it without spoiling even a single thing the game has to offer.
After 10000+ hours or so in my MMO's, 7000+ hours of other mundane games and total combined hours on Steam, being burned out isn't such a weird thing to expect; However. This game is everything a game is, should and ever will be; it reminds us as to why we love videogames and why we played them.
It's hard to say what the best game you ever played might be or was, since sometimes it's based on what is 'currently' your best game; but also because of the enjoyment it gave you. Undertale invokes so many things it's hard to say anything without trying it for yourself.
I have played a lot of games, a lot, many more so outside of steam. I can with ease say, that this will forever be with me as the most impactful experience I have ever had in a videogame. This is without a doubt the best game I have ever played in my life right now and it is impossible to see any game ever live up to what it made me feel.
It is so much more, I already said it, but this experience is one I will never forget.

I have played a lot of games, a lot, many more so outside of steam. I can with ease say, that this will forever be with me as the most impactful experience I have ever had in a videogame. This is without a doubt the best game I have ever played in my life right now and it is impossible to see any game ever live up to what it made me feel.
It is so much more, I already said it, but this experience is one I will never forget.

Overall.. quite an enjoyable game that is really hard to get a decent foothold on if you play by yourself. I spent all my game time just trying to estabilsh basic stuff for my charater only to wind up with something horrible happening to my character which results in death. Either a player, animal, starvation or cold kill you off. When this happens you lose all of your stuff and have to start up again trying to acheive the same thing.
It is a survial that uses a crafting system to try and create homes and things with the resources available to them. How you aquire these resouces varies and requires players to study the base list to find the best stategy to getting the items they want to make. After a short while you learn where you can get resources you need. Also helps to watch youtube videos to find out what else you can use.
The fort building system is the highlight as it allows players to build whatever they want in whatever stategic method they choose. As long as you reinfoce your fort beyond it's inital twig material, your home should hold together against most attack. No fort is perfect and can be destroyed by a determined enough opponent. If you die, you lose your key and lose access to your house. You wind up filling the game with ghost houses that can be no long accessed by thier orignal owners.
The players themselves are awful as most hate newbies and often kill them for sport.  Even the newbies themselves hate each other as they will kill each other given the chance. There are nice people that you can encounter but they are few and far between and you should try add them to your steam list if you find them. Otherwise you can't really trust most people and should avoid being seen by them.
Easily the most frustrating is the hunting with animals being able to clip though solid rock and thus becoming impossible to hunt. I've had to settle for boars and chicken until I can get enough cloth for a bow assumeing I can live long enough aquire it.
Some will also find it frustrating to lose all their stuff after death, however, if you use a sleeping bag then it can aleivate some of the stress by spawing back to your clans headquarters where you can restock. For loners however, it's back to the drawing board banging trees and rocks before you rebuild again.
If you can get the latter protion of the game then it does look like alot of fun. Base raids look fantastic and fun to play. I haven't gotton close to it yet but maybe I will if I find a nice enough clan to join.
So bottom line, presuade friend to play this with you as you will otherwise need to be very cunning to play by yourself.

So I guess I will write a review on a game I keep coming back to, Rust is my crack. With over 2k hours put into this game and playing from Legacy to the most current build, I still can't stop.  =]\
♥♥♥♥♥ if you want about early access for 2 years but the Developers are constantly updating the community on where they are at and what what is new and being worked on.
Whenever I explain Rust it usually goes like, "I'm a naked dude with a Rock, and I go around and kill other naked dudes with Rocks..." It's that and so much more, I enjoy building bases and the pvp aspect, but in it's essence it's a survival game where you start off naked with a rock, and that's it. By gathering resources and doing some searching you can make basic tools, building materials and weapons, oh and don't forget clothes, need to cover up your junk. You eventually learn better weapons, and items, build a base or♥♥♥♥♥♥hut,  join groups of other like-minded individuals and go out and rek fools.
The official servers are tough, be warned. Make friends, place a sleeping bag by a road or radtown and just go on blueprint runs till you learn enough to get established. Some must learns are hatchet, pickaxe, any gun except the eoka pistol, still blows. Check out the modded servers for extra resources, teleporting, setting home, insta crafting, kits and more to make learning a little bit easier. And not as bad when you log in dead, base raided and all your♥♥♥♥♥♥gone.

Rust: Single handedly the most fun survival game to play, IF you have friends to play with. Without friends you're an easy target. I found that most people are willing to help you out. Larger population servers are meat grinders. I spawned and died so many times because people would wait to get the kills.
Since FacePunch is finally nearly done with Alpha I can't wait to see what kind of optomizaitons they're going to do. My PC runs it like its nothing. My Surface Pro3 runs it like it's nothing as well. Great game!
ProTip: Play with friends to have the best experience.
StayAway: Don't go into a game thinking you're going to dominate. This game has a way of killing you at the most inopportune times.

At times myself, I smashed my desk asking myself why did I do that? You may ask yourself, "Why would I want to join a game as deadly as Rust?" The answer is simple, this game has thrills that some games barely perfect. When you are camping in a bush and hear footsteps all around you, hoping the enemy won't notice you, and then he does. So you have to fight like hell, to make sure its not you. Not many games have this thrill I seek. Yes some games have better graphics and better quality, but for what your getting, is something entirely better. The community is one of the best, because the staff listens to the community and there is an update every month or so. Some higher end companies have nothing compared to Rust of how the staff listen to us. If you do buy this game the best advice I have for you is this, trust everyone, but at the same time trust no one.

Most steam reviews for DayZ Standalone are very angry about a seemingly indefinite alpha, and with good reason. However, I think I'm going to be somewhat unbiased and review DayZ in it's current build as I would any other game. So far, the game's main mechanics are starting to take shape, and I'm saying you should buy this based on just how deep it is even in alpha.
First of all, like it's ArmA mod predecessor, there's heavy emphasis on realism in ballistics, player movement, and inventory management. The UI isn't counter intuitive like ArmA 2, and sorting your inventory and managing primary needs is a breeze. Ammo is commonly not found in magazines, making reloading a hectic chore in frantic PVP engagements.
With elements like heat, hunger, cold, disease, weight, and even clothing condition being vital to survival, there are many ways for the player to die. If you kill a player but he is without any food, you can butcher and cook his flesh and cannibalize him. One of the many ways in which DayZ steals my heart is it's brutal unforgiving atmosphere. Your hand certainly is NOT held at any point. The game rewards those who take advantage of the weak and those who have the will to fight back against all odds. It's a hostile, unforgiving gameplay is marred by one near-fatal flaw.
Bugs are rampant in DayZ. From low frames to disappearing items, you will become infuriated at times. That being said, I haven't really encountered any game-breakers yet.
All in all, good time waster with friends on a rainy day, shaping out to be a real nice game upon release (if it ever is released.)

Short Version: Infinite Alpha! Loot and Shoot! Banditoes... Banditoes everywhere...
Genuine Version: DayZ is the type of game that takes a while to get used to, but when you do, it becomes much easier. Starting out, I thought having a Crowbar and a Trumpet was good... Now I'm running around with Mosins, AK's, Aug's MP5's, Etc... Of course however, here are some things that I like, and dislike about DayZ
Likes:
Zombies: Without these undead ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, the game would be dull. It would be more like a world wide death match rather than a Zombie Survival game. Of course, zombies don't feel too overpowered or underpowered. They hit you A LOT giving you a lot of panic, they can cause bleeding easily, but at the same time, they still die the way you would expect them to.
Towns: The way certain towns are set up make me cringe, but with others, it's like being in heaven. Zelenogorsk is a very good example. I've been in Zelenogorsk for about... 4 days? Real days, with my friends. Zeleno has both a School for clothing, Houses and vehicles for food, Hunting stands for scopes, and a Military area for guns and ammo. Not to mention there is a Water Pump at the school, so you have an infinite water supply.
Equipment (Guns+Clothing+Etc): The guns in this game, sadly renamed due to copyright issues, look and feel like they should. What I noticed about DayZ as opposed to 90% of other FPS's is that the sounds of guns are VERY loud, making a lot of guns sound about the same, but still being that gun. You can clearly tell the difference between an AK74 and an SKS when you hear one in Cherno.
Other People: Being alone in the zombie apocalypse is no fun, which is why being able to meet randoms and befriend them is awesome. Course maybe you two are planning on betraying eachother, but who cares?
Dislikes:
Technical Difficulties (Like all the time!): One big issue with DayZ being in Alpha all the time is that the game has A LOT of problems. Prior to .57, logging out in 2 story buildings, without access to the one below would result in being forever stuck under the house, forcing you to kill yourself. Another problem is the "Signature Check Timed Out" which my friend is ALWAYS running into, atleast 7-8 times before being able to stay connected long enough to play. Other issues include zombies clipping through doors, certain houses not spawning loot, zombies hitting you from nowhere, and inventory issues such as not being able to equip anything into your hands or move object from the ground to your inventory.
Traveling: This is probably the one thing that most players of hardcore FPS's will avoid because it is tedious as all hell. This game is pretty much the running simulator of 2015, 90% of the game is holding SHIFT + W, I've almost worn the plastic on both keys just from holding them down for so long so much. Trucks only spawn in certain given locations, nowhere near where played spawn, making it very hard to actually progress quickly. The only thing you can hope to do is have a LOT of patience.
Bandits: This one is more based on people rather than the game. Playing on empty servers does not make you good at the game, of course however if you are like me, you like to meet up with friends first, then go to servers with people, then that's fine as long as you don't go to high loot areas. But of course, with every high populated servers, comes THOSE guys. You know those guys, the ones who even shoot new spawns because they think they're cool. Bandits are really just in-communicative♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥who don't know how to help others because their mommies bought them the game. But of course, with every Bandit comes every Hero. If you're like me, anyone I witness shooting at someone is my official target. When meeting new spawns, I give them some food and if I have one, a weapon (Minus ammo of course, trust issues).
Lag: This one is more or less based on my PERSONAL experience with the game, rather than general. My computer isn't the best, so of course I will have issues. Lag of course is the primary, and mostly only issue I have. You would think that having everything set to the lowest possible setting on a Gaming Laptop would do you any good, and it does, however I still have constant lag spikes lasting from either 5-45 seconds. Kind of agrivating.
Falling Damage: This one... Ooohhh boy. Listen Dean Hall, Just because I fell 5 feet doesn't mean I ruined my boots, and my pants. Seriously, it's like Earth's gravity x10, falling 5 feet damn near kills you in this game, or atleast, used to. in .56, falling that far would break your legs, ruin your pants and your shoes, and you would pretty much be screwed from all directions. In .57, now your shoes become Badly Damaged and your pants become Damaged based on how far you fell. But seriously, please be a little bit more realistic with your falling damage.
With all the pros and cons this game has, I would say that it is probably the best multiplayer survival game currently on the market.

I'd just like to interject for a moment. What you’re referring to as Linux, is in fact, GNU/Linux, or as I’ve recently taken to calling it, GNU plus Linux. Linux is not an operating system unto itself, but rather another free component of a fully functioning GNU system made useful by the GNU corelibs, shell utilities and vital system components comprising a full OS as defined by POSIX.
Many computer users run a modified version of the GNU system every day, without realizing it. Through a peculiar turn of events, the version of GNU which is widely used today is often called “Linux”, and many of its users are not aware that it is basically the GNU system, developed by the GNU Project. There really is a Linux, and these people are using it, but it is just a part of the system they use.
Linux is the kernel: the program in the system that allocates the machine’s resources to the other programs that you run. The kernel is an essential part of an operating system, but useless by itself; it can only function in the context of a complete operating system. Linux is normally used in combination with the GNU operating system: the whole system is basically GNU with Linux added, or GNU/Linux. All the so-called “Linux” distributions are really distributions of GNU/Linux.

Overall.. quite an enjoyable game that is really hard to get a decent foothold on if you play by yourself. I spent all my game time just trying to estabilsh basic stuff for my charater only to wind up with something horrible happening to my character which results in death. Either a player, animal, starvation or cold kill you off. When this happens you lose all of your stuff and have to start up again trying to acheive the same thing.
It is a survial that uses a crafting system to try and create homes and things with the resources available to them. How you aquire these resouces varies and requires players to study the base list to find the best stategy to getting the items they want to make. After a short while you learn where you can get resources you need. Also helps to watch youtube videos to find out what else you can use.
The fort building system is the highlight as it allows players to build whatever they want in whatever stategic method they choose. As long as you reinfoce your fort beyond it's inital twig material, your home should hold together against most attack. No fort is perfect and can be destroyed by a determined enough opponent. If you die, you lose your key and lose access to your house. You wind up filling the game with ghost houses that can be no long accessed by thier orignal owners.
The players themselves are awful as most hate newbies and often kill them for sport.  Even the newbies themselves hate each other as they will kill each other given the chance. There are nice people that you can encounter but they are few and far between and you should try add them to your steam list if you find them. Otherwise you can't really trust most people and should avoid being seen by them.
Easily the most frustrating is the hunting with animals being able to clip though solid rock and thus becoming impossible to hunt. I've had to settle for boars and chicken until I can get enough cloth for a bow assumeing I can live long enough aquire it.
Some will also find it frustrating to lose all their stuff after death, however, if you use a sleeping bag then it can aleivate some of the stress by spawing back to your clans headquarters where you can restock. For loners however, it's back to the drawing board banging trees and rocks before you rebuild again.
If you can get the latter protion of the game then it does look like alot of fun. Base raids look fantastic and fun to play. I haven't gotton close to it yet but maybe I will if I find a nice enough clan to join.
So bottom line, presuade friend to play this with you as you will otherwise need to be very cunning to play by yourself.

I feel like there's no shortage of praise for this game so even though I did enjoy it immensely I'm going to try to focus on being as objectively critical as I can. I will try to keep it spoiler free.
The story was, for me, the best part of the game though admittedly once you distance yourself from it a bit it is a little basic. Most of its impact comes from emotional highs, especially at the end, so you might not like it if you're someone who isn't easily emotionally moved or who doesn't care for that sort of thing. The story does have some twists and this is a game that loves to play with your expectations but I don't feel the revelations are the reason you'll remember it. The story is all about emotion. Whether or not that appeals to you should be your determining factor in buying this game.
Its humor might end up being the biggest turn off for some people. Not all of it works, and it is a little... internet-y, but personally I found that it didn't detract much from the game as a whole. The humor that did work was enjoyable and what didn't work never really became obnoxious, but for something as subjective as humor this will be different for everyone so it's probably the most understandable reason to not enjoy the game.
On the game play side of things the combat is sort of a combination of a traditional rpg with bullet hell dodging mechanics when you're being attacked. Its challenging and original even though it is technically two old things taped together. It's not incredible, but it is fun and I appreciate the effort put into it when Toby Fox could have easily thrown in standard RPG combat and called it a day.
However, the fact that the battles are initiated with Pokémon-style random-encounters-from-nowhere does get old fast, more so when they happen in the middle of a puzzle. I should also add that it can sometimes be unclear how to beat a character without killing them. For most of the monsters, figuring this out is the entire point, but some cross the line into "how the ♥♥♥♥ was I supposed to know that?" territory, most notably Undyne and Toriel. In both cases you have to repeatedly do the same action which (for the first few times) gives very little indication that it's actually working. This might have just been me being an idiot but it did stick with me as one of my biggest gripes with the game.
The puzzles were a personal low point for me. Sometimes they just felt time consuming rather than challenging, other times they just felt like they didn't need to be there at all. The puzzles that I did enjoy tended to be closely involved with the dialogue or not taken seriously, such as the ones with mettaton and alphys, or the earlier ones with Papyrus.
With Toby's track record it was no surprise that the sound design of this game is exceptional. The music is undeniably fantastic on its own but the implementation takes it to a new level. The way he combines sound and visuals for greater emotional effect is immaculate and I applaud him for knowing when to turn the music off when the tone demands it. One of the best soundtracks in years and I feel it's a testament to Toby's skill that the soundtrack feels more complete when you're hearing it in the game itself.
Despite some issues that are ultimately minor, I still feel that whether you like this game or not will come down to personal taste rather than flaws in the game itself. Its humor definitely won't appeal to everyone, and the more emotional parts are likewise going to mean more to some than to others. But despite that I'd still feel confident recommending this game to anyone. This is a refreshingly heartfelt and genuine game, a rare gem that deserves to be experienced.

Rust is probably one of the greatest games I've ever played. A while back I watched a video that described Rust as a social experiment, which I totally agree with. On the vanilla servers, as in the ones without mods/plugins, you might find people spending hours gathering resouces to build their wet dream base with traps and towers to shoot out of. The building has stability to it, so you can't really have floating buildings and you have to take into account things like pillars and such.
Raiding is probably the most amazing thing about Rust. Even though nothing in the game is scripted or setup, people form teams and organize their own raids with strategies and all these layers to their plan. In one of my experiences, me and 3 of my friends were scoping out this base with an absolutely massive tower in the middle. Suddenly some people in the tower were shooting at us, and since they had the higher ground we couldn't really fight back. Then we waited for them to go offline, and we came back with tons of explosives and we blew out the base of their tower, causing the whole thing to explode into thousands of bits of rubble. I remember sitting there, laughing while being showered in the remains of their tower. It was epic.

TLDR @ bottom of page
------
#OperationEA
This is our chance.
It's time we put an end to this scheme. It's time for the community to come together and make a stand.
It is very clear that the Early-Acess model is overall a money grab. It is a system that is SUPPOSED to help the developers create a finished game that the players will enjoy. However, I have yet to see an Early Access game go in the right direction so far.
It's not the developers fault, its the system. Because in the end, money makes the world go around.
Let's stop and think about this for a second. What reason do the developers need to finish a game when the companies have already made their money? A negligible percentage of the companies out there will actually waste their time and effort finishing a game when they've already made their money.
The Early Access system needs to change and to me, its simple. Game design companies from a business standpoint need to know that there is something in it for them to actually finish their product. I would GLADLY pay for a finished product and I know a lot of gamers out there would too.
So here's what needs to happen in order to promote a good environment for both the business and consumer-
When purchasign a game title for Early Access, Steam simply needs to sell the game for Early Access and then sell the game once again when there is a finished product. That is the Game studio's incentive! For most of the Early Access games I have played it would be as simply as splitting the price of the game in half! OR charge the same price, if it was a finished product I would pay!
It's up to us as a community to bring this to the attention of Steam. I know they understand the issues we have, because its evident in all of our reviews for almost every single Early Access. But this is something Steam can actually implement and take responsibility for.
Please share!
TLDR:
Steam needs to implement a purchase system that allows us to buy the game for Early Access and then after, when the game is finished. Maybe a contract with the game studio to sell the game half price now and half price later. Incentivising production.

Possibly the most overrated game ever, it's good don't get me wrong, but it surely doesn't live on the insane hype it has.
It's really original in its concept and that alone makes it a good game, it has some good plot twist and meaningful decisions, the gameplay works, with great musics and for the most part good atmosphere, it's a solid 4h experience with replay value but nothing more.
People are seriously claming it's the best game ever, you mean you want to compare this to stuff like "Final Fantasy VII", "Half-Life 2", "Metal Gear Solid", "Chrono Trigger", "Deus Ex", "Ocarina of Time" ... ? Are you joking ?
Let's start with the claim that you can play it however you want, you will always find stuff that changes and different stuff to do .... mmmm no, the only "real" way to play this game is the "true pacifist", that's obviously the intended way the developer wanted you to go through the game, the other playthroughs present different changes but it's nothing so big like in the true pacifist ( many lines of different dialogues and a whole new "dungeon" to explore ), some characters will say some different lines or some event won't happen, in one there's an additional boss, sorry but that's not enough to justify that you will have a total different experience.
Other than the approach with the characters, the game is pretty shallow in its content, there are really few items to equip or use, few locations to explore and the "act" option is original but the fight is trivial as hell ( another example of how the game is shaped to be played on pacifist ).
While i liked the artstyle and themes it's notable a lack of quality of ambients and locations during the second half of the game (hotland onward), knowing the engine i appreciate the way stuff is done at the beginning ( the fact that you read the story of the underground from writings with amazing music on the background for example ) but later on it's clear that it doesn't have the same meticulousness.
Gameplay wise apparently people never knew what bullet hell games are ... I liked how it's implemented in the rpg mechanics but that's all, reading what people say on the internet it seems it's the best inovation since the invention of the weel ...
Quoting from a review on metacritic :
"The Stanley Parable deconstructed gameplay mechanics and the nature of player decisions in a far more meaningful way. Spec Ops: The Line had more to say and contemplate on senseless killing than a genocide run of Undertale."
The game is artistic and i can't negate that, it's not some hipster fake game, but it's not that deep either, i recently played "Lisa" which i highly recoment, that game with its dark themes and morbid humor made me feel more engaged and care more for the fate of the characters and the world than "Undertale".

It will make you laugh, it may even make you cry. The music will inspire. The characters are much more interesting and nuanced than they seem.
You should really play it.
And really, despite temptation, don't kill anyone. Or do, I'm not a cop. But you will probably regret it.
This game may emotionally mark you in ways you are not prepared.

I've played this game enough times to become familiar with it and I've had my ups and downs. When you first start out, you need to find some food first and a weapon too. You won't be able to hunt anything to start with so you'll have to scavenge. this used to be reasonable, after a few houses you would find some food. Now though, server's have been looted so much that all that remains is junk, and very very little food. So you'll have to try and survive of apple trees and berry bushes. Searching in these becomes a painfully long progress. You'll need a weapon too, because you can't just stand around with zombies walking around, you will have to take at least one out.
So, you're still alive. Well, you're not hungry anymore, but you can't just stand at an apple tree all day looking for apples, so it's time to move on. You'll need to deal with thirst as well as hunger, so drink up at a well. You could try a pond, stream or river, but you might get sick. Best to stick with a well. Now it's time to leave your current place behind and go to some small lonely town up a dirt road. Because that's the sort of place people don't go to often, there's nothing good in those places, except for the canned food which spawns pretty much everywhere. However, there should be some here in this lonely town. So you go to this lonely town, well if you want to stock up on food, you'll need better gear. That's easy enough to come across at the start, you just need a hoodie or a wool coat. Cargo pants help too. If you're lucky you'll find a backpack, vest or the means to make a backpack. So, after killing yet more zombies and slowly losing more blood your screen is that irritating grey from blood loss, your almost out of rags and your cloths are damaged. But know you have some supplies for the longer journey. That or you're dead and you've just started over.
And so the longer part of your travels begins. You need better gear, so of to the larger towns with the better loot spots, such as fire stations, police stations and hospitals. Through out this time you'll be attacked by zombies, you'll need to replace your gear as you go along and repair what you can. So, now you've got some better stuff; medium sized backpack, wood cutting gear, bullets and a gun which uses other bullets you don't have. that or you've died.
So, know you're ready for some great gear or setting up a camp. A camp means nothing without a tent to store items in as you can create a fireplace anywhere you find a tree, which is everywhere. So, go get some military gear. Wait, don't bother, those places have already been looted to their bear bones, you'll want another server that doesn't have persistence for that. So you might get killed on the other server or you'll have to do without that loot.
Now, if you find a tent you'll want to set up a camp great! This is a great thing to be able to do. Except if you die you can say good-bye to your camp and everything with it. That's right if you die, and you will at some point, you'll have to start again from scratch. This just adds to the game when you die from something new or a mistake you made. But when you die because you were forced into a conflict with a zombie or because a sniper was watching the building you entered, or even if other players just shoot first you get tired of starting again and again. You'd expect that each time you die you'll have learnt something for the next time you try that again. In the latter cases the answer is no. Zombies will attack you, players will shoot at you. A single hit can kill you even if you are fully armoured and filled to the brim on health.
So, this game is enjoyable when you first start because it gives you a challenge to overcome. However, when you die for the 500th time, or so, you are no longer overcoming a new challenge, you are instead failing to the same challenge over and over. What breaks things, is that you can't change anything about this challenge. There's no way around a zombie being able to one hit you and you not being able to do that without having a high powered weapon. You used to be able to kill a zombie with a fireaxe with one swing, now it's anywhere between 2 and 10 swings. Shooting a zombie works provided you have the ammo to do so. In the stages I've given above, that doesn't happen until stage 4 or you got lucky. During that entire time you could have been killed by something well beyond your control. Maybe you could run away, but you'd normally have to run to the next town before anything, AI or player, decides to stop giving chase. when you run wildly into a town you end up with the same problem that you just left behind.
Given this game is still early access, it's got bugs and glitches to sort out. However I haven't seen any in a while, nor am I judging the game on it's bugs and glitches as it isn't finished yet. For me, without a group of friends to help you when things go bad, this game causes more grievances then good times.
So, my advice to anyone thinking of buying this game, either wait until it's at or near full release or get a group of friends to join you. If you've already got the game, see if any friends will join you or just keep and eye on it to see what updates it comes with. If you're not thinking about buying this game and are reading reviews for other reasons. I would advice against buying this game on the off-chance you like the sound of it from one of the reviews. It's not all gold digging, there's a lot of sour moments to get over.

Possibly the most overrated game ever, it's good don't get me wrong, but it surely doesn't live on the insane hype it has.
It's really original in its concept and that alone makes it a good game, it has some good plot twist and meaningful decisions, the gameplay works, with great musics and for the most part good atmosphere, it's a solid 4h experience with replay value but nothing more.
People are seriously claming it's the best game ever, you mean you want to compare this to stuff like "Final Fantasy VII", "Half-Life 2", "Metal Gear Solid", "Chrono Trigger", "Deus Ex", "Ocarina of Time" ... ? Are you joking ?
Let's start with the claim that you can play it however you want, you will always find stuff that changes and different stuff to do .... mmmm no, the only "real" way to play this game is the "true pacifist", that's obviously the intended way the developer wanted you to go through the game, the other playthroughs present different changes but it's nothing so big like in the true pacifist ( many lines of different dialogues and a whole new "dungeon" to explore ), some characters will say some different lines or some event won't happen, in one there's an additional boss, sorry but that's not enough to justify that you will have a total different experience.
Other than the approach with the characters, the game is pretty shallow in its content, there are really few items to equip or use, few locations to explore and the "act" option is original but the fight is trivial as hell ( another example of how the game is shaped to be played on pacifist ).
While i liked the artstyle and themes it's notable a lack of quality of ambients and locations during the second half of the game (hotland onward), knowing the engine i appreciate the way stuff is done at the beginning ( the fact that you read the story of the underground from writings with amazing music on the background for example ) but later on it's clear that it doesn't have the same meticulousness.
Gameplay wise apparently people never knew what bullet hell games are ... I liked how it's implemented in the rpg mechanics but that's all, reading what people say on the internet it seems it's the best inovation since the invention of the weel ...
Quoting from a review on metacritic :
"The Stanley Parable deconstructed gameplay mechanics and the nature of player decisions in a far more meaningful way. Spec Ops: The Line had more to say and contemplate on senseless killing than a genocide run of Undertale."
The game is artistic and i can't negate that, it's not some hipster fake game, but it's not that deep either, i recently played "Lisa" which i highly recoment, that game with its dark themes and morbid humor made me feel more engaged and care more for the fate of the characters and the world than "Undertale".

It will make you laugh, it may even make you cry. The music will inspire. The characters are much more interesting and nuanced than they seem.
You should really play it.
And really, despite temptation, don't kill anyone. Or do, I'm not a cop. But you will probably regret it.
This game may emotionally mark you in ways you are not prepared.

Undertale is a 2015 game released independently on Steam by Toby Fox. If you had not heard of Undertale last year, I don't even know how. Every YouTube gamer was doing it, and myself personally never watched anything. After my lack of inspiration to play RPGs over my personally disappointing Fallout 4, I decided I would give Undertale a go, considering I heard so many good things about it and was looking for something new to play. However, what I got was a gem of a game unlike any other game I played in 2015, perhaps unlike anything I've ever played in my life.
You play as a young child, who has fallen into the Underground, a place where humans locked up all monsters many, many years ago. You are swiftly met by Toriel (who is quite obviously a play on words of tutorial) who runs you through the basics of the game. However, to go back home, Toriel reveals you must cross through the barrier to go back home. The only way to do this is by obtaining seven human souls. Six of these have already been obtained by the king, Asgore, who wants to free monsters from the underground, and will kill you to do it. To set out on your journey, you must defeat Toriel one way or another, and can choose to spare her or kill her, which is the same with all battles in Undertale. You then set out on your journey into the Underground, meeting various characters throughout, solving puzzles and fighting your way to the end.
The story itself might not be the most complex story ever, but what truly makes it are the characters and the choices you have to make. There are three ways to play this game:
1. The True Pacifist Route, where you don't kill anybody.
2. The Neutral Route, where maybe you kill a few monsters here and there but balance it.
3. The Genocide Route, where
The choices you make deepen the story, where a decision you make at the beginning easily affects the outcome of the game later, but you wouldn't know otherwise, which is the genius of the game.
All the characters are also really well written, although the way that the dialogue happens can be annoying if the character keepings messaging you constantly.
Undertale is a very interesting game in terms of it's battle system. Instead of opting for some sort of side-scrolling, original-Zelda-esque system with swords, it plays more like Pokemon, for lack of a better comparison. You choose an option, which does not have to always be combat by any means. You can fight, which is to hurt your combatant(s), act, which is to try charm, plead, seduce, flirt, etc., etc.... there are a lot of ways to act, which can usaully be used to win over the affection of combatants. There is also items, which is for healing and more damage midfight and spare. If an enemy is low on HP, you can choose to instead spare them rather than kill them. You can also flee, if possible.
Gameplay is often one of the best parts of Undertale, deciding if you're going to kill the combatant or leave them, wondering what effect it could possibly have on the game.
I won't talk about the music in this game for long, since I won't be able to write about it for very long. But the music in this game is fantastic. Every song fits the mood of the area you're walking through, the thrill of a fight against a large enemy or the sorrow of a sad area. Paired with the plot in this game that can make you feel something, the music, and sometimes lack of, really adds to the game.
Undertale is without a doubt one of the best games I've ever played. The game is overflowing with charm, heart and humour. The story is great, mainly because of the decisions you make and how they affect the story in the long run. Undertale is a deeply thoughtful, charming and emotionally challenging game, in more ways than one.
Pros:

-Great visuals for a pixelated game
-The music is the best. I'm going to buy the soundtrack.

Undertale is a 2015 game released independently on Steam by Toby Fox. If you had not heard of Undertale last year, I don't even know how. Every YouTube gamer was doing it, and myself personally never watched anything. After my lack of inspiration to play RPGs over my personally disappointing Fallout 4, I decided I would give Undertale a go, considering I heard so many good things about it and was looking for something new to play. However, what I got was a gem of a game unlike any other game I played in 2015, perhaps unlike anything I've ever played in my life.
You play as a young child, who has fallen into the Underground, a place where humans locked up all monsters many, many years ago. You are swiftly met by Toriel (who is quite obviously a play on words of tutorial) who runs you through the basics of the game. However, to go back home, Toriel reveals you must cross through the barrier to go back home. The only way to do this is by obtaining seven human souls. Six of these have already been obtained by the king, Asgore, who wants to free monsters from the underground, and will kill you to do it. To set out on your journey, you must defeat Toriel one way or another, and can choose to spare her or kill her, which is the same with all battles in Undertale. You then set out on your journey into the Underground, meeting various characters throughout, solving puzzles and fighting your way to the end.
The story itself might not be the most complex story ever, but what truly makes it are the characters and the choices you have to make. There are three ways to play this game:
1. The True Pacifist Route, where you don't kill anybody.
2. The Neutral Route, where maybe you kill a few monsters here and there but balance it.
3. The Genocide Route, where
The choices you make deepen the story, where a decision you make at the beginning easily affects the outcome of the game later, but you wouldn't know otherwise, which is the genius of the game.
All the characters are also really well written, although the way that the dialogue happens can be annoying if the character keepings messaging you constantly.
Undertale is a very interesting game in terms of it's battle system. Instead of opting for some sort of side-scrolling, original-Zelda-esque system with swords, it plays more like Pokemon, for lack of a better comparison. You choose an option, which does not have to always be combat by any means. You can fight, which is to hurt your combatant(s), act, which is to try charm, plead, seduce, flirt, etc., etc.... there are a lot of ways to act, which can usaully be used to win over the affection of combatants. There is also items, which is for healing and more damage midfight and spare. If an enemy is low on HP, you can choose to instead spare them rather than kill them. You can also flee, if possible.
Gameplay is often one of the best parts of Undertale, deciding if you're going to kill the combatant or leave them, wondering what effect it could possibly have on the game.
I won't talk about the music in this game for long, since I won't be able to write about it for very long. But the music in this game is fantastic. Every song fits the mood of the area you're walking through, the thrill of a fight against a large enemy or the sorrow of a sad area. Paired with the plot in this game that can make you feel something, the music, and sometimes lack of, really adds to the game.
Undertale is without a doubt one of the best games I've ever played. The game is overflowing with charm, heart and humour. The story is great, mainly because of the decisions you make and how they affect the story in the long run. Undertale is a deeply thoughtful, charming and emotionally challenging game, in more ways than one.
Pros:
-Combat system
-Story
-Characters full of life and humour
-Great visuals for a pixelated game
-The music is the best. I'm going to buy the soundtrack.
Cons:
-Some annoyances with constant dialogue from characters
If you've ever thought about buying this game and haven't been sure. Let this be the review that sways you.
Overall score: 10/10

Positives:
+ The game is filled with very likable characters! Even the bosses you fight and monsters you randomly encounter have enough funny dialogue that you’ll start to like them.
+ The combat system is unique and entertaining.
+ You can interact with different objects in your surroundings to see what your character thinks of them. But unlike other rpgs, Undertale doesn’t waste that opportunity and provide some vague, dull information; instead it puts in a lot of personality and charm.
+Very nice music.
I really had to struggle to come up with any sort of criticism for Undertale. My thoughts below explain the only (slightly) negative thing I could find.
As a rule of thumb I would have wanted the game to be longer on the first run and not need multiple play-throughs to get the full story, but the game and story are designed to give you some very different choices on how to play and that drastically changes how the story will be. So far I’ve only done the basic, neutral route, but it was very awesome and I’ve heard equally good and exciting things about the other routes. It took me 7-8 hours to beat Undertale my first time, but there is a lot more to get out of the game once you attempt the other routes.
Conclusion: If you’re in the mood to play a top-down RPG then definitely check out Undertale! It is very unique and fun :D

Another reviewer hit the nail on the head when they summed up this game as "Call of Duty, naked"
...but Call of Duty actually has depth that this game doesn't even touch.
For a 2-year old game that was such a big seller and is presently still high-ranking on the Steam Stats I really surprised at how absolutely devoid of substance this game is. It is fairly straightforward what you're supposed to do once you figure out the controls: progress through the linear "tech tree" building better bases and acquiring better weapons until you're the one killing random players instead of being the random player killed.
Ah, yes, be prepared for much epic flailing of the default "rock" multitool you spawn with as another naked character (with blurred out genetalia... teehee?) flails a slightly more deadly weapon at you!
If you go unnoticed long enough you'll then gather materials from rocks and trees (but ONLY the special boulders that spawn and trees that grow, forget about that driftwood or stone-outcroppings)... and, we've seen this game how many times now?
As for the other players that you'll meet... in my limited experience the Stanford Prison Experiment was called to mind - if everyone were a guard. The players generally revel in their inability to play cooperatively and how unwelcoming the game is.

This game is pretty dope. I mean, if you like puns, irony, memes, anime, Earthbound, and/or self-awareness cuteness you might actually start foaming at the mouth while playing this, and then go into shock. But even those who aren't familiar with some (or any) of the concepts mentioned above, commonplace in certain internet sub-cultures, Undertale is still worth a try if nothing else for its interesting blend of Japanese RPG battle systems and old school arcade "bullet hell" shooters. But that would be selling the world and story of Undertale short.
You play as a child who has fallen down into an underground ruin that is home to a large community of monsters. Throughout the game you will meet, greet, fight, and/or befriend lots of very charmingly designed characters, all of whom are richly developed and often heart-achingly relatable. All of this is reflected both in the main world exploration and in battle. Though Undertale does at a glance look and feel like an amalgam of numerous games of also numerous genres with all the inherent pastiches and tropes therein, I've never really played anything quite like it. It takes a lot from other games but manages through immense ingenuity carves out an existence all its own. There's really nothing else out there currently quite like it.
The game is about 7-8 hours long if you play leisurely your first time through, but multiple playthroughs are absolutely necessary to get the most out of the game, due to the fact that the story and ending change in subsequent runs. Lots of games do this, but not to the extent that Undertale does. As I said before, this game is very self-aware, and this reflects on the new game plus (or plus plus, depending on which ending you get first).
So in short. Undertale is a charming little gem, with lots of fun characters, a unique battle system, and greatly rewards multiple playthroughs, and when I say that it rewards you for doing so, I really, seriously mean it. For me, the game didn't truly click until I played it a second time. It's only then that Undertale cracks open its soul and reveals to you the secrets of its universe.
It's real cool. Buy it.

To properly explain why Undertale is so special, and why it has garnered such a loyal following, would necessitate spoiling the entire experiance. Read the TL;DR, and just do it.
TL;DR: Undertale is the best game to come out in 2015. If you can look past graphics, then you'll find a deviously complex RPG that manages to get to the player in all the right ways. If you were on the fence, and still want to stay clean from spoilers, just bite the bullet and buy Undertale. It's worth it, trust me.
I talk a little about Undertale's sturcture, but nothing truly explicit about the game in terms of spoilers. I utterly reccommend going into Undertale blind, and just letting yourself figure out the game on your lonesome, but if you need to know a little more before diving in, then listen up.
Undertale is a game that relishes in creating impressions and facades, and then shattering them apart. Nowhere in gaming has going into a game unspoiled been so important than it is for approaching Undertale. What starts off seeing like a simple JRPG with a strange sense of humor eventually manages to shed its layers to reveal its true intentions, and depending on your choices, those intentions might be rather pleasent or horrifyingly grim. Undertale lives off the idea that you make your own ending. Where other games might have a few binary decisions that affect how the game ends in a small way, Undertale dares you to pick a way of life and stick with it. Pacifism has its own rewards, but sometimes you just feel like everything needs to die. Either of these are completely reasonable options in the world of Undertale, and the game actively rewards the player for sticking to their guns, whether they be literal or figuartive.
For adhereing to one dogma for a playthrough, you are provided with two starkly different games. Pacifism provides a more cheery and hopeful tone throughout the entire story, while choosing Genocide twists Undertale apart at the seams and shifts its usual quirks into stygian horror, allowing the player to dive deep into the depths of their depravity as they progress. Undertale is more like two games in one, an upbeat JRPG on one side of the coin, and a ♥♥♥♥ed adaptation of Heart of Darkness on the other. Both of these are fantastically written and immensly impactful, albiet for much,
different reasons.
Undertale has quite a lot to say about friendship, the values of life, the nature of video gaming, and even humanity's capacity for inflicting pain. Undertale forces you to question your actions and how they affect others, and manages to squeeze more heart out of $50,000 than any AAA developer in recent memory could with $50,000,000.
If you can appreciate a game that cares more about its characters than its graphics, and more about moving the player than making money, then Undertale is absolutely worth playing. Whether it inspires you, or makes you question your own morality, Undertale has something to say about who you are, and it's absouletly worth listening to.
