To properly explain why Undertale is so special, and why it has garnered such a loyal following, would necessitate spoiling the entire experiance. Read the TL;DR, and just do it.
TL;DR: Undertale is the best game to come out in 2015. If you can look past graphics, then you'll find a deviously complex RPG that manages to get to the player in all the right ways. If you were on the fence, and still want to stay clean from spoilers, just bite the bullet and buy Undertale. It's worth it, trust me.
I talk a little about Undertale's sturcture, but nothing truly explicit about the game in terms of spoilers. I utterly reccommend going into Undertale blind, and just letting yourself figure out the game on your lonesome, but if you need to know a little more before diving in, then listen up.
Undertale is a game that relishes in creating impressions and facades, and then shattering them apart. Nowhere in gaming has going into a game unspoiled been so important than it is for approaching Undertale. What starts off seeing like a simple JRPG with a strange sense of humor eventually manages to shed its layers to reveal its true intentions, and depending on your choices, those intentions might be rather pleasent or horrifyingly grim. Undertale lives off the idea that you make your own ending. Where other games might have a few binary decisions that affect how the game ends in a small way, Undertale dares you to pick a way of life and stick with it. Pacifism has its own rewards, but sometimes you just feel like everything needs to die. Either of these are completely reasonable options in the world of Undertale, and the game actively rewards the player for sticking to their guns, whether they be literal or figuartive.
For adhereing to one dogma for a playthrough, you are provided with two starkly different games. Pacifism provides a more cheery and hopeful tone throughout the entire story, while choosing Genocide twists Undertale apart at the seams and shifts its usual quirks into stygian horror, allowing the player to dive deep into the depths of their depravity as they progress. Undertale is more like two games in one, an upbeat JRPG on one side of the coin, and a ♥♥♥♥ed adaptation of Heart of Darkness on the other. Both of these are fantastically written and immensly impactful, albiet for much,
different reasons.
Undertale has quite a lot to say about friendship, the values of life, the nature of video gaming, and even humanity's capacity for inflicting pain. Undertale forces you to question your actions and how they affect others, and manages to squeeze more heart out of $50,000 than any AAA developer in recent memory could with $50,000,000.
If you can appreciate a game that cares more about its characters than its graphics, and more about moving the player than making money, then Undertale is absolutely worth playing. Whether it inspires you, or makes you question your own morality, Undertale has something to say about who you are, and it's absouletly worth listening to.

Pros of Undertale:
+Incredible storytelling
+A plot that's never quite feels finished, but is still satisfying
+A happy ending
+A horrible, sob-inducing ending
+Lovable characters who are fabulously flawed
+Hateable characters who you can't help but understand and even sympathize with
+Fantastic soundtrack which is as much a part of the storytelling as the plot itself
+Dogs
+Your choices actually matter. Yes. All of them. What you say, what you choose--it affects the outcome of each following interaction.
+Calls into question morality and the real meaning of good versus evil
+Graphics that are simplistic, but purposely so
+Nothing is meaningless, and everything has a point
+Simple gameplay allows the player to fully immerse in the story
+Not-so-simple bullet-hell mechanics allow the player to throw their keyboard across the room
+There's always something else to discover, some new puzzle to put together, even after you've seemingly finished the game
Cons of Undertale:
-
Conclusion:
The amount of love that went into this game is palpable. At every turn, the amount of attention to detail Toby Fox put into this game astounded me, and still does. I cannot imagine the hours it took to create this utter masterpiece. For only $10, Undertale is an absolute steal. Stop reading reviews and BUY THIS GAME. Experience it for yourself. I can guarantee you this: Undertale lives up to the hype. It goes beyond the hype.
Undertale isn't a game. It's an experience. And it's a damn good one, too.
Laugh, cry, scream, yell, smile, throw things, die, SAVE, load, try, and discover how DETERMINED you really are.
Buy this game.

When a friend referred Undertale to me, I initially dismissed it as just another RPG. I was eventually convinced to play it, after seeing the majorly positive reception for it, going in with little to no expectations.
Never before have I been so caught off guard.
The story itself starts off as relatively simple: Humans and monsters live separately, with humans on the surface and monsters underground, and a child (you) falls in and must journey to the surface. Sounds like your standard Earthbound type fare, right? Well, as soon as you exit the first room, everything changes. Encountering a wide cast of characters that you'll find yourself fawning over, rich environments to explore, a surprisingly deeper plot than you anticipated first going in, and so many twists and turns that can make replayability last infinitely.
What really stands out about Undertale is the combat interface. In Turn-Based RPG fashion, you and your opponent alternate between turns to beat each other. Ho ho ho, if only it were that simple. When enemies attack you, the interface shifts into a Bullet Hell scenario that varies with each fight, requiring you to avoid "bullets" from hitting your SOUL. And when it's your turn, that's when you get to a game changer. The interface will present two options: Fight and Act. Fighting will, of course, lead to killing your opponent and gain XP to help increase LOVE. Acting, however, allows you to take a more passive option against the monsters. Talk with them, get on their friendly side, and they won't fight you. Both options can lead down different paths, but the real surprises lay down the line.
Another of Undertale's high points is the writing. Toby Fox did an amazing job with writing all that happens throughout the game, both the random and the heartfelt. The tagline in the Game Overview about dating a skeleton isn't there just for kicks, ya know. At certain moments, the game really will tug at your heartstrings and make you feel for the game world around you.
That's all I can honestly say, Undertale is one of those special games that you need to experience first hand and cannot spoil. So what are you still doing, reading this review? Go and get this game, journey through the Underground, make friends and foes, and whatever you do, DON'T FORGET TO BUY A SPIDER DONUT!

I've hit a point in this game where I don't know if I'll continue, but I decided to put up a short review in the meantime. I can't imagine my opinion changing if I decide to continue this.
We all play games for different reasons, but ultimately it's to have a fun experience. This game will not bring that unless you just want to jump on a bandwagon of LV for a mediocre product.
The game is automatically being played off on false nostalgia. The graphics, sounds and part of the combat system is familiar to a lot of older gamers. However, the reason you played those old school console JRPGs was because they were fun. You had exploration, characters that were interesting, a variety of spells and attacks, and a reason behind everything.
In Undertale, the exploration is limited to different paths that sometimes lead to a funny/cutesy/quirky thing. In one scene, I saw a fishing rod that had a picture attached to it. I couldn't tell if the picture was a philosophical parable or a very simple joke. The combat has a feature to talk your way out of battle. I found the most useful feature is Fleeing a battle because the battle system is boring. This was the one aspect I was hoping would be a lot of fun. Instead, I found myself wanting random battles to never happen. I quit talking my way out of battles because the dialog that spews from an enemies mouth is, frankly, bad. It's not funny not entertaining. It's bland.
The music and graphics are something. They captured an era, and it's the one positive I can give the game as of now. They're ugly as sin and the main character looks like a reject from The Simpsons: Bart vs. The World, however, that's what this game was going for and they nailed it. When I left the first area start my quest home, the graphics went from Commodore 64 to a weird NES/SNES look. I could dig it. The music is charming, and probably the best part of the game. It fits the environments well and it's about the best reason to recommend Undertale.
You may have heard this game shares similarities to Earthbound. Yes and no. Yes, because it has some art aspects that look Earthbound-y, but no to everything else. If you want to play Earthbound, there's many options available. And it's actually going to make you happy playing it because it's fun, cute in a way that's relaxing, and has a decent overall plot line for an old game. Undertale just keeps dragging on and on.
I don't think this game was created with a bad vision. I think it's just a very poor game and has been grasped by a certain type of indie community that feels certain games that shouldn't be popular should be popular. There's people that are going to legitimately love this game. And good. Not everyone needs to love the same thing. But I think the overhyped community, the missionaries of this game, have spoiled it. This game having certain words associated with it like "feels" and "deep meaning" damages the game more than honors it.
If I finish the game, which as much as I don't want to, probably will to mark off my backlog, I will update the review if I feel it needs it. But as of now, I have to say don't bye into this weird hype. I don't watch My Little Pony even though it have a strong (non-physically) community. Undertale is no exception. Bad is bad and quirky isn't always good.

Well... what can be said about Undertale that probably hasn't already been said many times already. I imagine that most people looking at the reviews are the ones who have already played it and are looking for others to excitedly rave about it with (which they have legitimate reason to), while the minority are the ones who haven't heard much about it and want to know if it's worth getting. If you're within the latter group, the best advice I can give you is, if you think you're even the slightest amount interested in getting it, do it. Get it and learn the least amount you can about it. It's totally worth it.
I made the mistake of watching most of a playthrough of it before playing it myself. Although it didn't ruin the experience, I feel it may have tempered my reaction to it. This is one of those games where it will affect you the most if you go in blind.
You've probably already played a game before where your actions effect the story. This game takes that to another level. Keep this in mind while you are playing it.
If you're still not confident about getting it, here are some non-spoiler positives
+Great music
+Unique combat system
+Well-written dialogue
+Lots of dogs
+Stays interesting throughout the entire game / doesn't lose its pace
+Did I mention dogs?
Of course, I didn't find it to be a perfect game. It's not always the greatest to look at, and the puzzles can be rather simplistic. Beyond some minor flaws, though, I don't see why I wouldn't recommend this game to someone looking to play one of the most unique games that has come out in a long time.

For those who have played ARK, the style of gameplay is very similar.
Collect items from the world around you, build tools to colelct from new sources/more efficiently, and don't let the vicious animals see you or they will eat your face. In Rust, however, there is no character creation. You all spawn as a big naked dude. Thank goodness for the pixelation, or else I would have had a LOT of explaining to do to my mother.
It is quite difficult to figure out what you are doing in this game, especially on a server. I reccomend either finding an empty server or starting one in order to get used to what is going on. Early game, it's easiest to hang around the towns, where you can readily find blueprints, water, food, and items.
Right click is usually "throw" - avoid clicking this unless you want to fling your items into the bushes to be lost forever.
As far as finding your friends, navigating the map is rather hard. My suggestion would be to either find a rad town and follow the road/powerlines until you locate one another, or to have one person set up a quick base with a sleeping bag for the other person to spawn in.
Starting as a new player on a server with established clans isn't going to work. You are going to be killed repeatedly, it's going to be frustrating, and you're never going to get to actually play the game. PVE servers are great for learning, and the people there are usually very willing to help you along, just pay attention to the rules.
Helicopters are evil. If you hear a helicopter, RUN. You cannot win againt this thing without some serious firepower. Hide somewhere with a decent roof and away from open windows/doors.
Watch the sound levels, especially when first logging on. If you think the footsteps are loud? Wait till someone sets off a shotgun near your head. I about jumped out of my skin.
There are a few serious glitches in the game, but nothing that absolutely breaks it. Be warned: bear traps do NOT, in fact, work on bears. Doors can be glitched through under the right circumstances, and occasionally the naked people who logged off will float above the ground for no apparent reason.
Overall this is a fun game, but seems to be one where you can upgrade everything to a point and then have nothing left to do. This is solved on PVP servers by having others around to attack/be attacked by, however it leaves little to do for those on less populated or PVE servers. Hopefully there will be more updates for the game, as I am greatly enjoying it so far and hope to continue.

Undertale is an RPG/Bullet hell that really makes you think about what you have done. To tell you how effective the game is, I am a teenager who cannot cry for anything, but after a horrible mistake, I nearly cried. Now on to the real review...
Undertale is about a child who falls underground, and meets a cast of likeable characters with personality and traits, which makes the characters feel more real. The child tries to get back to the real world, but they find out that it's close to impossible, and comes a journey unlike any other (Until a fan game comes out), a journey of self discovery and friendship (don't mistake this for an indie film, because it's not.) Undertale is an enjoyable yet challenging game that really makes you want to keep going to help out your new friends and  get closer (unless you are a cold hearted killer, then you can just murder everyone in the game without mercy), while also finding out the truth of the underground and why it's in it's current state. I loved the bullet hell styled gameplay, classic yet new graphics, and especially the music, which fits the came to a T. Even as an experienced gamer (I'm more of a filthy casual),  the game gives quite  the challenge, which gives the game more diversity, and every enemy is different, so don't expect to defeat every enemy the same way.
Even though the game might seem bright and happy, but the story is quite dark and depressing, but it is still an overall amazing game. Undertale is one of my favorite games of all time and I would rate it a 9.5 out of 10.
BTW the fanbase for Undertale can be quite hectic, so be careful ;)
One of the best games I have ever seen.

is a fantastic game, full of character and heart. It's obvious the developer put a lot of time and effort into designing this game. While the comedy and somewhat didactic morality of this game may turn off some players, I think the humor is handled very well and the game's message is one that needs to be heard.
RPG purists should beware, as battles involve dodging attacks instead of watching your character be attacked. However, this gameplay mechanic (not to mention the enemies' characters) help alleviate the monotony that other RPGs can't avoid. In a nutshell,
prevents the player from feeling passive. It's up to you to defend yourself, to decide whether to kill--to make choices that affect your experience.
While I've only reached one ending, I intend to find the others as well and still encourage you to purchase this game, especially if it's on sale.

Undertale is an RPG game that takes many cliché elements in RPG games and creates it into this new type of game in which, just as the description mentions, you do not have to harm a single soul.
PROS:
+ Unique type of gameplay
+ Battles are unlike anything seen before
+ Surprising elements (planned crashes, (non-harmful) game file issues, etc.)
+ Many different characteristic entities, all with a very unique behavior
+ Intriguing artwork
+ Multiple "routes" and endings
+ Great amount of soundtracks
+ Trading cards with valuable crafting rewards
CONS:
- It's not really clear in some battles what you're supposed to do
- The protagonist character is rather bland and randomly constructed. It doesn't feel satisfying to be the "normal guy" in what is best described as a world filled with a colorful mismash of vivid characters
- A lot of the game and its areas and transitions make little to no sense
- Not exactly story-driven, despite the title being UnderTALE. Rather a loose collection of character dialogues, jokes and interactions that eventually bring you to the end
- The further you come in the game, the more it devolves into endless dialogues that really make you want to skip them (for example: the part where Alphys just keeps texting you over and over annoyed me greatly)
- You don't do much else than walking around, interacting with characters and having battles
Undertale is a pretty pioneering game when it comes to what we have seen in RPG games already. However, it's not exactly a game for everyone. If the humor didn't catch you, like it didn't with me, chances are you didn't enjoy the game altogether. Despite my generous rating for this game, because I feel that this game is certainly different than your average RPG, I did not enjoy this game a lot because the charm of it simply failed to capture me. Obviously it did click with other people. Even then, I still fail to understand how this game was dominating the gaming market for several months, and seemingly still raging on as I edit this review I typed months ago when the game's afterglow should've ended already.
My rating: 8/10 (read on for more information about this rating. Any more comments about this will get removed)
Edit: I usually don't break character in my reviews, but I want to share a bit of the bad experiences I had with both the game
the mentality of the fanbase.
I copied and pasted my review back after a mass fanboy downvoting parade flew over it rendering the score below 33%. It's not really fair to sketch my review off as "not helpful," because I give both pros and cons and explain why I don't recommend it. I'm not saying the game is bad or shouldn't be played, but it's not my cup of tea either.
I could also just write an awful joke or reference from the game here, like a lot of people do because the crowd deems it "hilarious," but that isn't helping anyone, but instead deprives people from helpful reviews that
help them getting an insight of what the game is like. And yet, those are the ones gathering all of the attention and upvotes.
This game enforces some kind of idea that if you don't like the game, you will be found and treated like a heretic and your choice on videogames is suddenly bad. I mean look at the helpful/not helpful ratio of the negative reviews. While most "singular-line reviews" in the positive section have a 90+ percentage of being "helpful" (read: completely useless), constructively crafted negative reviews kind of get looked down upon. I've seen some well-constructed "not recommended" reviews way better than mine being downvoted beyond belief. This kind of inability to witness people disliking something you love arose in some of my (former) friends and makes me feel like this game is mainly played by teenagers or people who find the hype of randomness and memes hilarious and can't at all take any negativity over it.
Of course, if you don't see yourself in this, you shouldn't feel guilty.
I'm not implying that you shouldn't downvote reviews that aren't going further than a few sentences, nor that you shouldn't voice your opinion over it, but instead encourage you to rate and argumentate fairly and considerate. Feel free to downvote mine too if it didn't give you insight or a different perspective. This is all besides the point of this review, but I'd like to have this addressed nevertheless. This seems to play a role in many reviews ever since Steam was invented, and it's a shame.

TL;DR: The game is hilarious, engaging, and enthralling, and is probably the greatest game I've played in the last decade.
Boy, where you do even begin with reviewing a game like this....
Undertale is an old-style RPG that refuses to take itself seriously, is damn proud of that fact, and is simply a beautiful and charming work of art.  It's precisely the sort of game that I would take joy from waving in Roger Ebert's face in an attempt to get the guy to understand and admit that video games truly are art, were Ebert still around to put up with my harassment.  Unfortunately, he's not, so I'll have to settle for dragging his name through the mud in a Steam review, instead.
Back on topic... I finished my two playthroughs of Undertale over a week ago, and I'm still somewhat in awe at it—amazed that something so phenomenal could be the product of just an artist and a preposterously talented dude.  It's the sort of thing that really makes you wonder what the hell the AAAs are doing with their huge teams and GDP-level game budgets.  How is that they've been pumping out games from their big-budget assembly lines for decades, but can't put together a game that actually makes people
things like Undertale can?  It seems so backwards, but, at the same time, it's not fair to make this review about the AAAs; Undertale is a brilliant accomplishment, no matter what it's being compared to.
Now, I've spent my opening paragraphs on slobbering over the game, but what is it that's so great about it, anyway?  Well, Undertale is incredibly funny and jam-packed with lovable characters you're not likely to forget anytime soon—special shout-out to my boys Papyrus and Mettaton!
Furthermore, Undertale's soundtrack is amazingly good and puts most of the music that you would hear on the radio—much less the music of most other video games—to shame.  The music is just
well-composed.  Since playing the game, I've been left in the state of continually listening to the soundtrack on loop and hoarding Undertale sheet music so I can play out the tunes, myself.  Does this indicate that I have a problem of some sort?  Maybe.  Or maybe it's you who has the problem, because you're not currently listening to the Undertale soundtrack.  It's not me who's missing out here!
Anyway, let's not forget about the quality of the writing, either.  The game is hilarious and witty, with writing that's probably funnier than whatever comedy show/movie/stand-up special you most recently watched, and that leaves you in constant state of wanting more.  You can rest assured, though, that, as you explore the world of Undertale, you'll find yourself in no shortage of things to chuckle about.  But it's not all laughs, either.  The game implores you to expect the unexpected at each turn, and there are some moments that really just sock you right in the feels.  At times, Undertale will encourage you to really stop and question some things (in a good way).  You might even learn something about yourself, in the process.
On top of that, despite being an RPG with a very purposeful old-timey feel, the game still manages to push boundaries with its features (e.g. there's some pretty meta stuff that goes on in the final battle), but especially in the department of RPG battle mechanics.  Indeed, the combat system is very unique for an RPG, and, unlike the antiquated RPGs of yore that Undertale so desperately wants you to believe are its kin, the combat seldom ever feels arduous.
It truly is a breath of fresh air that every enemy has their own particular strategy that is supposed to be discovered and exploited in order to defeat them, often blending together the mechanics of turn-based RPGs with shoot-em-ups (of all things) to create the Frankenstein monster's dashingly handsome twin brother of game mechanics—a combination of systems that you wouldn't have expected would work well together at all, but that actually could hardly work
together.  It's likely in large part thanks to this unique approach to RPG combat that the game continues to drive forward at all times without ever turning things into a grind, fostering a constant feeling of excitement about whatever might lie waiting around the next corner.
Now that I've sat here, lavishing the game with preposturous amounts of praise for paragraphs on end, you might be wondering if I'm not just some blind fanboy who can find no fault with Undertale and believes it to be an untainted relic of some sort, brought down to us from on high.  I will neither confirm nor deny the rumors of my fanboyism, but I honestly can't find a whole lot to complain about here.  Probably the biggest thing for me regards the game's innumerable references to Earthbound.  Don't get me wrong: Earthbound is one of my absolute favorite games, and I think that Undertale is actually the proper successor that Earthbound always deserved—and, yes, I say this as someone who has even played the "true" sequel to Earthbound from start to finish.  Earthbound and Undertale are both brilliant, masterful games, and shining examples of originality, wit, and humanity in video games.  Undertale is entirely deserving of any assessment that it gets that groups it together with Earthbound.
But my biggest problem with Undertale is just
it tries to associate itself with Earthbound.  It's one thing to be influenced by something and pay homage to it (as Undertale does with many other things, in tasteful moderation), but the frequency with which Undertale makes nods in Earthbound's direction is just too much for me.  There are
occurrences in Undertale that are references to Earthbound.  I dislike this, because Undertale is a game that is brilliant in its own right, and it really doesn't need to be leaning so heavily on Earthbound in order to stand tall as a delightfully fun experience that profoundly manifest its creators' passion and ingenuity.  This "too many references" problem isn't not a major point or a dealbreaker by any measure, but I just wish that the Earthbound references had been a bit fewer in number.  They simply weren't necessary, and started to take away from the game, at a point.
Anyway, the real moral of the story here is that Undertale is an game that I expect to love forever.  It's touching, incredibly entertaining, and reminds us that there's still room for innovation, even in a genre of games that's been existent and explored for some 30 odd years already.  Cherish your time with Undertale, and don't expect to see another game of its caliber anytime soon.
Instant classic.  Unforgettable.  9.75/10

A refreshing, original take on the survivor genre.  Rust is extremely high risk, high reward gameplay that will take a bit of patience during the beginning stage, but you'll find the slow progression totally worth it once you've built a base with solid defense set up.  As for the community, its generally fight or flight interaction, unless you have a mic in which case your PvP interactions may vary. You will be severely disadvantaged playing alone, although its still fun if you enjoy a challenge.  Finally, one of the best parts about Rust are the updates.  They are frequent and usually full of new content.  By the end of each year, Rust always feels like a completely new and more polished game.  It is clear that the developers released this as early access with the intentions of finishing it.

TL;DR: The game is hilarious, engaging, and enthralling, and is probably the greatest game I've played in the last decade.
Boy, where you do even begin with reviewing a game like this....
Undertale is an old-style RPG that refuses to take itself seriously, is damn proud of that fact, and is simply a beautiful and charming work of art.  It's precisely the sort of game that I would take joy from waving in Roger Ebert's face in an attempt to get the guy to understand and admit that video games truly are art, were Ebert still around to put up with my harassment.  Unfortunately, he's not, so I'll have to settle for dragging his name through the mud in a Steam review, instead.
Back on topic... I finished my two playthroughs of Undertale over a week ago, and I'm still somewhat in awe at it—amazed that something so phenomenal could be the product of just an artist and a preposterously talented dude.  It's the sort of thing that really makes you wonder what the hell the AAAs are doing with their huge teams and GDP-level game budgets.  How is that they've been pumping out games from their big-budget assembly lines for decades, but can't put together a game that actually makes people
things like Undertale can?  It seems so backwards, but, at the same time, it's not fair to make this review about the AAAs; Undertale is a brilliant accomplishment, no matter what it's being compared to.
Now, I've spent my opening paragraphs on slobbering over the game, but what is it that's so great about it, anyway?  Well, Undertale is incredibly funny and jam-packed with lovable characters you're not likely to forget anytime soon—special shout-out to my boys Papyrus and Mettaton!
Furthermore, Undertale's soundtrack is amazingly good and puts most of the music that you would hear on the radio—much less the music of most other video games—to shame.  The music is just
well-composed.  Since playing the game, I've been left in the state of continually listening to the soundtrack on loop and hoarding Undertale sheet music so I can play out the tunes, myself.  Does this indicate that I have a problem of some sort?  Maybe.  Or maybe it's you who has the problem, because you're not currently listening to the Undertale soundtrack.  It's not me who's missing out here!
Anyway, let's not forget about the quality of the writing, either.  The game is hilarious and witty, with writing that's probably funnier than whatever comedy show/movie/stand-up special you most recently watched, and that leaves you in constant state of wanting more.  You can rest assured, though, that, as you explore the world of Undertale, you'll find yourself in no shortage of things to chuckle about.  But it's not all laughs, either.  The game implores you to expect the unexpected at each turn, and there are some moments that really just sock you right in the feels.  At times, Undertale will encourage you to really stop and question some things (in a good way).  You might even learn something about yourself, in the process.
On top of that, despite being an RPG with a very purposeful old-timey feel, the game still manages to push boundaries with its features (e.g. there's some pretty meta stuff that goes on in the final battle), but especially in the department of RPG battle mechanics.  Indeed, the combat system is very unique for an RPG, and, unlike the antiquated RPGs of yore that Undertale so desperately wants you to believe are its kin, the combat seldom ever feels arduous.
It truly is a breath of fresh air that every enemy has their own particular strategy that is supposed to be discovered and exploited in order to defeat them, often blending together the mechanics of turn-based RPGs with shoot-em-ups (of all things) to create the Frankenstein monster's dashingly handsome twin brother of game mechanics—a combination of systems that you wouldn't have expected would work well together at all, but that actually could hardly work
together.  It's likely in large part thanks to this unique approach to RPG combat that the game continues to drive forward at all times without ever turning things into a grind, fostering a constant feeling of excitement about whatever might lie waiting around the next corner.
Now that I've sat here, lavishing the game with preposturous amounts of praise for paragraphs on end, you might be wondering if I'm not just some blind fanboy who can find no fault with Undertale and believes it to be an untainted relic of some sort, brought down to us from on high.  I will neither confirm nor deny the rumors of my fanboyism, but I honestly can't find a whole lot to complain about here.  Probably the biggest thing for me regards the game's innumerable references to Earthbound.  Don't get me wrong: Earthbound is one of my absolute favorite games, and I think that Undertale is actually the proper successor that Earthbound always deserved—and, yes, I say this as someone who has even played the "true" sequel to Earthbound from start to finish.  Earthbound and Undertale are both brilliant, masterful games, and shining examples of originality, wit, and humanity in video games.  Undertale is entirely deserving of any assessment that it gets that groups it together with Earthbound.
But my biggest problem with Undertale is just
it tries to associate itself with Earthbound.  It's one thing to be influenced by something and pay homage to it (as Undertale does with many other things, in tasteful moderation), but the frequency with which Undertale makes nods in Earthbound's direction is just too much for me.  There are
occurrences in Undertale that are references to Earthbound.  I dislike this, because Undertale is a game that is brilliant in its own right, and it really doesn't need to be leaning so heavily on Earthbound in order to stand tall as a delightfully fun experience that profoundly manifest its creators' passion and ingenuity.  This "too many references" problem isn't not a major point or a dealbreaker by any measure, but I just wish that the Earthbound references had been a bit fewer in number.  They simply weren't necessary, and started to take away from the game, at a point.
Anyway, the real moral of the story here is that Undertale is an game that I expect to love forever.  It's touching, incredibly entertaining, and reminds us that there's still room for innovation, even in a genre of games that's been existent and explored for some 30 odd years already.  Cherish your time with Undertale, and don't expect to see another game of its caliber anytime soon.

This game is not good. A bad game can be fun and that is exactly what Dayz is. The game offers a novelty that is rare, and can have some of the most intense moments in gaming. However, that alone is not enough to balance out all that is so wrong with this game. After 270 Hours and over a year of playing, this game has not improved in any meaningful way. Yes it is unfinished, but that is not an excuse for the lack of progress. So if you are going to charge for a product regardless of a disclaimer, normal business ethics demand that those selling it to improve their product, much more-so than if the alpha was free. But then again ethics isn't a very common thing in the gaming industry. This game has been in development since 2012 and the majority of the game's assets have been ported straight from ArmA II and the original DayZ mod, this game has not been built from the ground up. All of the updates have only marginally improved the game. The apologists always say "you have to wait its alpha!" and sure that's a reasonable point, but when this game is still in alpha 3 years from now, or the final release is just as terrible as the alpha (which it very well might be) it brings up the question of the developer's competence, and they certainly are no Rockstar or Naughty Dog.
Also the devs ban people on Dayz's steam forums for voicing criticism of their game on the basis that criticism is "Trolling" keep it classy Bohemia (I'm surprised they don't delete negative reviews too). I could elaborate more on the what is wrong with the games content, but plenty of other reviews cover that, I just wanted to cover the fact that this game develops at a snails pace and each update always disappoints.
TL;DR: This game is permanently an alpha. It's been in alpha for nearly 3 years and released to the public for 17 months. Game has only marginally improved, and the outlook is not looking good. 4/10 avoid.
Update 8/29/15: Recently played again... and its still awful. Yes player interactions, and gun fights are fun and intense, but nothing has improved. Lots of core features are still just as half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ as the rest of the game. Litterally every feature in this game does not work very well, and is half finished. I mean seriously, hotkeys still require at least 2-3 taps in order to change items (an issue since launch in 2013), and now if you log out with a hotkey item in your hand, upon logging back in it is removed from the hotkey slot for some reason (you do not lose the item). This game has not improved since the first vehicle was added and the vehicle system is also very unfinished.
With all the other survival games out, a lot of them offer stronger core mechanics, and a better functioning game, and have been developed in a shorter amount of time. Half-life 3 will release before this game is finished, and by them will anyone care?
I Have come to the conclusion that this game was never intended to be a finished product. Instead this game is running on the model similar to minecraft, where you pay for the unfinished game upfront and they slowly push out marginal updates, with occasional new features. The problem is minecraft does this much much better.

This game is not good. A bad game can be fun and that is exactly what Dayz is. The game offers a novelty that is rare, and can have some of the most intense moments in gaming. However, that alone is not enough to balance out all that is so wrong with this game. After 270 Hours and over a year of playing, this game has not improved in any meaningful way. Yes it is unfinished, but that is not an excuse for the lack of progress. So if you are going to charge for a product regardless of a disclaimer, normal business ethics demand that those selling it to improve their product, much more-so than if the alpha was free. But then again ethics isn't a very common thing in the gaming industry. This game has been in development since 2012 and the majority of the game's assets have been ported straight from ArmA II and the original DayZ mod, this game has not been built from the ground up. All of the updates have only marginally improved the game. The apologists always say "you have to wait its alpha!" and sure that's a reasonable point, but when this game is still in alpha 3 years from now, or the final release is just as terrible as the alpha (which it very well might be) it brings up the question of the developer's competence, and they certainly are no Rockstar or Naughty Dog.
Also the devs ban people on Dayz's steam forums for voicing criticism of their game on the basis that criticism is "Trolling" keep it classy Bohemia (I'm surprised they don't delete negative reviews too). I could elaborate more on the what is wrong with the games content, but plenty of other reviews cover that, I just wanted to cover the fact that this game develops at a snails pace and each update always disappoints.
TL;DR: This game is permanently an alpha. It's been in alpha for nearly 3 years and released to the public for 17 months. Game has only marginally improved, and the outlook is not looking good. 4/10 avoid.
Update 8/29/15: Recently played again... and its still awful. Yes player interactions, and gun fights are fun and intense, but nothing has improved. Lots of core features are still just as half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ as the rest of the game. Litterally every feature in this game does not work very well, and is half finished. I mean seriously, hotkeys still require at least 2-3 taps in order to change items (an issue since launch in 2013), and now if you log out with a hotkey item in your hand, upon logging back in it is removed from the hotkey slot for some reason (you do not lose the item). This game has not improved since the first vehicle was added and the vehicle system is also very unfinished.
With all the other survival games out, a lot of them offer stronger core mechanics, and a better functioning game, and have been developed in a shorter amount of time. Half-life 3 will release before this game is finished, and by them will anyone care?
I Have come to the conclusion that this game was never intended to be a finished product. Instead this game is running on the model similar to minecraft, where you pay for the unfinished game upfront and they slowly push out marginal updates, with occasional new features. The problem is minecraft does this much much better.

When I first saw somebody play this game, the graphics and just the overall odd design pushed me to believe that this was going to be a bad game. I came back months later, and man was I wrong. I discovered unique characters, funny jokes or references that play at the exact right time, and a developer team that seriously knows how video games are really made. What if the boss you were fighting knew that you would simply respawn after dying? What if Bowser could reset the game? This game reflects on that thought, and seriously breaks the fourth wall in a very subtle manner. The ending seriously reflects on your mid-game actions. If you chose to be a pacifist (the game obviously pushes you to this) then you get to see a really well thought out ending. If you do the genocide ending, you get a completely heartless ending. I watched somebody do a pacifist run and I decided to go on a genocide run, and I even surprised my self on how determined I was to beat the (WAY over the top hard) final boss. If your looking for a new game, this is an easy 20 hours of the best story you will see. Get past the graphics and quirkiness of it, and you will see how well made this game was. HUGE congrats to Toby Fox for making something like this, without the insane equipment that these big brand developers have. Without a doubt this is my new favorite game and I don't think anything will surpass it, unless Toby Fox decides to make another. Trust me, just try the game.

Other people have said it, and it's true: Rust, in its current Alpha state, is no fun for beginners (maybe not even for the more seasoned players).  Here's why, in a nutshell:
Starting out with just a rock and a torch is hard.  Duh!  But that's all fine and good if you can build something from that and start to make something of your naked self.  So you start out and you get killed (A LOT) before you can build anything up.  Ok, ok, you'll say- I might be dying and losing everything but it still seems like so much FUN and I think I can establish myself, so I'll keep trying!
So you keep trying.  Eventually, you are able to survive long enough to build a house!  Wahooo!  You add a door, you add a lock, you start to store things, you upgrade your twig hut to wood and now you're thinking- hey!  I've finally established a small little foothold here!  I got some clothes!  I got food!  I even found some way cooler weapons!  I'm on a roll!!
Then you log out to, you know, live your real life.
You return.  You end up naked on a beach.  You go back to your former home to discover that not only did someone break in and kill you, but they stole your house and changed the lock too!  You must once again live in the cold, dark world trying desperately to survive.
Over and over again, the same thing happens.  It's the inability to make a real foothold in this game for longer than a few hours that makes it so frustrating and, in my opinion, not really an enjoyable game to play.
The game is beautiful, and it has a lot of really positive traits- the ability to build your own house, raid for items, hunting, even running away from the bad guys and the bears can be exhilirating.  What it really needs though, in order to appeal to the masses, is a chance for people to actually establish themselves.  Otherwise, who really cares?  You'll just end up naked on a beach again anyway.

No trees, no wood to pick up to create tools with, just naked with only a unlit torch and a rock which seems weird until you learn that you can't craft anything without blueprints, and you can only get them through destroying man made trash cans randomly generated on the world....
There is no intro to this game. You literally start the game somewhere on land, or in my case water, and are suppose to know what to do right off the bat.
I was punching buttons for minutes to try and figure out the controls all while trying to play the game.
No health/condition/hunger stats were available that I could find, and when I did manage to kill something, it's health bar went right back up to where it was before I killed it! That's just not right, can't even go hunt properly....
Your rock is not an indestructible rock. And after you use it to its full potential it breaks in a few pieces and that's that. I had picked up over 1,000 rocks and couldn't use even just 1 of them to replace my starter rock when it broke!
No starter rock=no mining. No mining =no blueprint shards, and no shardes= no more progression in the game. This game is extremely frustrating for new players just starting out; no tutorial, no opening story mode... Nothing.
I hope that after a few months I will be able to get back on here and reevaluate this review I have of the game and hopefully have a better outcome playing the game then I did when I first downloaded it.
Why does there have to be blue prints? Why can I make ammo before I can make a base or even a basic tool? I will attempt to play again... And hopes that my new game will have a better outcome.
Until then, I highly do NOT recommend this game.

I will give this game a positive review soley because I, personally, enjoyed it. I even plan to continue.
Now, I do understand that the game has some flaws, perhaps large ones. I still thoroughly liked it. The game itself is fairly simple and straightforward in terms of combat. This, combined with a nice story that is altered and carried mostly by the emotions that the player invests in it, makes for a unique experience. This is not to say it's a good or a bad game, but it's a mixture of simple and complex, as the game world differs with each playthrough. That sort of immersion is pretty nice. The simple art style is charming as well, although in some areas it goes pretty crazy.
I won't sing this game's praises, nor will I tell anyone who doesn't like it that they have no soul. I will simply say that everyone is entitled to their own opinion. You may not like the game itself, the story, the combat, or anything about it. That doesn't mean that your opinion is fact, nor does it mean that anyone who likes the game is garbage. Likewise, you may think the game is fantastic, but that doesn't mean that it really is, or that anyone who doesn't like it is stupid.
Let people think what they want to think, guys. It's not that hard to live and let live.

I put in 8 hours into this game thus far. Its not a bad game but it does have it's annoyances. For example, when  I first launched the game I woke up on a beach with a rock and a torch. After about 15 minutes, I came across someone with a rifle and and of course they shot and killed me. This happened several times through the 8 hours of game play. In my opinion, In this type of game you really shouldn't be able to get up to getting a rifle and killing anyone just starting the game for ths first time. If the official servers provided a game type that was more a community style IE minecraft, state of decay, this would be a pretty rockin game. Theres also a bug where sometimes when you start the game trees and hemp plants don't respawn or spawn at all. You have to exit the game and go back in to correct this. I understand this is a work in progress game, I just hope the dev's balance the game better and correct some of the issues. Graphically the game looks solid there are some graphical issues but overall its pretty good.  Also the official servers wipe the maps every few weeks so it basically undoes all your hard work. In some other reviews people have complained of other people hacking/cheating, in my game play I haven't noticed this but maybe thats why theres so many people with guns?
Pro's:
- Graphics are pretty good
- Great idea
- Crafting system is pretty solid
- Worth the current sale price of 10 bucks
- Food and water dimish at an acceptable rate to give you a chance to forage and gather meat
- From my experience anti cheat system seems to be working
Con's:
- Guns shouldn't be permitted to give new players a fighing chance and actually enjoy the game
- Servers reset every few weeks which will undo all your hard work of gathering resources and building a base
- Sometimes required resources don't respawn forcing you to quit the game and go back in
- I would prefer there be an option to band together with other survivors to ward off the jerk players gunning down new players
Overall I would recommend the game if your into survival/resource gathering games at the 10.00 price point other wise I would hold off till the official release and see whats been improved on.

Undertale is a throwback to JRPGs of old, in that it has the quirkiness and art style of the Earthbound series and the monster barter system of Shin Megami Tensei (aka you can talk your way outta combat). The story and characters are amazing, but the game isn't without its flaws. The beginning drags a bit, the ending isn't satisfying until you either do a true good ending run or a bad ending run and the bullet hell combat mechanic is both a pain and a chore. But the worst part (not the game's fault tho) is that the fandom for Undertale are more extreme that your typical (insert beloved media here) fans in both their dedication and prejudice against anyone who doesn't profess their Undyne (heh) love to the game. But despite all that Undertale is still one of those games you need to try, even if you end up hating it. For me the true magic of this game comes from its deep metaness and constant fourth wall breaking. The game tries not to just subvert JRPGS, but video games as a whole and the gamers that play them in a particular way. So do yourself a favor and play this game, no matter how you feel in the end you definitely won't regret it.

I put in 8 hours into this game thus far. Its not a bad game but it does have it's annoyances. For example, when  I first launched the game I woke up on a beach with a rock and a torch. After about 15 minutes, I came across someone with a rifle and and of course they shot and killed me. This happened several times through the 8 hours of game play. In my opinion, In this type of game you really shouldn't be able to get up to getting a rifle and killing anyone just starting the game for ths first time. If the official servers provided a game type that was more a community style IE minecraft, state of decay, this would be a pretty rockin game. Theres also a bug where sometimes when you start the game trees and hemp plants don't respawn or spawn at all. You have to exit the game and go back in to correct this. I understand this is a work in progress game, I just hope the dev's balance the game better and correct some of the issues. Graphically the game looks solid there are some graphical issues but overall its pretty good.  Also the official servers wipe the maps every few weeks so it basically undoes all your hard work. In some other reviews people have complained of other people hacking/cheating, in my game play I haven't noticed this but maybe thats why theres so many people with guns?
Pro's:
- Graphics are pretty good
- Great idea
- Crafting system is pretty solid
- Worth the current sale price of 10 bucks
- Food and water dimish at an acceptable rate to give you a chance to forage and gather meat
- From my experience anti cheat system seems to be working
Con's:
- Guns shouldn't be permitted to give new players a fighing chance and actually enjoy the game
- Servers reset every few weeks which will undo all your hard work of gathering resources and building a base
- Sometimes required resources don't respawn forcing you to quit the game and go back in
- I would prefer there be an option to band together with other survivors to ward off the jerk players gunning down new players
Overall I would recommend the game if your into survival/resource gathering games at the 10.00 price point other wise I would hold off till the official release and see whats been improved on.

Undertale demands a lot from the player. It demands at least some knowledge of videogames (especially JRPGs), anime, and internet subculture. It also demands you have a sense of humor similar to Toby Fox, the game's developer. If your sense of humor isn't completely goofy and nerdy, you might think the game is far too silly. And if you're looking for a challenge, you're looking in the wrong place.
All of that being said, I found Undertale to be one of the most hilarious, well-written games I've ever played. It's not the prettiest thing to look at, and could surely use a visual upgrade, but the music is fantastic, the battle system is far deeper than it seems at first glance (most of the boss fights are pretty great), and few games will ever warm your heart like Undertale will. Undertale is not for everyone, and the fanbase would do well to remember this. However, I can say with certainty that Undertale is for me.

It's a fun game of survival,  if you log the hours to learn it properly.  At first you will start out roaming around trying to survive the wilderness,  hunt food,  collect resources,  ect.  all while trying to avoid as many players as possible,  for you don't know if they're friendly or not.  Most are not,  but soon you will learn to how build a base,  a home sweet home.  Somewhere to put all of your items that you have collected,  put up signs make it yours then when you log off someone will bust in your improperly placed front door ransack the place,  take everything you have,  kill you and lock you out of your own house.  Then you repeat the process untill you either build a great unraidable base or join a clan.  This is not a game for solo players,  so you will have to meet people which is the most pulse pounding experience of your gaming life,  because it's almost like an old west standoff,  if they pull a gun you will have to react fast to take them down and run home with their stuff.  Overall the game is great if you're the worst possible human alive,  murdering, stealing, burglarizing homes,  shooting at anyhting living on the beach,  and pretending to be a fresh spawn just to kill a couple of people an hour in the game to get guns and resources for free.

A game with so much potential, so many avenues for growth. And it all fell to the side of greed.
Welcome to DayZ, a game abandoned by its developers because, well, they made their money and ran. DayZ has to be one of the most realistic/fun survival games I have ever played. It has no real rules, other than physics. There are no leaderboards, you cannot play it like Call of Duty, it is in fact a simulator. Your environment is just a landscape full of things that may kill you, full of people that can kill you, and that will kill you merely by choice. Your character is not bound to any story lines or quests. If you die, you lose everything. It is a game that has no point, no ultimate goal, other than just last as long as you can, gear up and fight the onslaught of players and zombies looking to take you out. You can do this with friends, for the "roaming with my squad" party effect, or do it all solo, in constant fear that someone somewhere may be following you, to take you out and steal your loot.
The idea of a game in Alpha was to have the game grow with the players, to achieve absolute perfection. However, over time it seems those who originally started this project lost touch of what this was all about. This game after many years still has major flaws and holes that have yet to be fixed. It seems to me that the developers are merely pointless adding features/weapons/towns/etc just to sprinkle some new excitement into the game without actually having to work on it any further. There a number of hackers, making this insanely are to play without wanting to kill yourself after wasting hours getting gear and exploring just to have someone ice-skate across the map and instantly kill you. There also is the optimization issues. I have a relatively powerful computer, and this game still destroys my settings to the point where I cannot run anything on a decent graphic settings. There are also places around the world that tank your FPS for no real reason.
Apart from an abundance of technical issues, theres gameplay as well. Most of the weapons do not respond as they really should. Because there is no real goals/achievements you eventually are just looting places until either someone hacking instantly kills you or you die to some random environment glitch. So at the end of the day, it is completely pointless to play at all. The only thing worth mentioning, to even play for, is the chance that you will get decently geared and will get into some sort of scuffle with another group of people, depending on the server you join.
Theres also a community issue. There are DayZ communties out there but most have to be heavily funded to function. Hosting a group server costs upwards of $70 a month, which for a game that isnt even finished yet, is absurd. And there is no LAN function built in, so if you and a group of friends do want to play on your own set up, you have to buy Arma 2 and just use the mod, which is in fact more stable and has better support than this stand alone.
So would I recommend this to someone? Unfortunately I have to say no. There is no clear sign of progression for me to validate even continuing playing. I feel lucky that I only payed $17 for this. I almost feel dooped into buying this in the first place. If someone really wanted their game to be special, to have a community work on it, then make it free. Call them beta testers, and give them something shiny in game for their contribution. I honestly do feel stupid for paying to be a alpha tester.
In all, I hope someone somewhere will see what happened here and will make the effort to create a game just like this if not identical to it. The potential for this game to be fun and fulfulling is endless, but it was thrown away, all because of greed.

I believe DayZ has gone in the wrong direction ever since the .47 update: the update just before persistance was added to the game.  The development team appears to be dedicated to adding new and cool content to the game but they don't seem to want to work on the boring yet essential pieces of the game such as the infamous low frame rate - which I heard keeps the entire map rendered in - and the annoying bugs that result in my death.  Don't even get me started on the desync in battles! Before the .47 update, the game was so much fun and possessed the perfect amount of content so they could start working on the core engine.  Now I feel the development team is digging themselves into a pit of useless content that will only hinder future patches that fix fps - which may come in 5 years - just like they have been doing for the many years this game has been out.  At this point, I think we are looking at a Rust legacy where the devs start with a bad framework that they struggle adding onto it.  However, the game has its really fun moments and, for me, I didn't find them in battle but just hanging out with my friends next to a campfire.  I would have recommended the game in an instant a year ago but now the critics of the game, who I opposed so much, are starting to sound right.  I don't know why other games are progressing so much and the original survival game with 3 million purchases is releasing 10 items per update! All I can say now is wait...

Day Z in my opinion is often looked down upon because of its bugs and the fact that it's been in Alpha for as long as it has been. But all great games begin somewhere, the only difference is that the creators of  Day Z let us participate in the development of the game, anyways.... on to game play! Day Z can be really fun whether you like playing Hero, Pack rat (me), Bandit, or Survivor play style. Same goes with playing solo or with a group, there's many advantages and disadvantages to both. For example if you play solo a lot then you're going to be able to travel more quickly since you won't have to wait for anyone, also you won't have to split the loot with anyone else (not a problem with me,I like sharing :P), but if you're alone then you're more likely to lose gunfights and you won't be able to loot as much considering you can only carry so much. As for being in a group the advantages are as listed,except the ones listed obviously in the disadvantages portion of solo game play, you will be able to socialize which is a big deal in surviving the apocalypse, also you and your group can learn more about the game by helping each other, and just plain ole assisting your group. Such as when someone has a broken limb, and especially when someone goes unconscious. As for specific things in the game, guns, weapons, items, vehicles, these are all subject to change, but the game play that I just described is here to last. Overall I believe this game is a sound investment that has payed me back constantly through amazing social experiences.

Rust, a game where the inconceivable happens. A game where many feelings of joy, laughter, anger, and sadness, set foot in your adventure in the lands of Rust. I have played Rust for over one thousand hours now and I believe it's time to make a proper review on my experience of the world of Rust.
Rust is my favorite open-world, survival, crafting, building, tree-chopping simulator on the market currently. It is a game with enough to enjoy for a century. With the game updating every week with brand new guns, supplies, resources, and much more, it feels like the game never ends. If you don't know already, the creators of Rust are the same people who made Garry's Mod. You know, the famous Half Life 2 mod the basically everyone on steam owns? That means that this game is plenty funded and will not be in early access forever like some other games...
Rust is a game where many thoughts go through your mind while playing.. "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥geared guys, I'm screwed." - "Where can I censor the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that are flopping all over my face." - "Damn Koreans." Rust may have a very toxic community but the community is what runs the game. Think about it, if Rust didn't have any players the game would be♥♥♥♥♥♥because there would be no PvP. The games only fun and enraging because there are toxic players.
Early game Rust is consequential and very intimidating. I recommend (if you're in vanilla/community) grabbing a already raided base so you can start out using less resources. It's a good technique especially because raiders tend to see already raided bases to be unworthy of raiding.
Mid-Game Rust is where you make a lot of tough descions. "Where should I make my new and improved base." "What design should it be?" Base designing is really tough and that's why I recommend fortify or rumbled. These programs allow you to test your base design without the worry of losing resources. Remember, don't use wood to make your base because it can be burned by a flamethrower. Don't use sheet metal because it can easily be destroyed by explosives and don't use armored because it's just damn too expensive. Stone is perfectly right in the middle. If you want a guide on which items do what damage here it is:
End-Game Rust.. Oh.. Where do I start, well, end-game is where you choose what bases to raid, how to defend your base, what guns to make, and I guess if you're into this kind of stuff, slaves. Slaves are very useful for many reasons. One reason is they farm resources for you for a small pay and housing. Usually, big clans use slaves as a lower rank for new members that want to join the clan. This way big clans can see if they're trustworthy enough to join. The blueprint system was a much more effecient way of using slaves because you could just give them a blueprint after they do their work but that's old business.
My rating on Rust would be a solid 10/10 for great vibes and solid effort by the development team. Thanks a lot facepunch!

REVIEW FOR CASUAL PLAYERS.
Okay so i although i don't have masses of game time on Rust, i can honestly say it is well worth the £15 or so it is priced at. I'll start with the negatives of the game although there arn't many at all!
>Social - Finding your own friends is more difficult than you might anticipate. There's no select-spawn and most maps are completely different. I'd suggest if you need to find your friend you locate an easily recognised landmark NOT a mountain or river, because there's often loads of mountains and rivers in a map. No, i mean maybe a large building like a tower or a power plant or a large water tower.
>Getting started - Getting started can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥ especially on high-populated servers. The majority of the gaming community are total♥♥♥♥♥♥♥when it comes to fresh spawns so assume nobody and everyone wants your precious rock. Building a base worthy of logging off in is difficult, as you really need at least a stone base/house before you can really begin to feel safe, and it does take bloody forever to collect the resources. So if your new to a server, make sure you have a couple of hours of free time or you'll find yourself logging off in an unsafe building or even still in the wilderness.
>Server resets - The thing i hate most about pretty much every online survival game that involves building. Minecraft, DayZ, Ark, every game has this issue but it's still annoying. Obviously people build bases, then simply leave them for whatever reason. The structures remain and clutter the world, lowering FPS and land. Servers usually deal with this by wiping the server every so often so everyone has to reset from scratch. Nuff said, it's annoying as being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by a horse, and equally as painful.
That's all the negatives really, now might i just say i feel this game has done a great job at being a survival game but unique from others. I won't be able to list every great aspect about this game but i strongly suggest you get this game as you can play it solo or with a group of friends and still have hours of enjoyment.
>Optimisation - I don't know what they've done to this game but it runs smooth as hell. I can run max settings at 50FPS (GTX 960, I54590). This game is smooth as hell much more so than any of its counterparts such as Ark and it obviously pisses all over DayZSA.
>Community - The rust community obviously is majority tossers looking for easy kills on fresh spawns, however, it is much better than any other survival game i know of, ESPECIALLY DayZ. In some cases, whole servers are friendly.
>Gameplay - All of the gameplay is great. Rust is unique in it's own way, setting itself apart from other games of survival type. You may hate the fact that one day you can log on dead and your base destroyed and raided, however that's all part of the thrill. It means there's skill in basebuilding more so than in other games, and it also means that if you can be raided you can raid too, you can literally see a base and know it's not impossible to go in there and flatten it. Unlike in DayZ overpoch where most servers have indestructable bases meaning you can't get in or flatten it, and even if you do get in the chances are all your enemies items are locked away in a rock-hard safe.
>Building/crafting - Again, i love the crafting menu. It's confusing at first but its just so practical, as is the build system. Building may not be 'free' but all the objects are solid. It's incredibly difficult to bug through floors under any circumstance or anything, the build module even has a 'flip' option, so if you place a wall the wrong way, you don't have to completely demolish and rebuild it!
>Signs and paintings - I love this so much. You can paint on signs and canvas that you create and let your artistic side flow making your base ever more homely. Me and my good friend Meg have spent literally about an hour just adding to our picture wall.
>Wildlife - Although there's not much wildlife, chickens growl and deer givee you chicken breast, the hunting is bloody fun. Not buggy, and the bears and wolves scare the absolute living erection out of your trousers. Be careful!
>Gunplay - Very unique and really fun. The guns are just fun to shoot and although i haven't gotten into any real massive combet yet, i look forward to it!
>Adaptability - You can play this game however you want. You can raid people constantly, you can defend, you can bandit, you can be friendly, you can trade, you can war, you can raid secretly as people are offline or you can go all out and attack that person and make them watch you obliterate their base. The possibilites are endless! In fact, just recently we as a group conducted our first raid by using a charge to blow off the roof of a house, jump down, destroy the sleeping bag, loot the chests and get a jey to the door to let ourselves out, and instead of outwright murdering poor gavin asleep in the corner, we placed a land-mine right next to him as a farewell present. (Sorry Gavin).
That's all, but really if anyone does make it this far well done! And seriously, buy Rust you won't regret it!
And thanks to Meg for gifting me this!

Day Z in my opinion is often looked down upon because of its bugs and the fact that it's been in Alpha for as long as it has been. But all great games begin somewhere, the only difference is that the creators of  Day Z let us participate in the development of the game, anyways.... on to game play! Day Z can be really fun whether you like playing Hero, Pack rat (me), Bandit, or Survivor play style. Same goes with playing solo or with a group, there's many advantages and disadvantages to both. For example if you play solo a lot then you're going to be able to travel more quickly since you won't have to wait for anyone, also you won't have to split the loot with anyone else (not a problem with me,I like sharing :P), but if you're alone then you're more likely to lose gunfights and you won't be able to loot as much considering you can only carry so much. As for being in a group the advantages are as listed,except the ones listed obviously in the disadvantages portion of solo game play, you will be able to socialize which is a big deal in surviving the apocalypse, also you and your group can learn more about the game by helping each other, and just plain ole assisting your group. Such as when someone has a broken limb, and especially when someone goes unconscious. As for specific things in the game, guns, weapons, items, vehicles, these are all subject to change, but the game play that I just described is here to last. Overall I believe this game is a sound investment that has payed me back constantly through amazing social experiences.

Wanna start out by saying I went into this game completely blind and unbiased. I heard about this game called "Undertale" from some post on Tumblr (I only follow artists I swear), and honestly I though it was just another terrible flash game (some of the said artists I follow have collaborated on a few small flash game projects which I never cared about, I assumed it was just another one of those)
Then I saw it on Steam and was kind of surprised to find it on the store, as I said I thought it was just some flash game. And to my surprise it had surpassed Portal 2 to become the 2nd highest rated game ever on Steam. Within a week.  Picked it up for $10 and played it. So at this point I hadn't heard ANYTHING about it. At all. Not even seen any of the characters yet.
I was COMPLETELY taken aback by how good it was. This game is amazing.
Now that that's out of the way I'm gonna go over some pros and cons:
Pros:
+Every NPC is very well done. Unique design, good dialogue. Every character feels special and interesting.
+World design is really good. Every area has a different vibe and ambience to it. Makes it fun to go through the world and explore, instead of just repeating the same type of area over and over.
+Humor is on par. Might not be for everyone but I honestly found myself in stitches at some points.
+Soundtrack. Best soundtrack for a game I've ever heard, except for maybe Portal 2. Every song is memorable and I regret not getting the bundle that included the songs.
+Battle system is amazing. Sprites are insanely well done, the first game I've ever seen that doesn't just give you the options to fight or run, but also to try and solve battles through diplomacy. What other game does that, seriously, what game gives you the option to TALK your way out of a fight. Also, what appeared to be a pile of Jell-O stopped attacking me because I waved my hips at it seductively.
+You can date a skeleton in this game. Let me say that again; You can go on a date, with a skeleton.
+There are AT LEAST 5 dogs in this game.
+This game gives you options. Lots of options. You want to murder everyone in the world? You can do that. Wanna talk your way out of a battle and be a peaceful resident of the underground? You can do that.
+Why are there 6 dogs now..?
+No other game has made me feel such a range of emotions. It'll make you laugh, cry, be sad, be happy, or be angry. Sometimes all of these at the same time.
+Okay I lost count of the dogs, you'll have to count them yourself.
I love this game so much, however there ARE some cons.
Cons:
-The player sprite is obnoxiously designed. Toby Fox wanted the character to be of ambiguous gender, so you could project yourself and your personality onto it. He succeeded but everything else is just badly made. I mean the basic color scheme of this game is all dark colors. There are bright colors that are used well, but this player design has the skin color of a LEGO minifigure. The shirt is ugly and it all doesn't fit.
-Again, the player design. The face. It's literally just this face [-_-]. Nothing else. The entire game. It bugs me, all the NPCs are filled with emotion and expression, and here is this emotionless robot that is supposed to be me?
-Fandom is turning very sour.
-I had a lot of confusion with this game. Where to go, who to interact with. I didn't even know how to get the ending until I googled it, because when I thought the game ended it turned out there was more to it. In all honesty there is a 90% chance you will have to look up something really quick to figure out what to do.
All in all, pros and cons, I enjoyed this game. In fact it's one of my favorite games I've ever played, coming from someone  who does not enjoy most RPG's and the game he has the most hours on is Kerbal Space Program.

Undertale is an incredible game.
Please ignore my play time, I have actually played this game for hours in offline mode.
When i first heard about it, I was litterally blown away by one simple fact.
It was a RPG where you choose how you want to deal with you'r enemies. I'm not talking simple,
"I can spare this story character, at this time so I can get a bonus but I'll kill this one because I hate his guts," sort of inccidents that come with most RPGs, I'm not kidding when I say, you can Spare EVERYONE.
I remember I heard about it when my brother showed me a You tube video about it. I remember standing ther laughing as the guy tried to spare the first boss, who in truth I wouldn't want to finish off either. I remember thinking "Man, toughen up, that's just how these games are. It's sad but true, they make you fight." but as the fight progressed. I realised that wasn't the case. I stood there dumbfounded when the boss just... gave in, not even hurt. It was the way I would exspect the senario to go, but never hoped that a RPG would actually allow you to play it out. That was when I relised that this, was something very diffrent from other RPGs, and I added the thing to my wishlist and avoided all the spoilers I could.
This is a game you have to go in raw in order to feel the full effect.
It is emotional and thought prevoking, with witty lighthearted, (If not somewhat corny) banter, but quite a few gut punch moments, and a ligetimatly terrifying and tragic villian.
I should mention that how you play has a significant effect over the overall feel of the game... you'll figure it out, just don't take one look at the first playthough and think that's all there is to it.
then of course you can go into the games hidden meaning, but you'll only get that once you figure out the true ending, and you do have to think about it, I sure did. Let's just say, theres alot of meaning that can be hidden in a name.
Overal this is a great game. The graphics are old fastion, but they are done in such a way that the game has it's own special charm.
the battle sequenses are easily my favorite part of the game, as they each requier you to do something diffrent, and as you play you learn about the character you are faceing, and sometimes, you have to do something that no other RPG (That I've yet seen) would ever ask you to do, wich in of it'self forces you to think about what you have to do.
Perhaps I over analize games, Lol, but all in all, Untertale is a gem, that is at least worth a try. It's an RPG, but, it's a diffrent RPG, that may leave you looking at games in a diffrent way.

I decided to wait a little bit before buying in to this to see if it would just be another over-hyped mediocre game (kind of like FNAF was). It's not.
I hate RPGs (usually retro themed ones, like this), and I really don't care much about story. This game is the complete exception to that, this is a fantastic RPG, with amazingly funny while interesting story.
There's 3 different runs:
Pacifist
Neutral
Genocide
I chose the pacifist run, and honestly don't think I can bring myself to do genocide. If you're looking at my hours, thinking it would take that long, it won't. I had Undertale open to listen to the music quite a lot of the time, because I don't have enough cash to buy the OST right now.
All the characters are lovable, funny, and add a lot to the story. Look in to the game, and see if it's for you before you purchase. Before you fully experience the game it will probably be more than 2 hours, which is beyond the Steam refund time limit. If you look in to it, and want to experience the joy, sadness, and laughter that this game has to offer, do yourself a favor. Buy it.
Buy it all full price too if you can, support the developer as much as you can, he deserves it! (and the OST if you can afford it!)
