Sure it has its fair share of issues with bugs, hackers, and ninja zombies, etc, but I've never played a game like it before where there was so much freedom and interaction with other players. You can play however you want, whether it be as a hero, paramedic, bandit, survivor, hunter, trader; the list goes on. DayZ still has a long way to go but I think it has the potential to become a truly incredible game. As a lover of RPG games, this one is by far the best! Undertale has a great and very interesting plot that draws people into the world it takes place in. Depending on the choices you make throughout the game and how much you keep a close eye on things, the story is almost always changing somehow, weather it's drastically or only small details. You could play Undertale a million times and you would always see some type of change or secret you didn't see before.
The characters are well created and you get attached to them as you play. I don't know how many times I started to cry or felt bad or sad about the choices I made whenever I reseted the game and started playing from the beginning again every time I finished it. It felt like I was seeing old friends again, even though they no longer remember me. Even now, after playing and finishing Undertale five times, I still laugh and smile at the actions of these characters when I see them make the same jokes as they did all the other times.
Another amazing aspect of the game is it's soundtrack. The music really sets the mood of the scene, weather you're simply at the shop buying supplies or fighting one of the bosses. You always feel the emotions that each song creates when it plays. It really makes you feel like you're the character in the game, not the one controling the character. There are even times I listen to some of the songs on the sountrack when I'm doing homework, and they always fill me with determination to finish it, no matter how late at night it is.
I don't know about anyone else, but personally, I would love to see Toby Fox create a sequal to Undertale. I know if he did, I would buy it in an instant!

Undertale is an incredible game.
Please ignore my play time, I have actually played this game for hours in offline mode.
When i first heard about it, I was litterally blown away by one simple fact.
It was a RPG where you choose how you want to deal with you'r enemies. I'm not talking simple,
"I can spare this story character, at this time so I can get a bonus but I'll kill this one because I hate his guts," sort of inccidents that come with most RPGs, I'm not kidding when I say, you can Spare EVERYONE.
I remember I heard about it when my brother showed me a You tube video about it. I remember standing ther laughing as the guy tried to spare the first boss, who in truth I wouldn't want to finish off either. I remember thinking "Man, toughen up, that's just how these games are. It's sad but true, they make you fight." but as the fight progressed. I realised that wasn't the case. I stood there dumbfounded when the boss just... gave in, not even hurt. It was the way I would exspect the senario to go, but never hoped that a RPG would actually allow you to play it out. That was when I relised that this, was something very diffrent from other RPGs, and I added the thing to my wishlist and avoided all the spoilers I could.
This is a game you have to go in raw in order to feel the full effect.
It is emotional and thought prevoking, with witty lighthearted, (If not somewhat corny) banter, but quite a few gut punch moments, and a ligetimatly terrifying and tragic villian.
I should mention that how you play has a significant effect over the overall feel of the game... you'll figure it out, just don't take one look at the first playthough and think that's all there is to it.
then of course you can go into the games hidden meaning, but you'll only get that once you figure out the true ending, and you do have to think about it, I sure did. Let's just say, theres alot of meaning that can be hidden in a name.
Overal this is a great game. The graphics are old fastion, but they are done in such a way that the game has it's own special charm.
the battle sequenses are easily my favorite part of the game, as they each requier you to do something diffrent, and as you play you learn about the character you are faceing, and sometimes, you have to do something that no other RPG (That I've yet seen) would ever ask you to do, wich in of it'self forces you to think about what you have to do.
Perhaps I over analize games, Lol, but all in all, Untertale is a gem, that is at least worth a try. It's an RPG, but, it's a diffrent RPG, that may leave you looking at games in a diffrent way.

Rust is a game of hardship, trust, community and heartbreak. Over the course of a year, the game has changed, from being completely about killing everyone who came near, to working towards creating communities that band together to wage battle and besiege the enemy.
Each time I shut down Rust, I am constantly thinking about rushing right back to the game just for a few more hours. It all started with legacy Rust, just a month or two from it's
release. That was a subpar game by my standards, the community was volatile on almost every server, and no one was willing to help new players. It was plagued by easy to obtain raid gear, and overpowered endgame weapons. I put in roughly 60 hours despite this (
). When it got old, due to the previously explained shortcomings, I left the game for half a year, casually reading the update blog and becoming hyped at the amount of work they put in and propose to put in. The amount of time I put in after the forced updates, is ridiculous, 60+ hours in two weeks. Cramming in play time whenever possible, sometimes all night just to finish building an unraidable base. *Sigh*
Of course, without any people to compete against this game would be no fun as it would turn into a base building game...which it is not. The PvP aspect of this game is still a bit tricky, as you sometimes try to be humane, while some people will work with you only to be holding a thompson to your head when you finish a good run. It is situations such as this that make the game fun, i.e., the risk of losing everything on your person, with the potential to have a nemesis to raid in the near future. Teaming up against enemies to raid is fun to say the least, and that hint of danger is always lurking nearby, keeping you on edge.
In points:
Pros:
+Longevity
+Progression is well-paced (as there is no true progression system)
+Community
+Learning curve
+Combat
+Raiding
+Building system
+Constant danger
+Fun
Cons:
-Community (depending on the server, you can always ask assuming players are online on the server)
-No tutorial yet
-Quick progression to guns
-Raiding (Tool Cabinets can be frustrating)
-Time sink
-Mining wood
-Some optimization issues

A story with many layers to peel back and fun, well-written and fleshed out characters that will leave you wanting to return again and again. A gameplay experience that compliments this story by refreshing itself with new mechanics and unique confrontations consistently throughout the not-quite-too-short time it takes to make a single run through. Great character designs and awesome sound design despite the technical limitations. There are scenes to make you laugh and scenes to make you cry, and neither ever feel out of place because the pacing and storytelling are that good. Undertale is one of those rare pieces of art that's more well thought out than most releases 10x it's size, the kind of discovery that reminds me why thousands of years after the hero's tale was settled upon, we still come up with new stories to tell each other.
If there are gripes to be had they are that fighting enemies with the intent to kill requires no strategy, tactics or thought other than timing and dodging, making it a strictly less interactive and fun method than talking your way out every time. It can be argued as being intentional, but if all Undertale did was flip what most games do (make the violence interactive and the talking more like a menu) it suddenly seems much less original and interesting, and at times it felt a little like that. As it stands, I dread starting a Genocide run to complete seeing the rest of the story because just thinking of thoughtlessly button mashing my way through the game makes me bored. I have a couple minor gripes mostly relating to the game's ending(s) that I won't post here because, y'know, NO SPOILERS.
Undertale is an experience for people who love video games and stories. I'd give it at least a 9.5/10 as an honest-to-god rating. It's not the biggest adventure out there, the one with the most secrets, the most twists, or the most characters. But the amount of good ideas packed into this little package is full to absolute bursting. I honestly have a hard time thinking of anyone who I don't think would enjoy it at all.
But I'm sure I'm not telling you anything you haven't heard before. The hype surrounding this little game is, to say the least, DETERMINED. Stop fighting it and know that someday you're gonna end up playing it to see what everybody's talking about anyway.

Wow... Undertale... where do I begin? It's trully an amazing game.
I guess I should start with the game's best aspect: the story. (Don't worry, no spoilers!) Normally I don't give a crud about good story. There are only 2 game I have played where the story actully ADDED to the game, and this is one of them. Two of the charecters feel very real to me, and the others keap me laughing so much I don't care that they are a tad simple. (Of course in the normal ending you won't see much of the good story, really only in the good ending.) I'd rate the story a 9/10.
The gameplay is... a tad bland. The enemies are very diverse, and the bosses are amazing. The combat style is very different from most RPGs, becuase when the enemies attack they shoot bullets at you that you have to dodge in a bullet-you-know-what style, and when you attack it requires some timing, or it requires solving a puzzle if you want to spare the enemy. But with that being said, the player has one attack. Not a big deal if you are trying to get the good ending, but in the normal ending (and presumably the bad ending, which I have not played) you start to notice. The game is also very easy, I never died while trying to get the normal ending and only I died 3 times during the good ending. It's still a lot of fun story or no story, so I am giving the gameplay 7/10.
The art? Who gives a dang?! Sure the art is... not good, but again, who gives a dang? The art does not get in the way of the game, so it has achived it's gole.  Unless you are colorblind. You unforchanatly need to at least see blue, orange, and green to be able to dodge some of the bullets. (Being able to see yellow would also help) Not a big issue, but I would've liked it if the was an option for all you colorblind people. 7/10.
The music is probably the 2nd best part of the game. Absalutly amazing 10/10 (Don't ask me why I ranked the 2nd best part of the game higher than the best part, I have my reasons)
Probalby my biggest gripe about the game is that it is too short. Sure it has 3 endings to add replay value, but I beat both the normal ending and good ending in less than 12 hours.
Nevertheless this game is worth those 10 bucks. 9/10, an almost perfect game.

I am a huge fan of the RPGs of the SNES-era: Super Mario RPG, Terranigma, Final Fantasy, Secret Of Mana, Chrono Trigger, Earthbound, etc. The art, the story, the characters, the gameplay, the soundtrack. These games had it all and thus left a big impression on me and rank very high among my favorite games of all time.
Undertale managed to do the same for me. It stays true to the spirit of these games but at the same time it does something new: It messes around with your experiences, your expectations and parodies the core elements and clichés of the genre whereever it possibly can.
A little warning on that note: The humor is not for everyone. I'd describe it as random, meta and often rather blunt. I often couldn't really believe what just was happening on my screen. If you can't stand these kind of jokes you won't enjoy the game. Just read the game key features on the store page and have a look at the
and you get the idea.
√ awesome pixel artstyle
√ great world design
√ hilarious and lovable character design
√ turn based fighting system with minigames and non-lethal option
√ your playstyle and actions have consequences and have the power to alter the game and further events heavily
√ small and fun puzzles to solve
√ appealing story with a lot of unexpected events and twists
√ masterpiece of a soundtrack
√ great sense of humor, doesn't take itself too serious
√ 3 possible endings with alternate versions based on your actions
× only one save slot
x rather short game with ~7 hours
I recommend Undertale to everyone who is a fan of the good old-fashioned RPGs of the SNES-era but doesn't expect a 100% serious game and can take a lot of jokes.

Wow... Undertale... where do I begin? It's trully an amazing game.
I guess I should start with the game's best aspect: the story. (Don't worry, no spoilers!) Normally I don't give a crud about good story. There are only 2 game I have played where the story actully ADDED to the game, and this is one of them. Two of the charecters feel very real to me, and the others keap me laughing so much I don't care that they are a tad simple. (Of course in the normal ending you won't see much of the good story, really only in the good ending.) I'd rate the story a 9/10.
The gameplay is... a tad bland. The enemies are very diverse, and the bosses are amazing. The combat style is very different from most RPGs, becuase when the enemies attack they shoot bullets at you that you have to dodge in a bullet-you-know-what style, and when you attack it requires some timing, or it requires solving a puzzle if you want to spare the enemy. But with that being said, the player has one attack. Not a big deal if you are trying to get the good ending, but in the normal ending (and presumably the bad ending, which I have not played) you start to notice. The game is also very easy, I never died while trying to get the normal ending and only I died 3 times during the good ending. It's still a lot of fun story or no story, so I am giving the gameplay 7/10.
The art? Who gives a dang?! Sure the art is... not good, but again, who gives a dang? The art does not get in the way of the game, so it has achived it's gole.  Unless you are colorblind. You unforchanatly need to at least see blue, orange, and green to be able to dodge some of the bullets. (Being able to see yellow would also help) Not a big issue, but I would've liked it if the was an option for all you colorblind people. 7/10.
The music is probably the 2nd best part of the game. Absalutly amazing 10/10 (Don't ask me why I ranked the 2nd best part of the game higher than the best part, I have my reasons)
Probalby my biggest gripe about the game is that it is too short. Sure it has 3 endings to add replay value, but I beat both the normal ending and good ending in less than 12 hours.
Nevertheless this game is worth those 10 bucks. 9/10, an almost perfect game.

On top of all of this it portrays story through the gameplay mechanics themself, and you feel a direct connection to the story through what you are doing in the game.
Long story short, Undertale is a game that I think every gamer should playthrough in their lifetime.

If you think you'd like this game even a little bit, you probably will. This is especially true if you enjoy classic RPGs, moreso the Earthbound/Mother games as its style and humor are very similar.
Undertale is very well written, with a cast of all likable characters, a strong story and fun game play to boot.
The pacing is perfect, nothing overstays its welcome or feels like it ended too soon. The dialogue and text always leaves you wanting more in the next scene, meanwhile the game play segments tie in well with what's going on in the current scenario. You never feel like you're tediously trudging through an area or puzzle to get to the next cutscene, meanwhile you don't feel as if the cutscenes interrupt the game play.
After finishing it, Undertale became not only my favorite game of 2015, but my favorite game of all time. The hype may seem offputting for it, but after playing it the praise this game receives is all well placed and well deserved. Is it the best game ever made? I'll leave that for you to decide!

TL;DR: Mechanics and late-game equipment are good and well-done, early-game is incredibly difficult and the community is quite literally AIDS...
Beginning in Rust is very difficult by yourself, even playing with friends is difficult. You spawn with a rock and a torch, and you have to get wood and stone to create tools like hatchets and pickaxes, then you need cloth to make a sleeping bag for a spawn point, or to get your friends into the same area as you, and hope to find that one person who's willing to lend a hand. In Rust, morals don't exist. Everyone will try to kill you for the stupidest of reasons. Mining an ore node someone was nowhere near? Guess what, you died! That guy wants that ore node for himself and he's not gonna let you and your naked body take it!
But let's assume you got past all that, you built a base and have your materials in chests, all neat and tidy. You have an airlock for your house which is locked with armoured doors, which makes it all the more difficult for raiders to get in. You find other people who are willing to help you progress with your little game, and everything seems pretty nice. Everyone is still out for your blood, even the people you trusted. You may or may not come back to find yourself dead, because disconnected players don't disappear, oh no, your character goes to sleep, leaving you out in the open for someone to just walk by, somehow get into your house and then take everything you own.
Death is inevitable, like in all games, but it happens way too often here. The wolves and bears don't kill you, people do. People who have no liking for anyone else, and don't care how recently they spawned. People who are going to claim to be friendly, then blast your face full of bullets. People who just want to annoy the everliving crap out of you, just because they can.
If you're into the community more than the game mechanics (doubtful) then this is something to steer well clear of. If you're into mechanics and willing to lose your soul/morals to the game, go right ahead. It's not my $20 anyway...

On top of all of this it portrays story through the gameplay mechanics themself, and you feel a direct connection to the story through what you are doing in the game.
Long story short, Undertale is a game that I think every gamer should playthrough in their lifetime.

Undertale is one of those games I'm happy to have played, and won't soon forget.
It's an awesome narrative experience, with challenging and engaging gameplay. The minimal graphic style might turn you off at first but ultimately contributes to the experience.
You should play Undertale if you'd like to try a well paced game, with interesting takes on classic RPG mechanics, and great characters that will grow on you.

I'll preface this review by simply saying that Undertale should be played without any proir knowledge.
_______________________________________________________________
, which I found inconsistent in a couple of ways. Environments are occasionally sparse, and while many of the settings are nicely realised with environmental animations and elements to investigate or characters to interact with,  some areas lack that attention and felt empty as a result. For the most part though, the environments are interesting- even if I'd have liked a little more visual detail overall.
The second inconsistency in the visuals I found to be a real credit to the game- the character design. Each character is unique, with individual construction, animations, and expressions. Often typefaces are even exclusive.
There is no stock character that all others are based on- no template on how all character's eyes should look when they're angry or happy in Undertale. It helps define the characters as individuals, and makes them memorable as a result.
The final boss was initially jarring in terms of visual design, but it was a choice that makes perfect sense in a game that's constantly seeking to subvert expectations. There was no foucs-group meeting to discuss a glossy homognised visual style for the characters in this game- and it gives Undertale a depth of texture as a result. It's creative freedom at it's best.
, which is argualbly the star of the show in Undertale. The sheer amount of different arrangements  impresses alone- each boss having it's own tune, environments and short pathways often featuring songs that you will only hear in that area.
The music ranges from extremely catchy to devestatingly emotive, and combined with the previously dicussed characters, completely define Undertale.
in Undertale at it's worst is functional, and at it's best- fun. The battle gameplay mechanic is entertaining and frequently introduces surprises to keep each encounter interesting. RPG style elements add a bit of depth to the boss fights, but the system is more an engaging means to and end than something the game's success hinges on.
Overworld puzzles tended to be simplistic and a bit uninspired, I felt there could have been improvement here with some more invention. The gameplay isn't the sole focus of Undertale, though; It's one aspect of a larger package. One that contains a story, the outcome of which is decided by you.
The various elements that form Undetale are largely subjective. The visuals, music, and humour are all fair game for debate, but the amount of enjoyment had will likely depend on your own sensibilities. Once this description can be applied to something, you could reasonably call it a piece of art. What you derive from it is entirely up to you.

, which is argualbly the star of the show in Undertale. The sheer amount of different arrangements  impresses alone- each boss having it's own tune, environments and short pathways often featuring songs that you will only hear in that area.
The music ranges from extremely catchy to devestatingly emotive, and combined with the previously dicussed characters, completely define Undertale.
in Undertale at it's worst is functional, and at it's best- fun. The battle gameplay mechanic is entertaining and frequently introduces surprises to keep each encounter interesting. RPG style elements add a bit of depth to the boss fights, but the system is more an engaging means to and end than something the game's success hinges on.
Overworld puzzles tended to be simplistic and a bit uninspired, I felt there could have been improvement here with some more invention. The gameplay isn't the sole focus of Undertale, though; It's one aspect of a larger package. One that contains a story, the outcome of which is decided by you.
The various elements that form Undetale are largely subjective. The visuals, music, and humour are all fair game for debate, but the amount of enjoyment had will likely depend on your own sensibilities. Once this description can be applied to something, you could reasonably call it a piece of art. What you derive from it is entirely up to you.

TL;DR: Mechanics and late-game equipment are good and well-done, early-game is incredibly difficult and the community is quite literally AIDS...
Beginning in Rust is very difficult by yourself, even playing with friends is difficult. You spawn with a rock and a torch, and you have to get wood and stone to create tools like hatchets and pickaxes, then you need cloth to make a sleeping bag for a spawn point, or to get your friends into the same area as you, and hope to find that one person who's willing to lend a hand. In Rust, morals don't exist. Everyone will try to kill you for the stupidest of reasons. Mining an ore node someone was nowhere near? Guess what, you died! That guy wants that ore node for himself and he's not gonna let you and your naked body take it!
But let's assume you got past all that, you built a base and have your materials in chests, all neat and tidy. You have an airlock for your house which is locked with armoured doors, which makes it all the more difficult for raiders to get in. You find other people who are willing to help you progress with your little game, and everything seems pretty nice. Everyone is still out for your blood, even the people you trusted. You may or may not come back to find yourself dead, because disconnected players don't disappear, oh no, your character goes to sleep, leaving you out in the open for someone to just walk by, somehow get into your house and then take everything you own.
Death is inevitable, like in all games, but it happens way too often here. The wolves and bears don't kill you, people do. People who have no liking for anyone else, and don't care how recently they spawned. People who are going to claim to be friendly, then blast your face full of bullets. People who just want to annoy the everliving crap out of you, just because they can.
If you're into the community more than the game mechanics (doubtful) then this is something to steer well clear of. If you're into mechanics and willing to lose your soul/morals to the game, go right ahead. It's not my $20 anyway...

This game is both charming and emotional and is a lot of fun to play. Not only does it deliver a very intersting story with distinct characters, it also offers unique gameplay that combines rpg-style elements and bullet hell battles, and battles with enemies are unique so it doesn't ever feel like the gameplay is getting old. There are many humorous lines of dialogue and touching moments throughout the game that, despite being just a simple pixelated game, makes you feel very connected with the in-game characters, moreso than most games have ever been able to do successfully in the past.
Undertale is probably one of the best games I've played in quite some time and I would definately recommend it to almost anyone, both newer gamers and experienced gamers alike.

Undertale is a low-res RPG set in an undefinable setting. It borrows a lot of elements from several different archegenres, that I won't list here. The game takes place underground and across several different locations in this cavern.
This game uses turn based-combat with the command blocks similar to other RPGs that also employ this system, such as Attact and Item menues. While in combat, you utilize an "attack bar", where you must time your hits to the center of the bar for maximum damage during your turn. During the enemy's turn, you have the oppertunity to avoid their attacks, via verticle-shooter style, where you must actually avoid attacks to prevent damage.
Undertale uses Pixel-based graphics, much like the old Marios and a few newer games, such as Bit-trip runner and Cavestory.
The sounds for this game were very good, if you're into 16 bit sounds. The sound effects match actions well, such as movement through menus and attacking, and so forth. The music of this game is memorable, and some of it is quite catchy, to the point to where you never want to finish a combat sequence or leave an area. Of course, there were also a few tracks that didn't tickle my fancy, and ended up bothering me after a bit, but those were few and far between.
Undertale is about a boy who fell down a hole into a cavern. Inside this cavern dwell monsters of many different shapes and forms, but not all are inheriently hostile. Your journey through this cavern takes you through a few noteworthy areas, and introduces you to a colorful cast of very well designed characters. While the characters themselves don't have a terrible amount of backstory, their personalities are very well conveyed and make this experience a very entertaining one.
Undertale is a unique game for a few reasons. First of all, you don't have to kill a single creature. Not a single enemy. Second of all, it focuses heavily on comedy and puzzles as core elements of it. This is very well done in my opinon, as the jokes aren't forced (except for the blatanly obvious ones that are made by the characters), and the puzzles aren't particularly hard, but do require some thought and exploration to solve.
AND YOU CAN USE A CONTROLLER.
So... This game is wonderful. It's beautifully thought out and executed in an extremely great manner that could lead to several hours of playtime. There's a huge world of lore and tidbits that could have you reading for hours at a time. The bosses of the game are unique in their attacks and personalities too, and in the fact that you don't actually have to kill any of them, due to the mercy option on your command board. I loved just how much fun the characters were, and how well (or comically bad) they interacted with each other. The visuals, for me, allow for imagination about the world around you, due to just how few there are. None of the boss fights felt unfair or as though they were impossible to overcome. The story made me smile, laugh, shudder, cry, and even filled me with
.
I absolutely encourage anyone who enjoys games that take them on adventures to places forigen, both in reality, and in your own mind. It's truly an experience worthy to be had.

Well, I don't really know where to begin. Let's start with the ethos.
I am currently doing my 4th playthrough of the game, and I have achieved Neutral, Pacifist (Don't kill anyone), and True Pacifist (make friends with Papyrus, Undyne, and Alphys) endings (The current run is Neutral, then moving on to Genocide).
The game itself is revolutionary, but you may not know that from the screenshots. So, here are a few lists to show you basically what I mean.
GAMEPLAY:
+No one has to die! Except maybe you, if you ask
.
+Fun, classic RPG-style gameplay.
+Active attacks and defenses! This means that monsters don't just deal damage, you instead have to maneuver your heart (soul, whatever) around a box to dodge attacks, and you have to press Z with the right timing to attack (not that difficult).
+Bosses introduce new attacks and Soul States (movement modifiers) to keep things fresh.
-Bosses, especially Asgore, will mess you up BAD on a pacifist run.
-Can sometimes be difficult to figure out how to spare some enemies, especially bosses (again, notably Asgore).
-By the time you know you're gonna have a bad time, it's too late to change it.
-Fairly short, I've done about 3.25 runs in 15 hours.
Characters:
+Mostly lovable, quirky, and hilarious characters. Comes complete with spaghetti-obsessed skeleton, killer robot TV show host, and goat mom.
+Breaks the fourth wall ALL the time.
+All of the endings are very satisfying, and make you feel either very good about yourself, very bad about yourself, or repulsed (By the Neutral ending final boss
.
-Genocide runs make you feel like a terrible person.
-Onionsan. Onionsan is pointless. Luckily you won't have to endure a lot of him.
Environment/Asthetic:
+Lots of loving details put into every corner of the game, from changing the "Sparable Monster" names from yellow to pink, all the way to Lesser Dog's petting-induced snow art. Really creative.
+The music is great, and almost always fits the situation well (The duck flight scene is an apparently ironic exception).
-The areas get boring to look at if you stick around for too long, or on repeated runthroughs.
In the end, it's a great game, and definitely worth getting. However, if you want something to occupy you for a long time, this isn't the game for you. And be sure to tell Muffet NOT to pour you a brimming glass of spiders!
Also, Steam Awards! Pick this one for like every category.

This game is both charming and emotional and is a lot of fun to play. Not only does it deliver a very intersting story with distinct characters, it also offers unique gameplay that combines rpg-style elements and bullet hell battles, and battles with enemies are unique so it doesn't ever feel like the gameplay is getting old. There are many humorous lines of dialogue and touching moments throughout the game that, despite being just a simple pixelated game, makes you feel very connected with the in-game characters, moreso than most games have ever been able to do successfully in the past.
Undertale is probably one of the best games I've played in quite some time and I would definately recommend it to almost anyone, both newer gamers and experienced gamers alike.

Undertale is a low-res RPG set in an undefinable setting. It borrows a lot of elements from several different archegenres, that I won't list here. The game takes place underground and across several different locations in this cavern.
This game uses turn based-combat with the command blocks similar to other RPGs that also employ this system, such as Attact and Item menues. While in combat, you utilize an "attack bar", where you must time your hits to the center of the bar for maximum damage during your turn. During the enemy's turn, you have the oppertunity to avoid their attacks, via verticle-shooter style, where you must actually avoid attacks to prevent damage.
Undertale uses Pixel-based graphics, much like the old Marios and a few newer games, such as Bit-trip runner and Cavestory.
The sounds for this game were very good, if you're into 16 bit sounds. The sound effects match actions well, such as movement through menus and attacking, and so forth. The music of this game is memorable, and some of it is quite catchy, to the point to where you never want to finish a combat sequence or leave an area. Of course, there were also a few tracks that didn't tickle my fancy, and ended up bothering me after a bit, but those were few and far between.
Undertale is about a boy who fell down a hole into a cavern. Inside this cavern dwell monsters of many different shapes and forms, but not all are inheriently hostile. Your journey through this cavern takes you through a few noteworthy areas, and introduces you to a colorful cast of very well designed characters. While the characters themselves don't have a terrible amount of backstory, their personalities are very well conveyed and make this experience a very entertaining one.
Undertale is a unique game for a few reasons. First of all, you don't have to kill a single creature. Not a single enemy. Second of all, it focuses heavily on comedy and puzzles as core elements of it. This is very well done in my opinon, as the jokes aren't forced (except for the blatanly obvious ones that are made by the characters), and the puzzles aren't particularly hard, but do require some thought and exploration to solve.
AND YOU CAN USE A CONTROLLER.
So... This game is wonderful. It's beautifully thought out and executed in an extremely great manner that could lead to several hours of playtime. There's a huge world of lore and tidbits that could have you reading for hours at a time. The bosses of the game are unique in their attacks and personalities too, and in the fact that you don't actually have to kill any of them, due to the mercy option on your command board. I loved just how much fun the characters were, and how well (or comically bad) they interacted with each other. The visuals, for me, allow for imagination about the world around you, due to just how few there are. None of the boss fights felt unfair or as though they were impossible to overcome. The story made me smile, laugh, shudder, cry, and even filled me with
.
I absolutely encourage anyone who enjoys games that take them on adventures to places forigen, both in reality, and in your own mind. It's truly an experience worthy to be had.

Well, I don't really know where to begin. Let's start with the ethos.
I am currently doing my 4th playthrough of the game, and I have achieved Neutral, Pacifist (Don't kill anyone), and True Pacifist (make friends with Papyrus, Undyne, and Alphys) endings (The current run is Neutral, then moving on to Genocide).
The game itself is revolutionary, but you may not know that from the screenshots. So, here are a few lists to show you basically what I mean.
GAMEPLAY:
+No one has to die! Except maybe you, if you ask
.
+Fun, classic RPG-style gameplay.
+Active attacks and defenses! This means that monsters don't just deal damage, you instead have to maneuver your heart (soul, whatever) around a box to dodge attacks, and you have to press Z with the right timing to attack (not that difficult).
+Bosses introduce new attacks and Soul States (movement modifiers) to keep things fresh.
-Bosses, especially Asgore, will mess you up BAD on a pacifist run.
-Can sometimes be difficult to figure out how to spare some enemies, especially bosses (again, notably Asgore).
-By the time you know you're gonna have a bad time, it's too late to change it.
-Fairly short, I've done about 3.25 runs in 15 hours.
Characters:
+Mostly lovable, quirky, and hilarious characters. Comes complete with spaghetti-obsessed skeleton, killer robot TV show host, and goat mom.
+Breaks the fourth wall ALL the time.
+All of the endings are very satisfying, and make you feel either very good about yourself, very bad about yourself, or repulsed (By the Neutral ending final boss
.
-Genocide runs make you feel like a terrible person.
-Onionsan. Onionsan is pointless. Luckily you won't have to endure a lot of him.
Environment/Asthetic:
+Lots of loving details put into every corner of the game, from changing the "Sparable Monster" names from yellow to pink, all the way to Lesser Dog's petting-induced snow art. Really creative.
+The music is great, and almost always fits the situation well (The duck flight scene is an apparently ironic exception).
-The areas get boring to look at if you stick around for too long, or on repeated runthroughs.
In the end, it's a great game, and definitely worth getting. However, if you want something to occupy you for a long time, this isn't the game for you. And be sure to tell Muffet NOT to pour you a brimming glass of spiders!

Okay..I've had just about enough.  All of these people bashing this game are forgetting one, very relevant fact--Alpha is to building what Beta is to fixing.  Truth is, this game is buggy, servers are generally unstable, and many of the mechanics need a lot of attention.  All of these problems and many others combine to form a very jarring and infuriating experience.  That's alpha. Deal with it. That said, this game is also truly wonderful.  It sucks you in.  It provides you with a gameplay experience that will irritate you more than dark souls did (in that oh-so-good way, of course).  As you learn the game and its controls, you will find that your instinct to survive is perhaps stronger in-game than out.  You'll grow attached to the character after you've spent cummulative days finding gear, keeping it fed and healthy, and then you will turn a corner one day, and another player will be staring back at you, just as surprised to see you as you are to see him.  In that split second you'll both be thinking the same thing: what do I do?  Will he try to kill me?  Does he have friends?  Should I wait to find out? What is more important, my life or my morals?  And depending on how you answer those questions in the moment, if you have time to answer them at all, you will make a choice, and then you will face the consequences. Ultimately, as you are faced with those quetions time and again, you will come to understand the disturbing reality: the only right choice is the one that keeps you alive.  And THAT moral dilemma is why all of these nay-sayers are still on here reading and commenting.  They're filled with the thrill of walking a tight-rope, yet focused on the sting of sharp strands sticking into their feet, all the while ignoring the weaver saying, "You can try it out, but it's far from finished."  That, or they're upset that the developers were being honest when they said this wasn't going to be a run-and-gun pvp game, which is perfectly understandable.  Who wouldn't be upset by the developers doing exactly what they said they would? (Yes, I just implied that those of you who are upset about the pvp nerfs are both inattentive and narcissistic).  So take my advice, and give people's testimony the same amount of attention they give their opinions.
Also, to address the prevelant negativity (this isn't addressed to anyone in particular, but to everyone that has said the following), the phrase "They'll never finish it." is the most bull-headed and ignorant statement one could make about this game.  The dev team spent a very shiny penny with last years earnings to hire people to help them port this game to consoles, and they didn't do that for no reason. You don't invest into something without being focused on the return. Unless, of course, you are one of the people I am addressing, in which case I suppose that's exactly what you did.
The point is: had Rome been built in a day, it would have fallen apart by the end of the week.  The devs have an opportunity to expand the scope and possibilities of the MMO genre as a whole, and, what's more, they have the time and resources to make it perfect.  Why would you even want them to rush that?  Forgive my frankness, but your narcissistic need for instant gratification doesn't have a place in the history of this game's development, and your blaring  impatience shouldn't detract from the base of folks that haven't given this game a shot yet.  Who knows? They may turn out to be a little less narrow-minded than you, and they might, god forbid, enjoy their own experience.
To those of you that are among those newcomers, you really should give this game a shot, if only for a glimpse of what the game will be when it's finished.  And if you come across any of these detractors that feel DayZ is unworthy of their time or money, you be sure to grant them the peace that Chernarus isn't giving them.
To the devs: I will forgive and defend every bug and faulty mechanic, but I won't do the same for hackers.  You have people that are mocking your game on a daily basis by exploiting its weaknesses, and seemingly nothing is being done about it.  I think we can all agree that DayZ deserves better than that.  Please take the time to resolve this one issue.

This game, wow.
I bought this game day one, and was soon disapointed due to its undevelopment and lack of mechanics and items. Reason being I was very unfamiliar with the game, never playing the mod untill later, I strongly disliked this game, but now I realize how very wrong I was.
Though Early Access is still labled on this title, it still makes up for an A-Thriller game, bringing survival, horror, and simulation to the table. Based of the Military simulation ArmA II, it was a mere mod, and has become what we now know as DayZ Standalone. I will be setting this up into different catagorys reguarding performance, gameplay, etc.
Gameplay
This title offers in-depth gameplay keeping the attention of the user playing for hours, and making them want to quit for weeks. From hacking at the undead, to shooting your close allies for simple gear, that is DayZ. It makes you choose moral decicions while putting real survival instinct intertwined with the breath-taking gameplay.
Graphics/Audio
The engine of this game explains itself. As glaring at the open city of Cherno, to gazing at the open valleys, this games has its fair-share of breath-taking moments. Weapons look classic and real to the trigger, while sounds echo throughtout cities, the grapics and audio amaze me to this day.
Performance
Though, one of the only downsides, it is a downhill in development, as of now. As the game still remains in its Early Access stages, its optimization is poor. PCs must cost around 1200 to ever really run the game ideally with decent settings. But, at the end of development in the Early Alpha and Beta, we will see a beautiful work of art.
I reccomend this game to gamers who aren't afraid to dive into a game, spend hours looting, killing, or farming. Gamers who are willing to invest in a game so breath-taking that it drives Console users blemish of not owning a PC.
I rate this game an 8.5/10, and up to a 9 at beta.
This is a must buy.

Well, I don't really know where to begin. Let's start with the ethos.
I am currently doing my 4th playthrough of the game, and I have achieved Neutral, Pacifist (Don't kill anyone), and True Pacifist (make friends with Papyrus, Undyne, and Alphys) endings (The current run is Neutral, then moving on to Genocide).
The game itself is revolutionary, but you may not know that from the screenshots. So, here are a few lists to show you basically what I mean.
GAMEPLAY:
+No one has to die! Except maybe you, if you ask
.
+Fun, classic RPG-style gameplay.
+Active attacks and defenses! This means that monsters don't just deal damage, you instead have to maneuver your heart (soul, whatever) around a box to dodge attacks, and you have to press Z with the right timing to attack (not that difficult).
+Bosses introduce new attacks and Soul States (movement modifiers) to keep things fresh.
-Bosses, especially Asgore, will mess you up BAD on a pacifist run.
-Can sometimes be difficult to figure out how to spare some enemies, especially bosses (again, notably Asgore).
-By the time you know you're gonna have a bad time, it's too late to change it.
-Fairly short, I've done about 3.25 runs in 15 hours.
Characters:
+Mostly lovable, quirky, and hilarious characters. Comes complete with spaghetti-obsessed skeleton, killer robot TV show host, and goat mom.
+Breaks the fourth wall ALL the time.
+All of the endings are very satisfying, and make you feel either very good about yourself, very bad about yourself, or repulsed (By the Neutral ending final boss
.
-Genocide runs make you feel like a terrible person.
-Onionsan. Onionsan is pointless. Luckily you won't have to endure a lot of him.
Environment/Asthetic:
+Lots of loving details put into every corner of the game, from changing the "Sparable Monster" names from yellow to pink, all the way to Lesser Dog's petting-induced snow art. Really creative.
+The music is great, and almost always fits the situation well (The duck flight scene is an apparently ironic exception).
-The areas get boring to look at if you stick around for too long, or on repeated runthroughs.
In the end, it's a great game, and definitely worth getting. However, if you want something to occupy you for a long time, this isn't the game for you. And be sure to tell Muffet NOT to pour you a brimming glass of spiders!
Also, Steam Awards! Pick this one for like every category.

I received Undertale as part of a Secret Santa gift swap, but it's been as cheap as $7.99 at the time of this writing.  It took me around 6.7 hours to get one ending and around 10.7 hours to get another.  I played pacifist from beginning to end since I figured, why not?  The game's description outright says you don't have to destroy anyone, so I thought I'd see how that would go.  And I enjoyed my experience.
The backstory involves a war between humans and monsters that the monsters lost, resulting in a magical barrier to keep them trapped underground that humans can freely cross.  You are a human child who climbs a forbidden mountain and winds up tumbling into the world below, thus starting the plot.  I won't say anything more.  I know with most games, you're encouraged to go in blindly so that your reactions to what all happens is most genuine, but I'd honestly encourage you to try and avoid spoilers before playing.  And that's rather difficult given the game's popularity, so good luck.
I honestly did laugh a few times during the game.  It's seriously weird at times, silly, goofy too.  Some of the characters have...colorful personalities, and there are some great situations I find myself in too.  But that's how the game went when I was peaceful.  There are largely three routes with playing the game, between being completely peaceful, being completely violent, or some mix of the two, and the game will react to your actions, so that's something to consider when you start.
Undertale is probably one of the more unique games I've ever played.  It fancies itself as an RPG, and while it does have random encounters and stats and equipment and healing items and so on, I'd honestly say it plays a bit more like a puzzle game.  That comes in more if you decide to be a pacifist, since you have to figure out how to get the monster to become Spareable through various context-sensitive actions.  It's somewhat reminiscient of Shin Megami Tensei's demon contacting feature, though you're always given the same options for each specific monster type, and the 'solution' to the fight is the same for each copy you encounter.  Unlike in SMT, you won't invariably anger monsters by trying the same dialog options that worked before or whatever.  Of course, you can just cut the knot instead and kill the monster if you want.
The combat system also incorporates a unique dodge mechanic.  Unlike regular RPGs where dodging is based on stats or equipment, you physically get out of the way of attacks.  That in itself isn't novel, but how many RPGs have elements of bullet hells?  You control a tiny red heart during the monsters' turn and you're given a field you can move within to dodge their attacks.  It sounds and is simplistic at first, but of course the game adds new elements to keep you on your toes.  Most of the boss fights introduce a gimmick and you have to quickly learn how to work with it and still avoid getting hit.
The encounter rate I thought was on the low side.  Fights in this game use invisible random encounters so you can't just avoid monsters or lure them away from where you need to go, but the fights are nowhere near as frequent as some of the RPGs from ages past.  This can be good or bad depending on how you're approaching the game, but I kinda liked not tripping over a mook every three feet.
On the difficulty side, I thought it was about middle-of-the-road.  I had to look up solutions to beat two of the bosses, mostly because I ignored what the game needed me to know.  Whoops.  For the puzzles, they were a little harder than what I'm used to in other games, but I didn't have to look up help for them.  The game does throw quite a few at you, but it never got to the point where I was annoyed at facing yet another one.
On the visual side, Undertale works a neo-retro style with pixel graphics reminscient of SNES games.  During battle, monsters show up in two-bit black and white, stark contrast to them appearing fully-colored in the field.  Characters have their portrait in dialog boxes and their expression will change to reflect their moods since the character sprites are generally not detailed enough to show these.  Some characters also use completely different fonts when talking, so that was an interesting feature.
For audio...well, a lot of people say it has a great soundtrack and I agree.  Music uses cues from chiptunes though it's not all beeps and bloops.  Some of the songs are another song either sped up or slowed down, sometimes with different instruments.  You usually wouldn't notice this.  Sound effects were there, though each speaking character had their own sound effect to go with their text appearing, giving them a type of 'voice' so that was a cool touch.
If you have an open mind and are willing to try something different, I think you'd like Undertale.  Someone going in expecting a typical RPG might be annoyed at the character personalities when they the player plays nicely, but that's why there's always the option to just be a typical RPG protagonist, right?  You'd like it a lot better if you're already familiar with RPGs already since you otherwise wouldn't know the concepts that the game addresses and uses and turns on their heads.  So not a great game to break into the genre with.  And despite its cutesy appearance, I wouldn't recommend it for young kids.  It might look sweet and innocent on the outside, especially given the gentle nudge for not hurting anyone, but...
Also, there's a demo on the official website.  It's not 1:1, but it'll give you an idea of what to expect, how the battles work, and so on.  If you're interested, it might be worth a try, though I never tried it out because...I didn't know it existed.  Whoops.
Anyway, I really did enjoy my time with Undertale, though I don't think I'll be taking it for a spin again anytime soon.  I have a perfectly valid reason for that.

This is probably one of the best games I've ever played. I love choice and consequence games and this game puts a great deal of emphasis on the consequences of your actions. Be a kind but determined pacifist, and the story will feel rewarding. Be a ruthless killer, and the game is ruthless in return. Regardless of what path you choose, the narrative is powerful.
The gameplay is a twist on traditional RPGs, allowing the player to talk their way out of a fight instead of killing their enemy. The game also forces the player to dodge enemy attacks, instead of simply relying on a chance system to determine if the player takes damage. This unique fighting system is coupled with a solid story and an amazing soundtrack, making each fight feel rewarding.
All of these elements combine to create a fantastic experience that is fun. Even when the game goes a little easy or hard on you, it's usually to further the narrative. And, even when a boss kills you over and over again and you are forced to backtrack a little to get better items, the soundtrack manages to recreate a consistent thrill that makes failure much less tedious.
The only real downside to Undertale, in my opinion, is that the game can get a little too overwhelming. It works wonders for the overall experience, but players who are highly emotional or have anxiety issues should take breaks. Toby managed to make me incapable of harming these characters without feeling intense regret and you will probably have a similar experience.
TL;DR: If you want to play a RPG with a great narrative that puts emphasis on your choices, I highly suggest playing Undertale.

I received Undertale as part of a Secret Santa gift swap, but it's been as cheap as $7.99 at the time of this writing.  It took me around 6.7 hours to get one ending and around 10.7 hours to get another.  I played pacifist from beginning to end since I figured, why not?  The game's description outright says you don't have to destroy anyone, so I thought I'd see how that would go.  And I enjoyed my experience.
The backstory involves a war between humans and monsters that the monsters lost, resulting in a magical barrier to keep them trapped underground that humans can freely cross.  You are a human child who climbs a forbidden mountain and winds up tumbling into the world below, thus starting the plot.  I won't say anything more.  I know with most games, you're encouraged to go in blindly so that your reactions to what all happens is most genuine, but I'd honestly encourage you to try and avoid spoilers before playing.  And that's rather difficult given the game's popularity, so good luck.
I honestly did laugh a few times during the game.  It's seriously weird at times, silly, goofy too.  Some of the characters have...colorful personalities, and there are some great situations I find myself in too.  But that's how the game went when I was peaceful.  There are largely three routes with playing the game, between being completely peaceful, being completely violent, or some mix of the two, and the game will react to your actions, so that's something to consider when you start.
Undertale is probably one of the more unique games I've ever played.  It fancies itself as an RPG, and while it does have random encounters and stats and equipment and healing items and so on, I'd honestly say it plays a bit more like a puzzle game.  That comes in more if you decide to be a pacifist, since you have to figure out how to get the monster to become Spareable through various context-sensitive actions.  It's somewhat reminiscient of Shin Megami Tensei's demon contacting feature, though you're always given the same options for each specific monster type, and the 'solution' to the fight is the same for each copy you encounter.  Unlike in SMT, you won't invariably anger monsters by trying the same dialog options that worked before or whatever.  Of course, you can just cut the knot instead and kill the monster if you want.
The combat system also incorporates a unique dodge mechanic.  Unlike regular RPGs where dodging is based on stats or equipment, you physically get out of the way of attacks.  That in itself isn't novel, but how many RPGs have elements of bullet hells?  You control a tiny red heart during the monsters' turn and you're given a field you can move within to dodge their attacks.  It sounds and is simplistic at first, but of course the game adds new elements to keep you on your toes.  Most of the boss fights introduce a gimmick and you have to quickly learn how to work with it and still avoid getting hit.
The encounter rate I thought was on the low side.  Fights in this game use invisible random encounters so you can't just avoid monsters or lure them away from where you need to go, but the fights are nowhere near as frequent as some of the RPGs from ages past.  This can be good or bad depending on how you're approaching the game, but I kinda liked not tripping over a mook every three feet.
On the difficulty side, I thought it was about middle-of-the-road.  I had to look up solutions to beat two of the bosses, mostly because I ignored what the game needed me to know.  Whoops.  For the puzzles, they were a little harder than what I'm used to in other games, but I didn't have to look up help for them.  The game does throw quite a few at you, but it never got to the point where I was annoyed at facing yet another one.
On the visual side, Undertale works a neo-retro style with pixel graphics reminscient of SNES games.  During battle, monsters show up in two-bit black and white, stark contrast to them appearing fully-colored in the field.  Characters have their portrait in dialog boxes and their expression will change to reflect their moods since the character sprites are generally not detailed enough to show these.  Some characters also use completely different fonts when talking, so that was an interesting feature.
For audio...well, a lot of people say it has a great soundtrack and I agree.  Music uses cues from chiptunes though it's not all beeps and bloops.  Some of the songs are another song either sped up or slowed down, sometimes with different instruments.  You usually wouldn't notice this.  Sound effects were there, though each speaking character had their own sound effect to go with their text appearing, giving them a type of 'voice' so that was a cool touch.
If you have an open mind and are willing to try something different, I think you'd like Undertale.  Someone going in expecting a typical RPG might be annoyed at the character personalities when they the player plays nicely, but that's why there's always the option to just be a typical RPG protagonist, right?  You'd like it a lot better if you're already familiar with RPGs already since you otherwise wouldn't know the concepts that the game addresses and uses and turns on their heads.  So not a great game to break into the genre with.  And despite its cutesy appearance, I wouldn't recommend it for young kids.  It might look sweet and innocent on the outside, especially given the gentle nudge for not hurting anyone, but...
Also, there's a demo on the official website.  It's not 1:1, but it'll give you an idea of what to expect, how the battles work, and so on.  If you're interested, it might be worth a try, though I never tried it out because...I didn't know it existed.  Whoops.
Anyway, I really did enjoy my time with Undertale, though I don't think I'll be taking it for a spin again anytime soon.  I have a perfectly valid reason for that.

Key things to bear in mind:
* you'll feel better about the griefers when you consider them the human equivalent of the AI zombies in a zombie game.  It's okay to be killed and robbed - and actual players are far funnier about it.
* don't walk in with the initial idea that it's going to be a building game.  You'll invest a whole bunch of time in gathering resources and then just have them stolen.  Your base will be broken into as soon as you log out.
* make a sleeping bag and hide it somewhere so you can keep spawning at the same location and start to learn the surrounding area.  You can also use sleeping bags to bring in other players to your location by donating it to them.
* spend your first couple of plays collecting items from barrels and earning knowledge.
* play with others - go solo and you'll have a very hard time.
* play with voice comms enabled - it's fun to interact with the other dodgy survivalists.

For those who dont know what early access means:
Early access, alphafunding, or paid-alpha is a funding model in the video game industry by which consumers can pay for a game in the early stages of development and obtain access to playable but unfinished versions of the game, while the developer is able to use those funds to continue work on the game. Those that pay to participate typically help to debug game, provide feedback and suggestions, and may have access to special materials upon release of the game. The early access approach is a common way to obtain funding for indie games and may also be used along other funding mechanisms including crowdfunding.

Undertale is somewhat of an oddball game for me. I only became aware of this game through a friend of mine who got the game day one and was completely enthralled by it along with a ton of other people who were praising it to the heavens. But it didn't really hook me just from the trailers, screenshots and snippets of gameplay I saw at the time, yet it's premise was an interesting one and I eventually did want to check it out to see if it was truly deserving of it's praise. (Which I was able to do so thanks to that same friend of mine who gifted me the game)
And all I can say is, while I do think the game is a bit on the overrated side and one I personally wouldn't call an absolute masterpiece like a lot of people think, this is still a genuinely heartfelt and thoughtful twist on the RPG genre.
The gameplay while relatively simple in the overworld, the battles are where things get interesting with dodging attacks bullet hell shmup/WarioWare style which can get pretty challenging, ESPECIALLY the infamous Sans battle.
The game’s main attraction is the ability to either act your way out of a fight leading you on the “Pacifist” route or fight the games various monsters conventionally, though you’ll probably end becoming the real “monster” amongst them. (Which I have no plans on doing, I HAVE NO SHAME IN THAT FLOWEY! :p)
The plot I do find well written with it’s witty & even at point’s self-aware dialogue (with plenty of 4th wall breaks and jabs at RPG tropes), likeable characters, heartwarming, unsettling and memorable moments and how it brings up some pretty deep moral questions. While I don’t personally think this game is about “AURGH, YOU KILL THINGS IN RPGS AND YOU SHOULD FEEL BAD!! LOVE & PEACE ALL THE WAY!!” I did find this an interesting plot.
And the music is both catchy and can tug at your heart at points.
All in all, while I’m not a MEGA fan of this game, I did have a good time playing this game (but I don't have the stomach to have a bad time if you know what I mean) and if the concept sounds the least bit interesting to you, check it out.

This old-school-console-style RPG with turn-based combat(?) has simple and fulfilling gameplay with a few new twists, with silly-funny sideshows, puzzles, and characters (and serious story lines as well) - all of which have more depth than the low-def graphics can possibly convey at initial glance.
If you regret the price you paid for (name any triple-a title), here's your chance to make it up to yourself.  And listen up, game devs:  This is what games are supposed to be about - this is story-telling, this is entertainment, this is a retro sound track that actually works with the game moods, this is pure video game and RPG nostalgia bringing a new story - and even more important, this is just plain FUN.
And this is worth every penny it doesn't cost.  Just buy it.  Return to the days when the game itself meant something to both the author and the player.  Even if you're not a big fan of the genre, even if your sense of humor can't appreciate the silliness of the characters and stories, you'll still get something out of it anyway.

"Anime's real, right?!?!" -
"Anime is real." "Anime is not real." - You, the player, pondering the toughest decision in the game.
Undertale is an indie RPG developed and published by Toby Fox. The premise of the game is simple, humans and monsters once roamed the Earth. After a war broke out where humans emerged victorious, monsters were sealed below the Earth in the Underground by a magic barrier, preventing any monsters or humans from crossing. Sometime after the war, you, a human child, fall into the Underground. You then explore the Underground in a quest to escape it. And that is how much of the game it is possible to tell without spoiling anything, for Undertale is one of the most unique experiences I've ever had playing a game.
To say what makes Undertale so special and such a great game would be spoiling the entire game. Like the Stanley Parable, explaining why Undertale has had such an impact for everyone playing it would ruin the experience for you. Undertale is best experienced going in completely blind. Knowing the tropes of the RPG genre also will make the Undertale experience much more enjoyable.
The gameplay is simple, yet finds so many ways to surprise. Enemies attack you with "Bullet Hell" styled attacks, where you have to dodge and avoid the objects coming at you. You attack and kill enemies with a QTE styled minigame, where you can land your attacks within a certain space to do more damage. Or not. In Undertale, enemies can be interacted with in the games "act" menu, where you can talk to enemies, or act in different ways. Making the right decisions will eventually allow you to spare enemies, and avoid killing. While sounding simple enough, it never once wears it thin, for every monster encounter is extremely different and unique in its own way. Indeed, one of the defining features of Undertale is to play the entire game without killing a single monster.
Oh and it does impact the game. And in a BIG way. Every monster you kill, every boss you decide to spare or fight, which characters you befriend, deciding whether anime is real or not real, Undertale will remember EVERYTHING that you do. Even
One of the best moments in the game came for me in one of these moments, which I just HAVE to talk about. Some vague spoilers:
After that moment, I knew Undertale was going to be one of my favourite games of all time.
One of the best things Undertale does is acknowledging that it is in fact a "game," a "program" on your computer, and uses that to convey it's story. Video games have been in this strange spot, where they have been trying to emulate movies to tell story, usually with cutscenes and scripted moments. However, Undertale asks
It's not the first game that has taken this concept, but without spoiling the story, it is one of the best games that has utilized it to it's full potential.
One of the things that surprised me most about Undertale was how good of an RPG it was. Despite its artstyle on the surface emulating NES games, the exploration and roleplaying mechanics of Undertale are well fleshed out. Everything found in RPGs, puzzles, inns, taverns, villages, lore and most of all, exploration, is all found in Undertale. It's quite surprising how open the game is too, despite its small scale. The world building and lore, while simple, is fun to explore, learning about the monsters and their lives underground. Which leads me to one of the defining highlights of the game: the cast of characters.
Undertale has some of the best written characters I've ever seen in a game before. Without spoiling any of the interactions, every scene with the cast of Undertale is memorable. And it's hilarious too. Undertale is one of the most genuinely funny games I have ever played, rivaling even Portal 2's humor. You meet a monster who really likes spaghetti. His brother really like skeleton puns. Another character is completely obsessed with anime, who also happens to be a brilliant scientist. Oh and you can totally date a skeleton. Yup, in Undertale, everything goes. If I'm sounding too vague, it's because I want you to experience all the dialogue and character development for yourself. It's really that damn good.
I said that the characters were one of the best things about Undertale. By far the other best thing is the soundtrack. Wholeheartedly worth the purchase, I have not been able to stop listening to it ever since finishing the game. Repeating motifs are used often, in fact, there are about 10 themes that are used throughout the game, which all songs draw on in some way. It's almost impossible to group the soundtrack under one genre, every song is uniquely different in some way. If I had to pick ABSOLUTE highlights, they would be: "Ruins," "Enemy Approaching," "Home," Heartache," "Snowy," "Dogsong," "Snowdin Town," "Bonetrousle," "NGAHHH!!" "Spear of Justice," "Metal Crusher," "Spider Dance," "CORE," "Death by Glamour," "Undertale," "ASGORE," "Hopes and Dreams," "SAVE the World." And of course: MEGALOVANIA.
SERIOUSLY, HOW CAN YOU NOT GET PUMPED WHEN THAT COMES IN IN A BOSS FIGHT?. There are just simply so many good songs in Undertale, way to many for me to list, and each go perfectly with every scene. One of my favourite videogame soundtracks ever.
There's very little to criticize Undertale for. The first hour of the game is admittedly tedious, especially with the large number of random enemy encounters during the introduction, but the random encounters do slow down in frequency. Albeit, they can be a bit annoying at times. Undertale's humor may not resonate as strongly for some people, and some jokes do tend to drag on out for a bit.
Undertale is one of the best damn games I have ever played, and may become my favourite game of all time. YES, you should buy this game, and if you are a fan of RPGs, it is an absolute MUST OWN. I am sure that in the years to come, we will get a huge wave of Undertale clones, all that will try to emulate what has made the game such a success. But like any games that have tried to emulate a games success, it is unlikely they will succeed as much as Undertale. A truly genre defining game, and I daresay it will be a defining game that will be remembered throughout videogame history.

One of the best survival games on Steam, but given the field of survival games, that isn't saying much. Gameplay mechanics are intuitive, but the community makes this game, like all survival games, almost unplayable by yourself. Without a squad of friends, you'll spend the majority of your time collecting resources only to be shot in the back. Since resources are scarce, it's almost impossible to build a proper base without investing more than a few hours into the game. If you can play with a small group of friends, Rust is enjoyable. But if you plan to play alone, you're wasting your time, and will find yourself very often outnumbered and outgunned in encounters with other players.

One of the best survival games on Steam, but given the field of survival games, that isn't saying much. Gameplay mechanics are intuitive, but the community makes this game, like all survival games, almost unplayable by yourself. Without a squad of friends, you'll spend the majority of your time collecting resources only to be shot in the back. Since resources are scarce, it's almost impossible to build a proper base without investing more than a few hours into the game. If you can play with a small group of friends, Rust is enjoyable. But if you plan to play alone, you're wasting your time, and will find yourself very often outnumbered and outgunned in encounters with other players.

While my this specific account would say otherwise, I've been playing this game for almost 2 years now on and off. Heres how I've felt about it:
Rust started off as a real basic survival game with zombies and stiff & ugly animations. I understood that it was a super early access at this point, and I still had fun for what it was. Every time I keep checking back after several months away, the game looks even more beautiful and complex than the last time I played it. Its cheap, and you'll probably have a lot of fun once you start to strive off the land. You also get to look at a game thats attempted to be a different from other survival games. They aren't quite there yet, but more and more its getting there. The only knock though is that once you start to really make it in the game, it sort of gets boring and loses its replay value. You're fully stocked on materials, got all the weapons, have a dope house, tons of food & water. Its cool to get to this point, but once you're there the game loses its fun after awhile. Even after server wipes or getting your house blown up into while you're offline you're basically just set to start the process all over again, which is where I stop playing for awhile. It's a lot of grinding to get to that point (which they've said they want to fix). I'm curious to see how they step away from this problem of basically getting super-rich in the game and just running out of♥♥♥♥♥♥to do afterwards.
TL;DR, I enjoy myself everytime I fire up this game again. It's also fun to see where this game goes during its development. It's just once after 2 years I keep running into the problem getting super "rich" and not having anything to do afterwards.

Even though it's still in alpha, there are a lot of features and I have not run into any game-breaking bugs. There are a lot of community servers as well as official ones so chances are you'll find somewhere where you'll fit right in.

I hate this game. I hate everything about it. It sucks you in with the promise of being able to create something wonderful and then beats you down with the reality that is the murderous and psychopathic nature of the human race.
I started off a cheery faced and bright eyed naked man on some god forsaken beach. I get up and begin walking around while enjoying the beautiful, atmospheric, nature of the game. I eventually come upon another person and walk up to him. I press 'v' and introduce myself. The next thing I know, a large bang goes off and my headset is filled with the wailing scream of my now dying character.
I get back up. I think to myself that that interaction must be the exception instead of the rule. Oh how naive I used to be. Again and again I am shot at, stabbed, hacked upon, crushed with the rocks of other naked men. One second marvelling at my wonderful yield of supplies and the next, crying as a bear charges out of nowhere and tears me and my lovely dreams apart. Lives lost, houses obliterated, ambitions crushed. And why? Because that is life. That is rust.
But I keep getting up. I cry, I yell, I curse, I pray, I vent to my wife, but I get up. I need to collect, to build, to create. The promise of what could be overshadows the reality of what has been. And why am I writing this? Because after nearly 50 hours of game time, I just logged on to find my house raided and all of my possessions gone. I am hardly any better off than I was when I logged on for the first time.
But I get back up. I will smash at trees and stones, stare down the barrels of countless more weapons, slowly craft my way back to the top. Always looking over my shoulder, jumping at every little sound, clenching my butt hole ever so tight as the sounds of carnage echo in the distance. This is my new life. My new addiction. Please don't ask why.
I just get back up.

My god, Undertale. What can I say about this game that hasn't been said already? It's truly a masterpiece, you can see the quality and tender loving care that was put in this game.
Undertale is a retro RPG, the weird, funny ones that are also creepy at the same time, kinda like Eathbound and Cthulhu Saves the World. Unlike other RPGs, you can complete the game without killing anybody, which is a breath of fresh air.
At first, it looks kinda innocent and "childish", perhaps, but you're getting deceived. This game game's a trip on the feels train without brakes. There's just so much to this game, three main endings, plus quite a few other minor endings, and all of them are emotional rollercoasters. The plot is deep and the lore is rich, it's full of secrets and stuff you got to research in game through NPC dialog and reading, and well, there's just lots to see here. It's got a huge ammount of replayability, even if the main storyline can be completed in a few hours. Yes, this game is quite linear, and the puzzles aren't even that hard, which is something I truly enjoy, being a sucker at both puzzles and maze like games myself. It's one of those games where you can be a goody-two shoes, neutral, or a total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ if you want. And that's freaking amazing. Unlike other games where you can be a total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, this game really makes you feel sad for being one, because most of the underground's denizens mean no harm to you. You monster.
The graphics, are something you would expect from a retro game. Yet, sometimes, it's quite polished, and the backgrounds can be seen with glorious retro graphics. Sometimes stuff is colorful, but this game is mostly monochrome, for example, the battle sprites and most of the projectiles you have to dodge.
About that, this game is different from the good ol' classic RPG games. Instead of having to trust RNGesus to allow you to hit your mark or avoid being hit, this game is fully interactive with that. You have to stop your attack bar right in the middle for more damage, for example. But also, you have to dodge attacks yourself, as if it was some kind of bulletstorm game at times. This game is quite easy at first, but some of the bosses are truly legendary when it comes to their difficulty.
The soundtrack? It's just BEAUTIFUL. It's got an arsenal of memorable tunes, epic music, funny music, (Looking at you, Dogsong), music that's just heart warming or even tear jerking. It's got creepy tunes, too, during the genocide run, for example. Quite atmospheric. The soundtrack of this game is a masterpiece, too.
If you are a fan of RPGs, you MUST get this game. It's quite cheap full price, and even still, this game is totally worth it, compared to some other 60 buck games out there that feel quite dissapointing.
If you aren't a fan of RPG games, you should try this game, anyways, because it's not the traditional kind of "boring" "Hit and wait to be hit" kind of game with tons of grinding, if that's what you hate. Plus, fan or not, the storyline in this game and the emotional rollercoaster is completely worth it. It has become one of my favorite games of all time by this point, and I urge everybody out there to at least try this game. It won't dissapoint you.
This game is very well made; a very fun experience that'll keep you busy for many more than the estimated time of gameplay of 6 hours. So, so much more than that.
